- the oral question (b5-0004/2000) by mr désir and others to the council on the council's position on the idea of a capital tax - the oral question (b5-0005/2000) by mr désir and others to the commission on the commission's position on the idea of a capital tax.
- madam president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr commissioner, everyone was able to measure, at the time of the asian crisis of 1997 and after the one that hit mexico in 1995 or the ems in 1993, the damage to the economy of entire countries that financial speculation can produce, especially that which is exercised on currencies. 1500 to 2000 billion euros are traded every day on the financial markets, in three or four days, the equivalent of the entire annual world production, of the world gdp, which is about 6000 billion euros. this means that, for the most part, these financial transactions are purely speculative, unrelated to trade in goods or investments. but the erratic movement of these vast masses of capital can lead to the collapse of a currency, the collapse of a country's economy, and the plunge of its entire population into recession within hours. in this context, there has been renewed interest in the proposal of james tobin, nobel prize winner in economics, to create a tax on foreign exchange transactions, the rate of which would be very low so that it does not affect trade in goods or investment but operates like a grain of sand in the wheels of speculation, that is, it curbs the multiplication of short-term operations. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. one of the reasons for the success of this proposal, and the campaigns of ngos such as attac, solidar and others, which have popularised it, is also that it would free up resources that could be allocated to development programmes in the poorest countries, in areas such as education or health. it is its redistributive nature in a world where there are both more and more rich and more and more poor. many people and institutions have taken a stand in favour of this tax, such as the president of brazil, fernando cardoso, the government of finland, the parliament of canada last march, and lionel jospin in 1995. this question has been debated in several national parliaments of the european union. the answer has often been that it cannot be dealt with at national level alone and that the right scale to deal with it is the european union, hence the oral question to the council and the commission which we tabled with 37 other members. i welcome the compromise resolution we have reached with the gue, the greens, the liberals and the pse, which calls on the commission to report to parliament within six months on the feasibility of this tax and also to examine the pressures and financial sanctions that can be applied against countries that encourage tax evasion or maintain tax havens. it is often objected that such a tax would be avoided, but this could be said of any tax and if this argument had been maintained, no tax would have been created. the draft resolution also calls for a position paper drawn up by the commission and the council to be submitted before the next annual meeting of the imf. i believe that the european union must take the initiative and, as the draft resolution calls for, must also propose this initiative to the g7 because it is first and foremost a political issue. if the union takes the initiative, it will have a ripple effect because the debate is taking place everywhere, including in the united states and japan, and there is an aspiration that is being expressed more and more strongly in the world, that the world should be run not by traders but by citizens, their parliaments, their governments, their democratic institutions. i believe that europe must play a role in this new international regulation and i am extremely pleased that today, with this debate and with this draft resolution, this issue is on the agenda for european integration.
- madam president, ladies and gentlemen, my group warmly welcomes the fact that such a debate is taking place today, especially since we have made every effort with colleagues from different groups to achieve this. we do not, of course, have the same approach, and i believe that our debate and the motions for resolutions we tabled at the beginning bear witness to this. however, we are not indifferent to the progress made by the compromise resolution and call on the commission to submit a report within six months. we believe that the european parliament can play its part by taking the initiative, even timidly, on this subject, although it goes without saying - and i agree with the previous speaker - that if paragraph 9 were called into question, this resolution would obviously lose its substance. our debate is in fact about a vital question which more and more citizens are rightly asking themselves: what place should be given to man and to the financial sphere in today's economy? $1.8 trillion is the volume of money that flows through the world's foreign exchange markets every day, representing more than a quarter of the world's annual volume of real trade in goods and services. by placing finance in the command post, such a move has reinforced the requirements of profitability and hardened operating conditions everywhere. this is the view of the growing movement of mergers, acquisitions and corporate restructuring. the raising of huge resources in the ever-growing financial markets. unemployment and pressure on the working population worldwide are increasing. opportunities and real growth are being hampered. and the influx or abrupt withdrawal of speculative capital threatens the economies of many countries, until they collapse, as in asia, russia or brazil. in the face of this neoliberal globalisation, dominated by the financial markets, there is a growing demand, as evidenced by our demand, for a different view of the world, according to which the common law is that dictated by the duty of solidarity in an increasingly interdependent world. no one can ignore the challenge to civilization posed by the loss of almost a billion jobs. the need for unprecedented efforts in development, access to knowledge. in this respect, all ideas deserve consideration and we believe that the tobin tax is an important one, as are other forms of transaction which are possible. this tax can help curb speculation, without penalising the activities of the real economy, and allow new resources to be released for human investment, at a time when the undp estimates at 40 billion dollars a year the amount needed to eradicate poverty, provide access to safe drinking water for all, and meet sanitation needs. as the debate is being launched on a global scale on the ability of politics to influence the economic sphere, the introduction of this tax could become one of the symbols of the political will to regain the democratic spaces confiscated by international financial operators. and i would like to respond to the commissioner who said that a minimum number of industrialized countries was needed to achieve this. it seems to me that the european union is made up of a large number of industrial countries and i believe, as do harlem désir and many others, that the european union we are now able to take the initiative in this respect. in any case, i think that the european parliament would be honoured to echo the wish of the citizens to control the world in the sense of the well-being of all.
- madam president, i too welcome the holding of this debate, which has come too late. we know that each generation has, over time, blindly indulged in what might be called a dominant ideology, that is to say, a set of prejudices accepted as such by the prevailing conformism and which, nevertheless, end up revealing to the following generations how full of drama they have been. free trade and the permanent glorification of globalisation are, in our view, the dominant ideology of today, that is to say, the great error of the end of our century, as dangerous as the ideology of the dictatorship of the proletariat in the corridors of the kremlin was in the past, or, long before, the dogmatic certainty that the earth is flat. our world is now governed by a single logic, i was going to say a single god, that of money at work and not of man at work. with a trade in goods and services amounting to chf 36 000 billion, i.e. the product of only four days of speculation, the financial bubble no longer owes much to the productive activity of individuals. it feeds itself in a bidding war that constantly denies the humanity of man, the rich as well as the poor, even if the latter are the ones who, in the end, are excluded from most of the decision-making centres of the planet, which are dominated by a tiny minority, what jean-pierre chevènement very well called recently: "the globalized elites". it was natural that these elites should exclude all political concerns from their field of action, thus shielding themselves from any democratic control and, in short, being both illegitimate and irresponsible. but the people are resisting, as their reaction at the ineffable seattle summit showed, where the world's leaders rushed in slavishly - individuals or states - a more organized reaction than has been said elsewhere, especially in france thanks to the magnificent attac network which is campaigning with growing resonance for the limitation of free trade in general and, more particularly, for the taxation of international financial transactions. the creation of this tax, of the tobin type or of the more realistic type of professor lauré, would prove politically opportune, at least in its symbolic burden, even if its rate is low, in that it would mean above all that politics regains a foothold in a field from which operators whose profits are proportional to the degree of resignation of the states have been excluded.

mr president, the implementation of the fourth multiannual guidance programme in the fisheries sector is particularly difficult. the sector has already made substantial efforts to adapt its fleet capacity in previous plans. the commission nevertheless calls for further capacity reductions. but below a certain threshold, the fleet level is no longer sufficient to absorb and make the port and commercial infrastructure profitable, which may lead to relocations and reductions in the number of vessels that are totally unjustified, as long as we remain within our catch quotas. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the fishing fleet is kept in line with the community's fishing policy. that is why the members of the europe of nations group cannot adopt the cunha report as it stands. that is why our colleague dominique souchet tabled five amendments which are intended to recall that the capture capacity must be adapted and not necessarily, systematically and continuously reduced. our objective is to ensure the sustainability of the fishing fleets of the member states of the european union. our amendments also make it clear that comparison between the third and fourth plans is difficult to make because of the introduction of new elements such as the composition of the catches and the nature of the gear. they also point out that it is difficult for the member states to provide the many fine data requested in a very short time. the group of the european people's party will also oppose paragraph 6 of the draft resolution. the european parliament does not have to ask that the penalties for non-compliance with the plans or the notification procedure may consist of further reductions in quotas. firstly, we believe that there is no legal basis for this and that the principle of the guidelines should not be distorted, which, i repeat, are not aimed at the disappearance of fishing in europe but, on the contrary, at controlling it in order to ensure its sustainability. finally, because of the recent oil spills in france, our group has also tabled two amendments calling for the suspension of the implementation of the disaster relief plans. the whole of the european parliament was moved this week by this disaster. in our group, our colleagues dominique souchet and philippe de villiers found themselves in the heart of the disaster in the vendée and told us that it was urgent to take solidarity measures. it is obvious that fishing in these affected areas will be weakened for a certain period. in these circumstances, the attempt to apply restrictive measures uniformly throughout the european union, without taking account of these exceptional situations, could lead to further disasters.
mr president, i am speaking on behalf of the tdi group, even though i am speaking for one of its members. we are dealing with the question of ballasts in fluorescent tubes. what's this about? the electric current in fluorescent lamps like the ones that light us up here above our heads is regulated, stabilized, by little devices called ballasts. for 50 years, these ballasts have been made from a copper coil in a tin can. they're called ferromagnetic. but now there are electronic ballasts. traditional ferromagnetics would cause a loss of energy, in particular by resistance phenomena. the loss would be up to 8 watts per hour, while the electronics would only lose 3 watts. so they would save 5 watts and multiply by 130 million ballasts, we would save millions of tons of energy, less co2, less greenhouse effect and humanity would breathe better. the commission has therefore decided to switch from ferromagnetic ballasts to electronics within eight years. unfortunately, what mr turmes does not tell us is that the electronic ballast has a shorter life span than the ferromagnetic. this means that more must be produced, with more energy consumed, and the savings of earlier are partly lost. in addition, these electronic ballasts are made with transistors that contain heavy metals, such as tantalum, germanium, even arsenic, not to mention plastic, that is, pollutants that are not biodegradable, whereas copper and the sheet of the magnet are biodegradable. in other words, for an energy saving that is less obvious than it may seem, our green colleagues are dumping heavy metals and arsenic into nature. at the same time, besides increasing pollution, unemployment is increasing, because the components used in the manufacture of electronics and the machines that make them are not european. to avoid import costs, our manufacturers will relocate and thus reduce jobs. in the end, by wanting to save a modest amount of energy with electronics, while our manufacturers simply ask for a gradual and selective ban, we have at best an economy, but with pollutant emissions and added unemployment. and it doesn't address the real issue of waste, which is incandescent lamps that lose up to 50 watts compared to fluorescent lamps. but it is true that incandescent lamps are manufactured by two multinational companies, philips and osram. and perhaps among the globalists of the european commission, the globalists of the green multinational nebula and the transnational corporations of industry, perhaps the current is passing, but i do not ask that we shed any light on this point.
in writing. - the commission's proposal for a directive on ballasts for fluorescent lighting aims to improve their efficiency and reduce energy consumption. it proposes that measures be introduced in a gradual and balanced manner. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. this maximalist approach does not take into account all the technical and scientific arguments, both in terms of energy savings and technological progress. it seems to ignore, for example, that there are ferromagnetic ballasts with low energy consumption that are very popular on the market. much more serious is the fact that the report of the committee on industry completely ignores the impact of its proposals on employment. the abolition of the production of ferromagnetic ballasts would risk the closure of many production sites and the resulting redundancies, as for example at the vossloh-schwabe plant in colmar. that is why i voted against the final report after the adoption of many amendments whose implementation would be very dangerous for employment in this sector. i call on the council to reject the amendments which have just been adopted.
in writing. - the coastal regions of western france are now polluted by the sinking of the erika. everyone knows that the longer the time goes by, the more likely it is that this tragic incident will happen again. the us legislation adopted in 1990 following the exxon valdez oil spill off the coast of alaska prohibits oil tankers that do not meet the strictest and most stringent security standards from entering us ports. the inevitable consequence is that tankers which do not meet these criteria will - and increasingly will - return to european waters, thus increasing the likelihood of pollution risks. it is therefore essential that our european parliament addresses these problems as a matter of priority and that it obtains without delay from the commission first and then from the governments of the member states the introduction of a set of provisions to protect maritime and tourist activities along the european coast. it is essential that a european maritime agency be set up without delay, the primary purpose of which should be to coordinate the security checks on oil tankers using european ports in accordance with standardised and unified methods. ladies and gentlemen, it may be necessary to draw up and vote on a resolution, but what is important now is to take concrete, strong and courageous measures to prevent further disasters.
in writing. - the storm which has struck europe and france in particular calls for several remarks and observations on my part: 1 - while there is no clear link between this storm, the greenhouse effect and pollution, these events are at least a warning of what will happen in the future if we continue to pollute the atmosphere of our planet thoughtlessly. 2 - if, in europe too, we have often "built at a discount", if we have favoured open-air electricity grids, which are often very ugly visually, we are now measuring the real and heavy costs of these false economies. 3 - the measures taken to repair the damage caused by the storm showed our weaknesses, our lack of resources and, at the same time, the strong solidarity that has been shown and the equally strong importance of the notion of 'public service' in some of our public enterprises, which are often abused by the dominant ultra-liberal ideology. i would like to pay tribute to all the employees and staff of the companies who worked tirelessly and without counting to restore traffic, restore electricity and telephone, and help with the rehousing of the families affected. 4 - finally, if europe wants to stay or be close to its citizens, it must intervene financially in a significant way! the member states, which are often too frivolous, still have to provide the necessary financial means.
mr president, the european parliament's resolution on international capital movements, which we have just rejected, dealt with a very broad and interesting subject, but unfortunately it was treated in a superficial and sloppy way. frankly, the subject deserved better. after some careful consideration, the resolution revealed in paragraph 9 its real purpose: to ask that 'the commission draw up within six months a report on the interest and feasibility of a tax on international speculative capital movements'. if we approach the matter from this angle, i am sorry to say that the report requested was not to be produced. everyone already knows it's impossible. it is impossible to distinguish between speculative and non-speculative capital movements, except by using arbitrary and bureaucratic criteria which would distort trade. and even if we were to succeed in doing so, we would still have to distinguish between good speculation, which is aimed at challenging artificial situations in order to take account of the real economy, and bad speculation, which would be arbitrarily defined as essentially aimed at harming others. this exercise would be even more impossible than the last one. in short, the european parliament's resolution, in this form, was completely off the subject. however, the question could have been formulated differently. it could have been asked whether it was appropriate to impose a tax on all international capital movements of any kind, without making impossible distinctions. that's a more sensible question, but again, that question wasn't asked. the second question, however, is that such a uniform tax would probably not solve monetary crises, which are often the result of underlying real imbalances. instead of creating a new tax - and we do not know to what funds - it would be better to improve economic policies and reduce existing taxes and charges, particularly on labour.
in writing. - our economic system has shown its limits. the financial sector is out of step with the real economy and too often deregulates it; the high unemployment rates we are experiencing, the growing gap between the north and the south, the increase in poverty on a global scale are all proofs of this sad reality! the global capital flows are destabilizing! we must therefore look for measures to tax transactions on the foreign exchange markets, in order to reduce their volatility and to curb short-term speculative operations. a tax such as that proposed by james tobin - nobel prize winner in economics - would be a "grain of sand" in the well-oiled wheels of speculation, and the considerable sums it could generate are all arguments in favour of its application, when we know that, even if it were adopted at a very low rate (around 0.05%), it would yield nearly 600 billion francs a year, according to the most pessimistic estimates! the united nations conference on trade and development (unctad) therefore proposes that this sum be returned to the states where the tax would be collected and to a redistributive fund for the poorest countries. this wealth, thus captured from the big international capitalists, would be returned to the citizen and could constitute a formidable lever for development for the less favoured countries. we would finally be in a logic where solidarity would replace selfishness. for all these reasons i voted in favour of this resolution and i am glad that this house has put this matter back on the table, at the risk of upsetting the unscrupulous speculators who, by their actions, destabilise the most vulnerable economies and sometimes our whole system, as the recent financial crises in south-east asia have shown.
in writing. - we voted in favour of the request to put the tobin tax on the agenda because we are convinced that its application, even if limited, to europe would be a first step towards greater social justice and a different distribution of wealth. we are not under any illusion that this tax alone will eliminate the very causes of poverty, which are linked to the economic and financial system that dominates the world. we vote for everything that goes along with the invitation to the commission to examine the feasibility of the tobin tax. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy.
in writing. - the workers' representatives will vote against the compromise resolution on the taxation of capital movements. this resolution, under the pretence of "stabilizing" the international financial system and "clearing" it of its excesses, is both ridiculous and utopian, but above all it states that its objective is to preserve it. our perspective is that humanity will be rid not only of the excesses of the global financial system, but of the financial system itself and the capitalist organization of the economy of which it is one of the essential elements. it is not only capital speculating on the financial markets on a short-term basis that represents a huge waste of material, social and human resources for society, but capital in general. the current layoffs and job cuts, from michelin to alsthom, which almost all the large companies in europe are carrying out, with the sole aim of raising their stock prices: is this speculation or the normal activity of capital? if a resolution had clearly proposed the introduction of the tobin tax, we would not have voted against it, so that our vote would not be confused with that of the happy admirers of the capitalist system who regard any tax on big capital as an insult. for our part, the political objective we propose to the working classes is that they impose very high taxes not only on speculative capital but also on the profits of all the big capitalist enterprises, as well as on the private fortunes of the rich class, so that the money thus concentrated in the hands of the state can be used to create useful jobs in public services. but the tobin tax is certainly not a measure of social justice, it would not even bother the speculators and instead of preventing the waste and injustices of the capitalist economy, it would only serve to cover them up.

lives. it noted the measures already taken by the egyptian government to restore calm in the region and welcomed its commitment to bring those responsible to justice. she is eagerly awaiting the triggered by the violent reaction and incompetence of the police and not by sectarian behaviour on their part. recent events, however, seem to be religious in nature, although they were triggered by a simple commercial dispute. in upper egypt, as elsewhere, chronic underdevelopment can dangerously exacerbate religious tensions, which is why measures to restore harmony between different communities must go hand in hand with socioeconomic development. the commission shall, in its cooperation with egypt, seek above all to strike a balance between measures promoting economic modernisation and social measures, including measures to combat poverty and to promote civil society and human rights. upper egypt is one of the regions targeted by social measures and poverty reduction measures. as regards china, the commission shares the concerns of the members of parliament about the human rights situation in china and in particular in tibet. these issues were discussed at the highest level at the second eu-china summit in beijing on 21 december 1999. the union also made a formal approach to the chinese foreign ministry on 14 january, expressing its deep concern about the fate of political dissidents, the freedom of worship of members of christian churches and the treatment of certain falun gong practitioners. these issues, as well as conditions of detention, labour camps, freedom of expression, freedom of association and the rights of women and ethnic minorities, will also be on the agenda of the next session of the eu-china human rights dialogue to be held in lisbon on 25 february. the outcome of this session and the results of the dialogue will determine the position to be adopted by the union at the next meeting of the united nations commission on human rights. the union considers that the improvement of the human rights situation in china and the negotiations for china's accession to the wto are two major issues which should be dealt with separately through instruments and in specific fora. in general, the commission considers that economic opening and trade liberalisation, which will accelerate china's accession to the wto, constitute a favourable environment for the development of human rights, the strengthening of civil society and the establishment of the rule of law in china in the long term, and it will pay particular attention to the latter aspects in the context of the world trade organisation dialogue. the tibet issue is already being widely discussed through the existing channels of communication with the chinese authorities. troika ambassadors also carried out an observation mission to tibet in 1998 and the commission is committed to continuing this work. as regards the problem of the gulf prisoners of war in iraq, the commission, like parliament, is concerned about the lack of cooperation on the part of iraq in the case of the missing kuwaitis and is aware of the intolerable effects of this situation on the families. the commission calls on iraq to respect the relevant un security council resolutions and the international committee of the red cross, as you have pointed out, has been entrusted with the case of the missing kuwaitis in accordance with these un resolutions. but unfortunately iraq refuses to cooperate, even through this international body. the commission supports the efforts of the international committee of the red cross and, as the commission has no contractual relations with iraq, there is no formal dialogue with the iraqi government. i would also like to make sure that the commission fully complies with the un sanctions regime, which is a response to the dramatic human rights situation in that country. but, and i think this is an important point too, as some of you have said, despite these violations of the un security council resolutions by iraq, the commission will continue, through echo, to provide humanitarian aid to the iraqis to alleviate their suffering. the commission is the main provider of humanitarian aid to iraq, with €240 million since 1991, and under its programme for the year 2000 echo has provided €10 million in humanitarian aid to iraq. we are therefore distinguishing between the populations and the constraints on human rights that iraq has. the commission will support all the measures in this area. finally, as regards the violation of human rights in chad and cameroon, in connection with the current planning of the pipeline, the european commission is closely monitoring the situation with regard to the deepening of the democratic process, the defence of human rights and the strengthening of the rule of law. it is also focusing on the proposed oil project in the south of the country, which will pass through cameroon. the commission is not directly concerned with the financing of this project. but on several occasions it has shown its understanding of chad's right to exploit its only resource, provided that the necessary precautions are taken with regard to the protection of the environment and the defence of the rights of the local population on the one hand, and the real allocation of future oil revenues to the development of the country on the other. we will ensure that these concerns are conveyed to the european investment bank. in chad, oil production could be a very important factor in development and consolidation of the rule of law if these revenues are used wisely. the european commission will therefore endeavour to encourage the government to continue the dialogue on the issues raised by the oil project with the country's main partners, including the european commission itself, and to closely involve local authorities and non-governmental organisations in the preparatory actions. this is so that the progress already made on the most critical points of the oil project can be reinforced where necessary.

the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. i would like to start by quoting an expression used by mr harbour and take this opportunity to thank him for the great interest he showed in the hearing on 4 and 5 november. the commission always appreciates very much the participation of members in a hearing or other activity and i would like to emphasize this, mr president. mr harbour has therefore spoken of balance and this is obviously one of the commission's aspirations. you will understand, mr president, that i am not speaking only in my personal capacity or on behalf of my directorate-general, but also on behalf of the commission as a whole. this commission includes my colleague mr byrne, who is a strong advocate of consumer interests, and the answer i gave in this debate is of course linked to mr byrne's views, so as to show the face of a joint administration. we are also striving for this balance between the interests of the manufacturer on the one hand and the interests of the consumer on the other. the fact is well known and the arguments are also obvious. so we are trying to achieve that balance. and i think we have achieved that through the e-commerce directive. the principle of this directive states that the country of origin plays a major role in e-commerce litigation. generally speaking, i could say that there is a public policy exception, but that exception is subject to very strict specifications. these must be clearly defined objectives and no other. the derogation must also be necessary. the country in which the public order offence was committed must provide explanations in this respect. it must be given the opportunity to take action and the commission must be informed. the commission must be able to take action against the country which has allowed the infringement to take place. in other words, the basic principle of the e-commerce directive is country of origin, with a very strict exception. i would also like to take this opportunity, mr president, to urge parliament to approve the directive properly - that is to say quickly - so that it can find its way into european law at the end of the internal market council next may. everyone is waiting for a european directive on e-commerce and i hope that we can achieve this in may. mr president, i would now like to turn to another subject which has been raised by a number of members, including mrs palacio and mrs oomen, namely the brussels convention. i have taken note of the criticisms made by mrs palacio about the way in which the commission's proposal has been put forward. we'll learn from this for the future. i would however call on parliament, and in particular the legal affairs committee, to give its opinion on the thorny issue of article 15. i believe, mr president, that article 15 of the commission's proposal for the brussels convention departs from the original convention in one essential respect, namely in favour of consumer protection. the 1968 convention combines two requirements with the possibility for the consumer to rely on the law of his own country. one of these two requirements was not included in the commission's proposal. this is a very important issue, and has also raised concerns among the various organisations involved. the commission is also looking into the matter. we will have a small meeting next wednesday with four other commissioners - including commissioners byrne, vitorino and liikanen - and myself, to set out more precisely the ideas on article 15. if you, mr president, and mrs palacio allow me, i would also urge the legal affairs committee to pay attention to article 15, so that the commission will know what mrs palacio's committee thinks in good time. mrs wallis very rightly referred to the notion of 'joint administration'. in consultation with parliament, we now wish to define the concept of article 15 in more detail, in accordance with the commission's proposal. in addition, a number of members, mrs wallis, mrs oomen and, of course, mrs palacio, spoke of small claim procedures on the one hand and alternative dispute settlements on the other. parliament will readily understand that these matters do not fall within my direct competence. they are more the responsibility of my colleague vitorino. this does not detract from the fact that there is a close link with the subject as a whole and that, because of the relationship between these two accelerated and simplified methods of settling legal disputes, these methods are obviously very closely linked to the functioning of the internal market. that is why i feel very connected to this case. however, it is necessary to be honest and to recognize that antonio vitorino is the main responsible person in this matter. as i have just said, four or five commissioners will therefore be meeting next week. i am already under taking to stress the need to introduce the two accelerated and simplified methods mentioned earlier in order to put an end to small legal disputes arising from electronic commerce. i repeat once again and i would like to conclude on this point: we are striving for balance. we try to find that balance. firstly, we do not want what mr maccormick has said. we refuse long-distance scams. i thank mr maccormick for that colourful sentence. on the other hand, we also do not want to see what mrs wallis has said, namely that excessive protection will lead to infringements of the internal market. we reject both of these ideas. we must therefore find the most advantageous route for the internal market, that is to say for all european consumers, between charybdis and scylla.

- the next item is the report (a5-0082/1999) by mrs mcnally, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, on the communication from the commission 'women and science - engaging women to enrich european research' (com (99) 0076 - c5-0103/99 - 1999/2106 (cos)) (a5-0082/1999).
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let me first say that i find it a bit unfortunate that the debate on 'beijing + 5' was already postponed at the end of the parliamentary session a month ago, as was 'women and science' again. it seems that when it comes to women, the discussion is always postponed until after all the debates. i'm sorry about that. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when we read mrs mcnally's report we immediately know that we are dealing with a very important issue. "women and science" is a title which could be misleading if it were to be placed in an ever incomplete list of "women and "... on this or that subject: the enumeration is necessary but sometimes ineffective in explaining the importance of a problem. we are addressing a fundamental issue that has been the subject of controversy for centuries over gender equality. can women have reason like men? are women capable of scientific activity? some still doubt it, and yet the answer is now and forever: yes. but that's where the trouble starts. the situation of women in science is a cause for concern because of a number of problems that are difficult to solve. science, a symbolic activity, remains a male privilege, just as political responsibility is. the same blockages are found when it comes to sharing political power as well as the power of thought. in both cases, male power is at stake. let us then propose the same remedies, such as the establishment of parity in policy attempted by some countries of the union. girls are doing very well in school and there is no reason why they should be so few in the world of research. the obstacles to scientific careers are external to the research itself. in other words, it is not enough to have access to the scientific space, but it is also necessary that this space should be open to women, rather than to permanent guests, as the april 1998 symposium organized by the commission so well pointed out. school and university guidance remains a gender equality conundrum. the exact sciences are often organized in a way that discourages girls. the mixed nature of learning, as well as the possible sexism of teachers, parents and institutions, are problems that are far from being solved. as for the humanities, they will only make sense if they integrate the need to reflect on the "man-woman" dimension in all social and human problems. it is obvious that we must take a broad view of science and we must know that we cannot think of society without introducing the dimension of "man and woman". we are far from the number today. i think mrs mcnally's report, which i appreciate for its completeness as well as its complexity, is important because it stresses the remedies, if not the solutions, to the problem of the difficult exercise of science, namely data, figures of course, on the presence of women in the various fields, scholarships and degrees, the introduction of binding measures to develop the presence of women in research, as well as the promotion of studies on the mechanisms of sex discrimination, the establishment of working groups and monitoring bodies in the commission's directorates-general. i am glad that this report has not omitted the problem of women's power in science, ... (the president cut the speaker off)
the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area, including the creation of a european research area. i am pleased to note that this initiative has been very well received by parliament, which i thank for the important role it plays in the 'women and science' dynamic. the motion for a resolution under discussion today broadly supports the guidelines prepared by the commission. that is a strong and meaningful encouragement. but the question of women and science is part of a broader perspective on the union's research policy. as i have already indicated to the committee on industry, the aim is to develop a political strategy for creating a european research area. the commission has just adopted a communication to this effect on 18 january. the creation of such a space will help to better mobilise the potential of women scientists and address the common challenge of the under-representation of women in research. the commission is aware of the debate on the principle of quotas in the field of women's participation in general. the debate is also developing, of course, with regard to the participation of women in scientific research. the commission has not chosen the mandatory quota approach, preferring the quantitative participation objectives approach, coupled with monitoring and evaluation. the commission considers that this approach will help to increase the participation of women, while respecting the principle of scientific excellence. the report by mrs mcnally, unanimously adopted by the committee on women's rights, supports the commission's guidelines, which aim to achieve at least 40% female participation in certain aspects of the implementation of the fifth framework programme. this support is important. already, the representation of women is 26% in the advisory groups and 24% in the monitoring and evaluation panels, which is a considerable improvement over the fourth framework programme. there is still work to be done, but i think we are on the right track. mcnally also recommends that gender impact studies in specific programmes of the fifth framework programme be taken into account for the sixth framework programme. the commission has already published a call for tenders for these studies. the commission shall evaluate the tenders received. the results of these studies will help to define the guidelines for the sixth framework programme. but the promotion of equal opportunities goes beyond the mere framework of community research programmes and i understand parliament's concern to see this issue taken into account in other union policies. the commission is already doing something in this area and will continue to do so. for example, in the framework of the employment guidelines, fourth pillar, and in the regulatory provisions relating to the structural funds. in its white paper reform proposal, the commission sets itself the objective of achieving a broad balance in the representation of the sexes in all areas and at all levels of the hierarchy. mcnally suggests that the reasons for the gap between the number of women with degrees in science and those who eventually take up a profession in these fields should be examined. a number of speakers echoed this idea. the reasons for this discrepancy are complex and the recently published report by the etam experts addresses this issue. it is important to continue the analysis to better identify the obstacles and ways to overcome them. in this connection, the implementation of the action plan presented in the communication is proceeding actively and the report by the etam experts, which mrs sörensen referred to very pertinently, presented on 23 november in the presence of members of parliament, including mrs mcnally, takes stock of the underrepresentation of women in research. this report, drawn up by independent experts, is a very useful instrument for promoting discussion and for drawing up concrete measures.

mr president, the members of the europe of nations group can only agree with the intentions of a proposal for a regulation which aims to strengthen the dialogue with the fisheries industry. but at the same time we must say that some of the ways in which this dialogue is being organized leave us deeply perplexed. first, the necessary strengthening of dialogue: the common fisheries policy is applicable to all operators in the european union, but it has to deal with a considerable diversity of situations, depending on the fishing zone, the place where the vessels are moored, traditions, the gear used, the local market organisation, etc. so much so that some good people have wondered whether well-coordinated national policies would not be preferable to a unified common policy. in any case, given the uniqueness of the current policy and the diversity of the situations of the professionals, it is all the more important to establish very close contacts with them in order to take their needs into account as much as possible and to eliminate the adverse effects of certain regulations, or to avoid the outright non-application of these regulations, which is sometimes noted, unfortunately, because of a total lack of agreement with reality. that is why the members of our group will vote in favour of the three amendments tabled today, which are designed to improve the functioning of the advisory committee on fisheries and aquaculture, to bring it closer to the professions and to the needs of the states, and to ask the commission to submit an annual report to the council and the european parliament on the discussions there. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. however, certain aspects of the reform leave us with a deeply uncomfortable impression, because the commission is bringing into the advisory committee on fisheries a very diverse group of lobbyists, whose ties are mainly brussels-based, and who are dedicated to very general goals - development, environment, consumption, etc. at the same time, on the fishermen's side, it would like to use community funding to give a boost to european professional organizations, which at present exist only on paper. it seems that the commission is trying to counterbalance the national organisations, which are structured, well-established and properly representative, by a mass of diverse participants. it is as if the commission were trying to avoid discussions with difficult interlocutors and to create a more docile consultation structure out of thin air, which would give it the pleasant image of itself and its ideas that it expects. more worryingly, one ends up wondering how many other sectors have already been organised in this way and whether a vast network of associations or organisations has not been built in brussels without real representativeness, financed for the most part by community grants and participating in largely artificial consultations. the example we are considering today suggests that this hypothesis is likely to be correct. in such circumstances, it is not surprising that the institutions in brussels lose touch with public opinion. the member states would do well to take this seriously if they do not want to see the national democracies they represent soon ousted by unstable pressure groups. in the fisheries sector, which is the immediate subject of our discussion, we feel it is absolutely necessary to ensure that the various players are well represented on the advisory committee. all the member states concerned by the fishing industry must be represented, and so must their professions. they are the ones to be relied upon, not man-made organizations.

in writing. - it is pleased that the debate on mrs mcnally's report on increasing and facilitating the participation of women in research and science has been the subject of a fairly broad consensus. in writing. - parliament is today considering for the last time this text on so-called end-of-life vehicles and their destination: destruction; a laudable intention out of respect for our environment. but there are two things that we must be very careful about in this text. first, the financial responsibility for this destruction. let us all make sure that it is not always the same person who pays, i.e. the owner of the vehicle. it's already taxed enough for this car which is, in financial terms, nothing but a bottomless pit. we have recently been able to speak of the polluter pays principle, let us apply it rationally and carefully, without ideology and without mistaking the target. the other fundamental point that this text must contain is to expressly exclude collector vehicles from its scope. it is not necessary to write it down, because it is obvious, but i would like it to be written down because it is in our interest to adopt clear texts. so let us vote on these amendments to preserve these jewels of the automobile industry. these old vehicles are the testimony of a culture, a passion, which must be recognised and respected by europe, otherwise our specific features will be diluted. there are many examples in european texts of how vagueness or imprecision can provoke important disputes or debates. i shall only mention the cases of directives 79/409 and 92/43. the precision of the texts is a guarantee and a legal certainty for those who will apply or live these texts on a daily basis. the european parliamentarian is not meant to be a litigator or a facilitator of proceedings for judges of any kind, for then he would not be fulfilling his mission. on the contrary, it must adopt clear texts to limit litigation.
in writing. - i welcome with great satisfaction the two proposals for directives which seek to facilitate the free movement of workers from third countries while at the same time facilitating the free movement of services. the main thrust of these proposals is to introduce the ec/service card which will in future enable some 5 million third country nationals legally resident in a member state of the european union to provide services in other member states, something which is currently hampered by problems such as obtaining visas and work permits. the first proposal for a directive will allow undertakings established in a member state which employ workers from third countries to temporarily post such workers to another member state to provide services there. under the proposed provisions, the employer would simply be required to apply for a service card for each worker concerned. logically, in order to be able to hold such a card, the worker would have to be legally resident in a member state and be covered by a social security scheme. the second proposal confers the same rights on selfemployed third-country nationals. while i agree with the commission's proposals in substance, it is true that some of the provisions could be confusing. i therefore vote in favour of the amendments tabled by the rapporteur. this will help to clarify the provisions and thus prevent any abuse! other amendments aim to simplify administrative procedures, for example by allowing member states to designate a single authority responsible for issuing cards. i thought that such a change was essential to avoid the administrative burdens which too often hinder the proper application of new provisions. i can therefore only welcome the adoption of such amended directives; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's citizens are not subject to discrimination. this is contrary to the fundamental principle of non-discrimination enshrined in the founding treaties of our union.
in writing. - we were very wary of the council's proposals for amendments. how can we explain the need to increase the number of judges in the court of first instance, which is known to be overburdened, when at the same time it is proposed to increase its area of competence? the effects of the first measure will, de facto, be nullified by the second. some people may say that perfection is not of this world, but a brief historical review should help them to understand better our reservations: on 1 january 1995 the council reviewed the increase in the number of judges provided for in article 17 of the treaty of accession of 24 june 1994. in may 1995, during the preparatory phase of the amsterdam treaty, the court of first instance, concerned about the continuing increase in the volume of applications, had already stressed the need to take measures 'otherwise the court will soon no longer be able to satisfy the principle of the proper administration of justice and to carry out the task entrusted to it ... under such conditions as would compromise the protection of the persons subject to the jurisdiction'. what did we do in amsterdam? the burden has increased with the extension of community jurisdiction under the third pillar. you will also agree that the texts voted by our assembly always call for community jurisdiction, including the charter of fundamental rights which is currently being drawn up. the increase from 15 to 21 judges at the icc and the recent recognition of the possibility for the court to rule on certain cases as a single judge council decision of 26 april 1999. are not solutions but mere deceptions of evil grace, which expose us to belated realizations. the commission has also proposed that the court of justice should be able to give its opinion on the case before it. we cannot allow this, because such a drift towards a europe of judges is detrimental to the proper exercise of democracy in our states. we therefore believe that the time has come to start a thorough review of the community's judicial system in order to ensure that it is of a high quality. this question is inseparable from the current debate on the hierarchy of standards and better application of the principle of subsidiarity. the forthcoming intergovernmental conference is the best opportunity that can be.

the rapporteur. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioners and members of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, i have been asked to draw up the european parliament's report on the interreg iii community initiative programme. when we went to committee we considered more than 100 amendments and so far 17 amendments have been tabled again, some of which were already tabled in committee. before discussing the content of the resolution i am proposing, i should like to share with you the points i have taken into account and which have guided my work as rapporteur. first of all, i would like to remind you of the role of the interreg community initiative, which is based on the principle of transnationality and innovation. this programme is a driving force for development and has a european dimension. interreg is one of the four community initiatives planned for the period 2000-06 and will have the largest financial envelope, i.e. €4.875 billion, compared with €3.604 billion at present. the interreg initiative, which was set up in 1990, is based on the desire to prepare european regions for a europe without frontiers in the context of the completion of the single market. in the 1994 and 1996 reforms of the structural funds, the interreg icp incorporated new components contributing to the development of the trans-european energy transmission and distribution networks. these programmes have encouraged crossborder, transnational and interregional cooperation in the european union, with a focus on the balanced development of the community area. the interreg iii programme, the guidelines of which have been submitted to us today by the european commission, in accordance with the provisions of european community regulation no 1260 of 1999 laying down general provisions on the structural funds, continues this action. it is based on three strands: strand a, which organises crossborder cooperation between territorial authorities in the border regions, both internal and external to the european union, on the basis of common development strategies, the implementation of which is the responsibility of the member states and local and regional authorities; component b provides for transnational cooperation between national, regional and local authorities in several member states or candidate countries to the european union in the fields of spatial planning, transport networks and the environment. the implementation of this strand is the responsibility of the member states and national authorities; and strand c, which organises interregional cooperation between different regions of member states or third countries by networking experiences concerning strands a and b, and cooperation in the field of research, technological development, to be defined with the european commission, which is responsible for its implementation. the new interreg programme, as it has been transmitted to us, takes account of the needs generated by enlargement to the ceecs and the island and outermost regions. the commission proposes that the interreg allocation be distributed as follows: from 50 to 80% for strand a, 6% for strand c, the difference for strand b, i.e. from 14 to 44% at the most. the european commission draws up the list of regions eligible for strand a and strand b. it was based mainly on the map of eligible regions during the previous programming period. the outermost regions may receive support under strand b. the commission shall draw up a list of priority areas and eligible measures which shall be non-exhaustive for strand a but exhaustive for strand b. it reserves the right to propose at a later stage those themes which it considers important for the exchange of experience and enhanced cooperation between regions, for strand c. the procedure for adopting the programmes is laid down in the general regulation on the structural funds . the proposals are drawn up by the member states and submitted for approval to the european commission, which checks their conformity with the general guidelines adopted. these proposals should include a number of elements, an overview of the cross-border or transnational strategies and priorities, a description of the measures needed to implement them and an indicative financing plan. i am one of the vast majority of members who voted to effective as possible, but i know how difficult this operation is - and i regret that the work schedule was extremely short, since the text was examined in a parliamentary committee on 24 november and 26 january, and i also regret that neither the regions nor the representative regional organisations were involved in the preparation of the programme. by promoting crossborder, transnational and interregional cooperation, this transversal instrument is the very embodiment of a regional policy of european dimension which favours a harmonious and balanced development of the community's - madam president, my group was one of those who wanted to have a document allowing for an exchange within the group on the commission's strategic objectives before this debate, rather than being reduced to a mere warm reaction to a plenary speech. the first merit of the text of this communication is therefore, in our view, that of its existence. we are also not indifferent to a number of the findings and intentions which are set out in it, and which mr prodi has just underlined, and even usefully clarified in some points. the current process of globalisation is, i quote, 'more exclusive than inclusive and has increased inequalities' and the european union's ambition must therefore be to help define, i quote again, 'new rules of the game within itself and in international relations'. yes, many of our fellow citizens are, as i keep saying, 'disenchanted and anxious' because they do not see real and lasting solutions to essential if not existential problems such as unemployment and social exclusion, which reminds us of what must be one of our absolute priorities. yes, we need to rethink many aspects of the present community policy if we are to succeed in the great but difficult project of enlargement, and we also need, i quote, 'genuine strategic partnerships with our neighbours to the south and the east to contribute to stability and peace'. there is no shortage of areas where we can have serious discussions. we will study the white papers carefully and will make a constructive contribution to the many projects that are open or that are being proposed. it is in this spirit that i now wish to formulate three criticisms which we feel must be heard if we really want to give 'shape to the new europe' not in words but in deeds, to use the ambitious title of the commission document and of mr prodi's speech. the first of these criticisms, and in my view the most severe, is a certain tendency towards the commission's somewhat grandiose complacency with regard to the european union itself and a somewhat summary, if not condescending, view of our partners. the commission's communication is a perfect illustration of this vicious vice. it describes the european union as "a living proof of what peace, stability, freedom and prosperity can bring to a continent and a model for the world to follow", and concludes "that our neighbours have the opportunity to join in this prosperity and that we have the opportunity to enable them to do so". a slightly more nuanced and rigorous diagnosis would, i think, be welcome. similarly, the idea that the euro would have fostered a consensus on wage moderation does not seem to me to be very much supported by the nervous and repeated injunctions addressed by the european central bank to the trade unions, which were considered too demanding. my second criticism is actually derived from the first. this extreme difficulty in seeing reality in its contradictions and, if necessary, in questioning oneself, is the source of serious limitations on the will, appropriately affirmed by mr prodi, to meet the demands of the citizens. i doubt, for example, at least in the countries i know well, that the intention, repeated three or four times in the commission document, to, i quote, 'reform the social protection, health care and pension systems in europe, in a context of moderation of public expenditure', i doubt that this meets the expectations of those whose confidence we say we want to regain. my third criticism is the result of these two observations: the weakness of the diagnosis and the obstacles to the necessary changes lead to a project whose scope seems to me to be severely hampered by the abundance of generalizations, by a somewhat self-serving approach and, therefore, by a lack of breath. but nothing is lost. this is a starting point, we have five years to succeed, if the political will exists and is expressed with sufficient strength and clarity. my group is fully committed to contributing to this.
- madam president, the commission is presenting its strategic objectives for 2000-2005 today in the form of a very general document, all the rough edges of which have been removed in order to avoid too much clashing. in the first part, therefore, on the new forms of european governance, the words federalism or superstate are obviously nowhere to be found. but it is they who stand out when it comes to strong european institutions, decentralising only the day-to-day activities of implementation and promoting their collective vision in a blurred whole where national governments and parliaments are mixed with regional and even local authorities, as well as civil society, all designated, without any hierarchy, as, i quote: 'stakeholders in european affairs'. these ambiguities are accompanied by many misunderstandings, first of all about our values. it is not enough to claim democracy to be a democrat. above all, it is necessary to accept in practice that citizens are free to take their decisions at the level where the objective conditions for close, loyal and transparent democratic debate are best met, that is to say mainly at national level. the commission's entire communication is based on the opposite assumption, namely that, under the pretext of better defending the people, their margin of autonomy should be further restricted by new regulations, new policy integration or new binding legal structures such as the draft charter of what is wrongly called fundamental rights. i emphasize 'rightly so' because it will actually reduce these rights. in the europe of nations group, our principles are very different. we want to defend the countries of europe, but we also want to respect the choices of the people. it's not the square of the circle at all. we must get out of the old federalist schemes, the schemes of those whose ideas on european affairs are all taken from the memoirs of jean monnet. on the contrary, it is necessary to open up the european institutions to the modern world by inventing a dynamic of variable geometry which respects the nations. that is the big idea about new governance that we would have liked to have found in your communication, mr president, but unfortunately it was not there.
- madam president, mr president of the commission, you claim to be shaping a new europe, but unfortunately you lack one essential condition: trust. it is not possible to win the trust of millions of europeans if you are not worthy of it. and how can you be trusted after the mad cow case, after the santer commission resigned for corruption? you are responsible for millions of unemployed and millions of poor people, for the precariousness and growing misery of your ultra-barter and ultra-liberal policies, for the forced march to the single currency. you wanted and organised the disappearance of internal borders and thus delivered europe to the explosion of crime and insecurity, to the flood of uncontrolled immigration. today you propose to give all the decision-making power to a handful of civil servants by making states, local authorities and ngos, all of whom are also placed on an equal footing in their submission to brussels, mere executors of decisions taken from above. not once in your 14 pages is there any mention of national parliaments, which are elected by the people. but it is true that they have no role in your strategy. you dare not even call things by their name and you take refuge behind a pseudo-branched semantics to call "governance" which is nothing but a federal, autocratic and centralized government. after years of trying to convince people by talking about shared sovereignty, you now admit your ultimate aim: to sell all european sovereignty, whether national or collective, to a world government in which you do not even hope to have a prominent place. finally, you dare condemn and sanction, or let condemn and sanction, the free and democratic vote of millions of austrians on the sole ground that you do not like the result. and at schüssel, which is clearly not a show of sympathy but a political maneuver. your ramblings are not fooling anyone, because you know very well that whether you like it or not, you need austria to reform the treaties and harmonize the taxation of savings. you will use austria to further strip the states of their real powers in the construction of the european union, with cynicism, with hypocrisy, but you will use austria as a very convenient scarecrow. of course, you commissioners are not the only ones responsible. the governments that support you, whether by way of vigil or ideology, are also. brussels, we are not all as you say, you are all. stop lying, you don't care what the people of europe want. europeans are only free to choose between your best of all worlds and the stake. more than ten years after the collapse of the soviet union, your projects have a gulag feel, with a moralistic approach that is even more deadening. we were among the few who denounced the communist dictatorship. we are and will remain among those who are fighting the europeanist dictatorship and we call on all the peoples of europe to resist your monstrous projects. the salvation of european democracies lies in the nation state, in the nation state, and the salvation of europe lies in the cooperation of the nations of europe. - madam president, mr president of the commission, we can welcome the overall ambition of the objectives announced, objectives which go hand in hand with the challenges that europe will have to overcome. i note that you consider the fall of the berlin wall to be the essential element of the end of this century. this event must underpin enlargement. i would like to speak of reunification rather than use the word 'enlargement'. it seems to me that this has a much stronger political significance. you are returning to the idea of refocusing your activities around the most important missions, and this is part of the goals of your reform. the principle of subsidiarity is being applied. a clear application of this principle will only strengthen the actions undertaken and give citizens a clear picture of each skill level. but, mr prodi, it is one thing to say it, it is another to do it! you will therefore have to fight against the tendency of any institution, which generally seeks to develop its powers further. so i'll judge by the deeds. in the meantime, i support and encourage this wish, which is clearly expressed in your communication. however, two points are essential: simplification and application of community law. in 1998 there were 123 cases before the court of justice for failure to apply or transpose and 25% of environmental directives are not applied or are not transposed. the events of these last days show how necessary this is. community law must not be left unapplied because it is too complex or too cumbersome. the union must not fall into this trap and i regret that your communication does not go into more detail. you are realistic about the fact that the welfare state will no longer be able to provide the right answers to the problems we face and, among other things, unemployment. i regret, however, that no clear option has been put forward. the emphasis should have been on the rejection of any policy of assistance and, on the contrary, on the emphasis on initiative and responsibility. you are not stressing the ageing of our population, which will have fundamental implications for the structure of our society, not only economically but also in terms of public health. it is a silent revolution, and in that respect i expected more from you. finally, you insist on european research as the key to our future. however, you do not tell us what you intend to do. ethical principles are also at the heart of this research. your communication says nothing of that. mr president, you want to inform the public better. first of all, strengthen your links with parliament: we are the representatives of these citizens.
- madam president, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we had arranged to meet you today when we voted for your nomination. today is the day when the serious business begins, because today is the day when we are going to decide on your programme. let me, in your speech to this house, concentrate on what you have called the new governance. you're making it a tool for reconciliation with our fellow citizens. but behind this term 'new governance', it seems to me that there is simply the question of the functioning of the institutions, the question of the functioning of our public authorities, if we agree that the european union should be a public authority. the coordination between the union's institutions, the member states' competences and local and regional authorities is very good. but is this really how we reconcile citizens and the construction of europe? is this really how we are going to answer the fundamental questions, which are not so much 'who does what' but rather 'what do we do together'? because that is what is disturbing our fellow citizens. in your speech you mentioned the challenges ahead, those of globalisation, those of enlargement, and i would add the future of our social model. that is why my group and i are putting such great emphasis on this draft charter, because it seems to us that if we have included the drafting of this charter of fundamental rights in our timetable, it is because we are at a turning point in our history, when our union needs to redefine the values around which it was built within its present borders, but also in the perspective of the future enlargements which we are calling for, but not under any conditions. our fellow citizens expect more of europe from us, but not just any europe. they expect us, not to adapt to globalisation, but to be, on the basis of our social model, a capacity to organise globalisation. i would like to say that when you commit yourselves to political union - and we are in favour of this political union - it cannot be achieved unless it is based on our social model, on what constitutes our originality and our capacity to regulate the affairs of this world better.
