in writing. - this report sets out general guidelines for what it calls the urban regeneration strategy of the urban centres and suburbs hit by the crisis of the capitalist economy and its consequences: the development of unemployment, exclusion and crime. this report stresses that to ensure sustainable urban development, it is necessary to implement an urban policy which does not leave out the main victims of the economic crisis: the unemployed, immigrants, refugees, women and the excluded. but there is no mention of the causes and the people responsible for this crisis. the report is at best concerned with correcting certain aspects and setbacks. and again, with scandalously reduced resources, since, according to the report itself, the funds allocated to the urban ii programme for the period 2000-2006 are about 30% lower than those of the previous period, which were already very low (eur 900 million), not to mention that there are about 50 projects for the whole of europe, which is ridiculous when it is practically all the suburbs of the large cities of our continent, or even the city centres, that are hit. that is why we are voting in favour of the concrete measures announced to help certain of the most disadvantaged social groups, but we are abstaining on the report itself, denouncing the fact that it is mainly wishful thinking financed at a discount.
in writing. - madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, i must say that i am very pleased with the continuation of the urban community initiative, an initiative which aims to support the social and economic conversion of cities and suburbs in crisis, all with a view to promoting sustainable urban development. with some 80% of the european population living in an urban environment, cities are at the heart of europe's economic, social and cultural development. at the same time, the social and economic problems facing european society are more acute in cities. in fact, many european cities are faced with an internal territorial divide: the coexistence within cities of neighbourhoods with high value-added activities and high-income residents, and neighbourhoods with low income, high unemployment, poor and overcrowded housing and high dependency on social assistance. the concentration of social and economic problems in certain urban areas requires targeted intervention which takes account of the complexity of the problems. this is why our european parliament successfully called for the extension of the urban community initiative (ci) during the reform of the structural funds. the success of urban during the 1994/1999 programming period is undeniable. the results are tangible in terms of improving the quality of life in the target areas. this ci has fostered the development of good practice in the economic, social and environmental sectors. it has also strengthened the role of local authorities, the non-governmental sector and local communities and fostered new forms of partnership in the field of urban regeneration. the new initiative will pursue and strengthen these objectives, with particular regard to the promotion of equal opportunities for men and women and the integration of socially marginalised and disadvantaged groups. we can therefore welcome its adoption; but we must admit that we cannot claim victory financially. the financial envelope allocated is far from being up to the challenge. the amount was €900 million for the period 1994/99, it is €700 million for the period 2000/2006, a drop of 30%! this reduction in funding has led to a reduction in the number of programmes under the new urban initiative. the ceiling seems too low. it was set at 50 projects. it should therefore be increased to take account of regional and local factors while maintaining the financial allocations for member states. given this concentration on a limited number of projects, the publication and dissemination of the results of the new community initiative urban may play an important role in achieving a multiplier effect.
in writing. - the mccarthy report on the community initiative urban gives us an opportunity to reflect on the desirability of community action in the field of cities. the situation in some urban areas is alarming, with social distress manifested in the face of unemployment, poverty and crime. drug trafficking in particular fuels insecurity and petty crime. in the face of such social challenges, the effectiveness of the structural funds remains questionable. subsidiarity should lead us to recognize that the state, in the exercise of its royal functions, and local authorities are best placed to intervene in an appropriate manner, the state by ensuring public security, the local authorities by helping people in difficulty. while the desire to create a system of exchanges of successful enterprises is to be welcomed, the problems specific to each urban area cannot be placed on the same level. the urban community initiative is part of the european union's drive to make urban policy more community-oriented. it would be more appropriate for the union to concentrate its financial efforts on existing european policies. some, of course, are taking the opportunity to engage in a new budgetary bidding war, a particularly unwelcome bidding war at a time when the emu convergence criteria impose a severe thinning of national budgets. mrs mccarthy suggests increasing the funding for urban and promoting the community initiative through a costly communication campaign to promote the benefits of federal europe. is it worth recalling that the effectiveness of an expenditure is not measured by the volume of funds allocated to the project? on the other hand, those who receive too many and too high subsidies will eventually take them for granted. the aim should not be to assist citizens, but to empower them. finally, the report places great emphasis on actions in favour of ethnic or sociological minorities. we cannot but condemn a policy of minorities which is necessarily dangerous for social cohesion. on the one hand, it encourages the integration of immigrants where it is necessary to promote their assimilation into the culture of the host country in order to avoid the emergence of ethnic ghettos which will be like urban dustbins. on the other hand, it is a manipulation of the principle of affirmative action, a politically correct chimera that is just as harmful as the precedent in the united states has shown. for all these reasons, the french delegation of the uen group could not approve mrs mccarthy's report.

in writing. - as a member of the european parliament from a border region, i welcome this third interreg initiative with great interest. the difficulties faced in the past by border regions, both land and sea, which were economically, socially and culturally separated, will never be sufficiently recalled. the presence of frontiers has turned them into peripheral areas of the states to which they belong, which has too often led the national authorities to neglect these regions in the context of national policy. this is why the interreg community initiative was set up in 1990. the objective of this programme was to encourage crossborder, transnational and interregional cooperation and a balanced development of the community area, in order to strengthen economic and social cohesion in the union. interreg is mainly intended to finance joint approaches in the fields of sme development, training and education, cultural exchanges, health problems, protection and improvement of the environment, energy networks, transport and telecommunications. it stresses that interregional cooperation contributes to involving local and regional authorities in the european integration process. the more active participation of local and regional authorities in community initiatives must be promoted, bearing in mind that local and regional authorities often have very limited capacities for cooperation because of the diversity of legal frameworks and the disparity in levels of development on both sides of the same border. in the context of crossborder cooperation, greater emphasis should be placed on improving the operating conditions of small and medium-sized enterprises that create jobs. in the same vein, and given that 50% of unemployment is attributable to structural unemployment, the resources made available under interreg must be sufficiently large to complement national measures to promote employment. more specifically, obstacles too often linked to taxation (double taxation) and social protection prevent, slow down or make crossborder mobility particularly problematic. i hope that the projects in the programmes will help to find solutions to these problems and give concrete substance to the principle of free movement of workers, a principle which in my region is very much in vogue! interreg funding should also contribute to the creation of a european research area. last but not least, in the regions, expectations of this initiative are high, with the localities not eligible for objective 2 hoping to find compensation through interreg! the challenges are therefore important: the integration of border regions will be an essential element in the development of a future european spatial planning policy! may everyone, like f. decourrière, whom i congratulate, be aware of this!
in writing. - the interreg community initiative is an element of a harmful european regional policy. this policy, which appears to be generous since it is officially intended to help the regions in difficulty, is a market for dupes for french taxpayers. france, which contributes 17% to the european budget, will receive only 8% of the regional structural funds. between 1994 and 1999, our regions received an average of chf 15.4 billion each year; the commission has already taken a number of measures to improve the situation. my region, nord-pas-de-calais, will be particularly affected, with french hainaut losing the aid paid to objective 1 regions. unjustified suppression in a region whose main activities have been ruined by free trade europe. european regional policy also reinforces brussels centralism, with which regional authorities are invited to negotiate directly the use of the structural funds. it is the europe of the regions, regions which, less solid than our nation states, will easily submit to brussels. the interreg initiative, which was set up in 1990 to prepare - and i quote: 'the border regions for a europe without frontiers, and therefore without nations, fits well into this philosophy'. however, mr decourrière makes some common sense remarks, denouncing the shortcomings of the brussels technocrats. these will result in particular in a late implementation of interreg iii and thus in financial losses for the beneficiary regions. we also agree with him that we should pay more attention to small and mediumsized enterprises and, of course, reject the use of an external service provider. the commission's own resources are used to finance the budget. however, these paragraphs, which are marked in the corner of common sense and which we voted in favour of, do not correct the euro-federalist philosophy which characterizes community initiatives, particularly interreg. that is why the national front voted against the report.
in writing. - the european parliament delivered an opinion on the commission's guidelines for the interreg community initiative on crossborder, transnational and interregional cooperation. i would let us not leave it without innovative and pilot community programmes which will help to define the new geographical and economic map of europe.

in writing. - all the members of the union for a europe of nations group voted in favour of almost the whole of our colleague mr procacci's report on the leader+ community initiative. however, we have amended the draft report as adopted by the committee on agriculture to clarify certain points which would make this community initiative more operational. in particular, we believe it is essential to simplify the administrative and financial procedures which have proved to be too cumbersome and too slow in the context of the leader ii initiative. we also believe that it is essential to ensure that the development priorities of local actors are better taken into account and that the benefit of leader+ funds is not limited to agricultural regions with a low population density. amendment no 10, tabled on behalf of my group, refers to the concept of 'economic and social cohesion' instead of 'spatial planning' because the european union has no recognised competence in this area. amendment no 11 replaces the words 'government or municipal administration' with 'all public administrations'. while it is true that the local action groups must constitute a balanced representative body of partners from the various socio-economic sectors of the territory, at the decision-making level the public administrations as a whole (municipalities, departments, regions, states) must be fully represented, whatever their level. the rapporteur's wording was therefore, in our opinion, too restrictive. amendment no 12 meets the expectations of the committee on regional policy of our european parliament. it includes the necessary coordination between leader+ and community cooperation and partnership programmes such as interreg, phare, sapard or meda. in the territory of the member states of the european union, the candidate countries or the efta states, there may be interrelations between the various community initiatives. it should be remembered that the real priorities for the european continent are to establish an operational level, within a european framework and not a global one, as the rapporteur proposes. the creation of organisations similar to lags can be usefully encouraged by the european union, provided of course that the corresponding costs are borne by the various partners. in substance, we are of course in favour of this community initiative leader+. it should be remembered that at the conference on rural development held in cork from 7 to 9 november 1996, rural development was identified as one of the priorities of the european union, since it is essential to preserve the integrity of our agriculture and the whole rural fabric (infrastructure, public and private services, etc.). in this context, we in the committee deplored the appropriations for rural development and supported the amendments calling for an increase in the budget for this community initiative, so that it would be in line with the previous leader i and leader ii initiatives. compared to the last initiative, which was limited to 6 years, the budget allocated to leader+ for 7 years is 50%. this is not acceptable in view of the importance of rural development and the consequences for farmers of the fall in prices and aid as provided for in the reform of the cap following the berlin agreements. finally, among the priority parameters to be introduced at european level to allow local registrations, particular attention will have to be paid to the quality and originality of projects which have already been carried out by lags under the leader ii initiative, but which could not be completed due to the time-frame and the burden of the planned management arrangements.
- doc. a5-0015/2000 by mr graefe zu baringdorf, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 70/524/eec on additives in animal nutrition (com (99) 388 - c5-0134/1999 - 1999/0168 (cns))
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report on additives in animal feedingstuffs deals with a technical and economic problem of restoring the competitive balance between different additives in animal feedingstuffs and between the producers of these additives. but today, after the serious dioxin crisis which struck belgium and other european countries last summer, we cannot simply dwell on a simple question of competition. in his day, although this went unnoticed by the general public, the commission's scientific experts had discovered industrial lime residues laden with dioxin in the pulp of citrus fruits imported from brazil. it is therefore time to take a look at all the elements in the chain that are involved in the production of feed for farmed animals. i would like to add that the problem is much less serious for the food we give to our dogs, cats and other pets. is it because of the fierce and globalised competition between the industrialists in this sector that it has become a recycling sector for all the waste from the agri-food industry? such a serious matter cannot be confined to a technical debate, even though the directive itself limits the authorization of antibiotics and other growth factors. the same precautions we are about to take with regard to animal feed must also be applied to the food of farm animals, the very same ones we find on our plate. as this report emphatically points out, labelling is an absolute necessity if every farmer on his farm is to know all the ingredients in the feed he is feeding his livestock. he also needs to know if any gmos have gotten into his protein-pellets bag. these components may pose a potential risk to public health. in any event, the precautionary principle requires that we ensure that traceability is clearly displayed at all levels of the marketing of these products. but before labelling, clear rules must be established. simple questions must be asked, such as the real purpose of using animal flour. if we look at all the problems they have posed, from an ethical and health point of view, it is their very use that must be questioned today. the chapter on animal feed in the white paper on food safety must therefore serve as a basis for our work, which goes far beyond simple commercial matters. the commission has repeatedly used the example of 'fork to fork'. our colleague from the epp emphasized this earlier. it's a good formula, but it still needs to make sense. and to make it meaningful, we have to address both the animal-related and the consumer-related health problems. it is therefore important to accept amendment no 2 in recital 4, which avoids the risk of monopoly if the companies which have already been the first to place an additive on the market are the only ones allowed to operate it during the review period. but above all, we must accept amendments nos 4 and 5 to the new article 2a, which will make it possible to clearly identify genetically modified additives in order to enable users to make an informed decision.
- mr president, commissioner, i too would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent work and, above all, to welcome the unanimity that has prevailed on this matter at group level. it is therefore foreseen that the commission will replace existing authorisations by authorisations linked to those responsible for placing additives on the market, by means of regulations, and that these replacements will be carried out at the same time for all additives concerned. a coherent legal framework must be restored. the commission proposed to introduce a legal basis in directive 70/524/eec as from october 1999 for the replacement of authorisations. however, we must be careful not to create distortions of competition, as mr kindermann and mrs auroi have pointed out. i believe that there is also a need to clearly identify genetically modified additives in animal feed to enable and guarantee the final consumer to choose a food that is gmo-free or based on gmos. the consumer must retain his freedom of decision in full knowledge of the facts. this proposal has no financial implications for the community budget, commissioner. this is why, in food safety, there must be full transparency for producers and consumers. i am sure that the commission will be able to follow the rapporteur, who, let us recall, was unanimously elected by the committee on agriculture and rural development.
commission. - i should like to begin by thanking the committee on agriculture and rural development and its rapporteur, the chairman of the committee, mr graefe zu baringdorf, for examining the commission's proposal. the commission's proposal is, as some of you have pointed out, quite technical. however, the aim is quite simple: to harmonise the procedures governing the authorisation of food additives. at present there is a difference in the treatment of authorizations, which depends on when the applications were submitted, i.e. before or after 1 january 1988. the aim of the commission's proposal is to harmonise these procedures to ensure that such differences no longer exist. the subject of the proposed amendment is therefore very limited. five amendments were tabled by parliament. i regret that the commission is not in a position to adopt these amendments despite the fact that i am well aware of the views and commitment of parliament, the committee on agriculture and, in particular, the rapporteur, mr graefe zu baringdorf, on these problems. i intend to examine each of the amendments separately. the first amendment proposes to amend the legal basis of the proposal by replacing article 152 with article 37. i would simply point out that the commission proposal makes no reference to health and consumer protection. the technical nature of the proposed amendment does not allow it to be interpreted as having as its primary objective the protection of public health. i note that the committee on legal affairs and the internal market also considers that rule 37 is the appropriate legal basis. i would remind the house that the primary objective of article 152 is the protection of health. i recommend that you read the arguments in the letter from the legal affairs committee, which, in my view, describes the situation precisely, clearly and with commendable conciseness. amendments nos 2 and 3 go much further than the commission proposal, since they seek to introduce additional provisions on genetically modified additives. i am the first to admit that gmos are a very serious problem. i also acknowledge and concede that a number of initiatives are needed to update eu legislation in the field of gmos. however, this technical amendment is not the appropriate instrument for introducing such initiatives. the commission is of the opinion that it is premature at this stage to amend the provisions currently laid down in directive 70/524 concerning genetically modified additives. however, it is appropriate to await developments in the common position on the amendment to directive 90/220, which is currently under second reading in parliament. the commission intends to go much further than what is currently proposed by parliament in its amendments. i can also assure parliament that i will ensure that the relevant provisions of directive 90/220 are included in the proposal for the recasting of directive 70/524 which the commission has proposed in the white paper on food safety and which will be presented to parliament before july 2001. i can also assure the house that all the remarks made today will have our full attention. amendments nos 4 and 5 are also unacceptable because they give undue preference to copies of products by giving them authorization to be placed on the market even before an application for authorization has been submitted. the commission stresses the need to examine these applications for safety and efficacy before granting an authorisation. i can only ask you again to bear in mind the technical nature of the commission's proposal and to wait for the independent proposal for a new directive on food additives to address wider issues. i should like to examine some of the specific problems which have been raised in the debate. first of all, with regard to the comments made by mr graefe zu baringdorf, i would like to assure you that we will amend the procedure for the authorisation of genetically modified additives in directive 70/524 on additives and not in the novel food directive. this is a directive whose subject-matter is more concerned with raw materials than with additives. the text referred to by parliament is from the directive which was adopted in 1998. however, the vertical legislation of directive 90/220 on how to carry out the environmental risk assessment of gmos has since been amended and is still amended today. it is submitted to parliament for second reading. i am convinced that we should wait for the final version of directive 90/220 and more particularly article 11 thereof. reference was also made to the question whether the present proposal might create a risk of monopolies. mr kindermann and mrs auroi raised this issue. i would just like to make a few remarks on this matter. firstly, the project has been under way since 1993 and, therefore, it cannot be said to have caught any other producer of goods by surprise. any such applicant may always submit his application for a particular product. i would also like to stress the fact that the commission has never approved any application for authorisation of gmos for inclusion in additives. mrs roth-behrendt referred to the question of the appropriate legal basis, whether that basis should be article 37 or article 152. i repeat what i have already said on this point and i assure him and the house that it would be extremely inappropriate for the commission to seek to justify a measure taken on the basis of article 37 by simply excluding from the provision any reference to public health. this is a problem which has been examined on at least two occasions by the european court of justice, which has established the legal criteria for situations identical to the present situation, which require that the appropriate legal basis be taken into account when a legislative text is presented. the case-law of the court appears to be quite explicit on this point. as a general comment on the amendments suggested here, particularly with regard to the problem of the legal basis, it would, in my view, be inappropriate to base the legal basis on article 152 in these circumstances, as this would very certainly run the risk of being contrary to the objective criteria which have been defined by the court. a number of you - mr nicholson in particular - have referred to the problem of labelling. directive 70/524 deals with the labelling of genetically modified additives. this point is already settled at present by the "indication of the special characteristics due to the manufactured products". so this problem will be dealt with. this formula allowed us to oblige the applicants to indicate on the label that genetic modification techniques have been used in the product for which the application is made.
commission - i would like to emphasize that no gmo has been approved under this directive; this directive applies only to additives. as far as labelling is concerned, i would also say that it is a very complex subject. it is dealt with and will continue to be dealt with exhaustively, particularly in directive 90/220. this matter is currently before parliament and other directives will follow, which will also have article 152 as their legal basis, which grants parliament full codecision rights. i would like to assure mr graefe zu baringdorf that i have no intention or desire to engage in a conflict or a showdown with parliament on this matter. i intend, as i have always done, to work in collaboration with parliament and to ensure that the results we achieve are the best possible. the best way to deal with this issue is to go through the legislative proposal which is currently before parliament and the legislative act which is being prepared rather than going through this technical document and working in a context where the issues which are raised and need to be discussed in the context of directive 90/220 might not be fully taken into account. it is better to wait for the debate which i understand will take place very soon. all these issues will be addressed in this legislative document.
- thank you, chief. parliament takes note of your remarks. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at 11.30 a.m.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0027/2000) on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council decision on a framework for community action in the field of water (9085/3/1999 - c5-0209/1999 - 1997/0067 (cod)) (rapporteur: mrs lienemann).
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, the question of water will be one of the great environmental and planetary questions of the 21st century. whether it's climate change, resources across the globe, the quality of our rivers and the quality of our groundwater, we know that these big issues pose risks to our common future. we will either be able to restore a quality of water that corresponds to the planet's ecosystem, or we will see a whole series of disruptions threaten the development of some regions, threaten the living conditions of the inhabitants in others, and even, more fundamentally, the global balance. i take as proof an excellent report drawn up by our colleague, mario soares, in the international bodies on the state of the seas and oceans. when we talked about climate change, we rightly referred to the greenhouse effect and the state of the atmosphere. but we also know that the deterioration of the oceans will dramatically destabilize entire parts of our planet. it is therefore appropriate that europe, both because it has to promote a certain model of development and because it itself is faced with serious problems of pollution and deterioration of its waters, whether groundwater, surface water or sea, should be, in some way, exemplary in its practice. in fact, our europe has signed international conventions. i am thinking in particular of the ospar convention, where it has made commitments. it said: 'within a few years we will have to stop the dumping of pollution, we will have to stop the increase in pollution and even we will have to get close to a level of almost zero, as far as toxic or dangerous substances are concerned.' europe is therefore basing its signature on international agreements, and then the directive arrives, along with the concrete policies on the ground, and there it announces that it will not be able to achieve the objectives set or it delays them to dates such that the very credibility of the signing of these international conventions is questioned. that is why, when it opened the debate on the water framework directive, the european parliament, from the first reading, sought to ensure that the framework directive was consistent with the international objectives, and in particular, with regard to compliance with ospar, that there was effective, concrete convergence which would involve us in action. the european union's water policy does not start from scratch. many directives have been adopted, and the commission is determined to make them more readable, more compatible with each other and with clearer objectives. it is therefore a concern for rationality that has led to the implementation of this framework directive. but our parliament, at first reading, insisted that the current directive not only be compatible with the commitments we have made - like ospar - but also allow us to reverse the course of events. because despite these many directives, despite the frequent declarations about the effort that must be made in the field of water protection, when we look at the state of the environment in europe, we see that the objectives have not been achieved. in many cases the situation has deteriorated and we cannot therefore be satisfied with an effort to rationalize the texts. we must set ourselves targets that are commensurate with the challenges we face and we do not have much time, because if we do it, as the commission proposed, with too long deadlines, while it and the council have extended the deadlines again, we will not only have a problem of credibility with public opinion, but we know very well that the efforts will be postponed until tomorrow, and tomorrow they will be postponed again and so we know that we will not achieve the objectives. i insist on this because we should not wait for the umpteenth time for disasters to be reported every day in our newspapers and then say: 'ah, europe did not do that, ah, europe should have done that' and then, in a rush, pretend that we are going to solve the problems that we did not want to tackle in good time. the example of the danube today, the pollution that is happening in romania, shows very clearly that if we do not put in place a new model of economic development, clear requirements, precise controls and measurements on the state of our rivers, we know that this type of incident will not only happen again, but will multiply over time. we also know that if we do nothing, the development of our agriculture will continue to be carried out with great imbalances. already now the rivers of brittany in my own country are in the midst of eutrophication and this is hurting tourism. i would simply like to conclude, mr president, by saying that the issues are clear at second reading. do we want standards compatible with ospar, that is to say, for dangerous substances, to be close to zero? do we want to shorten the time limits proposed by the council for this directive? do we want to have a pricing policy that gives all public and private stakeholders the ability to clean up, act on cleanup and save our water? are we serious about meeting the aspirations of our people? most of the amendments voted by the committee on the environment are in line with this objective; i hope they will have the support of the house.
mr president, every satellite image proves that we do inhabit the blue planet: this abundance is, however, an illusion. the recent catastrophe on the danube reminds us that rivers and streams are the lifeblood of our planet and that pollution knows no bounds. water is a renewable and limited natural resource. it becomes scarce when it is not well managed and when geographical and climatic conditions are not favourable. within the union, this issue is of crucial importance in the mediterranean region, but also in other european countries where we are witnessing the gradual drying up of wetlands. we would like to point out that sensitive areas, wet or dry areas, inequalities between states, inequalities between the different regions within states, climatic, economic, geographical and geological particularities are all obvious, but they must not lead to distortions of competition in the community. we have, however, tabled amendments to recall the importance of the specific relationship between agriculture and water, which is a key factor in the occupation and development of the territory. it is understood that the needs of agriculture in the south are much higher and that this specificity must be taken into account in this framework directive. it is not only the member states of the union which are seeking solutions to these problems: in october, in turin, the euro-mediterranean partnership countries demanded a marshall plan for the southern mediterranean coast. we are not there, thankfully. in europe, there are droughts, desertification in some areas, but also floods, and the directive emphasizes this. we have suffered recently in france, and also in the rhine valley and in central europe. we need this framework directive as an essential element of a sustainable development policy which will have to make the different uses of water compatible with each other. but it is necessary to integrate the protection and conservation of biodiversity into this new management. the water issue will not be closed today anyway. indeed, the issue of enlargement and climate change are opening up new perspectives.
- commissioner, i refer to one of your replies to the previous questions in which you mentioned what i call the possibilities of blocking the treaty in the face of the risks of deviation, and in particular the diversification of the sanctions which can be imposed on a member state, under article 7, for violation of fundamental freedoms. do you think that these proposals, or proposals of this nature, can be part of the igc's mandate as defined in helsinki? i don't feel like it. are you not afraid that such sanctions might slip and be used to punish not violations of human rights but mere disagreements, opinion crimes or disagreements with the dominant european thought?

the rapporteur, mr president, has already had the opportunity to examine this report at first reading and i understood in committee that there was a broad consensus in this house. life is the only - mr president, the european union's environment programme, which has considerable funds (eur 613 million), raises many questions about the proper use of public funds. a financial instrument of this magnitude should be transparent and efficient, which is not the case for the following reasons: poorly defined selection criteria, dubious and uncoordinated operations, unpublished balance sheets, absence of evaluation policy. we therefore propose that the rules be amended as follows. first, to reserve the acquisitions made with the help of life funds exclusively for public structures, even if the management of these sites is entrusted, following a call for tenders, to associations approved for the protection of nature. it is a question of the sustainability of purchases, since private law environmental protection. second, define the eligibility and allocation criteria for life funds, to avoid any suspicion of clientelism or ostracism. thirdly, we must require prior consultation with the users and the communities concerned. for example, the life-nature in france grand-lieu, developed without any consultation, has led to a real ecological catastrophe. the clearing, carried out in defiance of the french water law, has resulted in a major silting of the acheneau, a downstream watercourse, with destruction of spawning grounds, filling of wetlands, and the like. in fact, the vase was moved three kilometres away, at a cost of 6 million francs, a cure worse than the disease, a predictable consequence announced by all the actors on the site. results, litigation and a cost of rehabilitation in excess of the program's budget. that's what we're trying to avoid. fourthly, to include representatives of parliament and at least one member from each political group in the monitoring committee. what is more legitimate than for members to monitor the use of the appropriations voted? fifthly, to publish annually the scientific, technical and financial balance sheet of the life operations carried out. sixthly, to carry out a serious and regular evaluation of the programmes. seventh, allowing these funds to be used in the event of an environmental emergency, for example, reforestation after storms, restoration of natural areas after a flood, etc. the commission's proposal is a concrete, sensible and easy-to-implement proposal, capable of limiting local conflicts and justifying the proper use of public money, which we propose to you before any increase - plus 40% anyway! - in the life budget line. - mr president, we cannot vote in favour of this report. the european union should put social issues at the heart of its construction. it is social rights that should govern economic choices and not the other way around. we are therefore opposed to the introduction of mechanisms for social protection which are based on the luxembourg process and which run counter to this logic: the broad economic guidelines, then the convergence criteria and finally the social aspect, which is treated in a residual way. the european union should affirm a general principle: social rights acquired in the states cannot be reduced. all community action should aim to supplement and then harmonise the existing guarantees from the top down. to strengthen the financing of social protection systems, a policy of general wage increases is needed, the establishment of a legal smic in each member state. in the fight against poverty, the right to an income and the right to employment are inseparable. finally, to avoid any commodification of health, the european union should speak out clearly against pension funds and oppose the access of private insurance companies to the health system. i really believe, in conclusion, that social europe cannot be satisfied with speeches and wishful thinking. the situation is too tragic for millions of people.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, it is with great pleasure that i address this house for the first time, on behalf of the presidency of the council, in recognition of the important role which the european parliament will have to play in the very near future in the deepening of development policies at the level of the european union. the theme of the statement i have the honour to make before you today is that of the coherence of the various policies of the european union with development policy. i will leave it to the commission to complete some of the observations i will have the opportunity to make and i will begin by stressing the need for all of us, at the level of the european union, to make compatible the extraordinary development and progress achieved in many areas of life, especially the strong technological impulse that has increased in recent decades and which has benefited broad sections of the world's population in terms of well-being and improved living conditions, with the simultaneous increase in the profound imbalances between certain regions and geopolitical areas of the planet, which undermines the stability of the international system, threatens peace and therefore imposes on us all the duty of conscience to try to adapt our policies to the objective of achieving greater stability and balance in the various parts of our planet. this has led to a re-evaluation of development policies in response to the globalisation of economic and financial markets. the imbalance in the conditions under which these markets operate has increased, and this naturally leads to the need for major adjustments which in turn necessarily impose new options for development policies. we are therefore on the threshold of a new paradigm of development policy which requires action in four key areas, which i would like to stress. first, greater coordination between all international actors at donor level, which requires greater coordination, greater coherence and better coordination between humanitarian aid and development policies, the strengthening of the multilateral system, greater attention to the problem of debt and to the problem of financing and development. however, new references are also needed at the level of the countries receiving aid, in particular the requirement of the fight against corruption, the requirement of democracy and good governance as fundamental principles of the development of political systems and also the need to pay particular attention to the policies of these countries, to policies focused on poverty reduction. a second aspect of this new development policy paradigm is the need for a more integrated approach to development. we must not reduce our view of aid to the development element alone, but on the contrary give ever greater weight to the role of other policies in the financial, trade and investment fields, of course, but also in relation to the need to consider this integrated view of development both at the level of global policies and at the level of the policies of the various donor states. a third aspect of this new paradigm which i would like to highlight relates to a policy oriented towards the pursuit of objectives. from 1995 onwards, following a concerted effort among the major donor states at international level, and in particular a major reflection at the level of the oecd development assistance committee, it was possible to establish certain important objectives which should guide the orientation and implementation of development policies, both at national and international level. as you know, these goals are to halve poverty by 2015, either by raising the schooling age, or by significantly reducing child mortality, or by a set of social welfare interventions that actually achieve this goal. that would mean lifting the extreme poverty in which a third of the world's population lives, lifting the extreme poverty of about a billion people, which is extraordinary but certainly requires strong participation and strong intervention by the entire international community. this is the fourth aspect of the new development paradigm that i would like to emphasize: development policies are being considered today, especially in recent years, as an increasingly global issue that suffers from a lack of strong international leadership. the concerted actions of the institutions of the united nations system have contributed significantly to this, as has the bretton woods system. the strong impetus given to this debate by the world bank, notably through its comprehensive framework, and the international monetary fund should be noted in particular. for the first time an institution of this nature has put the problem of poverty reduction at the centre of its policy and has established a link between debt relief and poverty which has been unimaginable before by such an institution. it is also in the light of this new role of international organisations in relation to development problems that we must reflect on the role of the european union in this context. the portuguese presidency stresses the need for the european union to make its important role at international level, as the main donor, more compatible with a leading and more active role in this movement for renewal of development policies at international level, by increasing its capacity for articulation and coordination, in particular with the united nations system and the bretton woods system. in order to strengthen the role of the european union in the context of international development policies, we believe that it is necessary to develop three basic types of action. first, to improve the effectiveness of development policy. as everyone knows, an overall evaluation of development policies was carried out in 1995. the conclusions of the european council were presented during the german presidency. the main conclusions emphasise the need for a more coherent european union policy and an overall strategic vision of the european union in relation to development problems. they emphasise the need for greater coordination and complementarity between the policies of harmonisation and organisational simplification, the framework within which the union's cooperation policy is implemented, and the need to make aid management more efficient, in particular by reviewing its intervention mechanisms, as well as the need to strengthen the evaluation system and ensure greater transparency in the way aid is applied. the second aspect to be stressed concerns the need for greater complementarity between the union and the policies of the member states. it is well known that a significant part of aid today is channelled through the national policies of the member states, which are not always complementary or coordinated; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. we also believe that it is essential to do everything possible as soon as possible to strengthen the mechanisms for complementarity and coordination between the policies developed by the member states and the policies of the european union. the third aspect to be stressed is that of strengthening and coherence of policies, which is the central theme of the debate proposed today. firstly, we all agree that it is not enough to improve the conditions for aid, but that other policies of the european union must be better coordinated so that development objectives can be achieved not only through aid but above all through a more integrated view of the different policies which contribute to the development objectives. as you know, a council resolution was adopted in june 1997. the commission was required to submit evaluation reports, the first of which was sent to the council in may 1999. the commission is already setting out certain aspects of policy coordination, particularly in the fields of peacebuilding, food security, fisheries and migration. as everyone knows, the commission should make a communication on coherence at the same time as the communication on development policy. it is only natural that this debate will be enriched in the coming months, again under the portuguese presidency, in the light of the contributions which the commission intends to submit to us in the coming months. the coherence of policies will always be limited, of course, and it is natural that a certain contradiction between policies will still be a factor of balance and balance between the conflicting and conflicting interests operating in the union's space; it is only in this way that it is also possible to manage a certain contradiction between policies. but regardless of this, we would like to stress that the strengthening of the coherence of the policies of the european union, in the present context and in the conjuncture of the union, requires a reflection on certain aspects related to the dynamics of the european union. and so to the internal dynamics of the european union. we know that the european union has its own dynamic, which is mainly derived from the treaty of amsterdam and which strengthens its political dimension, which has important consequences for the presupposition of policy coherence in the field of development. we will also have to look at the developments in the work of the intergovernmental conference, see what the dynamics of enlargement will be, to see to what extent the internal dynamics of the european union are geared towards strengthening the coherence of its policies and, in particular, in the field of development, contribute to institutional arrangements which are also adapted to this objective. the second aspect to be considered in relation to policy coherence is that of development policy in the context of the union's external policy. we know that the union is experiencing a new dimension in its external policy, we know that with the creation of the high representative, the rapid reaction force, the military crisis management centre, there is a whole dynamic of european union assertion that we cannot ignore when we consider the role of development policies and also that there are aspects related to political dialogue, the adoption of common positions or actions, the preparation of common strategies, preventive diplomacy, the development of regional capacities for crisis prevention and management. all these aspects will undoubtedly make a significant contribution to strengthening the role of development policies in the context of the european union's external policy, in terms of its implementation and development. let us say that at this level too, at the level of the european union, the framing of development policy in the context of foreign policy will certainly have to follow the same path as that taken by the development policies of many member states in the context of their respective foreign policies. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the european union's external relations is based on the principle of subsidiarity. in this context, we believe that we must move from a post-colonial paradigm to a truly european paradigm of development policy, knowing, as we know, that development policy has been strongly conditioned in the european context by the policies of certain member states, in accordance with the post-colonial references of the policies of these states. the third aspect to be considered is that of the policy of the european union and the policy of the member states. policy coherence at eu level certainly requires better coordination of member states' policies with the european union's development policy. if it is not possible to establish better mechanisms for coherence between national policies, it will certainly be difficult to think of a more coherent framework for the european union's development policy. the fourth and final aspect i would like to raise, which is always related to development policies, concerns the role of the development council. the role of the development council in the context of union policies has been discussed, particularly in recent months. we know that the difference in status between development policies and other policies at union level is glaring - one need only look at the difficult conditions under which the communityisation or non-communisation of the edf was settled - and it is hard to believe that we can develop more coherence in european union policies without a more active and more interventionist role for the development council in the taking of political decisions which are of vital importance to development competence and which take place in other councils, other decision-making centres, ranging from the agriculture and fisheries council to the environment council, but in relation to which the development council has so far had no opportunity to be heard or to intervene. therefore, without a more active role for the development council in the overall coordination of policy decisions which are developed outside its decision-making centre and directly affect the development policy of the european union, it will certainly be difficult to develop a more coherent policy of the european union with regard to development objectives. the european parliament's views and reflections will certainly be timely and welcome here as well. commission - let me begin by saying a few words about the successful conclusion of the negotiations between the eu and the acp countries. i would like to point out that participating in these negotiations has been a very positive experience. i have seen member states working together as a team, and it has been a great experience indeed. both sides were deeply satisfied at the end of the negotiations, not only because they had ended, but also because we all knew that we had achieved something together, the eu and the 71 acp countries. the world needs this and the signal sent is very positive in the context of the general discussion on globalisation. i will highlight some of the new features of this new agreement. we explicitly address the issue of corruption; we are setting up a framework to deal with the immigration problem for the first time. we encourage participatory approaches, we ensure that civil society is consulted on reforms and policies that the eu should support. we are refocusing development policies on poverty reduction strategies. we base the allocation of funds not only on an assessment of each country's needs, but also on an assessment of their policy performance. we are creating an investment facility to support private sector development. we are streamlining the instruments and introducing a new system of rotating programming which allows the community and the beneficiary countries to adjust their cooperation programmes regularly. we are decentralising administrative, and sometimes financial, responsibilities to local levels in order to improve cooperation. we are improving the policy framework for trade and investment development. we are strengthening cooperation in all areas of commercial importance, including new areas such as labour standards and the links between the environment and trade. after seattle, i'm sure you'll realize the significance of these agreements. i now move on to some of the more important points. first, the agreement on political questions. the new agreement will involve a firm commitment by both parties to good governance as a fundamental and positive element of the partnership, a subject to be the subject of regular dialogue in a sector which enjoys active community support. secondly, a new procedure has been devised for cases of violations of human rights, democratic principles and the rule of law. compared with the current procedure, the new procedure places more emphasis on the responsibility of the state concerned and allows for greater flexibility in the consultation process with a view to productive dialogue leading to measures to be taken to redress the situation. in the event of a particular urgency, namely serious violations of any of these fundamental elements, action will be taken immediately and the other party will be notified. thirdly, the eu and the acp countries have also agreed on a new specific procedure to be used in cases of serious corruption. this is a real innovation, both in the eu/acp context and in international relations in general. this procedure will be applied not only to cases of corruption involving edf money but also, more broadly, in any country where the ec is financially involved and where corruption is an obstacle to development. it is therefore not limited to the activities of the ec. this is a very important aspect, given the financiability of public finances. by adopting such a provision in the partnership agreement, the eu and the acp states together send a clear and positive message which will undoubtedly be appreciated by taxpayers and, hopefully, by european investors. migration is another new feature of the acp-eu agreement. we have reached a balanced agreement on cooperation in this area. this new dimension to the partnership agreement reflects the guidelines followed by the eu in accordance with the treaty of amsterdam and the conclusions of the tampere european council in finland in october 1999. the european union is committed to developing and implementing an asylum and immigration policy based on the principle of partnership with countries and regions of origin. the agreement with the acp countries opens the way to new initiatives, in particular concerning the rights of third country nationals within the eu, and to measures to facilitate their integration. we have also agreed on provisions to deal with issues related to illegal immigration. the eu and the acp states will begin the process of defining, within a framework to be negotiated with each acp country, the means and instruments for the repatriation of immigrants staying illegally in the territory of one of the states. this also covers persons from third countries and stateless persons. these highly innovative approaches provide a good opportunity to improve government management standards. the agreement also provides an adequate framework to underpin the mutually reinforcing effects of trade cooperation and development assistance. we have agreed on a process to establish new trade regimes promoting trade liberalisation between the parties and to formulate provisions on trade-related issues. we have responded to the acp states' concerns about the timing of trade negotiations. the negotiations will not begin until 2002 at the latest. this two-year preparatory period will serve to strengthen regional integration processes and the capacity of acp countries to conduct trade negotiations. we have a six-year timeframe for these negotiations. we will address the economic and social constraints of the acp countries in two ways: first, through human and social development policies associated with economic and trade reforms, and second, by helping the acp countries to become active players in the international economic and trade system through capacity building and cooperation in multilateral fora. this approach will lead to a regime which is fully compatible with the wto. economic operators will be more inclined to establish close relations with their acp partners. domestic and foreign investment will increase and more know-how and technology will be transferred. all this will boost the competitiveness of the acp countries and facilitate their gradual integration into the world economy. moreover, agreements with the eu will lead to anchoring. they will irrevocably fix economic reforms, just as each party's commitments under the agreements will stabilize national and economic reforms. the reasoning behind this new approach is also based on the idea that combining free trade policies with social development policies will lead to economic growth and poverty reduction. another important aspect is the improvement of the eu trade regime for all the least developed countries, 39 of which are actually part of the acp group. this process will take place over the next five years, so that by 2005 virtually all products of developing country exporters will have free access to the eu market. the eu has made a financial proposal for the volume of the next edf. it is based on the principle of reconciling the need to maintain a substantial level of financial resources in a period of limited official development aid budgets with the need to increase the effectiveness of community aid. today, some eur 9.5 billion from previous edf resources is not committed. the eu commits to mobilise these remaining balances, in addition to the new edf resources, over a period of 7 years, i.e. before the entry into force of the next financial protocol. this will enable the community to increase substantially the annual flows of commitments and payments during this period. so we are not heading for a period of reduced activity in the coming years, but for a period of increased activity. such a commitment implies a thorough reform of procedures and enforcement on both sides. there is a very real link between the reform process within the commission as such and our ability to deliver on our promises on the ground, which is the basis of the agreement with the acp countries. i come now to our development policy. i would say that the overall context has changed completely. the marginalisation of many economies, increasing global poverty, the need for better management of environmental interdependence, the destabilising effects of migration and the worrying consequences of armed conflict and pandemics are all major concerns. it is in this changing world context that we must find our place. fortunately, the evaluations of eu aid provide us with a valuable tool to improve our actions and also, hopefully, to address the challenges i have just mentioned. in particular, as regards the contribution of these evaluations, i would mention the following problems: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this is due to the complexity of our own structures, but also to the real inconsistencies that exist between policies and sectoral interests within the member states. the commission's aid scheme is too complex and fragmented in terms of instruments, procedures and institutional mechanisms. policies are often determined by the instruments available rather than by clearly defined policy objectives and priorities. human resources are too small for the volume of aid we are supposed to be handling. on average, to manage us$ 10 million, the commission employs 2.9 workers, compared with 4.3 workers at the world bank and 4 to 9 workers in the largest member states. this is a real problem: there are too many different financial instruments, each with its own characteristics and, in particular, a series of different budget lines. it is difficult to reconcile this with the requirements of an effective management system. in order to face and solve these problems, the community must engage in an effective dialogue with the member states and parliament. it is absolutely crucial that we solve the problem of coherence in a realistic and pragmatic way, which means that we must hold this debate in the appropriate institutional framework, namely the council and parliament. the lack of concerted action between the 15 member states and between them and the community is also an issue that needs to be addressed. by focusing community development policy on internationally agreed objectives and strategies, we will pave the way for better complementarity with the member states. this approach is in line with the approach which has just been put forward by mr amado. when we talk about politics today, we are engaging in a process of convergence. that's part of the solution. we are engaged in the process of formulating new policy guidelines and we need to define the priorities for community action. everything has become more and more complex. the same applies to development cooperation. no single donor is able to address the full range of issues from macroeconomic issues to policy frameworks or sectoral policies to a range of new cross-cutting themes such as gender, environment, good governance and institutional reforms. it is important to find flexible mechanisms that promote a division of labour according to the skills and abilities of the different donors in each developing country. this should be done at member state level and should lead to the formulation of sectoral policies for community action. that is what we want to achieve. in defining the ec's priorities, account must be taken of the specific characteristics of the community in relation to the member states and the international institutions. i will mention just a few: our ability to combine development policy with trade policy and to ensure synergies between aid and economic cooperation; our neutrality and our defence of community interests in general; the fact that we represent a critical mass and are able to carry out relatively important tasks compared to what the member states can normally do individually. there is also our presence on the ground: in fact, in my view, our greatest value is that, as a successful regional cooperation enterprise ourselves, we are seen as a neutral, welcome partner in this global experiment - something that no one else can claim to be. it is vital to increase the effectiveness of community policy and to develop a more operational policy framework. the commission is faced with this double challenge when it prepares a proposal for a general policy statement in the coming months. we will initiate a broad and open consultation process to gather the views of all interested parties. for me, the process is not as important but almost as important as the content and we will put all our resources into active participation, and we invite everyone to participate. at the same time, we are also working to improve consistency and to clarify and highlight any real or imagined problems we encounter in this respect. it will be a continuous process which i see as a kind of continuous quality control effort and i invite parliament to take part in this continuous effort to increase the coherence of our actions.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, let us say at once that in matters of cooperation, consistency is far from being a requirement. the treaties provide that the european union should help developing countries in their development, but as the other members have already very well said, there are many distortions in these statements. the first inconsistency is the absence of consultation between the union and the member states on their respective cooperation policies. this leads to major dysfunctions, since some community programmes are added to national programmes, whereas they could have helped other projects which have not been followed up. it should also be remembered that the de facto neo-colonialist policy of some member states does not contribute at all to the development of the countries which are supposedly receiving aid. the second inconsistency is the support given to despotic regimes. good governance and an end to corruption are declared mandatory, but hundreds of thousands of euros continue to be deposited into swiss accounts through the pockets of a number of heads of state. the third inconsistency relates to human rights. we say we want to protect them. developing countries are encouraged to respect them. we have even voted on a number of resolutions condemning any violation of these rights. we also join protests, international campaigns. but at the same time, the arms trade is allowed to grow, without even bothering to restrict the trade in the most atrocious weapons: landmines, for example. and little is being done to actually prevent human rights violations. the fourth inconsistency in the european union's cooperation policy is this: how can you help development by plundering the natural resources of those you are helping? the european union must leave its fish to local fishermen to feed the local population, instead of systematically destroying the seabed with its intensive fishing. the raw materials must be left to local producers to process. we shall not even talk about oil, because unfortunately we know the policy of groups like elf or total in africa. to go further, and this may soon be the fifth inconsistency, we ask for respect for biodiversity, among other things to enable everyone to produce with their own seeds and to preserve natural wealth. but at the same time - and this was also the case in the last negotiations - the acp countries are being forced to sign the trips agreements, even though there is a risk that they will be extended in their lifetime. however, this would mean the death of biodiversity and a return to de facto slavery for small farmers in the south to multinational companies. but, and this is a sixth inconsistency, we do not defend the application of the existing treaties. so on the one hand we vote for a budgetary envelope for the fight against aids, and on the other hand we do nothing to enforce compliance with compulsory licences within the framework of the said trips, which would allow developing countries to produce their own medicines and curb the aids-related slaughter. in the same vein, during the wto negotiations, and while the second paragraph of the schwaiger report noted that the current process of trade liberalization is of little benefit to large sections of the population in developing countries, especially the poorest, the european union continues to advocate trade liberalization and puts an end, albeit with a few transitional years, to the favourable regime granted to the acp countries when it would have been necessary to strengthen it, especially for the poorest countries. the eighth inconsistency is political and practical. we always say: think globally, act locally. yet local development actors are neglected, preferring to talk to national governments, subsidizing northern ngos at the expense of local programmes and southern ngos. agriculture, the environment, there are other problems, other inconsistencies that could have been identified, not to mention research, emigration and health. in short, we claim to want to help developing countries and at the same time encourage market liberalization, while recognizing that it is contrary to such an objective. let us say it again: the european union's cooperation and development policy is not consistent. i therefore call on parliament, the institutions and the commission, on behalf of the green group, to try to bring about some coherence in our policy.

in writing. - i welcome the quality and ambition of this life report. i will briefly recall that life is a financial instrument for environmental policies within the european union and in third countries, whether neighbouring mediterranean countries, countries bordering the baltic sea or candidate countries. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy proposed a number of amendments, most of which were accepted in the common position adopted by the council. for the third phase of life (2000-2004), this instrument will be divided into three axes: life-nature (47% of resources), life-environment (47%) and life-third countries (6%). the most important changes in my view are: - life's contribution to sustainable development in the community, as well as to the development of community environmental policy, in particular as regards the integration of the environment into other policies, and to the implementation and updating of environmental legislation; in writing. - as a member of the european parliament, and above all as a consumer citizen, i welcome the european commission's proposal which marks a further step towards better food security in the european union. the proposal is twofold: first, to amend the 1991 council directive on animal health conditions by deleting the provisions on scrapie in sheep; and second, to introduce a new regulation laying down rules for the prevention and control of certain transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (tses) or bse-like diseases affecting sheep and other animal species. the interest of this new legislation lies in the fact that it creates a specific legal basis for the fight against scrapie. i am all the more pleased that this was one of our main demands in our follow-up report on the mad cow crisis. it also seems to me essential, for reasons of consistency, to merge the existing legislation on scrapie, which is limited to trade in ovine and caprine animals, into a single comprehensive set of new rules governing tses affecting all animals throughout the european union, rules designed to prevent the consumption of food or feed. this regulation is particularly welcome as there are still doubts about the sheep's trembling. some scientists hypothesize that sheep's rattle may have evolved into bse in cattle and thus be the cause of bse epizootic disease. although the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on the prevention and control of certain tses requires further clarification and strengthening, particularly as regards the detection and control of scrapie, it represents a significant improvement. this is a pledge to the european citizens who have repeatedly expressed their concerns about european food policy. their concerns, echoed by our european parliament, have been heard. the debate on the precautionary principle, traceability, accountability and transparency led the european commission to present a white paper on food safety. the white paper sets out a number of lines of thought, including the proposal to set up an independent european food authority. this is all part of a european strategy to regain consumer confidence. it is up to us, the european leaders, to show that the single market and the free movement of goods can go hand in hand with food security!
