in writing. drinking, eating, washing, growing, water is the basis of all our daily activities. water mistakenly considered to be an unchanging and inexhaustible resource. because a simple act like opening a faucet seems to be flowing. but the spring is threatening to dry up... all scientific studies are now formal: water will be the key issue in the coming years, starting tomorrow. but tomorrow it will be too late. it is time today to clarify the rules of the game, before we are all losers. the european parliament adopted the water directive on wednesday, 15 february, in a statement affirming its ambition to protect surface water, coastal water, inland water and groundwater. europe now has a framework to prevent water quality deterioration, promote its sustainable use, protect ecosystems, help to combat floods and droughts and eliminate discharges of hazardous substances. it's a life raft launched into the water.
in writing. - i welcome this ambitious proposal for a framework directive on water. the ecological disaster on the banks of the danube is a timely reminder that human negligence too often puts natural resources such as water at risk. the aim of this 1997 proposal for a directive is to put an end to the fragmentation of water legislation and to protect surface water, coastal water, inland water and groundwater. it provides a framework to prevent further deterioration, protect ecosystems, promote sustainable water use, help to combat floods and droughts and phase out discharges of hazardous substances. specific directives will then be adopted within this framework. the procedure for drawing up this text was lengthy. the proposal for a directive was amended twice, first in 1997 and again in 1998. a technical working group composed of representatives of the council and parliament met in january 1999 to try to bring the positions of our two institutions closer together. however, the amendments tabled by the committee on the environment remain numerous. i support most of them. as regards the timetable and objectives, the council envisages that the objective of achieving good surface water status should be achieved no later than 16 years after the entry into force of the directive, the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy wants this deadline to be reduced to 10 years. the committee also calls for an end to all spills or losses of dangerous substances by 2020. the ultimate objective should be to reach values close to zero by 2020. the council hopes to achieve good groundwater status after a period of 16 years, but the commission intends to halt the deterioration of the qualitative chemical status of groundwater in order to achieve good groundwater status within 10 years. all the standards and objectives for protected areas must be achieved within 10 years, not 16. i must say that i am in favour of these reductions in deadlines, especially since there are exceptions. as regards costs, i support the proposal that by 2010 member states will have to ensure that water pricing policies encourage a more efficient use of water resources. in the same vein, i expect the european commission to make a clear statement committing itself to present a proposal to ensure that water prices reflect environmental and resource costs by 2012. i would like to end by quoting one of the amendments of the committee on the environment, which calls for no comment: 'water is not a commodity like any other, but a heritage belonging to the peoples of the european union, a heritage which must be protected, defended and treated as such'.
in writing. - the council's common position on this proposal for a framework directive has disappointed us. it is minimalist in many respects, particularly as regards the dates of entry into force of too many provisions and the number and conditions for implementing the derogations. the main problem, however, is to define the objective which the european union wishes to pursue through this text. the aim is, of course, first and foremost to create a clear general framework which will finally simplify the law applicable in this field. however, the union must also have the ambition to improve the quality of surface water and groundwater. the issues involved are public health and the supply of drinking water, the quality and biodiversity of the water, and the preservation of landscapes and species. the common position is weak in this respect. i wanted our parliament to take a more ambitious position than the council, but i also wanted it to be credible. the requirement of zero discharge and zero pollution, including for substances naturally present in water, is not realistic. i am not one of those members who thinks that it is essential to adopt 'extremist' amendments at second reading for the sole purpose of leaving room for manoeuvre in the context of negotiations with the council of ministers. on the contrary, i reject this now systematic strategy. it is damaging to our parliament. our messages to the citizens and to the council are confused and not credible. environmental objectives that are too strict and do not take account of reality will not be applied, because they can never be achieved. is that the message we wish to convey? in writing. - water is a renewable and limited natural resource. its proper management is essential. the water framework directive will become the cornerstone of community policy in this area. his goals are clear and ambitious. we share them. it sets environmental levels close to zero. but we believe it is more prudent not to impose unrealistic deadlines that neither our governments nor our industries would be able to meet. we certainly need a timetable, but more gradual. the legal obligation to achieve zero emissions and no more discharges within 20 years would mean a ban on all identified substances. such provisions could pose significant problems for crossborder areas and for candidate countries, and could complicate enlargement. i would of course like to speak of a particular sector which i am very familiar with, agriculture, which is the main water consumer: it must, as it is already beginning to do, accept its share of being the polluter who pays, but it is also necessary to take account of its peculiarities and constraints, particularly in dry regions. as regards the amendments on radioactive substances, i am naturally in favour of controls, but the question is of the legal basis which is the responsibility of the euratom treaty.
in writing. - the present difficulties of our social protection systems are mainly due to a deficit of revenue due to unemployment, poverty and the ageing of the population, and not to an excess of expenditure. the european union, through its policies, bears a heavy responsibility in this situation. we must adapt these systems. in france in particular, it is necessary to stop making work alone the source of the financing of health insurance and pensions. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the first thing we must do is to pursue a family policy of population growth, an economic, monetary and fiscal policy of growth and the reconquest of our internal market, which will create jobs. what the commission and the andersson report are proposing is not a social policy, it is a way of giving brussels exorbitant decision-making powers in the financing, and therefore in the organization and delivery of the social protection systems of the nations of europe. that is why we voted against this text. social protection must above all reflect national solidarity. and it is first and foremost the responsibility of the national state. social protection must be based on the principle of national and community preference. otherwise, it is nothing but the financial treatment, at the expense and detriment of european citizens, of the unbearable social situations created by immigration.

president of the czech republicoriginal speech in czech. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, ladies and gentlemen, the question of whether the soul of europeans is animated, in addition to the conscience or the feeling of national belonging, by a sense of europeanism, is very often on the agenda today. in other words, do europeans really feel european, or is it an abstract idea, a theoretical construct that tries to exalt a geographical element to make it a state of mind? this question arises, among other things, from the debate on the share of sovereignty that national states can and should transfer to the common bodies of the european union. some point out that if a clearly felt national attachment were too quickly replaced by a european attachment that was felt only weakly or even perceived as illusory, this could only go wrong. so what about our europeanism? if i ask myself how european i feel and what unites me to europe, i am at first slightly surprised: it is only now that i am asking myself this question, under the pressure of certain topical political issues and duties. why didn't i ask myself that a long time ago, back when i was just starting to navigate the world and think about it and myself? did i consider my membership of europe to be a purely extrinsic, unimportant element, one that should not be the subject of torment or even concern? or did i, on the contrary, regard my europeanism as something taken for granted that merited no questioning, no study, no extension? the second possibility is more likely: everything i have always been attached to was so naturally european that it had never occurred to me to consider it as such. i simply did not think it useful to call it that and, more generally, to associate my thought with the name of any continent. i feel that in my youth i would have felt a little ridiculous if i had declared or written that i was european, that i perceived and thought in a european way, or even if i had claimed to be explicitly european in some way. that would have seemed very pathetic and presumptuous; i would have felt it as a more proud version of that patriotism that always embarrassed me in national patriots. in other words: i was so obviously and naturally european that i didn't think about it. and this is probably the case for the majority of europeans: they are deeply european, but they do not realize it, they do not describe themselves as such and, in public opinion polls, they are a little surprised to have to claim loudly their europeanism. reflective europeanism does not seem to have a great tradition in europe. i do not regard this as a positive element and i welcome the fact that our europeanism is now beginning to emerge clearly from the vast sea of 'self-evident' concepts. by asking questions about it, thinking about it, and trying to define its nature, we make a significant contribution to our understanding of ourselves. this becomes decisive in the face of our multicultural and multipolar world, where the ability to perceive our identity is the first condition for a good coexistence with other identities. moreover, if europe has so far been so unconcerned with its own identity, it is probably mainly because it wrongly thought of itself as the whole world or at least as something superior to the rest of the world, because it did not feel the need to define itself in relation to others. with unfortunate consequences, of course, in terms of practical behaviour. to reflect on europeanism means to ask what set of values, ideals or principles evokes the notion of europe, or even what is characteristic of europe. more than that. it also means, starting from the very essence of the thing, to make a critical examination of this whole. and so it is not long before we realise that many european traditions, values or principles are characterised by great ambiguity and that most of them can lead to hell if they are exaggerated, exploited or abused. if europe is entering an era of self-reflection, it means that it wants to define itself in relation to others, but also that it is looking within itself for what is good, what has stood the test of time, what is of the future. when i had the honour of addressing this house for the first time six years ago, i had mentioned the need to stress the spiritual dimension, the importance of the values of european integration, and i had expressed my fears that the spiritual, historical, political and civilizational meaning of the construction of europe could be dangerously obscured by technical, economic, financial or administrative questions, which could then completely confuse the public. at the time, my remarks sounded somewhat provocative and i was not sure that i would not be scolded in the european parliament. none of that happened, but today i am pleased to see that those same words no longer have that provocative character. the dramatic changes that europe has undergone in the ten years since the fall of the iron curtain, the ever more evident need to enlarge the european union, the ever more rapid economic integration and the range of new threats generated by the present period are all factors that have necessarily led the european union to open itself up to a new, more intense reflection on itself, a definition and a search for new values that unite it and give meaning to its existence. it is sometimes suggested that this research is too late, that cultural and political integration, self-reflection, should have preceded economic integration, in other words, that we started at the end. i don't think that's a fair judgment. after the second world war, democratic western europe was confronted with memories of the horrors of the two world wars and the danger of the expansion of totalitarian communist rule. at that time, it was almost superfluous to talk about the values to be protected. they were obvious. on the contrary, it was necessary to unite the west, so to speak technically, and as quickly as possible, in order to prevent the eventual emergence, or even the proliferation, of a dictatorship, but also the relapse of old national conflicts. i am sure that my sense of europeanism is the same: it was so natural to me for years - even decades - that it never even occurred to me to call for it explicitly. for western europe, all that it had to protect was so obvious that it did not feel the urgent need to define it, analyse it, deepen it or translate it into various political and institutional facts. and so, just as i have only now been led to ask myself whether i feel european and to reflect on what this means, the democratic europe under construction has doubtless been forced by the historical events of the last decade to undertake a thorough reflection on the very foundation of its unification and on its objectives. the great european values - as shaped by europe's turbulent spiritual and political history and taken up by other parts of the world - at least some of them - are, i would say, clear: respect for the unique human being, his freedoms, his rights and his dignity, the principle of solidarity, equality before the law and the rule of law, the protection of all ethnic minorities, democratic institutions, the separation of legislative, executive and judicial powers, political pluralism, respect for private property and free enterprise, a market economy and the development of civil society. the current form of these values reflects, of course, also countless modern european experiences, including the fact that our continent is becoming a multicultural intersection of the first order. let me focus on one of these fundamental values for reasons i shall explain. this is civil society. in the western world, i.e. the euro-american world today, a highly structured, open and decentralised civil society, based on the confidence in the sovereign independence of its citizens and their multiple associations, is the basis of the democratic state and the guarantee of its political stability. if the european union is soon to open its doors to new democracies, which i believe is of vital interest to it, it is very important, if not essential, that it helps to rebuild and develop civil society in these countries. it is no coincidence that the communist dictatorship, shortly after its arrival, hastened to violently tear apart the fine fabric of civil society and finally liquidate it. it was because it knew very well that it would never have real control over the population as long as the various structures of civil society, constituted from below, continued to function. what was left of a genuine civil society lived and developed in direct or indirect resistance. european values have thus survived in this environment, not because of the political system, but in spite of it. the self-structuring of society cannot, of course, be ordered from above. but we can create an environment, conditions, for its development. support for new democracies should therefore be part of a broader framework: that of the sustainable deepening and strengthening of civil society at pan-european level. the more varied, differentiated and interwoven the various civil structures in europe are, the better prepared the new democracies will be to join them, and the more quickly the principle of trust in citizens and the principle of subsidiarity will be established within them, thus strengthening their stability. but that is not all: the foundation of the european union as a supranational community will be all the more strengthened. in practical terms, this means, among other things, that certain social solidarity duties should be transferred to local authorities and to non-profit or public-law organisations. the lower the level of redistribution of resources, the more transparent and economic this equalization will be, the better it will cover the most varied needs of society, which are difficult to identify from the centre, the more authentic social solidarity will be because it is more clearly linked to concrete persons or their associations. this genuine solidarity of citizens, social groups, communities and regions is therefore the best soil for this solidarity which can only be provided by one entity, namely the state. and in a supranational entity as large as the european union, which must function as an instrument of solidarity, its real civic foundation must be even stronger, richer. the viability of the european union therefore depends, among other things, and perhaps most of all, on how its citizens adopt the spirit of european civic belonging. a growing sensitivity to all symptoms or manifestations of national egoism, xenophobia or racial intolerance should obviously be part of this new sense of european belonging. the appeasement policy which led to a capitulation to evil in munich is one of the bitterest chapters in modern european history. this experience calls for vigilance. we must fight evil when it is in its infancy and it is not enough to have governments to do it. the attitude of governments must be the result of the attitude of citizens. (applause) i would like to thank concern for safety is another expression of social solidarity. it is the responsibility of the state or a supranational grouping. the european union is beginning to work intensively on a new approach to its security policy. this policy should be characterized by the ability to take decisions quickly and to translate them into action just as quickly. that seems to me to be extremely important. it's about time. i think that the recent experience in yugoslavia tells us a lot about this. in my view, the nato intervention was a relatively clear demonstration of several things. first, respect for life and human dignity, as well as concern for european security, may impose, where appropriate, the need to intervene outside the borders of the european union. the stronger the mandate for such intervention, the better, of course. but unfortunately we can also imagine a situation where the un mandate is lacking, whereas intervention would be in the interest of many, of the whole of europe and of human civilization as a whole. i am not sure that europe was prepared, even recently, to face such a disastrous eventuality. she is no doubt much more so now, at least psychologically. i think it should be used quickly, also to make a hardware or technical improvement. secondly, more efforts are needed in the field of safety prevention. in kosovo and serbia, as in bosnia and herzegovina and other parts of the former yugoslavia, tens of thousands of lives and countless properties could have been saved if the international community had been able to react adequately earlier, at the very beginning of the conflict. idea of two europeans living side by side, the idea of a democratic, stable, prosperous europe on the way to integration and a less democratic, less stable and less prosperous europe, is in my view completely false. it's like the idea of sustainable coexistence in a room, where one half is flooded and the other half is not. europe, however diverse it may be, is indivisible, and anything serious that happens to it will have consequences and repercussions for the rest of its territory. as a single political entity, europe has a chance today that it has never had in its turbulent history: to organise itself in a profoundly equitable, peaceful way, on the principle of equality and cooperation of all. nor should acts of violence by the powerful against the less powerful, but understanding we all know that the process of enlargement of the european union must be accompanied by a continuous and equally bold reform of its institutions. i am convinced that the intergovernmental conference will bring forward realistic proposals which will move the european union in the right direction. however, i do not believe that institutional changes within the european union can stop there. on the contrary, i believe it will be the beginning of a very long process, which may take decades. it should be marked by a constant concern to speed up, simplify and make decision-making in the european union more transparent. i would like to mention two more concrete points which i have already mentioned on several occasions and which i believe could help to achieve these objectives in the more distant future. firstly, i believe that the european union should sooner or later have a constitution which is concise, clear and understandable to all. (applause) a constitution that all children in europe can learn in school without much difficulty. this constitution would, as is customary, comprise two parts. the first would set out the fundamental rights and duties of european citizens and states, the fundamental values on which the unified europe is based, and the meaning and purpose of the european construction. the second would describe the main institutions of the european union, their essential competences and their mutual relations. the existence of such a basic law would not automatically bring about a radical transformation of the union of states as we know it into a super-large federal state that haunts eurosceptics, but would only allow the inhabitants of a europe in the making to have a clearer idea of the nature of the european union. this would enable them to understand it better and to identify with it. (applause) i would like to thank one of the important issues, often and rightly raised in connection with the institutional reforms of the union, is how to ensure that the smaller member states of the union are not made into a minority by the larger ones, while taking proper account of the size of the individual states. it seems to me that one of the possibilities could be the creation of a second chamber of the european parliament. the vote would not, of course, be direct, but the various parliaments would delegate their representatives to it, say three per state. while the first chamber, the current parliament, would reflect the size of the individual member states, the second would strengthen their equality: all member states would have the same number of representatives. in this situation, the commission, for example, would not have to be composed by national membership and national parliaments could be involved in a much more operational way. whatever the evolution or outcome of institutional reform or the reform in question, one thing seems clear to me: disagreement or lack of consensus on institutional matters must not hold back the enlargement of the european union. if this were the case, too long a delay in enlargement would risk having consequences infinitely more dangerous than the eventual failure to complete institutional reform. ladies and gentlemen, the technical civilization which has arisen on european soil and which now covers our entire planet has been considerably influenced by elements of euro-american civilization. europe is therefore particularly responsible for the state of this civilization. however, this responsibility must never again take the form of a violent export of one's own values, ideas or goods to the rest of the world. on the contrary, europe could finally start by itself and set an example that others can, but do not have to, follow. the whole modern conception of life as a constant material growth and progress, based on the assurance of man who considers himself the master of the universe, is the hidden, regrettable face of the european spiritual tradition. this view of life also predetermines the threatening nature of present-day civilization. who else but this part of the world, which has started the great movement in this direction, even the free fall of our civilization, should vigorously oppose these threats? it seems to me that at the turn of the century, it is up to europe to reflect courageously on the ambiguity of its contribution to the world, to understand that we have not only taught the world about human rights, but also shown it the holocaust, that we have not only led it, spiritually, to achieve the industrial revolution and then the information revolution, but also to disfigure nature in the name of the multiplication of material wealth, to plunder its resources and to pollute its atmosphere. it is a question of understanding that we have indeed opened the way to a huge development of science and technology, but that we have done so at a very high price: that of the elimination of a whole set of very important and complex human experiences that have been formed over several millennia. europe must start with itself. it can economize, impose privations on itself, respect - in accordance with the best of its spiritual traditions - the higher cosmic order as something beyond us, and also respect the moral order as its consequence. humility, agreeableness, kindness, respect for what we do not understand, a deep sense of solidarity with others, respect for all that is different, the willingness to make sacrifices or to do good deeds that only eternity can reward, that eternity which silently observes us through our conscience: these are all values which could and should be the programme for european construction. europe has, in whole or in part, borne the brunt of the most horrendous events of the 20th century: the two world wars, fascism and the totalitarian communist system. in the last century, europe has also experienced three positive events, although not all of them were exclusively its own doing: the end of colonial domination of the world, the fall of the iron curtain and the beginning of the european construction. the fourth great task facing europe would be, in my view, to try to show by its very existence that it is possible to counter the great danger which its civilization, full of contradictions, is posing to the world. i would be happy if my country could participate in all this as a full partner. - mr president, the launch of the euro could well be a blessed time for the fake money-makers. the citizens, who will lose all their currency references at once, are in danger of accepting counterfeit euros easily, since they will not be familiar with the real ones. it is therefore natural that the council should be concerned and should seek to provide for penal sanctions, including criminal sanctions, applicable in all european countries in the face of such offences. to this end, it could have simply adopted a resolution recommending that member states adopt national legislation to this effect. that's what i would have preferred. but the council, no doubt because of a lack of confidence in the zeal of some of its members, preferred instead the implementation of a more binding legal instrument at european level, the framework decision. the difficulties begin here, because criminal law is a matter of national sovereignty and the maastricht treaty, in order not to frighten the electorate by overloading the boat, did not provide anything specific for the euro in this case. the draft framework decision before us today therefore tries to cover up this shortcoming by referring to articles 31 and 34 (2) (b) of the treaty. but these visas don't seem appropriate. article 31 provides for common minimum rules for criminal offences only in a limited number of cases: organised crime, terrorism and drug trafficking. counterfeiting is not one of them. article 34 of the treaty of amsterdam merely defines the new wording of the framework decision, but this is of course only applicable to the existing powers of the union. so we're back to the previous problem. in other words, the council has failed to give this text a credible legal basis. it is a kind of deferred punishment for the dishonesty with which he presented the maastricht treaty to the electorate at the time. i would also like to make a more general point. some time ago we had to deal with one or more reports on questions of principle on the euro almost every part-session. but for the last year, nothing. just a few little technical reports, like this one on counterfeit currency. the commission's communication on its strategic objectives for 2000-05, which we discussed this week, contained absolutely nothing on this broad subject, except for the reminder, in one line, that euro coins and banknotes should enter into circulation on 1 january 2002. it's really very thin. yet many of the underlying problems remain unresolved. the worrying disinterest of public opinion, the definition of monetary policy objectives that are abused and reduced to the fight against inflation alone, the strange combination of a monetary federalism without fiscal or budgetary federalism, the status of the commission - (de) mr president, madam rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, to what extent is the euro a safe currency? this is a question that is very frequently asked by the public. this question will of course be asked with increasing urgency as we approach 1 january 2002, the date on which the euro will be in everyone's pocket. this issue of the euro's security concerns not only the stability and external value of the euro, but also its protection against counterfeiting. these are also issues affecting the people, because this money will be, as has been very well said, something new for the citizens of the union, both for the eyes and for the hands that will handle it. the fact that this currency will be valid over a much wider territory and will be used as the main currency throughout europe will also be new for european citizens. you'll have to get used to it. so clearly the question is what is the eu doing to protect the euro against counterfeiters. that is what we are discussing in this evening's sitting. it is a subject which is of great interest to the citizen. it is therefore regrettable that he should be approached at such a late hour. but it has to be. of course, the european central bank has been dealing with this issue for a very long time. it is responsible for technical security against counterfeiting. as already noted, the commission presented a communication in the summer of 1998 listing all the areas where action is needed, namely the information field, the field of continuing training - an important point - the field of cooperation between the euro area states and, of course, cooperation beyond this simple framework and in the field of criminal measures. this is the subject of the framework decision under your examination. madam rapporteur, i would like to thank you very sincerely on behalf of the commission and, above all, i would also like to thank parliament for having been able to draw up an opinion in such a short time. i value it very much. the framework decision envisages that the member states should use the definition of counterfeiting. having the same definitions is obviously the essential condition for reacting in the same way everywhere, because, as already emphasised, the main thing is to ensure that the euro is protected even before it is physically put into circulation. of course, the commission is also grateful to parliament for its swift decision - i hope the text will be adopted just as swiftly - which now allows the framework decision to enter into force as soon as possible. implementing measures may therefore be initiated. the commission is now invited to present, in the first half of next year, a report on the implementation of the framework decision in the member states, so as to know whether the importance of the subject is reflected in adequate actions. it was noted that this framework decision falls precisely within the scope of criminal law. this innovation, this advance, must therefore be recognised, even if mr schulz points out that, in supplementing this rather old convention, the advance in question is rather timid. the commission was asked whether it considered that the framework decision was based on a sufficiently sound legal basis in accordance with the treaty. the commission considered that the legal basis applied was the correct one. however, the framework decision will subsequently have to be supplemented by other legal acts. the commission will propose a proposal for a regulation on cooperation between all competent authorities and on cooperation with europol. the proposal should include a duty of cooperation and should also oblige national authorities to report cases of counterfeiting to europol and to submit the seized counterfeit currency to the ecb for identification and classification, which will allow effective action to be taken in this area. as regards the coordination of the various measures, since 1998 the commission - and subsequently olaf - has been working with the experts of the member states, the ecb and europol in order to be able to combat counterfeiting of the euro effectively in advance. the commission has already put forward a proposal for an information campaign on the euro, as mr karas has pointed out, with a proposed budget of €32 million. that is a sum that can be spent wisely, a substantial sum. this campaign will of course focus on the security of the euro against counterfeiting. i think that this debate, which is taking place shortly before midnight, is also helping to teach a lesson to all the forgers who think that they own the night because the eu is no longer watching at that time.

in writing. - i welcome with great satisfaction this report on the pre-accession strategy for cyprus and malta, accessions which are vital for the mediterranean future of the european union. the aim of this proposal for a regulation is to establish the first programme implementing the strategy for cyprus and malta, starting in 2000 and for a period of five years (2000-04). the proposal therefore aims to facilitate the approximation of legislation to the acquis communautaire and the correct application of that acquis. this is a new step in the wake of the one taken last december at the european council in helsinki. in view of malta's progress, it was decided to open bilateral conferences as early as february 2000, i.e. before the end of that month, in order to start negotiations on the conditions for accession to the union and the necessary adjustments. as regards cyprus, the council maintained, and i quote: 'that a political regulation will facilitate the accession of cyprus to the european union', its 'decision on accession will be taken without the above being a precondition', which i welcome. i have always considered it completely unfair to make the opening of negotiations with cyprus conditional on a settlement of the situation in which a third of the territory of the republic is occupied by turkey. more generally, it is true that the socioeconomic situation in these two countries is much more favourable than that of other candidate countries. however, they have been granted technical and financial assistance from the european union for the transposition of the acquis communautaire. this technical and financial assistance was provided until the end of 1999 under the fourth financial protocols (b7-4011). these two countries are also eligible for financial support under the meda programme (b7-4012). in its first and second readings of the 2000 budget, the european parliament stressed that the new heading 'pre-accession' (b7-0) proposed by the commission in the previous draft budget should not be limited to the associated countries of central and eastern europe, but should also be extended to malta and cyprus. however, because of the council's refusal to negotiate the necessary revision of the ceiling for heading 7 (pre-accession) of the financial perspective, the european parliament agreed, exceptionally, and i stress this point, to finance this expenditure under heading 4 (external actions) of the financial perspective for the year 2000. at the same time, the european parliament created a new chapter on the 'pre-accession strategy for the mediterranean countries' (b7-04). within this chapter, two new articles on the pre-accession strategy for malta and cyprus were created, pending the presentation by the in writing. - as a member of the committee on economic and monetary affairs in the previous parliament, i welcome the adoption of this framework decision to strengthen the protection of our single currency. the union shall use all the means at its disposal to ensure its protection against counterfeiting. consumers and traders are not really familiar with the euro. this means that counterfeit money can be easily put into circulation in supermarkets, exchange offices and banks without being detected at first. as for the coins, the fact that they may have a national face will make them even more difficult to identify. the information centres on europe, which already play a key role in raising citizens' awareness of the single currency, will have to step up campaigns to draw public attention to counterfeiting. at another level, cooperation between community and national institutions will have to be ensured and an information system will have to be set up to enable data on counterfeiting to be collected and exchanged. at the criminal level, measures are also needed to ensure that the protection of the euro is brought into play. it is in this context that the european parliament has presented the draft framework decision to strengthen the criminal framework for protection against counterfeiting. the framework decision is intended to supplement the provisions of the international convention for the suppression of counterfeiting currency of 20 april 1929 and to facilitate its application by the member states. each member state shall take the necessary measures to ensure that the offences provided for in the framework decision are punishable. such infringements must also be punished if they concern future euro banknotes and coins and are committed before 1 january 2002. it's a fundamental part of the device! i can only agree with the rapporteur when she laments the fact that the current national currencies that the euro is replacing are not protected. we must realize that national currencies will be able to continue to be exchanged for twenty years! they should therefore be protected against counterfeiting by criminal law when they are no longer in circulation. in the interests of the union, it also seems desirable that all member states should participate in the protection of the euro, in particular sweden, denmark, the united kingdom and greece, which will not yet have adopted the euro on 1 january 2002. if this draft framework decision is a step in the right direction, it merely strengthens criminal protection: in fact, it seeks to harmonize substantive criminal law by setting minimum standards. there are still no uniform criminal provisions on counterfeiting, but 15 different national regimes. this is a reference to the more general problem of the necessary criminal harmonization called for by the tampere european council.
in writing. - in its communication on the strategic objectives for 2000-05, the commission reiterates that europe must become a 'global player' that speaks with a strong voice in the world. what would be the objective of this global player? the citizen would undoubtedly expect a reply such as: 'better to defend the countries of europe', since this is the traditional and primary mission of political association. but that phrase is nowhere to be found. there are only vague phrases about "strategic partnerships" and the new possibilities for the development of trade which would be offered, it seems, by the full integration of europe. the omission of the main objective is very revealing. it shows one of the major flaws of the european union, a little known, almost always implicit, but which explains in large part the disaffection of citizens. the work programme for the year 2000, which is attached to the strategic guidelines, contains a very revealing passage in this respect. addressing the key issue of relations with the united states, the commission mentions this single priority: 'we will endeavour to reduce and eliminate as far as possible conflicts concerning transatlantic trade' (page 5). where we would expect a firm statement showing the will to defend the interests of europeans in the many trade confrontations that are taking place (to say nothing of that), we find only the will to eliminate conflicts, which does not show, on the part of the commission, a very great will to fight. why this strange simultaneity of integration and loss of the defense instinct? i will mention three reasons: (1) the european institutions, in wanting to go beyond the nations, cut themselves off from the peoples, and by cutting themselves off from the peoples, they become malleable to foreign interests; 2) the men who work in these institutions, once cut off from the peoples, get used to thinking not as the exclusive defenders of these peoples, but as international officials charged with regulating a global system; 3) integration may bring economies of scale and productivity gains, but it also loses much more, because by breaking up nations, subtle solidarities are broken down, and with them the will to defend ourselves together.

development. the acquisition and dissemination of management and technological know-how is therefore all the more urgent in order to encourage new production methods and to promote a tourist offer that responds as closely as possible to market developments. the adoption by the member states of tax measures favourable to smes in order to reduce, in particular, the burden on labour would, as the report indicates, be an excellent means of promoting employment growth in labour-intensive sectors and, consequently, in the tourism sector. this field of activity is also a decisive element in the economic and social development of the less favoured regions: i am thinking in particular of the outermost and island regions, whose advantages in this field are undeniable. it should be borne in mind that tourism is the largest industry in terms of revenue in these outermost regions. the income and employment generated by tourism contribute to a large extent to reducing imbalances and encouraging convergence of their economies towards the average rate of community development. tourism can also promote a certain cultural and economic rapprochement, since it allows greater awareness of the different european cultures and thus contributes to the development of respect for european ways of life. it is therefore clear that tourism, if properly developed, must in the long term provide a sustainable source of income for local economies while safeguarding and enhancing the richness of the landscape, culture, history and environment. finally, i would like to stress the key role that the - mr president, the 1997 directive, published on 21 january 1998, which initiated a partial liberalisation of postal services in europe, provided for a subsequent revision, in an otherwise complicated form, since it was to be the subject of a commission proposal before the end of 1998, then decided on before 1 january 2000, and finally to enter into force before 1 january 2003. but at the moment, time is now tenable. in these circumstances, it is only natural that our assembly should be concerned today by asking an oral question which urges the commission to show the definitive and unquestionable feasibility studies that no one has yet seen. what are the scenarios and possible risks? the main risk is that the commission, without sufficient justification, will upset the existing balance by proposing to move fairly quickly to a second stage of liberalisation which would unbalance the financing of the universal postal service in some countries and make it unmanageable. today, following the 1997 compromise, member countries can entrust public monopolies with the postal service for mail and items whose cost of distribution is less than five times the basic rate, or whose weight is less than 350 grams. it is assumed, for example, as commissioner bolkestein suggested during his hearing on 6 september last, that the commission might propose to reduce these limits to 50 grams and two and a half times the basic tariff. we do not think that this would be a fair solution, and the commission would not have any irrefutable figures to support it. but unfortunately, we know from seattle that she does not need a serious review of the previous stage to propose moving very quickly to the next stage. the second scenario we prefer is to postpone the revision and to maintain the current situation until we have a serious, detailed and objective study of the effects of the 1997 directive. in saying this, we are not seeking to protect monopolies, the harmful effects of which we are already well aware, but we want to be sure that we can combine the progressive evolution of organizations with the maintenance of the essential principles of public service. finally, the europe of nations group wonders whether the idea of imposing unified management rules on the postal services of the 15 member states would not, in itself, be flawed. in france, for example, the unequal distribution of the population over a large geographical area makes the existence of public service obligations in the distribution of mail absolutely essential if citizens' equality and social cohesion are to be maintained. but other countries, in other situations, may have different analyses. we believe that everyone should be able to make their own organisational choices. article 86 of the treaty establishing the community, formerly article 90, provides that services of general economic interest are subject to the competition rules in so far as the application of those rules does european parliament, it is the people of each member state who are deliberating democratically. to do otherwise would be to divert the spirit of our institutions.

commission - (it) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, last july i made a solemn commitment here in front of you to reform the commission. i would like to return to what happened last july: a crisis had hit the previous commission, i had just been appointed and you had accepted this appointment for the first time. the highlight of this episode was my commitment to reforming the commission, a fundamental reform which must be translated into a real revolution in the way it works. my commitment has not been unrealised and the reform announced is before you today in the form of a white paper which the commission has just adopted. i would like to emphasize that the commission voted unanimously, with one vote, in this case too. what are the main points of this reform? first, the definition of political priorities and their translating into concrete actions, through the targeted use of resources. these two elements will be at the heart of the system, to enable politics to assert its primacy and to assume its responsibilities fully. to this end we have created a completely new policy planning mechanism which enables the college to define annual policy guidelines, to establish the budgetary procedure on the basis of these data and to entrust the directorates-general with well-defined objectives, as well as to have control over the relationship between the resources available and the activities entrusted to it, which is a fundamental problem. the gpa (management by activities) approach will be the key instrument to ensure the necessary alignment of objectives, actions and resources. secondly, the optimal use of human resources. it is the backbone of the system, insofar as it touches upon what constitutes our real wealth: our staff. this is a staff of exceptional qualities, qualities which are difficult - if not impossible - to find in national governments, precisely because of the methods and criteria for recruitment. this is the impression i had when i became president and it has been confirmed in my daily work. at the same time, however, i found the morale of the administration to be very low. before, we felt the pride, the pleasure of being part of an institution admired by all; today, it is more about demoralization caused by months and months of criticism. all this must change, and this is one of the basic motivations for our reform. recruitment, career structure, mobility, disciplinary regime: everything will be governed by new criteria: more meritocracy, more credible and above all verifiable evaluation systems, continuing training, better accountability of management. these are some of the most striking aspects of the proposals. thirdly, financial management. this is a very delicate element and the key to the previous crisis, because management and control operations must combine efficiency and safety. we will create a management and control system in each directorate-general. this implies a shift from the current system based on centralised microcontrols to a new control system which will combine decentralised management controls with an efficient central audit system. in other words, we will have a central financial service to guide and advise financial management, a decentralization of the whole chain in each general direction, namely programmes, bonds, contracts, expenditure and ex ante control systems, and an external audit service to control all these operations. this is a real revolution in the way the commission works, both in terms of organisation and culture. we are aware of the problems associated with this transitional phase. this is the one that has raised the most concerns among our staff. we will therefore ensure that it is accompanied by all the necessary safeguards. the commission's reform aims to make it an administration that serves as a model of excellence for europe and the world. we want to be a model for the advanced use of information technology. we want to be a model of fully computerized administration. the commission was accused of being swamped with paperwork. we will therefore be a paperless commission in order to be more efficient internally and to promote the use of new technologies externally. the revolution here will be technical but also organizational. i will leave it to neil kinnock to explain the content of this reform in more detail, not without first paying tribute to the intelligence, enthusiasm and energy with which he carried out this work. i would also like to thank those who have worked on the project and all the staff of the commission, who have taken part in the largest debate ever held within the institution. i would like to point out that this method of debate is quite new and that, in my view, it has forced us to make a radical change in our thinking. the white paper before us is the fruit of their contribution. they have understood that only a thoroughly reformed commission can become the internationally admired institution that was at the heart of european history. the commission's aim is to turn the page on the white paper. a chapter of the past is closed, i hope for sure. we are now looking to the future, to the challenges facing the union, as we have indicated here in front of you in the past few weeks in the programme 2000-05, in the objectives of the five-year plan. this is the fundamental political reason for the reform. we need, the whole union needs, a strong commission, a commission which is again able to act as a political subject, which is a political entity recognisable as such in all its actions. that is why we are redefining all the priorities on which we will focus our work. that is why, and this is another important aspect, we are now freeing ourselves from activities which it is no longer appropriate for us to manage, in accordance with the principles of decentralization and subsidiarity. to this end, we are reforming the administrative machinery to create the conditions which will enable us to carry out our tasks effectively. we will make the best use of the limited resources available to us and which we are using to the full. but if it proves necessary, i do not rule out coming back here to ask for additional resources in case we are given new tasks. in september we made a commitment to reform with the presentation of the white paper. today we are fulfilling that commitment in the terms we expressed before you. the commission wants to be judged on facts, only facts, on the basis of what we will achieve. but i would remind you - and this will be my last point - that the commission is not the only community institution. parliament and the council will also be called upon to fully accept the challenge of reform. the commission has resolutely paved the way. i hope that all the institutions will follow it to the end, putting themselves at the service of the european citizens, for an ever stronger and more transparent europe. (applause) i would like to thank
commission. - i am pleased to be here with president prodi and my colleague, michele schreyer, to present the white paper adopted by the commission this morning: 'commission reform'. as the honourable members will see from this document, which will be available to them today, the unprecedented consultations with commission staff, parliament and the council, which began after the adoption of the consultation document in january, have been very productive and have led to useful improvements. i would like to thank mr prodi and the house and the many people who have given their time and effort to give us constructive answers. the white paper puts the reform in the right political context. within the commission, systems and structures have accumulated over 40 years during which successive enlargements have taken place. the treaties have been revised, new management tasks have been assigned by this parliament and the council to the commission, and many other changes of great importance have taken place within our union, on our continent and in the world. these realities, together with the approach to future enlargements, all strongly recommend the modernisation of the commission so that this essential institution can fulfil its primary duties of policy design and development, treaty implementation and management of public resources, and that it can do so with maximum efficiency and accountability. the commission's independence and sustained strength are certainly fundamental to this mission, as this house has repeatedly acknowledged. reform and renewal are also essential to this objective. the commission is not and will not be a secretariat of any kind, and all the institutions know this very well - everyone has understood this very well. but the commission is there to serve the union and its citizens with high performance standards. that is what the citizens are entitled to expect, and that is what the people who work for the commission want to do and will do. the house knows, of course, that the commission cannot achieve these objectives on its own. all the institutions of the european union will have to face the problems of reform in an honest and responsible manner. i know that my colleagues and i can count on the support of many members of this house from all sides of this house. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very important one. last month, as romano prodi has just said, we launched a thorough assessment of the activities and resources of the whole commission and we will report back in detail in september. our aim is for the commission to focus on key policy priorities and on core activities in line with our strategic policy objectives for the next five years. it will therefore inevitably be necessary to define the activities which could and should be reduced or eliminated. this means that we must look very carefully at how we can more effectively balance the use of internal and external resources in the interests of the union. this means that staff must be allocated to areas of high political importance, both in the departments and within the commission. once this assessment is completed, we will be able to say whether the resources at our disposal are up to the task assigned to us. if it is proved that this is not the case, we will ask the budgetary authorities to grant us more resources. if we do not get a positive answer, then not only the commission but also parliament and the council will have to tackle the difficult problem of determining which activities are less priority and which should be discontinued. i do not say this because i want the prodi commission to give up activities or responsibilities. on the contrary, as many members of this house understand, i am making these remarks because we want to assume our responsibilities with maximum efficiency and accountability. this means that any significant gap between the obligations and the operational resources must be closed, either by reducing activities or increasing resources, or a combination of both. for each of the three pillars of reform, the active cooperation and support of this house will be absolutely crucial. the new activity-based management system, which the president has just mentioned, will link political priorities to the availability of resources and therefore to the budget for the first time. the role of budgetary authorities in the application of activity-based management (abm) will therefore be vital. attempting to micro-manage the commission's operations clearly serves no one's interests. a strong and practical interinstitutional agreement will therefore be a prerequisite for the effective functioning of activity-based management. parliament will inevitably have to participate in human resources policy as an employer of civil servants and as a democratic institution to which the commission is accountable. again, this will be a very difficult challenge. and finally, in the area of financial management, where the court of auditors, the committee of independent experts and other internal and external analyses have strongly advised radical change, the support of this house in implementing the recommendations for total money security and value for money will be of the utmost importance. it is obviously impossible in the time available for this statement to examine our proposals in detail. i have no doubt that we will do so again and again in the coming months and years, and i look forward to the questions from the honourable members this afternoon. it is clear, of course, that in many ways the really hard work begins now, with the implementation of our proposals. i look forward to working with parliament, the council and the staff of the institutions to ensure that the reform strategy is implemented in the interests of the union and all its peoples. high representative for the common foreign and security policy. - (es) madam president, as you can imagine, i am very pleased to be back among members here in the european parliament. a lot has of parliament, and in particular to the presidency, is the inauguration of the intergovernmental conference and the opening of negotiations with the future members of the european union. the events in between the european union and the latin american countries. chechnya has also undoubtedly held a special place in our hearts and i shall have the opportunity to say a few words about it at the end of my speech, following an important conversation i had this morning with the representative of the council of europe, mr álvaro gil-robles, on his recent visit to the region. but i know that you have asked me to come and speak more directly to you about foreign policy and especially about security policy in europe after helsinki. i will briefly speak about it, and if you have any questions at the question time, i will be happy to answer them. let me remind you that the summit under the finnish presidency was held in helsinki not so long ago, just two months ago. during this summit, key decisions were taken on the foreign and security policy of our continent. there are three main types of decisions, which i'm going to talk about. first of all, it was decided to create three types of committees within the european union for decision-making in crisis management, including a political and security committee and a military committee representing the chiefs of staff of the 15 countries of the union. decisions were also taken on the relations of the european union with third countries and other organisations. i am referring mainly to the relations between the european union and nato and the relations between the european union and those countries which, being european in geographical terms, are not part of the european union or at least not yet. i shall confine myself to these three points to inform you of what has happened. firstly, as regards the decision-making bodies, the political and security committee (psc), set up at the last general affairs council, met for the first time this morning, 1 march 2000. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them, but i am afraid that the council will not be able to accept them. i can tell you that you can be happy and content. the 15 countries have appointed diplomatic experts at the level of ambassadors to deal with one of the most important issues we will face in the coming months. secondly, the military committee, which represents the various chiefs of staff of the 15 countries, will hold its first meeting on 7 march, that is to say, two months and a few days after the helsinki declarations. this military committee, as you can imagine, will have several obligations. during the interim, provisional stage, its main task will be to advise the council and me, and to take the first decisions on how to set up the final bodies which we will undoubtedly try to get going by the end of 2000 or the beginning of next year. thirdly, the military staff will represent the senior military officials of the 15 countries who will form with me the civil and military secretariat, whose task will be to prepare, with the assistance of the military committee, any operation that may be launched at any given time in the field of crisis management within the european union. this crisis management will not be a purely military one: the military, the military committee, will also be responsible for formulating logistical recommendations for possible humanitarian operations which may require the participation of military forces. today, mozambique is certainly a beautiful example of the fact that military logistics may have to be used not for military purposes but for purely humanitarian purposes. we are working very hard and, ladies and gentlemen, if i had told you a few months ago, when i had the pleasure of appearing before you for the first time, that on 1 march 2000 i could announce to you that the political affairs committee met for the first time today, that the military affairs committee would be launched a week later and that the first elements of the military staff would start arriving the next day at the building we have within the european union, many of you would certainly have thought that the high representative was going mad. we were not crazy, we worked hard, hard, hard and we certainly had the support of the members of the european parliament and the heads of state and government of the countries you represent. few initiatives in the field of the european union have evolved with such determination, energy and perseverance as crisis management from helsinki to today. in less than two months we have launched a mechanism in collaboration with the commission. i would like to thank commissioner patten, who is here with us, for his support and for the tremendous energy he has put into making sure that all these matters can be resolved in a relatively short time. ladies and gentlemen, allow me to turn to the second subject i wanted to discuss with you. we have already spoken about the bodies we have set up, but we have an essential obligation to be credible, which is that europe must be able to provide itself with the military capability to act in times of crisis. i would like to reiterate that with these military capabilities, the european union is not seeking to make war but to make peace, to participate in crisis management to go where there is war or conflict situations, in order to calm them down, to relax them and to avoid them, in the line of helsinki which, as you will remember, intelligently agreed to set up with the help of all european states a force of 60,000 soldiers capable at any given time of deploying in 60 days - two months - to avoid a crisis and to remain in place for a year to avoid conflict. this is a major operation, a major objective we have set ourselves, but i can tell you that we are capable of meeting the challenge that the heads of state and government set themselves in helsinki. on monday, exactly two days ago, in sintra, a beautiful town just outside lisbon, the defence ministers of the 15 countries represented here met and took important decisions to implement the headline goal set out in helsinki. the timetable they have proposed is a strict, important timetable which will require great determination on the part of everyone - including parliament. i'm going to define it in five points. first, before the next general affairs council in march, we will be able to define precisely - and to limit ourselves to the point of view that military planners may think adequate - the deep and specific meaning of the headline goal. there is a difference between saying we are going to deploy 60,000 troops in a peacekeeping operation or in a peacekeeping operation. we must therefore have all the scenarios in place so that we have the capacity to do this and do it well. before the 24th we shall therefore have this timetable fixed so that the general affairs council of that day can do it and do it well. secondly, we must look at the capabilities of each country, so that this overall force of 60,000 soldiers can be distributed in an orderly and efficient way among the 15 countries. third, we need to see what the differences are between the headline goal and what each country can bring. it is possible, ladies and gentlemen, that we do not have enough capacity in the 15 countries and that they all have to make an extra effort to meet the needs we have proposed. how are we gonna do this? we want to do this by convening a conference of the 15 countries to see what differences remain between the objectives set and the means we have to achieve them and to see how what we lack is distributed among the 15 countries that make up the european union. ladies and gentlemen, madam president, we want to set the timetable so that during the french presidency, in december 2000, we can conclude this process with a major conference bringing together forces from all the countries so that needs and capacities are equal and we can therefore honestly say that we already have the plan for what we have to do from the end of 2000 to 2003, when we have decided that the capacities will be in operation. ladies and gentlemen, that is what we are doing, what we have committed ourselves to. i think we have done a good job in the last few months, in the last few weeks, and i think we can do it for the rest of the year 2000 under the portuguese presidency - which is doing a really extraordinary, magnificent job - and continue under the french presidency, which will no doubt continue to work with the same promptitude and the same capacity as it has shown on other occasions. i wanted to tell you that in the meantime there will be at least four european councils, the lisbon council, the feria council and two european councils during the french presidency. at these councils, the heads of state and government are also prepared to continue to examine these issues so that we do not ration the train and that we are able, by 2003, to deploy what we have agreed, if necessary. i therefore believe, ladies and gentlemen, madam president, that we are working in this area with determination, with energy and with the broad support of all governments and all heads of state and government. ladies and gentlemen, i would like to add two more points. the european union is obliged to carry out this whole operation by maintaining contact with the third countries to which i have referred, countries which, although geographically part of europe, are not yet part of the european union. these are countries with which we have to work, which we have to integrate, because if a crisis were to occur, god forbid, all forces and all countries would be more than welcome. secondly, we must be able to establish a fluid and transparent relationship with nato. the operations we will have to carry out in the future will be of three types: the first is operations in which european forces participate within the framework of nato; the second is operations in which european forces participate and are led by them, but using nato's means and infrastructure; the third is the operations where the europeans will act alone. for the first two types, we will need the cooperation of nato and therefore a framework of transparent, positive and trusting relations between us and nato, which will of course be good for nato and for us. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i have told you about the capacities we are prepared to put into operation, the timetable we want to apply and what has been done in the last few months. i would also like to say that we do not forget that from a civilian point of view we will also have to deal with crisis operations. humanitarian crises, police crises, such as the ones unfortunately happening in kosovo, in the balkans. we also contribute or try to in writing. - we know that the commission will soon be reforming the common fisheries policy. this proposal for a council regulation is the first in a series which will make it possible to develop this reform. the collection and management of fisheries data is essential for the good management of the common fisheries policy. this data must be reliable, independently developed and accepted by all stakeholders in the sector, policy-makers and those responsible for the implementation of the cfp. the text of the proposal for a regulation has been amended in a relatively significant way in the committee on fisheries. all the members of our group voted in favour of these amendments both in committee and in plenary. amendment no 1 makes the text significantly clearer. the data collected should not be used for scientific purposes alone. scientists must process this data and pass it on to the relevant political authorities, who are responsible for decision-making. however, it is essential that the method of collection is carried out in a scientifically justified manner. amendment no 2 modifies the original commission proposal. the commission's proposal requires very detailed ship-by-ship and company-by-company studies. in addition to the extraordinarily high cost of such a proposal, the burden of management could lead some administrations to use these complexities as an excuse for not providing information in a timely manner and to create a certain feeling of distrust among professionals in the sector, if they are thus subject to heavy additional bureaucratic constraints. as regards the second part of this amendment, it is important to count and identify job losses in the sector much better. the management of the common fisheries policy must not be forgotten, but it must include a social dimension in terms of statistical analysis. amendment no 3 allows an important dimension to be added, namely the collection of environmental data. the particularly serious effects of the failure to take account of this type of data can be seen, for example, in the decision to ban driftnets, which is absolutely unjustified from an environmental point of view, since it concerns one of the most selective fishing gear. if this environmental dimension is not integrated into the data management, the commission could unilaterally prohibit the use of certain fishing gear at its discretion. amendment 4 specifies the obligation for scientists to process and transmit all data to the competent authorities, including national and regional authorities, so that they can contribute to the decision-making process. amendment no 5 makes it possible to lighten the commission's proposal. the information requested from the authorities must be reasonable in order to have an operational knowledge of the fishing activity, without removing the essential right to confidentiality, for example in the tax field, where there is no community competence. amendment no 6 is designed to make the commission's participation in the control procedure more binding. it is necessary that all data be transmitted annually and that the commission regularly reports on the aggregation of results. finally, amendment no 7 requires the commission to report before the end of 2001. since the reform of the common fisheries policy is scheduled for 2002, it is necessary that all the political players should be able to have access to the information which will form the basis of the commission's proposal.
in writing. - the amendment to the directive, as presented to us by the commission, is important because it deals with a particular disease, infectious salmon anaemia, a contagious viral disease. it is transmitted through water, through organic substances such as blood, fecal matter, mucus, etc. there is no scientific evidence that the disease can be transmitted vertically through eggs or milk. however, it is known that other species such as trout, eel or herring can carry the virus without being affected. the disease was detected in norway in 1984 and in canada in 1996. the virus does not survive above 26°c, so it is harmless to humans. the disease mainly affects the scottish salmon sector. it was detected in this region in may 1998. today, the ais covers 240 salmon farms. it is therefore important to contain this disease in order to avoid its spread to all aquaculture farms in the different member states of the european union. the council proposal aims to establish a system for the phasing-out of affected fish and a vaccination plan. as regards the phasing-out plan, we can only support this proposal. it is necessary to help the farms concerned to 'clean up' the infectious outbreak and to avoid any spread of the disease through commercial movements of live fish. as regards vaccination, it should be remembered that the original directive prohibited the use of the ais vaccine. the new commission proposal would allow the use of vaccines, but it is important to note that no vaccine has been found at present. the usefulness of this proposal is limited, at least in the short term. canada has a vaccine with a 76% success rate. as the canadian strain is different from the european strain, this vaccine cannot be used as such, but could serve as a basis for developing a vaccine against the european strain. it is therefore important that the commission should provide sufficient financial resources to support the development of an effective vaccine against european strain ais.
