for example, continues to be a reality. yet we know the importance of seeing many women in politics. only they can devise policies that can change structures that have been designed by men for men. women are faced with structural discrimination, whether in politics or in the labour market. it is therefore up to european political parties to open up to women. in fact, article 191 of the treaty (ex 138 a) emphasizes, and i quote, their 'important role as a factor of integration within the union'. the article goes on to state that they contribute to the formation of a european conscience and identity and to the expression of the political will of the citizens of the union. although such a provision has no legal value, it is nevertheless highly symbolic. it gives political parties an important role in the construction of a democratic europe. this can be done, for example, by implementing positive actions, by promoting parity within our political parties. some parties presented equal lists in the 1999 european elections. this is good practice and should be generalized. i do not know if there is a causal link, but it is still the case that the proportion of women meps has gone from 25.7% in 1994 to 29.9% in 1999. it has also been headed by a woman since the 1999 elections. i will conclude by reiterating the conclusions of the april 1999 conference organised by the commission, entitled 'women and men in power'. gender equality is not a problem that concerns only women, it is a problem that affects our whole society!
in writing. - women suffer from growing inequalities because they are victims of sex discrimination which can be exercised in an open way (violence, rape, sexual harassment, domestic violence, etc.) but also in a more insidious way. this oppression is based on a sexual and social division of labour which values men's work over women's. wages are unequal, their work is still perceived as "ad-hoc" and, more generally, women employees do not have access to the same positions of responsibility as men. furthermore, the family responsibilities are primarily theirs. women must have the right to fulltime employment on the same basis as men. coercive laws must be passed to promote equality in the workplace. states must develop a public early childhood care service. finally, to enable everyone to participate in public life, there must be a massive reduction in working hours. we need a real mix of political, economic and social life. we are fighting the idea that the biological difference between women and men will give rise to two different worldviews and two different value systems. women have the right to be present in the decision-making process as 'individuals' and not as representatives of the female sex.
in writing. - i would first like to warmly congratulate the rapporteur on the audacity of his proposals. i shall continue to deplore the frivolity of the right wing of this european parliament, which, by adopting a whole series of amendments, has emptied the work of my colleague of its substance! this report is, i remind you, based on the commission's annual economic report for 1999, the first published under the euro system. it therefore concerns the unified european economy rather than a series of national economies. it was a matter for the european parliament to take this opportunity to make imaginative and 'activist' proposals, to use the adjective used by the rapporteur, to give a new direction to the economic activities of the european union. europe has an incomparable potential for economic and social progress which, for reasons that are still partly unknown to us, remains largely untapped. hence the very interesting suggestions contained in the initial report of the economic and monetary committee to revive economic activity by setting ambitious objectives (employment rate of 75%, recovery of growth, etc.) and by providing the means to achieve them! the original proposals called on the council to adopt measures to ensure full employment while maintaining price stability and budgetary balance throughout the economic cycle. this is not, as some people tend to believe, a question of calling into question the stability policy adopted in recent years. measures, including fiscal measures, to encourage private and public investment must be adopted. the transeuropean networks programme as proposed in 1994 must be put back on track, and a major research and development programme must be launched to give investment the necessary innovative content. how can we consider that investment should not be used as a demand management tool but should be carried out on its own merits? we need to promote better management of working time and the mainstreaming of good practice policies in the member states in order to increase the level of employability, particularly among the most disadvantaged sections of the labour force. some measures, such as retraining in the form of lifelong learning, are particularly relevant. they should be an integral part of the ongoing institutional transformation that will have to accompany the transition to a knowledge-based economy. such a proposal is in line with the line of thinking adopted for the extraordinary employment summit to be held in lisbon in march. all these measures, which were too voluntary for the taste of some on the right, were of course swept away. i must deplore him ! the same fate befell an amendment referring to the taxation of speculative capital movements.
in writing. - our position is determined by our project for europe. we are for a europe that gives the highest priority to meeting the needs of a decent life for all, and in particular for the unemployed; a reduction in working hours with a duty to hire, without flexibility; wage growth in line with productivity; a tax reform that upwards homogenizes the taxation of capital income; a tobin tax to discourage financial speculation; and finally, the implementation of a planned energy saving programme. this policy should put the ecb's cold monetarism into perspective and break with the neoliberal principles of privatisation and the questioning of social protection. the resolution turns its back on such guidelines. on the contrary, it is a satisfaction for the stabilization policy which has only created unemployment and poverty and risks, through monetarist obsession, leading to breaking the current recovery rather than accompanying it. the rejection of the proposed amendments by the liberal right therefore leads us to vote against the resolution.
- mr president, we voted the resolution on the sinking of the erika in solidarity with the victims of this ecological disaster. we are, however, denouncing the deliberate nature of the resolution. to merely deplore the disaster and to complain to its victims, without taking any enforcement measures to oblige total to make good all the direct and indirect consequences of pollution for which it is entirely responsible, is to do nothing. it is outrageous that total is leaving it to volunteers and local authorities to repair the damage it has caused. it is equally outrageous that the state is providing funds, which are insufficient, which are only a disguised subsidy to this criminal enterprise. to merely raise the question of flags of convenience is to avoid the essential point. whatever flag of complacency total uses, the oil company responsible is widely known and present in all the countries of the european union and the authorities concerned could, if they wished, seize all its assets until the company pays. and above all we want to denounce this economy where, in order to make extra profit, a company can pollute a region as it can ruin it by closing factories.
in writing. - i welcome the almost unanimous adoption by our assembly of the resolution on the consequences of the erika oil spill, to which our group contributed a great deal. taking into account better than our previous resolution the scale of the disaster, which appears every day to be much more considerable than the first judgments had suggested, it is more demanding, more precise and more urgent. the overall assessment of the damage caused to the fisheries, marine cultures and aquaculture professions as a whole is still difficult at this stage. but we already know that they will be considerable. new pollutants add to the bill every day. the deterioration is not only in the turnover of companies, but also in the value of assets. the damage to the image of seafood is still difficult to quantify. the damage suffered by upstream and downstream businesses (traffic, supplies, tourism, etc.) and the overall costs borne by local authorities for pollution abatement and tourist repositioning will also have to be taken into account. fisheries and tourism, the twin essential resources of most of our atlantic coast, are both therefore very badly affected. hence the need to set out very clearly, as our resolution does, the principle of the polluter who cleans and the polluter who pays. it is the responsibility of the polluter to clean up the areas affected by the pollution and to restore the ecological balance that has been destroyed. as regards the compensation system, people are concerned because the first reimbursements made to victims by fipol are limited to 25%. this is outrageous. of course, every victim must be compensated 100%. it would be unthinkable to make victims bear some of the damage they have suffered solely because of the impertinence of a polluter. the resolution also welcomes the initiatives taken by some local authorities, such as the department of vendée, to draw up a precise inventory of the state of the coasts before the first waves of the black tide arrive: this process should be taken as an example, because it will make it possible to speed up the compensation of victims, whether private individuals or public authorities. finally, our resolution makes it clear that we must, in the field of maritime safety, break out of this infernal spiral of generalized irresponsibility, of this perverse system of mutual paralysis where the states dispose of the union and the union dispose of the states, for the greatest benefit of the polluters. let each play his part. the commission, whose american tropism has not played a role for once, although it would have been beneficial, should define as soon as possible a general framework for maritime safety. this must include minimum access constraints to community waters and ports concerning the age and characteristics of vessels; the commission has also proposed a general principle of environmental responsibility which makes it possible to clarify the responsibilities of the various actors, in particular the charterers, and to impose heavy penalties on them. the commission should ensure that information is coordinated, that it is not afraid to confront the laxity of certain large ports or major shipowners, and that it puts the issue of flags of convenience at the heart of the negotiations with malta and cyprus. i remind you that the erika was registered in valletta. however, the states must not, of course, discharge themselves of their own and essential responsibility towards the union: the rigour and effectiveness (and therefore the means) of port state control are essential for the safety of all. we must and will continue to be particularly vigilant in the months ahead to ensure that the victims, who obviously bear no responsibility whatsoever for this disaster, are fully compensated by the polluter and that the lessons of the oil spill are actually drawn this time on maritime safety, so that the polluters are definitively dissuaded from playing with the lives of our maritime populations. the most effective prevention is to put any potential polluter at risk of very heavy financial penalties.
in writing. - the commission communication sets out a series of objectives and proposals, including the need to continue efforts in the field of control and surveillance, to adopt new technical measures on the selectivity of fishing methods, to monitor the application of existing legislation, etc. but the commission's communication also states that it is not in a position to enforce compliance with this legislation. the commission has a whole arsenal of binding provisions, measures and decisions (both international and community) already in force in the fisheries and marine environment protection sectors. efficiency and over-regulation are not the same thing. it should be remembered that the maritime industry is prepared to apply community legislation provided that it is applied fairly in all member states, is technically acceptable and applicable and is based on real scientific evidence. i find it unacceptable that in the committee on fisheries one of the european commission officials dared to state publicly that the financial means given by the commission to certain scientific bodies make it possible to check their conclusions. this is a very serious error: the commission must not, of course, claim any right to influence the conclusions of scientists in order to be able to apply the policy it considers desirable in the light of its own interests. as regards the reduction of fishing pressure on the resource, it is important to emphasise the international nature of this obligation. what would be the point of reducing our european fishing fleet if at the same time third countries continued to put pressure on the fishery resources? it should also be noted that the development of the globalisation of trade has the effect of considerably reducing the effectiveness of controls and monitoring of fishing activities. transhipment has become a very common practice and it is not uncommon for fishery products from one member state which cannot be released into the union because of tacs being exceeded to be marketed as imported products or as products from another member state. the latter is very common in the case of companies whose capital originates in a member state other than that of the flag of the fishing vessel (this is in fact a disguise for 'quota-hoping'). food safety in the seafood sector also plays a key role. it is necessary to preserve the positive image of seafood and to prevent unhealthy products from being marketed in the european union. the report also calls for the establishment of a european union fisheries fund, which would be a means of promoting the conservation of fishery resources.

- the next item is the statements by the council and the commission on the extraordinary european council in lisbon on 23 and 24 march. i have the great pleasure of giving the floor to the prime minister, mr antónio guterres.
counsel. - (pt) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is with great satisfaction that i take part in this debate in parliament on the extraordinary summit in lisbon. i am not doing this as a formality, but with the same enthusiasm and determination that portugal puts into the european project. we can say that the european union is gaining substantially at the moment. after the success of the single market and the single currency, it is now the turn of the area of security, freedom and justice and the common security and defence policy. at the same time, the negotiations on enlargement are gaining momentum and we are entitled to say that enlargement is irrevocably becoming europe's rendezvous with itself and with its history. europe is also experiencing a period of economic recovery and optimism. but let us not be fooled: while it is true that economic conditions are improving, it is equally true that we still have to face the serious problems of unemployment and social exclusion; many people have pointed to the serious risks to the sustainability of our social protection model. it can be said that the economy and society are facing a new paradigm today, the paradigm of the knowledge economy and society. knowledge has become the main factor in wealth creation, the main factor in the divide between rich and poor countries. the real raw material of work today is knowledge. europe is facing this new paradigm of the knowledge economy at the same time as three other challenges: the globalisation of economies and markets; the speed of technological change and its ageing population. it is therefore only natural that european society today should be concerned about two things: first, that europe will irrevocably lose its leadership of the world economy to the united states of america; and second, that the united states will lose its influence on the world economy. the second, and perhaps the most serious, is that in order to regain this leadership, in order not to lose ground irretrievably, europe must not question its own social model, must not allow exclusion to worsen and thus affect its own citizenship. it is important to distinguish between reality and myth here. it is true that the us economy has experienced higher growth rates and improved productivity in recent years. it is true that the us economy has been faster in turning ideas and projects into businesses, goods and services available on the market. it is true that the north american financial system has been faster and better able to support the progress of the new knowledge-based economy. it is true that venture capital is doing better in the united states of america than in the european union. but it is also true, and we must not forget it, that: first, european society is more humane, more equal and more just; secondly, no society will be competitive in the medium term if it does not rely on social cohesion, which is stronger, more solid, more rooted in tradition in europe. finally, it is true that europe has an immense wealth of cultural diversity and that it has already shown that it can be better, if it wants to be. i would like to give two very simple examples of the most modern technologies: europe is clearly at the forefront of mobile telephony and digital television, which will be the two decisive technological factors for internet access in the near future. we all know that the internet is now more than a new network, it is the real network around which much of the world's exchange of knowledge and experience revolves. we must recognize, however, that europe is facing this new paradigm with three deficits: a political deficit, a strategic deficit and a deficit in the coordination of its policies and measures. firstly, the political deficit: we are not one country, but 15 countries, and our political union is only in its infancy. moreover, there is no single european public space, no single european public opinion: there are fifteen national public spaces, fifteen national public opinions. the communication between political society and civil society, which is the essence of the decision-making process in a modern democracy - according to the conception of democracy of the german philosopher habermass - is working well in each of our countries, but it must be admitted that it is not yet working as it should at the level of the european union as a whole. our political deficit is not just a deficit in the organization of institutions, it is something deeper that concerns the very sociology of our societies. that is why we need a strong political will to build a european political opinion all the more. that is why we need ever more our will to combat the resurgence of national egoism, which has tended to resurface in the union's institutions since the end of the cold war. i think that the next intergovernmental conference is a crucial moment for the various countries to give a clear signal of their willingness not to assume power at the expense of others, but to contribute to the strengthening of europe's political union. it is in the spirit of this debate and with this orientation that the portuguese presidency has embarked on this phase of preparation of the igc's work. the main theme of the lisbon summit will be the political deficit. but there is also a strategic deficit in relation to the major questions of economic and social life. i should like to make our objective clear here. our objective is to transform the european union into the most dynamic and competitive knowledge-based economy in the world within ten years, not at any price but by building on a society capable of managing social cohesion and high levels of employment and growth. to do this, we need a strategy that is based on four main pillars: creating the basis for a knowledge-based economy and an information society across our union; implement the economic reforms necessary for competitiveness and innovation; but at the same time, deepen social cohesion; and finally, to invest heavily in more and better jobs, to modernise our protection systems to ensure their sustainability in the future and to invest in macroeconomic policies which not only guarantee stability but are also more favourable to growth and employment. the first pillar of the strategy is to create the conditions for europe to successfully meet the challenge of the knowledge economy. the whole range of measures and policies relating to the information society is of enormous importance here, and we have the excellent work of the commission in this area in the e-europe initiative. we must create the conditions for a reduction in the cost of telecommunications in europe, so that access to the internet is not a factor of exclusion and division but a real factor of equal opportunities and citizenship. we are creating the conditions in europe to connect all schools and training centres to the internet and to equip them with the staff that is properly trained to carry out their tasks properly. we are trying to get all our public services online as soon as possible, including public tenders. we are creating the conditions for the development of e-commerce by removing the remaining barriers - including legal ones. we are investing heavily in content because the information society is not just a network, it must live primarily on content that values the diversity of cultural and scientific creation in europe. but it is not enough to rely on the information society. our vision is to integrate the information society into what we call a genuine education society, as europe's answer to the knowledge economy. this requires coordinating our scientific and research policies. this is why the commission's initiative on the european scientific area is so important, since it involves combining science and research with education and training policies at the level of the union, so that our society can in fact become a genuinely educational society, providing equal opportunities for access to the technologies of the future. the second pillar of the strategy is based on economic reforms for innovation and competitiveness. we're in the middle of the cardiff process. we are of course in favour of reforming the telecommunications, transport and energy markets. we consider that the integration of our financial markets is essential; in this respect, and again, the commission's contribution to the financial services action plan is of enormous importance. it is essential for europe to focus on creating the conditions for a genuine venture capital market which can support, above all, small businesses that are born with the technologies of the future. the commission's action plan on risk capital and the excellent work of the european investment bank in preparation for the lisbon summit are particularly important here. however, i do not think it is enough to confine ourselves to the internal market reform mechanisms that were envisaged in cardiff. i would also like to welcome the initiatives prepared by the commission in the field of enterprise and innovation policy, which are aimed at creating the conditions for us to have a scoreboard with which we can coordinate our action at the level of the member states, but also between them and the european institutions. the third pillar is perhaps the one that elected officials and voters feel most deeply about, although it is less prized by political discourse. this is the pillar of social cohesion, the one which concerns the creation of more and better jobs in europe, the one which concerns the creation of conditions for combating the social exclusion which is present in our societies, which is undeniable and which we must combat in a coordinated and determined way, the one which concerns the modernisation of our social protection systems to ensure their sustainability. first, the employment policies. we have a solid starting point here, the luxembourg process. it is a process that is clearly embedded in the functioning of our institutions. i would like to draw your attention to the question which seems to me to be the most interesting for the future: that of continuous learning as the essential basis for supporting social change and as an indispensable condition for a new stage in the social dialogue, in the dialogue between partners within europe. the second is the question of combating exclusion. the fight against exclusion in employment, social security, education and training policies, but also - it must be admitted - the fight against exclusion which requires specific measures for the target groups particularly affected by this deficit of citizenship which is found in many sectors of our populations. finally, the sustainability of our social protection system. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social protection system is not only financed in the most efficient way possible, but also that it is not only financed in the most effective way possible, and that it is not only financed in the most efficient way possible, but that it is also financed in the most efficient way possible. in this connection, i would like to draw attention to three aspects. first, the growth of employment in services, both in high-tech and low-tech services. secondly, more flexibility in the way the question of retirement age is approached. finally, and this is particularly important, the greater participation of women in working life. in this connection, it is absolutely essential today that our societies provide services in the area of child care, a three-fold winner because it leads to job creation, it leads to the creation of effective equality of opportunity between women and men, and it leads to the creation of better conditions for women to work and to a higher employment rate that is better able to support our social protection model. finally, the fourth pillar is that of macroeconomic policies for growth and employment. we have been able to coordinate our macroeconomic policies to ensure the stability that was the basis for the launch of the euro. well, we must ensure that this same capacity is put to work in the service of a more favourable economic environment for job creation and economic growth. in this connection, let me say that it would be highly desirable if europe could achieve, in a sustainable way, in the medium term and of course respecting the natural differences in pace between countries, a level of economic growth of more than 3% and job creation that would allow us to move closer to the regions of the world where these rates are highest, above 70%, instead of our current levels, slightly above 60%. we have a political deficit, a strategic deficit, but also a deficit in the coordination of our policies and measures. we are not starting from scratch here, we have two experiences on the basis of which we can build the future in all other areas: the coordination of economic policies guaranteeing the launch of the euro, the coordination defined in maastricht, and the coordination of the luxembourg process in relation to employment policies which, as i said, is now firmly rooted in the collective life of the european union. after the luxembourg, cardiff and cologne processes, we do not want to launch a new process in lisbon. first, we want to create the conditions for articulating, simplifying and deepening the three existing processes, converging them towards the common goal. secondly, we want to add new essential dimensions to it, such as those relating to the information society and the knowledge economy, but also those relating to the modernisation of social protection and the fight against social exclusion. finally, to adopt as broadly and generally as possible, in compliance with the principle of subsidiarity, an open method of coordination which can above all take advantage of what we have at our disposal in the formulation of our policies, namely the luxembourg process, with clear objectives and instruments, quantified as far as possible. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. the commission's proposal is based on a system of indicators which enable the exchange of good practice between the various member states, now called benchmarking, which is based on national plans or national initiatives which can bring our policies closer together towards the same objectives, while respecting our own diversity and in objective forms of 'monitoring' and comparison, which also enable us to emulate and at the same time compare our economic and social achievements with those of other particularly dynamic regions in which we live. of course, not all of these objectives will be achieved in lisbon. what matters is our continued, joint determination. we want to gradually eliminate our political deficit, our strategic deficit and our coordination deficit. we want above all to increase the political and strategic leadership capacity of the european union in economic and social matters, because this is an indispensable condition for europe to win its bet on the new information and knowledge society. i believe that we can have a two-pronged strategy: gain in stability, but also gain in growth; gain in competitiveness, but also gain in economic and social cohesion. of course we want to be at least as competitive as the most competitive and modern economies in the world - the current practice of referring to the us economy as the most dynamic. but be careful! we do not want to do it at any cost, we want it to be done with respect for our own identity. the central question of our identity concerns the social model, which is more than a set of rules, it is a genuine form of civilization, the european civilization of which we are proud and which we will never accept to be called into question. (parliament adopted the resolution)
- i thank the president-in-office of the council, mr antonio guterres, and i give the floor to mr romano prodi, president of the commission.
the commission. - madam president, i would first of all like to congratulate prime minister guterres on the initiative he has taken in organising the lisbon summit and to congratulate him on the quality of the preparatory work. we fully agree with his analysis, which has been so warmly applauded, and we support his initiative. i believe that together we can make the lisbon summit a success. in this speech i shall confine myself to presenting the commission's contribution to the lisbon summit: our long-term strategy and our vision for the summit. in lisbon we will have to decide on a very simple point: whether europe can regain the leadership position it has long since lost in the fields of economics and technology. it depends on us, on the economic growth we are able to impose on the european system, on the number of jobs we are able to create, on the level of education of our citizens, on the training of our working class. as prime minister guterres has stressed, these are not new issues. we do not want another luxembourg, cardiff or cologne, but we want to tackle these issues, which have already been tackled, by adopting a completely new approach: not one topic at a time, but all together to finally establish a system of interventions. we're doing it now because that's when all of this can come together. we have a unique opportunity, an opportunity which has been built on the success of the recent policy: low inflation, a generally healthy balance of payments, sound public accounts and, finally, very strong economic growth. but, as the portuguese prime minister pointed out, these forecasts do not guarantee economic growth. never before in the last generation have european experts predicted with such unanimity a possible long period of high growth. the increase in oil prices has not stopped this growth nor has it caused a return to inflation, as might have been feared. there are, however, some worrying signs which do not, however, prevent us from pursuing a development policy as we had thought and planned. the lisbon challenges are therefore very simple: we must meet the technological challenge by taking back ground in the fields of knowledge, knowledge, technologies, particularly the technologies of reclassification. that is how we can once again take the lead. that is why we have taken the e-europe initiative, through which the commission has decided to set a concrete example in its administrative reform. we have committed ourselves - and i confirm this commitment before you - to creating a commission, or more precisely an e-commission, in the sense that all supply, research, etc. with this institution will no longer be done on paper but by direct electronic means. this is a very complex endeavour which we are nevertheless able to provide because we have a very specific mission, a limited dimension and a high cultural level. it can be a powerful example for all european governments and administrations, with whom we will have to interact not on paper but electronically. we also have a social challenge to tackle, namely unemployment and social exclusion. president guterres' speech shows a systematic formulation based on a new use of technology, but also on an important commitment to preventing these technologies from generating social exclusion again, which represented a real risk for development in the 1980s but also for that of recent years. i would like to stress - and i express my concern on this point - that the divisions in european society in terms of income are constantly increasing: this aspect of social division is of fundamental importance and must be taken into account if we do not want to find ourselves faced with a broken society in a short time. so we have a summit for sustainable growth and employment. as we have done, sometimes with some contestation in the minds of some, we should and can point to the goal of full employment as an attainable goal. this passage has been quite difficult, but i can assure you that this objective is not unrealistic. this is an objective within our reach because we have a solid macroeconomic environment, to which we must now add the lisbon summit, namely human resources, new ideas on the market and on the use of knowledge and research. human resources are synonymous with education, training and reform of social status to deal with the problem of ageing. we have not always been able to successfully solve this problem, which is facing all our countries and which is getting worse by the day. the problem remains and i hope that the lisbon summit will enable us to make progress by combining our experience of benchmarking with our proposals on such an important subject. we have a lot of work to do in the market. it would be wrong to say that we already have a perfect single market. we still need further structural reforms; we must complete the picture in the services sector, e-commerce, energy and transport. there are many public services which have not yet entered into a system of maximum competition and efficiency. if we are to curb inflation despite the increase in oil prices, we must act at european and national level to improve these services, as well as financial and banking services. we therefore need - and i say this because the situation has been stagnant for some time - european company statutes, a european patent, a more liquid capital market and better standards for tendering. these are operational points that we cannot escape. we will fulfil our obligations within the commission and, as i said earlier, we will start using all these new technologies in all our procedures and in our relations with the outside world. but since we want to be a model of effective administration, we must strive to make this happen throughout the continent, so that it can serve as an instrument for the multiplication of knowledge and technology. on this point we must mobilise citizens, local authorities, national governments, businesses and trade unions. as president guterres has already stressed, the lisbon summit will focus on putting all this in place. to achieve results we need a new method and, as the portuguese prime minister said at the end of his speech, very clear macroeconomic parameters. so we are not starting a new process, we are not bringing anything new, but for the first time we are complementing existing processes with a chance of success. we must, however, bring a new element: we must find a way of measuring this progress, we must be concrete to public opinion and use benchmarking - a word almost unknown until a few years ago - or, in simpler terms, the comparison and measurement of progress achieved in a completely homogeneous way. we must be aware, inexorably and seriously, of the areas in which we have lost ground - and there are many: just think of the biotechnology sector where we have suffered, in recent years, relative failures. we must spread best practice in all areas and try to bring it to the european level. in lisbon we hope to achieve what we have tried to prepare together with the cooperation - which i can only welcome - of - mr president, commissioner, amateurs know that good chocolate is made with cocoa butter. any addition of other fatty substances deteriorates the taste. it is to defend this quality that the 1973 directive prohibited the use of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter. with the entry of new countries into the european union, exceptions to this strict prohibition have come into force. in the name of the free movement of goods, harmonization was necessary. the commission could then choose to align the european standard upwards and extend the ban to all member states. but under pressure from multinational firms who wanted to reduce their production costs, the commission proposed a directive in april 1996 allowing lower amounts of vegetable fat to be added. in its first reading, parliament has put its finger on a dangerous gearing which amounts to accepting the directive on certain conditions. the council has entered the breach by adopting its common position, which recognises the name 'chocolate' even when other vegetable fats are added. it is, once again, the victory of profit for the few against quality for all. but the european parliament, at second reading, can overrule this directive, the application of which would have serious repercussions. consumers and chocolate makers would suffer a drop in quality and a levelling down. the acp cocoa-producing countries, on the other hand, would suffer a significant drop in their outlets and incomes. more than $300 million for ivory coast alone. it goes without saying that they are very worried. in the interests of consumers and the acp countries, my group, in its vast majority, is therefore in favour of a ban on vegetable fats in order to defend the authenticity and quality of real chocolate. that is why we have tabled a - mr president, consumer protection is our first concern. the challenge of the directive on the production and marketing of chocolate is equally important. the union must lead the way in simplification, trust, authenticity and respect for differences. since 1973, european legislation stipulates that the name 'chocolate' must be given to products containing only cocoa or cocoa butter. some states have been granted a derogation since accession. all right, everybody stay king of the chocolate bar at home. i want to be able to buy a chocolate bar in my shop in reims, in accordance with the gastronomic traditions of my country, without having to turn the product around, wearing my glasses at the same time, to ensure its quality. of course, this labelling frenzy is necessary since trust no longer exists. but if you, ladies and gentlemen, are going to give up a certain definition of chocolate, at least do so in a clear and visible way. i therefore ask you to support amendments nos 29 and 18. it is certain that tastes are cultural. if you give in to the compromise, a food that we don't consider chocolate will enter our territory. we are advocating an authentic conception of chocolate. cocoa butter is the essence of chocolate. let's respect the taste guarantee. it is not enough to publish a white paper on food safety to reassure consumers. it is not for artisans and small businesses to invent a way of promoting their know-how or to mark their differences with a label such as 'pure chocolate' or 'pure cocoa butter'. it is the whole fabric of the artisans and smes that we condemn if we accept a different definition of chocolate. this vote today is symbolic. we must give priority to consumer information and the interests of the african cocoa-producing countries associated with europe in the lomé convention. in the kingdom of the absurd, are they not planning an impact study on their economy, years after the implementation of a directive? to satisfy multinationals, consumers should make life more difficult for themselves, labels should be creative and reassuring, artisans should create a label for "chocolate quality", cocoa exporting countries should adapt... and you talk about a europe that is close to its citizens, generous, transparent and respectful of the diversity of cultures! we do not want your compromise chocolate, we know the federalist recipe all too well. the culinary understanding between peoples is difficult, it reflects our differences too well, too concretely, which is not in the sense of an all-round harmonization. i would like to say to the commissioner that i am very pleased that he has taken this opportunity to speak on behalf of the commission.
- mr. president, for centuries, cows ate grass and chocolate was made with cocoa. then, a few years ago, britain, which gave mankind the meat with jam, the hooligans and adam smith, began to feed cows with corpses and make chocolate without cocoa. these aberrations should have been confined to the british isles, but the removal of borders has allowed the adulterated chocolate to circulate. so much so that today, in seven out of 15 countries, consumers are unknowingly swallowing manipulated chocolate, including in mr haider's austria, which now finds itself with mr guterres' portugal. to reassure us, we are told that counterfeit cocoa will be limited to six tropical products: borneo ilipe, shea butter - also used in aircraft engine oils - and so on. but, with the amendments to the directives, the six products will become seven, eight, nine, until soybeans, rapeseed and gmos are included. we are also told that fraud in the cocoa sector will be limited to 5% - at first, then 10% - and that no checks will be carried out, just as, for example, the cartons of chiquita bananas, which are supposed to weigh 18 kg and actually weigh 20 kg, are not checked. the controls are useless, because we are told that the margin of error is 1%, when scientists tell us that it is actually 40%. we are told, "eat, drink, swallow without fear, there is a label to protect us". but the label is a graphic fraud, since it is illegible, and a scientific hypocrisy, since, for example, the mention "palm oil" will be drowned in a list of ingredients. it's like the port: we don't get told, "it's a south african counterfeit". we are not going to be told that cocoa is counterfeit. so, in the absence of arguments to justify the fraud in chocolate, the multinationals say: 'we must accept 5%, otherwise the fraud will be total. what 's the big deal ? it is enough that the product is called "karitelat" if it is shea, "sojalat" if it is soy, but not "chocolate". the 388 000 tonnes of french chocolate, for example, must be made with cocoa, and the 19 billion francs of french turnover, for example, must be earned honestly by the artisans. it is a legal obligation to côte d'ivoire, to the african farmers. we are bound by the lomé convention and the commodity convention to which the european union has acceded, as far as cocoa is concerned. it is also a financial obligation: if we fail to comply with it, we will be obliged, through the stabex mechanism, to compensate these countries for their losses. this is a health and food safety requirement, as cocoa substitutes such as brazil nuts can cause immunological pathologies. it is, after all, a question of truth, a question of morality. we must put an end to the widespread lying, because we start with fake chocolate and end up with a fake european commission whose members are american-modified bodies and whose flag is a flag of complacency hiding a world commodity.

- mr president, i voted in favour of the common sense considerations concerning the ecological catastrophe which threatens the planet if present trends continue. but the concerns are drowned out in a jumble of well-intentioned statements. neither the brussels commission nor the european parliament is inclined to act or even to clearly identify those responsible for a disastrous ecological development. the european institutions, for example, are content to make pious promises to protect the tropical forest, while the large timber industry trusts, which are the industrial slaughterers of the forest in many countries of south-east asia and africa, are imposing their actions on the local populations, and these slaughterers are well known. of course, in many poor countries, it is the people who are destroying the forests by clearing them, either to make a modest income or to clear land and gain access to land that they otherwise would not have. but to claim to integrate the environmental dimension into the development process is pure hypocrisy when the ruling classes of rich countries are actually blocking the path of development from poor countries and keeping the majority of their populations in poverty.
in writing. - the text of the report before us today responds to a need to preserve tropical forests. the european union and its member states have a responsibility to protect an ecosystem which is essential for the balance of the environment of the entire planet. this responsibility is linked first of all to the history and commitments of the member states to countries where the majority of these forests are located. these historical links, this expertise must be put to the service of protecting this ecosystem. on the other hand, we have a responsibility as consumers: many of the products consumed in europe come from these regions and generally have a negative impact on the forest. finally, the european union has large areas of tropical forests in the territory of its member states, particularly france. the department of french guiana in particular is almost entirely covered with this type of vegetation. in particular, it is necessary to allow these areas to be developed in a genuine way, while respecting the culture and traditions of their inhabitants, without confining them to a purely passive role of ecological conservation. the european union can make a contribution in this area if it is able to coordinate efforts and competences without seeking to control and impose a single strategy on the member states. we therefore supported the epp-ed amendments which maintain the flexibility needed for the whole system.
in writing. - the recent sinking of the oil tanker erika off the coast of brittany has raised public awareness of the problem of, among other things, "de-gassing", the uncontrolled discharge of waste oils, debris or other waste from ships' cargoes, which is carried out by unscrupulous captains on the high seas. while the cracks in the wreck were officially closed, oil continued to wash ashore, indicating either that other leaks were occurring, or that passing ships were using them to clean their tanks, or possibly both. in the shipping jungle, unfortunately, this is common. they contribute to turning our seas and beaches into garbage and to endangering the ecological balance of the marine environment. it just so happens that the european parliament is today considering, at second reading, a draft directive which has been under discussion for two years and which draws the consequences at community level of the 1973 marpol international convention, which has been ratified by all the member states. the convention requires ships to deposit their waste at port reception facilities when calling at ports and in return requires states parties to set up adequate facilities. we can therefore only applaud the draft european directive which will make it possible to apply these principles. but at the same time, we want to ask the big question: what about controls? the draft provides that ships calling at a community port may not leave the port unless they are provided with certificates proving that their waste and residues have been effectively disposed of in appropriate facilities. but what about ships coming from outside the community? will they be asked for certificates too? and how will ships passing without stopping be controlled? we believe, first of all, that ports in the member states should be closed to ships without such certificates, even if they come from outside. in addition, member states - which will undertake to strengthen their controls in ports by the directive - must also commit themselves to strengthening their control systems at sea. we know all too well what the competitive pressure is in shipping. there is no point in adopting conventions or directives if they are to remain dead letters in the absence of means of control.
in the light of the recent events in the gulf, the commission has decided to take the necessary steps to ensure that the situation in the gulf is not further complicated by the fact that the gulf crisis has not yet been resolved. i would remind you that the proposal for a directive under discussion today is aimed at improving the availability and use of port reception facilities for industrial waste and cargo residues. it is in line with marpol 73/78 (prevention of pollution from ships), but focuses more particularly on waste management in ports. it is part of the community's overall strategy for waste management and requires all ports to provide adequate reception facilities, meeting the needs of ships. today we are faced with problems of marine pollution that we must tackle hand in hand with bold action. as the rapporteur has pointed out, there are already regulations, but they are not being respected. the system which applies generally is that governed by the polluter pays principle, a principle which is conspicuous by its inefficiency! that's why we need to find an alternative. this alternative is proposed in an amendment which i supported. the aim is to introduce a system of fees to be paid systematically by all ships when they call at a port, whether or not they use waste disposal facilities. the levy will be used to finance 90% of the installations in question. this will inevitably encourage ships to discharge their operating residues or other waste in ports rather than off-shore, a practice which is now commonplace and which is condemned. it is well known that some ships have even taken advantage of the pollution caused by the sinking of the erika to dump their waste into the sea. it is absolutely outrageous and unbearable. however, there are examples of good practice, as the countries bordering the baltic sea have already been operating in this way since 1998. i am well aware that this will lead to changes in the organisation of ports in many member states and will lead to additional costs for ships. but is this not the price to be paid for ensuring the cleanliness of the marine environment, especially since the directive provides that the least polluting vessels should be able to be identified and benefit from reduced fees? i think that system is fair, and i am voting in favour of it.
in writing. - this proposal for a directive is welcome within the european union. it is part of the overall community strategy for the reduction of marine pollution and for the management of waste and requires all ports in the union, including marinas, to provide adequate reception facilities to meet the needs of ships. international regulations already existed, since the marpol convention imposes binding international rules on all ships, according to which any discharge at sea is prohibited. but the problem is the application and observance of these standards! the honourable principle of 'polluter pays', to which many member states, including my own, are committed, is far from being respected! the erika disaster is a sad illustration of this, as are the 39 gassings that have taken place with impunity in the space of a week! the european parliament and its committee on regional policy, transport and tourism have therefore, confirming the first reading of the previous legislature, proposed that each ship entering a member state's port should bear 90% of the costs of receiving and handling waste, irrespective of the actual use it makes of the facilities. we believe that this is the only real and fair way of avoiding these unintended discharges into the sea. if port facilities were financed (at a significant rate) only by the ships using them, there would be a strong fear that many of the latter would escape this burden, since the cost of dumping at sea would be lower. we also want to set the proportion of compulsory inspections at 25%. at the dawn of the french presidency of the european union, this is the position that the french socialists are preparing to defend. i can only urge our assembly to do the same. this is a political fight; but is it not our role to lead it, even if this means taking ambitious policy decisions which sometimes go further than those of our governments and which are always far-reaching and hopeful?
in writing. - we cannot ignore the coincidence of this second reading of the proposal for a directive on marine pollution with the tragic news of the sinking of the erika. the text does not deal with accidental causes of pollution, but we know that the consequences of pirate practices of offshore degassing are no less serious. in the last week of february, 39 wild gas discharges were identified in the only area where the erika wreck is located. these practices are intolerable, but they are difficult to control, especially at night or in foggy weather. this proposal for a directive and the amendment to introduce a universal port tax on ships in all european ports to finance the treatment of their waste have a twofold purpose: to oblige ports to equip or organise themselves to treat the waste from the operation of ships, whether directly or by subcontracting, to competent specialised operators; and above all, to dissuade ships from evading their waste treatment obligations, since they will pay the price anyway. however, it is necessary to ensure that this universal taxation measure is as mutualised as possible and accompanied by national or european financial provisions enabling small ports to access waste treatment services without unreasonably burdening their economy and thus their sustainability. under these conditions, what this directive proposes is a first exemplary response by europe to the legitimate emotion aroused by the pollution caused by the sinking of the erika. it is, in a sense, the beginning of the recognition and establishment of a european maritime area governed by common rules.
in writing. - the council had already had to debate this directive on port reception facilities for ship-generated waste at length, but the text it had reached respected the principles of strengthening the protection of the marine environment by taking account of the realities of each member state, without upsetting national practices, which is not the case with the text of the report which has just been submitted to us. a state such as france has already implemented the provisions of the marpol convention by guaranteeing in each port quality reception and treatment facilities, entrusted to private companies, which invoice the shipowner directly according to the type of waste and its nature: the reduction in the cost of use for the so-called ecological ships is therefore 'natural'. this solution, which favours the most environmentally friendly vessels, seems much more fair than an arbitrary reduction which would benefit - on the basis of what criteria? - ships bearing the 'ecological' label, and a contribution independent of the use of the facilities applied indiscriminately: we therefore refuse to substitute a taxation which takes account of the nature of waste for a blind policy of taxing the flow of ships, irrespective of their danger to the environment. it should also be noted that unfortunately 'unpacking' at sea is largely independent of the taxation system: only checks at sea and more frequent inspections of the fleet calling at the port would be likely to limit discharges at sea. for all these reasons, the uen group, while reiterating its agreement with the council's common position, opposes the text of this report which distorts the principles of the common position. it urged the member states to assume their full responsibilities by implementing control measures as quickly as possible, which, together with a system of penalties illustrating the 'polluter pays' principle, might help to avoid the recurrence of disasters such as the one which so scandalously disfigured the french coast recently.
in writing. - the european parliament has today delivered its opinion on the proposal for a directive on the technical roadside inspection of heavy goods vehicles. it is essential to improve the level of safety and to reduce the environmental impact of these vehicles, whose traffic is constantly increasing. the introduction of mandatory random road checks to check the level of road maintenance throughout the year is a good idea, but it needs to be implemented effectively. this proposal for a directive would be a very useful complement to the efforts made in the cities, in particular through the urban travel plans, and in particular in the rouen agglomeration, which is crossed by 5 000 heavy vehicles every day. it is also urgent to consider alternative modes of transport for goods (river, rail, etc.) and the development of clean vehicles. that is why, ladies and gentlemen, i have today supported the proposal for a directive on the technical roadside inspection of heavy goods vehicles.
- the next item is the report (a5-0064/2000) by mr duff and mr voggenhuber, on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the drawing up of a charter of fundamental rights of the european union.
the committee on petitions has tabled a number of amendments. - madam president, first of all i would like to congratulate all the rapporteurs on the richness of their work. they were able to affirm the importance of this subject for parliament, europe and its citizens. the aim of this report is to give our colleagues, members of the convention, a clear and precise mandate of the european parliament's expectations and to convey to our fellow citizens a strong testimony of our commitment to the effective respect of their fundamental rights by the institutions of the union. the committee on petitions' area of competence legitimises its interest in the drafting of the charter. the numerous petitions it receives help to determine how citizens perceive the union and the rights they believe it protects. the committee on petitions' opinion is intended to highlight the aspirations expressed by europeans who refer to parliament for non-respect of a right granted by the european union. the petitioners who write to us show a stubborn and unwavering conviction that they have a set of rights, thus giving the impression that the european citizen is convinced that there is already a material constitution of the union in which all these rights are enshrined, anticipating the decisions of the convention. our opinion thus underlines two essential points which the rapporteurs seem to share. first, the necessary visibility of the charter as a reference text for citizens. this requires clear and concise wording in a single, understandable text. secondly, the binding force of the charter, which is confirmed by the effective justiciability of the rights recognised. the natural consequence of this will is the inclusion of the future charter in the body of the treaties. in conclusion, i would say that we need to make a qualitative leap in the protection of fundamental rights. this report must be a unanimous message from parliament so that the council and the convention can meet the expectations of the petitioners.
- madam president, mr council representative, mr commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i believe that the exercise we are engaged in today is timely, and that the current events are there to remind us every day of the urgency of this charter of the european union. this is the framework in which we find ourselves. a charter of the european union clearly means that the charter will be addressed to each of our fellow citizens, of course, but also to residents, to persons passing through the territory of the union ... it matters. this is important at a time when the european union is experiencing upheavals within itself; this is also important - and we want to stress this in the text to be voted on tomorrow - as we embark on the process of enlarging our union to include countries for which respect for fundamental rights is a matter of meaning; finally, this is important at a time when we consider - and we want to make this clear in the text we will be voting on tomorrow - that the union has moved beyond the stage of economic integration and is clearly engaged in a process of political and social integration. this charter must contribute to that. the resolution we are voting on tomorrow is certainly not intended to give our colleagues - and therefore myself - an imperative mandate in the context of the convention, since we have already started work. it is rather a question of saying what parliament expects from the convention. i would like to stress two points. first of all, what do we expect from exercise? i am not saying that the european parliament should be the only institution in the world to have a right to vote, but i am saying that the european parliament should be the only institution in the world to have the right to vote. we want more. it is in this spirit that we are working within the convention, both in terms of timing and form. my second point concerns the content. our resolution contains little on this subject, but parliament has already had the opportunity, on at least three occasions, to say what it wanted from a charter of fundamental rights. this was not the subject of today's debate, but three points should be noted. firstly, if we do not have an original body to codify the existing law to the letter, i do not think it would be worthwhile to create this new body. secondly, if the convention is to be content with simply copying all or part of the european convention on human rights in order to empty the question of whether the union should accede to it or not of its substance, i also believe that we would be going the wrong way. thirdly, i believe that, as regards the content, we have here the opportunity to reaffirm at union level a number of commitments to which each member state subscribes, but which we must confirm on behalf of the european union as such: the recognition of a number of rights, particularly in the economic and social field. i can see how difficult the mandate given us in cologne is: to recognize social rights which are more than just objectives. but this is also the main thrust of the work that will be carried out in the convention, and on behalf of my group i would like to say how much importance we will attach to the content of the charter in these matters. in this spirit, i fully support the proposal just made by ieke van den burg: if the union is considering its accession to the european convention on human rights, it should also be considering its accession to the european social charter. finally, i believe that the european parliament will be on the right track so that this charter is ready - whether in substance or in terms of timing - to be incorporated during the french presidency. it would allow for the proper recognition of fundamental rights in the place they deserve in our internal legal order, an order which is today being observed with great attention by citizens within the european union, of course, but also by countries that aspire to join us.
- ladies and gentlemen, the charter of fundamental rights must be an essential step in the construction of europe. we must give ourselves the means to make it the founding element of european identity which would make europe take the qualitative leap it still needs to feel that it really exists. in this context, i would like to join my colleagues in stressing the need to make this charter binding. citizens would not understand that the european union is working to define fundamental rights which are not legally guaranteed. fundamental rights, and i emphasize this word, must be compulsory, otherwise the european construction itself would lose its fundamental character in the eyes of many. the future charter must therefore be included in the treaties, and this at the next igc, probably the last one involving 15 countries. france, which is widely recognised as the motherland of human rights, must make the most of its presidency in the second half of 2000 to put this amendment to the treaties on the agenda. this is a solemn appeal to the french government. but there are two points i would like to make here. on the one hand, i would like to stress the need for the charter to develop the concept of european citizenship of residence. it is more imperative than ever to prevent different categories of people enjoying distinct rights from coexisting in europe. for example, how could it be accepted that an algerian who has worked and paid taxes in france for thirty years cannot vote in european municipal elections, while a european who has been living in another eu country for six months can participate? this charter must do everything possible to change our definition of european citizenship from the notion of residence. the rights we define, to be fundamental, must apply to everyone. secondly, i would like to stress the urgency of introducing effective protection of personal data in the charter. the european parliament voted last month for an amendment calling for the creation of a european commission on information technology and freedoms. but it can only really exist if it is based on a sound legal standard. the charter must therefore be careful to define the limitations of the content of the files, the means permitted for collecting the information and the access procedures. moreover, at a time when certain communication systems, such as espionage, are being condemned, we must guarantee the rights of citizens in the face of the new european institutions that are developing, guarantee the rights of citizens through parliamentary control, but also the rights of consumers in the face of new marketing techniques on the internet. this is a major challenge for guaranteeing fundamental freedoms in the 21st century.
- madam president, my speech will be very different from that of the previous speakers, since i would like to show you that the charter of fundamental rights of the citizens of the european union, as drawn up by the duff/voggenhuber report of the european parliament, would in reality be a charter restricting fundamental rights. the report proposes that the rights of citizens, which have been defined at national level, should be enshrined in a uniform, detailed, binding european charter, the application of which would be monitored and thus interpreted by the court of justice of the european communities. i should like to stress before going any further that in the context of the cologne council, which was set up to prepare a preliminary draft charter, i am not sure that all the other participants representing the heads of state or government and the national parliaments agree with this position of the european parliament. so, for now, what i'm about to tell you applies only to the duff/voggenhuber report. it is clear that the promoters of the charter, whatever they may say, see the defence of fundamental rights, which are well protected in europe today, as a pretext for concealing another purely ideological objective: to provide the basis for a european constitution, the crowning achievement of a superstate, even though the peoples of europe as a whole do not want either. and they are right, for this detailed, binding charter, giving for all europe uniform definitions of the rights of citizens, would impose a rigid legal cover enclosing each people in rules which would not be entirely their own. if we say that the charter thus provided would reduce the rights of citizens, it is for three reasons. firstly, under the pretext of better defending citizens, it would remove them from the place where their rights are defined. it would weaken the control they have today. it would mean that a people could no longer change the rights of its citizens without the agreement of the other fourteen, a stifling formula which is not suited to the nature and interests of europe, as i explained in the minority opinion attached to the report. secondly, the charter would provide a new pretext for a delusional uniformity of citizens' rights in europe. i am surprised that governments are so willing to do this. have they not learned the lessons of the past? i am not saying that the commission should not be involved in this. finally, this charter would tend to circumvent the rights of the communities and, above all, of the national community, which are very precious rights for citizens, since it is in this circle that the most real and legitimate democracy is expressed. we are at the heart of what we have called the process of reducing duties. this process would go much further than is generally believed, because a whole series of commanders and minorities have begun to show themselves, understanding that if the charter is uniform and binding, adopted in addition under the dubious conditions of so-called european democracy, it could in the coming years constitute the weak link in the democratic chain. that is why the europe of nations group believes that the charter, if there is a charter, should be very brief, and present only the essential values, the fundamental principles of the countries of europe, in the form of a political declaration. it is also possible that the candidate countries will join the union by the end of this year, in order to show that they belong to the circle of european values. in this case, the proclamation of the charter by the present and future members should be common. what is certain, madam president, is that it is necessary in any case to avoid imposing on the countries of europe, under the pretext of building the post-national society that mr duff was calling for a moment ago, a uniform and binding text which would be perceived as an attack on the freedom of choice of national democracies. each country must continue to be free to choose its own rules in accordance with its own culture and development. we would like the intergovernmental conference, as it begins its work, to keep this great rule of respect for national democracies in mind.

mr president, the question we have heard many times in this debate is: what is the purpose of the charter of human rights when there are one or more universal conventions on human rights, a european convention on human rights, and human rights appear in the constitutions of all the member states, in those of the candidate countries and, generally, in the constitutions of all the countries, even those which do not respect them? it is certainly not, as has been said before, to improve or strengthen human rights within the european construction. no, and we must pay tribute to mrs berès for having just given a clear sense to this debate which marks an absolutely fundamental turning point in the history of european construction: the transition from an economic, commercial and market europe to a political and institutional europe. of course, the charter of human rights is the first step in that direction, but, as with everything that characterizes the construction of europe, the approach is oblique, hidden, circumvented, i would dare to say "jesuitic". we are not dealing with a constitution and its content, we are dealing with a charter of human rights, which is obviously the preamble to a constitution, on the understanding that the preamble to the constitution would eventually give rise to the constitution and then eventually to a state. the interesting thing about this approach - and we must pay a second tribute to mrs berès for her lucidity and honesty, even though, as she knows, i totally disagree with her on the purpose - is that it tends to determine the principles that will be those of the european communities, or the community of human beings living in the european union. when mrs berès speaks of rights which apply not only to citizens but also to people who are passing through and to residents, she is addressing a question which i believe should be developed in the texts which have been submitted and which will be submitted to this parliament, namely, what will be the basis of the rights which will govern the european union? will it be citizenship in the traditional sense, with rights that are specific to men belonging to a particular community? or will it be rights extended to others than citizens themselves, with a shift, or at least a beginning of a shift, between democracy based on citizenship and democracy based on equal treatment of individuals who live, reside or transit through the territories of the european union? i think we are only seeing the beginnings of this problem, but i think it is absolutely essential to see the beginnings of it in order to be able to follow the thread.
