the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. we have discussed this today at the commission meeting, particularly as regards the link with the directives on habitats and birds. the basic principle is clear: actions co-financed by the structural funds and the cohesion fund should contribute to the protection and improvement of the environment within the european union. this is confirmed in the new regulatory framework for the structural funds and the cohesion fund, as well as in the relevant commission directives. it should be remembered that both the cohesion fund and the structural funds finance major investments in environmental infrastructure such as water treatment plants or waste management systems. let me make one thing clear so there's no misunderstanding. the general regulation on the structural funds states that 'the actions financed must be compatible with the provisions of the treaty, with the instruments adopted within its framework and with community policies and actions'. contrary to what was suggested in one of the oral questions, this is not a new obligation for member states. in fact, its basis is closer to the previous framework regulation on the structural funds for the 1994-1999 programming period. the structural funds regulation has been approved by the member states and the council. as far as site protection is concerned in the framework of the habitats and birds directives, it is important that we do not grant funding for measures which harm sites which deserve protection - on the one hand, we would grant funding and on the other hand, we would fine a member state. we confirmed this this afternoon in the commission and michel barnier will present our decisions in a letter to the member states in a few days' time. in this connection, the commission intends to make full use of the possibilities offered by the new framework regulation for the cohesion fund and the structural funds. following the letter sent to the member states by commissioners wulf-mathies and bjerregaard on 23 june 1999, the commission will insist that the programming documents for 2000-06 must reflect a firm and irrevocable commitment to ensure that programmes are consistent with the protection of sites in accordance with natura 2000. member states will have to communicate sites, if not already done, in accordance with an agreed timetable and they will have to formally guarantee that they will not take any action leading to the deterioration of sites potentially eligible for natura 2000. the commission will now use all the means at its disposal to ensure that the commitments included in the programming documents are fully respected. it intends to monitor the situation in the member states and to carry out on-the-spot checks. the commission representative on the monitoring committees for each programme will also ensure that the obligations of the member states with regard to natura 2000 are fully respected. in addition, if a member state were to fail to meet its commitments to provide a list in accordance with the habitats and birds directives within the timeframe set out in the programming documents, the commission would take immediate action. in particular, this includes - except in specific situations and in accordance with the principle of proportionality - the possible recourse to the provisions of the cohesion fund and structural funds regulations concerning suspensions of payments. of course, all this is in addition to infringement proceedings against a member state for failing to apply these directives. in short, we decided today in the commission to insist that the member states send us their natura 2000 lists, which should have been sent to us already, as was said several years ago. we will use the means at our disposal to ensure that they honour their commitments. without these lists, neither the member states nor the commission can guarantee that we will protect these important natural sites when we carry out operations under the structural funds for the simple reason that we do not know where these sites are. i would like to add a comment on the habitats directive. the commission does not agree that this directive lacks clarity. the directive aims to establish a reference framework which, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, leaves the detailed application to the member states. although the commission has no intention of revising this directive, its services are ready to provide assistance to the member states with regard to its application and we are finally starting to make progress. the only sites that the commission takes into consideration in the framework of the habitats directive are those which have been submitted by the authorities within the member states. the so-called 'ghost lists' can only be an aid to the identification of sites in the member states. at community level, they may contribute to scientific reference material for the creation of inventories of existing natural habitats and species.

in writing. - the brussels commission's directive on the authorization of the incorporation into the composition of chocolate of a number of vegetable fats cheaper than cocoa butter clearly serves the interests of the five multinational companies which share three quarters of the european market. since the product misnamed chocolate will not even be cheaper, the consumer does not regain in purchase price what he loses in transparency with regard to the nature of the product. while we do not share the protectionist concerns behind the defence of 'real chocolate', we see no reason to vote for the brussels directive.
in writing. - after more than two years of delay, the council adopted a common position on the directive on cocoa and chocolate products in october 1999. as it stands, this text does not protect the interests of consumers, chocolate makers and cocoa producers, nor does it guarantee the quality of chocolate. it trivializes the use of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter, does not provide for rigorous consumer information and makes little provision for the absence of a reliable method of analysis and measurement of fats in chocolate. the proposal thus does not in any way respond to the concerns expressed by meps during the vote on first reading on 23 october 1998. this text opens the door to the industrial production of cocoa butter equivalents made from palm oil, which is much cheaper than cocoa. adoption of the new law would result in a dramatic fall in income for the 11 million people living off cocoa in west africa and for all the producing regions. to make us swallow this bitter potion, efforts have been made to give the text a social flavour by claiming that it defends the interests of the poorest countries producing shea butter, such as mali or burkina faso. however, there is no guarantee that the chocolate industry will use shea nut oil, which can in any case only replace up to 50% of cocoa butter. this is a largely artificial opposition between cocoa producers and shea producers, between poor countries and poorer countries. in reality, this proposal for a directive expresses above all the position of the multinational chocolate companies and ultimately safeguards only their interests. so she can't satisfy me. that is why i fully support the amendments which give priority to the concerns of the artisan chocolatiers, the interests of consumers and the future of millions of cocoa farmers.
in writing. - i would first like to congratulate the rapporteur on the tenacity he has shown in this 'chocolate' dossier. i shall briefly recall the main points of this report. in 1996, the european commission proposed to us to amend the 1973 directive which allowed the united kingdom, ireland and denmark to derogate from the current standard by replacing part of the cocoa butter in chocolate with other vegetable fats (vgm) up to a maximum of 5% of the total weight. with the accession of new member states, the number of countries authorising gmms other than cocoa butter has increased to seven with finland (which authorises 10%), austria, portugal and sweden. the other eight countries (belgium, france, germany, greece, italy, luxembourg, spain, and the netherlands) have banned it. the proposal therefore aims to give member states the possibility, in general, of authorizing the addition of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter in chocolate products up to a maximum of 5% of the total weight of the finished product. this has, of course, occasionally generated heated debate and, above all, has reawakened legitimate concerns among consumers. the latter, who felt particularly threatened a few years ago when europe tried to impose "european products" on us through harmonization directives, have shown their willingness to defend their culinary traditions. a life-saving trend has emerged to promote food quality alongside food diversity. in the present case, while it is not disputed that member states using gmms instead of cocoa butter are entitled to market their products, it remains to be seen whether it is legitimate to market them under the name 'chocolate'. the substitution of cocoa butter by other gmos raises the question of safeguarding the very nature of chocolate. the market must therefore be governed by sufficient guarantees for consumers, but also for cocoa producers. we must demand: - a method of analysis to determine the exact content of gmms other than cocoa butter, which was not provided for by the european commission; unfortunately, this requirement has not been included in the council's common position, but i still believe that it is a sine qua non condition for compliance with the 5% rule. - a very explicit statement for consumers so that they can buy with full knowledge of the facts; - the reservation of the term 'quality chocolate' for products containing cocoa butter; - the limitation of gmos as substitutes to tropical plant material not obtained by enzymatic production processes and not derived from genetic engineering; i agree with these demands, which are reflected in the amendments tabled by the rapporteur. i am a consumer who is concerned about the quality and taste of traditional chocolate. i also believe that consumer protection policy, which is a community policy, is not just about food safety and health protection. it must aim at the promotion of quality food as part of a more general philosophy, that of quality of life!
in writing. - this 1996 proposal for a directive is part of the achievement of the harmonization of the internal market, the commission thus giving member states the possibility of authorising the addition of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter in chocolate products up to a maximum of 5% of the total weight of the finished product. it also provides for the marketing of such chocolate products containing vegetable fats (vgm) in all member states, subject to labelling indicating the list of ingredients. like the rapporteur, i am of the opinion that we should go back to the first reading that parliament had in 1997 and not allow this addition and marketing. i still think that we should reserve the label 'quality chocolate' for chocolates containing no gm substitution and recommend an impact study on cocoa exports from developing countries; finally, i would like to see clear and precise labelling for consumers. this is a principled position, which is difficult to negotiate, since it is a matter of defending quality products and the consumers we all are. i therefore urge the house to vote in favour of the amendments tabled by our rapporteur and, in doing so, to vote against the position of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy.
- we're stepping on the head. in a europe which declares its will to protect the consumer, which speaks of quality and authenticity labels, we are faced with a common position of the council which prefers to distort a hitherto high-quality product, chocolate, rather than to offend the multinational agro-food companies. this is not surprising, since the same europe produces mad cows, trembling sheep, chickens with dioxin, imports hormone-laden meat and genetically modified cereals. the consumer is indeed 'informed' that the product he is buying is counterfeit. but what hypocrisy ! what a piece of information ! in tiny print, in a language that you can't understand, on the back of the packaging. you are used to doing everything in the name of your dogmas, of free movement, of free competition, of free trade. please do not make any more mistakes with our gastronomic traditions, our quality products or the terroir. stop playing with the food. that would be real progress. you will have understood: my colleagues from the coordination of the european right and i will vote for the 'zero option', zero vegetable fat other than cocoa butter in chocolate.
in writing. - this directive changes the very definition of chocolate which we believe should be made from cocoa beans and cocoa butter. we have no right to mislead the consumer by using the term 'chocolate' to describe products which are not necessarily made from cocoa. consumers demand clear and unambiguous information. they can't stand being cheated anymore. today's vote was about more than chocolate. it's the confidence of our fellow citizens that's at stake. that is why i voted for all the amendments to improve this directive which were tabled by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy.
in writing. - despite the laudable efforts of paul lannoye, i personally did not vote in favour of the text submitted to us, which aims to allow the inclusion of 5% vegetable fats (vgm) in chocolate, because it is the very type of european regulation that causes misunderstanding among our fellow citizens and breeds euroscepticism. where a clear and unambiguous labelling requirement would have been sufficient for the marketing of all types of chocolate in europe, we are being offered one of these unusual compromises, the secret of which we know: it will not be 0% vgm as in 8 countries, it will not be 10% as in others, the cut-off has fallen to 5% throughout europe! 5 per cent of the total value of the goods, which is obviously uncontrollable, for the greatest benefit of the industry which will soon have flooded the market with cheap counterfeit chocolate and also caused a rise in the price of real chocolate, which has been made into a luxury product for privileged consumers. will we harmonize the composition of ketchup, mustard, meat products, cheese, beer or pizza in the name of a single market to promote a single taste with the sole aim of facilitating food business? while it is legitimate, for reasons of public health, to legislate on manufacturing processes and the traceability of products, it is equally legitimate to want to impose a gastronomic 'maoist' on the whole of europe in the sole interest of large-scale industry. if the construction of the internal market is a means of strengthening europe in world competition, it must not become a totalitarian dogma and interfere with every aspect of our domestic life. in particular, the diversity of europe's gastronomy and food habits is part of its heritage and culture, albeit at the expense of local specificities that are foreign to the internal market. europeans do not want a standardised consumer europe, free to settle in a large, uniform internal market. they expect europe to have great political ambition rather than fleeting and incidental regulations.
in writing. - the new 'chocolate directive' is a first example of the extraordinarily cumbersome and slow legislative process in the community. the 'simplification' of the 1973 directive, which was launched at the edinburgh council in 1992, was not completed until 1996 with a commission proposal, which was considered at first reading by parliament in 1997, and it took another two and a half years for the council to adopt a common position which is being tabled before us today. does such a long process at least lead to a useful text? the answer is clearly no. the new directive does not meet any need. the 1973 directive clearly and unambiguously defined chocolate as a product composed of sugar and cocoa. to take account of the dietary habits of some northern countries, some exceptions were made. so the situation was satisfactory. why change it ? why, under the pretext of 'simplifying', is the 1973 directive being subverted? would the acquis communautaire then no longer be inviolable? in fact, the change in the content of the directive was brought about by pressure from the five multinationals (nestlé, suchard, mars, cadbury and ferrero) which already share more than 70% of the european market, but whose production was still hampered by the current double legislation. for example, a site in france cannot produce chocolate that does not meet french standards, which require that it contain no vegetable fat other than cocoa butter. but above all, these multinationals want to minimise the cost of their raw materials. it is not a matter of denaturing the composition of the chocolate. cocoa butter accounts for 8 to 9% of the total price of chocolate. shea butter is one third the price of cocoa butter and palm oil is ten times cheaper. by adopting a list of cocoa butter substitutes and providing for a percentage, the new directive creates a gap, and that is the main point. it will be enough tomorrow to extend it, to increase the percentage and to add soybeans, for example, to the vegetable fats we are offered today. shea butter will have played its role as an alibi and its producers will then suffer the same effects as those which will be felt by cocoa producers in the sense of lower prices as a result of the adoption of a directive which resolutely ignores its own developmental consequences and cynically defers their examination to the greek calendar. to achieve their aims - to produce and sell cheaper fake chocolate under the name of chocolate throughout the union - these multinationals have constantly allowed the 1973 derogations to become the rule, in defiance of the interests of chocolate and cocoa producers. the common position fully meets their requirements by proposing to make a derogation which corresponded to a dietary habit confined to some of the 15 member states a uniform and binding rule for all of them. does this at least raise the level of demand and quality for all member states? i'm not going to. it's the opposite. the alignment is, as usual, to the lowest common denominator. what is generalised is the lower quality level, to finally impose a standardised european taste, to the detriment of taste quality. and the burden of proof of quality paradoxically falls on the chocolate maker, who, to his relief, is not forbidden to indicate that he has not added vegetable fats other than cocoa butter! ! will the new text at least enable the consumer to distinguish easily between real and fake chocolate? no, because the text of the directive is dishonest, in that it provides for the possibility of introducing a very precise percentage (5%) of vegetable fat other than cocoa butter into the chocolate manufacturing process, whereas we do not have, as everyone knows, a reliable method of analysis to control this. the commission therefore sets a percentage which it knows is unverifiable. it's called deception. the text also contains dishonest labelling provisions. our parliament had appropriately adopted at first reading, on the initiative of mr lannoye, an amendment providing for the obligation to have a clearly legible indication on the front of the product indicating the presence of vegetable fats other than cocoa butter. the amendment was not adopted by the council and the consumer will not be properly informed. in all countries and for all consumers who are fond of genuine chocolate, the name 'chocolate' can now legally cover a product that has been completely denatured. in favour of a community mechanism which constantly dilutes the responsibility of everyone, the definition of a basic product of our food is changed, and this for the sole purpose of allowing a few multinationals to maximize their profits. chocolate lovers, please enjoy your next easter eggs with a religious heart. this will be the last time you can be sure that they are made of real and genuine chocolate, the kind that existed before the harmonization. and after the chocolate, who's next?
in writing. - labelling, when you hold us... here is a distinctive sign at european level which we want to give new strength here. this label, like the french nf environnement label, is voluntary, i.e. it is up to the industrialists to apply for it. it is based on the principle of a global approach, which takes into account the entire life cycle of the product. however, not all national signs should be placed in the background. because consumers, buyers, have their own codes, and they've built their trust on the logos that they know. the desire to replace the national logo would again be tantamount to confusing the citizen living in the european union, lost among the lists of ingredients, quality labels, logos, references to regions... a forest of indications. it's almost like a chocolate bar. we are keen to defend smes in terms of facilitating access to the community eco-labels which should be considered, and we support the rapporteur.
in writing. - waste management is a very complex task and lobbying is important. the european union has therefore adopted a comprehensive strategy to address this major environmental and health challenge. the directive we are discussing today is one of them, since it aims to regulate the thermal treatment of hazardous and non-hazardous waste. i must say that i have always been personally concerned about the incineration of hazardous and non-hazardous waste being dealt with in the same legislation. i have already expressed my concerns and questions during the first reading. a majority decided in favour of co-incineration, which does not satisfy me. that is why i am today campaigning for measures to be taken to ensure that there is no lowering of the emission standards for hazardous waste. everyone knows that the volume of waste to be incinerated within the european union will increase. as for municipal waste, 31 million tonnes were incinerated in 1990, and the figure will be over 56 million this year. there are several reasons for this, which are related to the increase in the volume of waste produced and the decrease in the amount of waste sent to landfills. it is well known that the incineration of waste results in emissions of substances which seriously pollute the air, soil and water and are therefore hazardous to health. the pollutants emitted depend on both the nature of the waste to be treated and the technologies used to treat it. this is why our concerns are focused on emissions of heavy metals, dioxins and furans. the debate has particularly focused on co-incineration plants. i would remind you that these plants use hazardous waste as fuel in the production of energy or material elements. it is true that the provisions of the applicable directives require the use of hazardous waste to be limited to a maximum of 40% of the fuels used. that percentage is too high! particularly stringent control standards should apply to these installations and these standards should be as stringent as those imposed on incinerators. i would also like to stress that the widespread use of hazardous waste must not lead us to accept the production of such waste. the risk is particularly great that tomorrow we will hear that investments have been made to build co-incinerators and that we now have to make them profitable! i strongly reject in advance these arguments which will lead to an increase in the volume of transport of dangerous goods with all the risks this entails for the environment and for safety. in conclusion, while recalling that infringements must be punished and that communities that standardise their incinerators must be supported, it is important to stress that our priority is and must remain the prevention of the production of waste, whether hazardous or not.
in writing. - the impressive volume of waste generated by our industrialized urban societies is undoubtedly one of the great challenges facing the european union in the 21st century: the planet is gradually and insensibly being overwhelmed, and every year no less than 2 000 million tonnes of waste are produced by the member states of our community. in these circumstances, it is inconceivable to approach the management of this waste according to the law of the least immediate cost: indeed, the flourishing industry (tens of thousands of jobs, billions of euros) which thrives on this growing need will undoubtedly have much to invent to fulfil its mission properly, in particular by avoiding, in turn, to pollute, under the cover of recovery: incineration returns particles of heavy metals and dioxins to the atmosphere, sewage treatment generates unwanted sludge, and some recycled materials have not found their market. the best possible protection of the environment and health therefore requires significant progress in the implementation of waste management legislation, which is still far from being transposed satisfactorily, according to a recent commission report. it is therefore necessary to encourage the member states and their industries to make rapid efforts to adapt - from their national legislation to the principles of precautions and environmental protection, and from their techniques to eradicate and not to move the problem of pollution - but at the same time it would be wise for the european parliament to chart realistic paths towards achievable objectives, rather than indulge in its lyrical inclinations and idealistic statements to the detriment of its credibility in environmental matters: it is only by going through the immediate possibilities that it will preserve the chances of achieving the desired sustainability. the uen group has therefore not supported amendments which are not applicable in our states and whose foreseeable economic consequences would be very harmful. as for the rest, and as a local elected official, i hope that a merger and simplification of the community directives will make the regulatory framework within which the departmental waste management plans must be included clearer and easier.
in writing. - i examined this report as mayor, since the commission's proposal is mainly concerned with strengthening the existing legislation on the incineration of municipal waste, which, incidentally, shows the usefulness for a member of the european parliament of being able to exercise the highly complementary mandate of mayor, a possibility that the current french government intends to prohibit us in a way that is both unfair and absurd, because it is in no one's interest to cut off the european parliamentarians from the field. the aim of the directive is to prevent and reduce the negative effects of waste incineration and co-incineration. but we cannot support the proposal to subject all installations to the same emission standards. this is not the way to deal with the problem of overcapacity in incinerators in europe. the rapporteur agrees: some waste streams are easier to treat in a co-incineration plant. we believe that some of the proposed amendments to the common position are in fact likely to disrupt the upgrading of existing installations and to penalize the co-incineration of hazardous waste in cement works, which mainly concerns france and belgium. i would like to make a few comments on municipal waste. first, it is not appropriate to create confusion as regards the definition of 'mixed municipal waste' in the context of co-incineration. the equation between 'partially separated waste' and 'untreated mixed municipal waste', as is done in amendment no 14, risks affecting the development of waste sorting systems, which we are seeking to develop, and whose residues or certain fractions would be likely to be co-incinerated. on the other hand, if article 7-4 were amended, thus removing the qualification of municipal waste as 'untreated', this would amount to prohibiting the co-incineration of fractions of sorted municipal waste (paper, cardboard, etc.) which could not be recycled unless they were collected separately. finally, the lowering of the threshold of 6 tonnes per hour, above which existing domestic waste incineration plants are subject to an atmospheric emission limit value of 200 mg per cubic metre for nox, cannot be accepted, as the planning by local authorities of the adaptation of existing equipment operates on this threshold (see annex v-a). although we know that incineration is not a perfect solution, it is an important step forward for many communities, which have invested heavily in developing modern municipal waste management. this must be taken into account, although, of course, further reflection and research must be carried out. the waste treatment industry will probably have to invent a lot in the future to avoid polluting in turn. we will therefore need to develop wider waste management strategies and actively promote research and development in this area which is essential to the lives and future of our local communities.
in writing. - according to the texts of the ancients, the disposal of waste was already a problem in ancient rome, although since then, this waste has been the joy of generations of archaeologists. back then, most waste was biodegradable, which is far from the case today. we talked about chocolate. well, here's a practical way to illustrate this by, for example, following the path of a chocolate bar pack from the trash to the incinerator and discovering that the combustion of the aluminum foil produces toxic gases. we are facing a very important challenge in waste management. i believe, however, that some countries are not prepared either materially or intellectually. today, three hundred incinerators are responsible for one third of the household and similar waste treated by the french waste disposal system. incineration generates pollutant emissions: dust, metals and dioxins which need to be controlled by a flue-gas treatment system. the regulations on the limitation of emissions have gradually become more stringent. of course, action is needed to ensure that the rules are respected, because health and the environment must be protected, but we do not want the scope of application and the definition of co-incineration plants to be changed. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the environment is not affected by the new regulations. on the other hand, changes in legislation on co-incinerators or the specific treatment of hazardous waste risk distorting costs and even leading to unjustified waste tourism. there is a real risk of favouring one sector at the expense of others by means of ill-adjusted limit values, when we need all four incineration sectors; the commission has already proposed that the member states should set up a specialised unit for hazardous waste, a specialised unit for non-hazardous waste, a specialised unit for co-incineration and a specialised unit for incineration by suitable combustion plants. i would like to draw the attention of my colleagues to another point, albeit a secondary one. however, i believe that communication work is necessary following the merger of these directives. the public has the impression that special waste, hazardous waste, non-hazardous waste, municipal waste, all of them will be mixed and treated together in the same furnace, in the same facility. the sorting of waste would therefore seem to be useless at their level. this would require a real effort to inform and explain.
in this debate on air quality, we are discussing, through the davies report, the problem of ozone in the ambient air. all experts agree that it is imperative to raise air quality standards so that citizens throughout the european union are effectively protected against the health risks posed by ozone in the air. the health effects of ozone are varied: irritation of the eyes, nose and throat, respiratory discomfort, cough, headache, etc. ozone also contributes to asthma attacks, impaired respiratory function and increased responsiveness of the bronchi. in the long run, it can even cause premature lung aging. this is a frightening observation to say the least, which is why i welcome this proposal for a directive with great satisfaction! the aim is to amend existing community legislation on ozone in accordance with the requirements of council directive 96/62/ec on the assessment and management of ambient air quality. it sets long-term objectives and intermediate target values for ozone in ambient air. it also introduces a framework of standards to protect human health and the environment. it also called on the member states to monitor ozone concentrations and to make the results public. the directive will therefore be a reference instrument for the level of ozone in ambient air. the commission proposes to use the air quality guidelines adopted by the world health organisation in 1997 to set long-term objectives. the first objective is to prevent these ceilings from being exceeded and thus to avoid harmful effects on human health and the environment. however, the commission's proposals do not set a date for their implementation. it's a pity. in the first stage, target values are established. the aim is to achieve them, as far as possible, by 2010. these values are also based on who guidelines, but it is accepted that they may be exceeded on a number of days per year. it should be stressed that the commission proposal does not take account of the changes which could result from the commitments made by the community on climate change. the eu is also proposing a reduction of 8% in greenhouse gases. and if these commitments are met, member states should be more ambitious in their targets for reducing ozone levels. in conclusion, i am relatively satisfied with the text of this proposal for a directive because it is an important step towards achieving the main objective set out in the fifth environmental action programme: never exceeding critical levels of ozone in ambient air.
in writing. - we are debating today a legislative proposal which concerns us all directly, since it aims to improve ambient air quality. this is a proposal for a directive on national emission ceilings for certain air pollutants (a directive under the framework directive on air quality). it is part of the community's fifth environmental action programme (eap). the main objective is to limit emissions of acidifying and eutrophicating pollutants and ozone precursors in order to improve the protection of the environment and human health against the harmful effects of acidification, soil eutrophication and ground-level ozone. the ceilings set out in this text must be respected by 2010 at the latest. with this in mind, member states should draw up programmes for the progressive reduction of their annual national emissions and report to the commission before the end of 2002. the programmes will be reviewed and updated in 2006. they are also required to prepare for 2010 and regularly update national emission inventories and emission forecasts for so2, nox, voc and nh3. these inventories and forecasts must be communicated annually to the commission. the rapporteur has proposed amendments to strengthen this proposal. it suggests, in particular, that stricter standards be set for the emissions of the four pollutants in question. i can only support such proposals in principle. indeed, when it comes to health and the environment, we must be ambitious if we are to claim to be improving the situation. however, setting the bar too high can be counterproductive. i therefore think that for the time being it is better to stick to the objectives set in the international conventions, while being aware that the ceilings may be revised in the light of the progress made. the report also calls on the commission to propose further amendments to the directive by 2004. the commission will be able to review the ceilings set in the text, the interim environmental objectives and the new measures taken to ensure compliance with the ceilings. these possible corrections will make it possible to adapt the directive to technical and scientific progress and would make it possible to achieve the objectives for 2010 eventually. i think it's a good compromise. the rapporteur also proposes setting target dates for achieving the agreed objectives; i think that is essential. without a deadline to be respected, texts too often remain declarations of intent without action. the same applies to the system of penalties for infringements of the provisions of the directive.
in writing. - the ambition of full employment, which is a term that is back on the agenda with the return of some growth, is certainly a laudable intention, but without addressing the real causes of unemployment, it will be difficult to achieve it. we all know that despite growth, job creation in europe is notoriously inadequate. they are also marked by precariousness, especially when they concern women and young people. the only thing to do is to go beyond declarations of intent, even if they are positive. in the face of extremely high social expectations, it is urgent to set measurable and verifiable objectives. i would have very much liked to see a commitment to the proposals in my group's resolution, for example: - the launch of a process of reducing working time without reducing wages or flexibility; - a revision of the directives on european works councils and collective redundancies, in order to strengthen the rights and powers of employees and their trade union organisations, particularly in the event of mergers and restructuring; - the introduction, at community level, of a tax on speculative capital movements and a reinforced fight against tax fraud and tax evasion. i deeply regret that we are not engaging in a new type of sustainable development, based on a fairer distribution of wealth, on increasing the purchasing power of households and on the revival of public and social investment. for all these reasons, we shall not vote on the joint resolution.

mr president, mrs ferrer's report has a title which seems to us to be at best incomplete and at worst a cover-up. it would be more correct to speak of an eu-nafta agreement, rather than an agreement associating mexico alone with the european union, because this agreement, which the rapporteur himself has described as the most important agreement ever signed by the european union with a third country, will not only affect our relations with that country, but will have consequences for all our relations with the countries of north and central america. the ferrer report, in a style that is clearly in vogue in this parliament, sets itself the objective of helping to create a new framework for european companies to compete on equal terms, particularly with the united states and canada. this is an objective which is not achievable in the near future and it is clear to whom the measures advocated in the text are designed. indeed, who can see that the decline in european exports to mexico is the result of the nafta agreement, which makes the whole area a single free trade area? who then seriously believes that, for example, european textile and automobile products, which are currently taxed at 35% and 23% respectively, will soon be able, whatever the details of the system put in place, to compete on equal terms with us exports of the same kind taxed at 1.8%. what's the matter? in these circumstances, who can justify the opening up of the respective markets at different rates to the detriment of the europeans? finally, who is not afraid that the consequences for employment in europe in sectors open to mexican products will, on the contrary, be felt immediately, particularly in the weakest sectors - textiles, to name but one - which do not need additional competition, the counterpart of which is the opening up of markets closed by the americans? in addition, the terms which are supposed to reassure us about the rules applicable to the protection of designations of origin and more generally to intellectual property would have the opposite effect, since their vagueness and wording seem to us to constitute more of a threat than a guarantee.
- mr president, 'the best is the enemy of the good' is a saying in france, and i am afraid that mrs read's report is a striking illustration of this. no one will deny the importance of the means of communication, and in particular the internet, for the future development of our societies, nor the delay which the member states of the european union are currently allowing in this respect vis-à-vis the united states, nor the need to codify the potentially anarchic development of these means in such a way as to limit the deviations to which they can give rise and to ensure their widest possible success among our populations. i am afraid, however, that the catalogue of good intentions which we are hearing today is actually detrimental to the objective pursued. instead of moving forward step by step by setting a concrete and quantifiable short- or medium-term objective for the member states, parliament is sending a mixed and confused signal, which is, admittedly, largely due to the quirks of committee work. we would have liked to have received more details on the specific nature of the european approach to this matter and, in particular, on how the commission intends to help the member states to curb the rapid standardization, modelled on the american model, which will certainly facilitate the development of these tools based on purely technical and commercial considerations. the report's educational and social concerns are certainly commendable, but they will ultimately weigh relatively little against the immediate repercussions that the extension of this tool as it stands will have on the peoples of europe. how compatible is the commission's text with the existence of specific taxation of trade and employment in the various member states? what possibilities are there to enforce our conceptions of individual freedom and freedom of expression, which are not yet harmonized at world level? what guarantees are there that the security of our states will be assured in the context of the development of a technology whose main operators belong to a great power which, while giving lessons of liberalism to the whole world, never forgets, for its part, to ensure that its companies scrupulously respect its conception of the national interest? - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with the e-europe initiative the commission is reminding us that europe has lagged behind in the development of the information society. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. but beyond this, we must also consider the quality of this backwardness: economic, political and social. how do you measure it? the commission wants to launch a political initiative, so let us take it at face value. yes, there is a european backlog in the access to the information society as a tool, a tool of knowledge, a tool of creation, a tool for exchange. yes, there is a lag in the development of commerce made possible by the internet. but are these two delays the same? some will say 'whatever', that we must develop this wonderful tool of digital information in all directions and that this objective is sufficient in itself. this may be the impression given by the commission's initiative. indeed, can we be satisfied with a catalogue of objectives, where the development of small businesses is placed on the same level as the development of public services, where e-commerce competes with university training? the absence of such a system raises the question of the content of the information which is supposed to circulate through the digital tool. standardized content or content reflecting europe's cultural and linguistic diversity? social content or merchant content? the information society is already creating social networks, developing new cultural experiences and creating spaces for political debate and opinion. the question is to measure it. the commission speaks of the european backlog and the urgency of closing it. between delay and urgency, we must not be content with speeding up a process to the detriment of reflecting on the democratic and political conditions for its implementation. technological progress is a well-known slogan. the change we are witnessing is analogous to the birth of the printing press. the challenges and changes that this brings require serious reflection. if the objectives are the development of employment and democratic access, as mrs read's report so well recalls, it would be a pity to see them evaluated only in terms of the market and economic development.
- mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to thank mrs read for this report and i should like to make it clear at the outset that i shall simply concentrate on the social aspects which we feel deserve further development. with the lisbon summit only a few days away, it seems to me that the european parliament must send a clear signal to the governments of the member states that europe's entry into the digital age, and therefore into a new economy with enormous potential, must not be at the expense of social cohesion. the need for a strong social anchoring, the taking into account of the real needs of citizens are, in my view, the sine qua non conditions for the success of the information society, as we understand it in europe, which cannot be built on the basis of market forces alone. we must be very vigilant in ensuring that all sectors of society benefit from the information society, and we must not create a society in which access to new technologies and the exploitation of their potential are conditional on social inclusion or exclusion. i think that three elements should be considered, together with the risks and concerns they entail. the first concerns users, and the risk of having a gap between the different victims of social exclusion. the cost of internet access, the exclusion of entire groups of the population (young unemployed, housewives, elderly), and the shortcomings in education and vocational training systems are all mortgages on an information society that must benefit everyone. the second concern is the number of people working in this sector; the flexibility of the labour market means that workers must be provided with organisational structures and guarantees of their rights, whether in the field of social security, pensions or the exercise of employment in the necessary safe conditions. the third and final item concerns the question of public service and the improvement of democratic systems of development of procedures....

in writing. - at its meeting on 7 may 1999, the european parliament approved the eu-mexico comprehensive agreement, although no member was aware of the terms of the negotiations on its trade side. in addition, impunity, human rights violations, repression of social movements and an undeclared war against the indigenous people of chiapas - all of which have been denounced by the united nations high commissioner for human rights and the inter-american commission on human rights, among others - continue in mexico and are contrary to the commitments made by the mexican authorities in this agreement (title i, article 1). the association agreement was designed to serve the interests of large transnational companies on both sides of the atlantic, as is shown by the content of title iv of the text, which refers to 'capital movements and related payments'. the trade section contains several of the most dangerous parts of the mia (multilateral agreement on investment). finally, this agreement ignores most of the proposals of the social, trade union, human rights and environmental organizations of mexico and the european union, which want social, cultural and political collaboration to take precedence over mercantilist aspects. for all these reasons, we are voting against ratification of the agreement.
in writing. - we voted against the joint motion for a resolution because it constitutes a quitus granted in advance to the european commission, which we disapprove of both in form and substance. we abstained on the gue resolution because, while we agree with many of its criticisms of the commission, in the recital it calls the commission an 'indispensable institutional instrument', which is not our position.
mr president, we heard a lot yesterday from the speakers of the federalist majority in this parliament that the charter of fundamental rights in preparation was going to give a great boost to the rights of citizens. however, the conditions under which this operation was launched show a disregard for the lives of citizens and can give rise to serious concerns about the future. firstly, we saw a few months ago, in paragraphs 44 and 45, in the cologne conclusions, the decision to launch the drafting of a charter of fundamental rights. who was consulted before the meeting ? no one, especially not the national parliaments, had ever heard of it. but it must be remembered that the fundamental rights are essentially the prerogatives of the national parliaments and, for the most part, of the various peoples of europe. of course, some will say that this was just a new display of existing rights, but it is clear that the operation will go much further, with the european parliament already calling for an innovative charter. in any case, there was no reason to exclude the national parliaments. the latter now find themselves in the convention which is preparing the charter, but as one partner among others, who will serve as a guarantee for a work which they will not have mastered. worse still, they will not even participate in the final stage, since the cologne conclusions provided for the charter to be proclaimed jointly by the council, the european parliament and the commission. yes, i did say "the commission". the national parliaments are thus being replaced by a body of civil servants who will "proclaim the charter". we 're stepping on heads ! democracy is being pushed aside, supposedly for the good of the citizens, but isn't that how europe usually works?
in writing. - our abstention from voting on the charter does not in any way represent an objection to its european character. we are convinced that the future belongs to a europe without frontiers between people united from one end of the continent to the other. yet the european institutions, like the national institutions, are infinitely more representative of the interests of big business than of the peoples in general, and of the working people in particular. the democratic rights and freedoms, like democracy itself, can only be truly expressed in so far as they do not run counter to the interests of the large industrial and financial groups. whether one or the other of the two institutional developments implicit in the debate centred on the charter is taken into account, these groups can take economic decisions that are catastrophic for an entire population, leading, for example, to the closure of factories, the ruin or pollution of an entire region. we therefore believe that a truly unified and democratic europe can only exist if it is rid of the de facto power of the big industrial and financial groups, which is a necessary condition for the people to have real and democratic control over their institutions.
in writing. - it was with great satisfaction that i learned in june last year of the decision of the european council in cologne to convene the convention (composed of representatives of the heads of state and government, the european parliament, the national parliaments and the commission) to draw up a charter of fundamental rights. this charter is indispensable for the continuation, under good conditions, of the political deepening of the european union. it will fill a gap that has existed since the union and the european community have seen their powers expand, with the european institutions taking decisions that increasingly directly affect the lives of european citizens. the latter must have a text to which they can refer in support of their defence before the court of justice of the european communities. to this end, provision should be made for direct recourse under certain conditions. the charter will also help to define a 'collective heritage of values and principles in which citizens recognise themselves and which inspires the policies of the union', a heritage which we must constantly defend against the racist and xenophobic influences which have unfortunately not disappeared! as the representative of the peoples of the european union, our parliament must be particularly vigilant about the content of this document. the expectations of european citizens must lead us to be bold. our demands are clear. the charter should be legally binding, as it is incorporated into the treaty. to this end, the committee on constitutional affairs requests the council to include the charter on the igc agenda. any amendment to the charter will have to follow the same procedure as for its elaboration, including a consent of the european parliament. any secondary legislation which may affect fundamental rights will have to be approved by the european parliament. the indivisibility of fundamental rights must be recognised and its scope extended to all the institutions and bodies of the union, and to all its policies (including those under the second and third pillars), within the framework of the competences conferred on it by the treaty. member states will have to respect the charter in so far as they apply or transpose union law. as regards the content of the charter itself, it seems desirable to divide rights into three categories. the charter would enshrine civic rights directly linked to european citizenship, such as the right to vote, the right to petition, the right to refer cases to the ombudsman; the european union has also adopted a number of measures to promote the protection of human rights, i.e. all the rights protected by the various international organisations and the new rights (bioethics, protection of personal data), social rights: the right to a minimum income, the right to strike, the right to unemployment benefits. i will conclude by saying that this charter must be seen as a central part of a process which must lead to the european union being given a constitution!
in writing. - the debate on the charter of fundamental rights reveals the lack of legitimacy and transparency in the construction of europe. the right to competition and profit is now above human rights. we are in favour of a different logic, starting from the requirement that the economy be subordinated to the satisfaction of human and ecological rights and needs. the charter should be drawn up through a broad public debate involving all the peoples, including those of the candidate countries, and involving trade unions, associations, women's movements and the unemployed in a constituent process. on the basis of the most advanced achievements, such a charter should combine social rights with democratic rights. radical reduction of working time which requires hiring and not flexibility; prohibition of dismissals; requisition of empty houses; the commission's proposal is based on the principle of equal treatment and the right to choose for women, the right to vote and the right to move for immigrants. such a charter would be a point of reference for all those who are fighting against a europe which dismisses workers or expels those without papers.
in writing. - the charter of fundamental rights is the latest incarnation of the constituent drift of community legislation. the interest of such a text is obvious if it is considered as the possible preamble to a european constitution; on the other hand, it would be double-edged in the case of member states which include these rights in their own constitutions and legal traditions and confirm them by ratifying international texts such as the european convention or the universal declaration of human rights. solutions can always be found to improve the application of existing texts, but the technocratic nature of community construction is still required today by the use of the elaboration of a supplementary text whose repetitive character will be difficult to avoid. what worries me most, however, is the content that is meant to be given to these rights. in fact, during this same part-session we are discussing reports from the committee on civil liberties which present a libertarian vision of society. it is not so much a question of defending and promoting human rights as of wiping out all the landmarks on which our societies are based and replacing them with an individualistic magma "without god or master". this construction is the basis for a new totalitarianism in which man finds himself alone in the face of a community administration as distant as it is impersonal, the intermediary bodies - and especially the most essential of them, the family - having been gradually destroyed. our society will no longer be a community of destiny but a juxtaposition of "minorities" each with its own rights and no common duty. the conclusion i draw from these texts is that the just struggle for human rights has become the ideological plaything of irresponsible and selfish people. it is the death of the common good and, beyond that, of the very meaning of life that they offer us today, who, concerned only with human rights, have forgotten what man is first of all and what his roots and aspirations are.
in writing. - the french members of the union for a europe of nations group are very committed to the preservation of natural heritage in general and of ecologically sensitive areas in particular. we share the concern to preserve an environment which we have a duty to pass on intact to our children. this is a commendable and necessary ambition. however, the commission, true to its nature and its habits, cannot help but take the opportunity to burden states and their citizens with new directives and petty, cumbersome rules, often unsuited to local realities. the result of such an over-bid is to paralyse economic operators a little more every day and to restrict the freedom to undertake. this was the case, for example, with the tecs which are trying to turn our farmers into environmental officials, paid not by the fruits of their labour but by subsidies paid to reward their submission to the brussels gosplan. we therefore categorically reject the proposal by mrs jackson to link payments from the structural funds to the transposition of community environmental legislation by the member states. this would be a very dangerous mix of genres which would open the way to a widespread practice of financial blackmail, blackmail all the more unacceptable since the money from the structural funds remains, it should be recalled, above all the fruit of the contributions paid to the community budget by the member states.
in writing. - while we share some of the report's concrete concerns, particularly on women's rights, and while we vote for some amendments which are in the direction of progress, we do not intend to endorse the european union's claim to make 'respect for and promotion of human rights and fundamental freedoms ... the fundamental objectives of its foreign policy'. within the european union itself, one of the fundamental human rights, the right to make a decent living from one's work, is trampled on by nearly 20 million women and men. a more or less significant fraction of immigrant workers, those considered as undocumented, are excluded from any legal existence. and outside, several of the most powerful states of the european union support, arm and finance infamous dictatorships, especially in their former colonial empire. and what about the demonstration of respect for human rights that has been the bombing of kosovo and serbia for several weeks? in these circumstances, we abstain on this report.
in writing. - in this joint discussion on human rights, the report analyses the instruments available to the union to promote these rights in the world and their practical application from 1 june 1998 to 30 june 1999. as you know, the union's international action to promote and protect human rights is based on several instruments, be they cfsp or development cooperation. with the implementation of the amsterdam treaty, the union's international visibility has been enhanced by the appointment of a high representative for the cfsp, javier solana. the treaty of amsterdam has made respect for human rights one of the major objectives of the union's common foreign and security policy. the european union has many instruments in this field. these include common strategies (a new instrument created since the treaty of amsterdam, which aims to strengthen the overall coherence of the union's action at international level), common positions (which define the union's approach to a particular subject) and common actions (which concern certain specific situations and involve immediate responses, on the model of humanitarian aid). there are also specific and horizontal actions on a given policy. this is particularly the case in the fight against the death penalty. finally, the so-called 'human rights' clause, inserted since the 1990s in most cooperation and development agreements with third countries, allows the union to maintain pressure on the countries with which it is linked in the field of human rights. this clause does not change the fundamental nature of the agreements but allows both sides to reaffirm common values and principles as a precondition for all cooperation, whether economic or otherwise. the rapporteur, however, believes that the current european human rights policy is fragmented and must be replaced by a coherent common strategy marked by better interinstitutional cooperation. i agree with that, of course. i believe that through initiatives such as the setting up of an advisory group comprising representatives of the institutions of the union, the member states and human rights experts - a group to discuss strategic aspects of activities in this field - it would be possible to achieve greater coherence and thus greater effectiveness. in the same vein, the development by the union of its own indicators to measure respect for human rights, the appointment of a special envoy of the european parliament for prisoners of conscience and the creation of an eu website on human rights on the internet are proposals that deserve to be taken up. the report also stresses that the systematic elimination of discrimination against women must become a priority in the european union's strategy. i would like to give my unconditional support to such a demand!
in writing. - the european parliament, in adopting the haarder report on human rights in the european union, has just committed one of those outrages which are too commonplace for them not to be in its nature. among other things, it calls for equal rights of all kinds for homosexual couples and traditional families, and the lowering of the legal age of consent for homosexual relations. i would simply like to recall that according to the universal declaration of human rights (article 16) 'the family is the natural and fundamental group of society and is entitled to protection by society and the state'. the family is defined in the same article as the marriage of a man and a woman. the international covenant on economic, social and cultural rights echoes this idea, stating in article 10 that 'the widest possible protection and assistance shall be afforded to the family, which is the natural and fundamental group unit of society'. the traditional family is entitled to this care from the public authorities because it provides a service that has no price: the renewal of generations, the perpetuation of society, the education of children and the transmission of values. this service is a major reason why the family is entitled to special benefits reserved for it alone. by ignoring this fundamental law, the haarder report shows that, on this point as on many others, european mechanisms are not only playing against nations but also against society itself.
in writing. - i welcome the work done by the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy on the annual report on human rights, for the part concerning the european union. this report replaces, i would remind you, the traditional memorandum on the union's activities in this field which the council had previously sent to the european parliament each year to inform it of the union's action in the field of human rights in the world during the previous year. the document aims to explain the union's motivation, as well as the institutional structures and instruments at its disposal to implement an active policy of respect for human rights. more specifically, the report states that new provisions have been created by the treaty of amsterdam in the field of human rights in order to strengthen the basis for union action in this field, in particular in the framework of the cfsp. we must exploit these new opportunities. the treaty thus established as a principle the respect for fundamental rights as guaranteed by the council of europe convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. the union thus 'founds' its action on the principles of democracy, respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms. with enlargement, the european union has clearly announced that any candidate country will have to respect democracy, the rule of law, human rights and minorities as a basic criterion for membership. our european parliament is a key player in the design and implementation of the union's human rights policy. our powers have gradually expanded to the point that parliament has become a forum for discussion of human rights, a recognized forum, as our debate today proves! the report we are discussing reminds us that although the european union claims to export its model to third countries, the situation within it is not without flaws. for example, 11 out of 15 member states were cited in amnesty international's 1999 report, which accused them of more or less serious violations of human rights. the rapporteur, beyond criticism, makes concrete proposals which i support, for example the extension of the right to vote and to stand as a candidate in municipal and european elections to all non-nationals of an eu member state who have been resident in the national territory for more than five years. there are other proposals for improving the asylum law which i think are very interesting and which need to be put into practice quickly. as regards the situation in the applicant countries, much progress remains to be made, particularly with regard to respect for minority rights. the european parliament must therefore remain vigilant.
in writing. - i would like to commend the quality of the report on respect for human rights in the european union by our colleague mr haarder. adheres to the general philosophy of the text, which aims to consolidate european policy on the civil and political, but also economic, social and cultural rights of residents of the union. i would nevertheless like to draw the attention of my colleagues to two requests in the report which i consider to be problematic. point 19 of the report, on the protection of national minorities, and point 20, calling for the ratification of the charter for regional in writing. - i would like to draw a parallel between the reports of mrs ludford and mr haarder and that of mr duff and mr voggenhuber. the european parliament intends to take part in the elaboration of a european charter of fundamental rights. why not ? - why not ? however, it is not clear what this additional text will bring to the fight for human rights, if not a little more legal confusion. and above all, what should we think of the idea that our assembly is making of these rights? the ludford and haarder reports give us a first idea of what this means: the project of a libertarian society, based on rights without duties, on freedom without responsibilities. freedom is not something you decide. but the community's construction does not seem to be aware of this reality: it would not only seek to make people happy ex nihilo, ignoring their differences and aspirations, but also to set up a society without benchmarks, without distinction between what can be done and what cannot be done, a society that is addicted to hedonism or the culture of death. the human person cannot conceive of himself as an entity independent of those around him and concerned only with his immediate well-being. it is true that women have rights, but above all the right to life, which is paradoxically the right which is most often denied to them, and which must be defended and promoted. but you seem to have forgotten that human beings need objective boundaries to be established, necessary for all social life. man needs not only the means to live, but also and above all the reasons for living. a supplementary charter, even a european one, will probably not be enough.
in writing. - i wish to explain the reasons for my vote against the annual report on the respect for human rights in the european union. two of the provisions of this text call on a number of countries, including france, to ratify swiftly the european framework convention for the protection of national minorities and the european charter for regional or minority languages. first of all, i must clear up the misunderstanding that is at the root of all the regional language debates: it is not a question of prohibiting anyone from speaking, teaching or promoting a minority or regional language, whatever it may be. as long as the learning and use of these languages remains a matter of personal choice, i am in favour of any measure to promote the preservation and transmission of these languages, which are part of the cultural heritage of nations. i have spoken against this report because, by calling for the ratification of the european framework convention for the protection of national minorities and the european charter for regional or minority languages referred to above, the haarder report seeks to promote a conception of european construction based on a communitarian vision, which i cannot subscribe to. in this view, the individual has special rights because of his belonging to a territorial, ethnic or religious entity, the community being the indispensable mediator between the individual and the right he claims. although the recognition of the community may appear, at first sight, as a factor in the protection of the integration of minorities, it is, on the contrary, in fact, a powerful factor in segregation and social regression (think of the situation of young turkish or north african girls, excluded from the emancipatory benefits of school brewing, relegated to an archaic status of women). similarly, while the recognition of a special status for communities seems to protect the weakest and most deprived, it is, on the contrary, a social division which triumphant liberalism is happy to see. it is also true that the enlargement of the european union requires us to take into account the particular situation of certain national minorities, but the community solution does not offer any prospects for the future for the threatened or oppressed populations. on the contrary, recent history has shown how the intensification of community feeling can be a ferment that can revive millennia-old ethnic strife and lead to fratricidal conflicts. i prefer the universalist vision of a republican europe to this conception, in which each individual is fully, as such, an active subject of his rights and freedoms. i prefer a europe which gives a chance of integration to all those who subscribe to its common values, whether they claim to belong to a religion or do not practice any religion, whether they speak the language of their ancestors or have chosen to transcend their roots. this europe affirms the primacy of a principle absent from the haarder report, the principle of secularism, which contains and synthesizes all the other freedoms: the right to respect for private life, freedom of conscience and religion, freedom of expression and association. the republic of europe is still to be built: let us hope that the charter of fundamental rights, currently being drafted, will constitute the first act and the cornerstone of this europe. for the same reasons i abstained on the report on combating racism and xenophobia in the european union.
in writing. - the annual report on the respect for human rights in the european union is usually the occasion for a rather distressing bidding of political correctness. the libertarian ideologues never miss an opportunity to make a list of demands that are more absurd than others, all of which are cloaked in good feelings. perhaps the exercise itself wants it that way. the cru 2000 is not exempt from this peculiar tradition. from the right of non-eu nationals to vote in municipal and european elections to the unification of the asylum procedure throughout the union, to 'equal rights for homosexual couples and traditional families', nothing has been forgotten, with the added bonus of the eternal desire to grab new powers for the benefit of brussels. as a member of the committee on women's rights, i will simply insist on equality between men and women on the one hand and on the family on the other. if the persistence of discrimination between men and women, for example in pay, is unacceptable, then to oppose men and women as is too often done by certain feminist organizations would be fruitless and dangerous for the cohesion of the social body. we therefore categorically reject any policy of quotas and positive discrimination, which is the cream of politically correct discourse. such a policy would, as we said in brussels on 1 march, be a profound disregard for women: women should not be given political or administrative positions by the mechanical play of a quota, but by the recognition of their merits and skills. women have a specific role to play in society: a family role essential for the generation of new generations indispensable for the survival of society, a role in the education of the younger generations, an economic role, as a mother of a family but also in family enterprises (farms, shops, smes). this role has been devalued for too long, when it is of vital importance. this means, on the one hand, giving a stable status to women selfemployed workers participating in the life of the family business and, on the other hand, recognizing the economic and social role of the mother of the family. this means, finally, that women must be able to reconcile family and professional life, that they must be given the opportunity to make a genuine choice: how many women, forced to make sacrifices because of economic constraints, have only two children when they would like to have a third? how many are forced to devote more time to their working lives than they would like? such a policy would require giving full priority to the family. but the family is under equally dangerous attack in this report. it calls for "equal rights for homosexual couples and traditional families" while forgetting the essential role of the family in the cohesion of the social body. let there be no mistake: everyone has his own private life, there is no such thing as a police force in the alcove. however, homosexual unions as such are of no use to society, are sterile and can only bring about the sterility of society; so society doesn't have to recognize them and give them rights; it has to ignore them. the family, on the contrary, is the basic community of society, which it ensures stability. its purpose is to provide the most stable framework possible for the renewal of generations, their education and thus the sustainability of humanity. already, with the help of european resolutions, some, under pressure from rights groups, are preparing to recognise the right of homosexual couples to adopt children. imagine what the psychological development of children would be if they had two fathers and no mother, or two mothers and no father? a child needs a father and a mother to grow up, he needs the stability of the family. in the face of the culture of death, we have the duty to bear witness to the culture of life. we are committed to a high idea of the dignity of the human person, of every human person, without discrimination, from conception to natural death. this requires breaking with the materialistic and individualistic view of the human person and considering that there is in every being a part of the sacred, the foundation of his dignity. only then can we effectively and consistently ban human cloning or discrimination on the basis of genetic heritage, discrimination to which people with down's syndrome are too often subjected, for example, in the name of better feelings. only at this price will we be able to break with the unacceptable hypocrisy which allows us to peacefully deface human rights by turning a blind eye to an economic and commercial system which, in the name of the dogma of free trade, encourages the exploitation of children in many third world countries. we can thus free ourselves from the politics of minorities, the legacy of individualistic thinking which threatens social peace, from the ideology of minorities, the new expression of class struggle which neglects the deep unity of the human family in order to establish superficial divisions based on race, sexual orientation, age or ethnicity and to claim specific rights for each of them. man is not a social security number, nor a pawn on the social and economic chessboard, to be manipulated at will and thrown away after use. he is worth much more than that: every man is a sacred story.
