expressed in amendment no 53 to article 16. however, i propose that the text be reformulated to ensure that equivalent comitology arrangements are adopted. i also welcome the intention expressed in amendment no 45 to annex viii, but i will call for flexibility in determining the exact length of the quake-free period. i reject amendment no 55 to annex viii, which reduces the protection against scrapie. in addition, i reject, for lack of scientific evidence, amendment no 56 to annex viii, extending the ban on the marketing of the offspring of animals suffering from tse. finally, on laboratory techniques, i accept amendments nos 47 and 48. thank you again for your cooperation. i sincerely hope that this proposal will remain an extremely important proposal and that our cooperation - directive 93/104 was already very restrictive in relation to the worker's output. it does not harmonize social legislation from above, quite the contrary. it creates a european framework which falls far short of the expectations of employees: eleven hours of rest per day, 48 hours of work per week, 24 hours of rest per week. in addition, it excluded certain categories from its scope of competence. the compromise which has been put to the vote by the members of parliament today after the conciliation committee meetings is not satisfactory in our view, either for the health or the safety of the workers. it extends flexibility, particularly for fishermen at sea, by introducing systematic annualization of reference periods. it will also allow for derogations from the already excessive 48-hour week legislation. and it will take nine years, at best, for doctors in training to see their workweek reduced from 58 hours to 48. in fact, this project to organize working time is organizing social deregulation at the very moment when, in france, doctors in training are struggling to obtain decent working conditions and real security for users. the real adjustment would be, we repeat again, a real reduction in working time with sufficient job creation. as it stands, we cannot support this report.
mr president, the draft directive on the organization of working time for certain categories of workers, such as doctors in training, offshore workers and so-called mobile workers, is a sign of the slow and ridiculous nature of social europe. the recitals to the draft text stress the particular importance of this dossier, which is the first major dossier in the social field, and even add that it concerns the health and safety of 7 million workers. in france, for example, several recent strikes by medical interns have drawn public attention to the unbearable length of the working day for this category, which is detrimental to the doctors in training themselves, but also to the quality of care provided to patients. the question arises, with at least as much acuteness, for other categories such as offshore workers or transport workers. this should have resulted in a rapid decision with a consequent reduction in working hours. the project intends to reduce working hours, but in stages. during the first three years, 58-hour weeks are allowed. it will take five years for the maximum time limit to be reduced to 48 hours and the commission has the cynicism to mention technical reasons for granting an additional two-year period for application. who is to believe that these measures could not be implemented almost immediately if there was the political will to go in the direction of the interests of the employees concerned rather than to give priority to the employers' arguments? even a small limitation on working hours is better than no limitation at all. we shall not vote against this text, but we shall draw the conclusion that the workers have nothing to expect from social europe and that, in order to change the legislation in favour of the workers, nothing will replace their collective pressure.

the rapporteur. mr president, i should first like to thank all the colleagues who have combined their work with that of the rapporteur to present these two reports which i believe are very important for the future of the railways. what's this about? the first is to take stock of the implementation of the 1996 directive on the interoperability of the high-speed rail system and to draw lessons for the future. secondly, and this is the essential report, we must discuss and vote on a proposal for a directive on the interoperability of the transeuropean conventional rail system. my dear colleagues, we must realize the importance of this matter. there is an unacceptable contradiction between the discourse and the reality of european transport today. as might be expected, the construction of the internal market has logically and considerably developed trade in goods and the mobility of people within the union, which recorded growth rates of 21% and 15% respectively between 1990 and 1997. of this explosive growth in inland mobility, which is expected to continue in the coming decades, road transport, and in addition sea cabotage in the north sea, have captured the bulk of traffic. while here in the european union, and in most of the countries, we have a rail network and rail technology unparalleled anywhere in the world, while a recent study estimates the external costs of road transport in terms of public health, infrastructure and pollution at some eur 480 billion, while the goal of sustainable mobility and respect for the environment is now commonly shared by europeans, rail accounts for only 8.6% of the freight market and 5.8% of passenger traffic. there is not one but several explanations for this paradox: the reduced competitiveness of rail, due to a social differential with the road sector, but also to the distortions of competition introduced by the considerable external costs of the road, a priority of prestige given in recent years too exclusively to high-speed passengers by most of the major railway companies, but also an excessive nationalisation of railway cultures, techniques and protocols which jeopardises the fluidity of railway traffic across the continent. the situation of european transport networks today is a caricature: there is only one single transport area, the road network. there is as yet no single european sky or maritime area, let alone a continuous railway area within the countries of the union. the challenge of railway interoperability is naturally to abolish the technical boundaries inherited from the national railway heritage which has gradually been built up since the nineteenth century. today, the europe of the fifteen has no less than sixteen electrical signalling systems, six voltages, five track gauges and several types of equipment and therefore of infrastructure. the new high-speed rail infrastructure is naturally a prime area for interoperability, since it is obviously a new or recent network dedicated to very little differentiated technology. directive 96/48 was adopted for this purpose. the report on its application, four years later, examined for an opinion by parliament, gives a mixed but ultimately more positive picture than it appears. firstly, there is a long delay in legal and regulatory transposition, as only two countries have transposed it to date and the first technical specifications for interoperability are just being finalised and published. it will be concluded that the time-limits for transposition and publication should be more stringent in the future. however, this delay in transposing the texts did not hinder the development of interoperable crossborder lines, the thalys being the only example of perfect interoperability, even superior to eurostar, despite its efforts to scale. these two international lines provide an example for future developments. but beyond that, in the absence of any tangible results, the directive on high-speed interoperability has above all helped to define and implement a working methodology. for the first time, industrialists, railway companies and infrastructure managers have started working together to define technical specifications for interoperability. they have been fed by the more general work of the international union of railways. they have formed a working forum within the european association for railway interoperability, which now has a methodology and experience that can be transposed to conventional rail. the committee also stressed that article 21, which brings together the representatives of the member states and the commission, allows for political and technical control of interoperability work and for discretionary intervention by the states in its direction. in other words, if the committee on transport has been careful to remind the member states of their obligations to meet the deadline and to transpose, it must be admitted that high speed has been a first-class testbed in the vast field of interoperability. in this connection, it must be borne in mind that the network and the conventional fleet pose otherwise formidable problems of harmonization because of the national and historical dimension of the networks, the diversity of the fleet and their considerable size. it must be very clear here that it is not a question of requiring railway undertakings and infrastructure managers to replace their equipment immediately and in full, which is absolutely out of the question. firstly, if interoperability is the objective, it must be achieved by the quickest and least expensive means to achieve decisive progress. in this respect, interoperability can be achieved by means other than harmonisation of equipment, provided that equipment can be adapted to various configurations, such as four-wheel locomotives. the commission is therefore proposing a pragmatic and realistic approach to avoid imposing additional costs on the competitiveness of rail in comparison with other modes of transport. the main principles of this draft directive are a limitation of the geographical scope of conventional interoperability to the transeuropean network as defined by the 1996 decision of the european parliament and the council. a logic of gradual convergence rather than systematic renewal, which is expressed in a phasing of priorities and interoperability, giving priority to the subsystems that provide the fastest and least expensive access, with priority given only to new investments in creation, extension, renewal, maintenance and operation. a hierarchy of objectives which distinguishes between the cross-cutting objectives which must be imposed on all standards: safety, reliability, health, environmental protection, technical compatibility; the objectives inherent in each technical subsystem: infrastructure, energy, rolling stock, etc.; a separation of the technical work of developing tsis, which is entrusted to a common representative body, of standardisation, which is entrusted to european standardisation bodies, and of control and certification, which is entrusted to notified bodies. the logic of consultation with users proposed by the committee on transport is unimaginable, ladies and gentlemen, without a parallel consultation of the staff representatives, the subject of an amendment which we will have to discuss tomorrow. finally, continuous monitoring of this work by the member states and the commission through the article 21 committee set up by the high speed directive, which allows the states to request derogations, to include in the technical specifications for interoperability specific cases for isolated historical or regional networks, as well as for certain equipment originating in third countries, also authorization systems notified by the member states to the commission. in other words, for countries with very strong specificities, safety valves exist and they still have the possibility, within the body of the institutions provided for by the directive, to assert these specificities and impose them on the work and publications of the tsi. finally, during the transitional period, the aim is to avoid a growing divergence of these networks. to this end, new investments will have to comply with an agreed technical standard by the time the tsis are published. a register of railway equipment in the union will be set up to identify the stock, its renewal and its ageing, as is still imperfectly done in maritime matters. in addition, we must look further ahead, and that is why it was proposed by both the committee on transport and the committee on industry to involve representatives of the enlargement countries in this work so that they can anticipate this future acquis communautaire. in the same way, we must already, and we recommend it, consider ways of making the different modes of transport interoperable, in line with our general objective of developing intermodality. naturally, ladies and gentlemen, it would be presumptuous to expect everything from this directive and the long work of upgrading it requires of railway operators. it is obvious that europe is proposing a long-term and very large-scale project on its vast rail network. it will not, on its own, resolve the question of distortions of competition, access to the network or pricing, which should be decisive steps towards a new golden age of rail in europe. the technical interoperability of our old national networks is a necessary condition for the reconquest of the railway, which this balanced, reasonable and flexible text should make possible in successive stages under acceptable economic and social conditions. to all of you, many of you who have contributed to this, i renew my gratitude and my thanks.

as we have always advocated - better quality employment. we have always insisted on this. the flexibility of the labour market implies many other things: we can talk about the organization of working time, but also about the removal of all the obstacles which currently hinder work, including for example taxation-related aspects. the development of investment was a major concern during the debate. it is true that the main directions of economic policy are based on the attempt to increase the growth potential of the european union. if we are unable to do this, it is quite obvious that the prospects for growth, which are currently positive above 3%, will be affected in the short term and that we will not be able to maintain this trend. therefore, public and private investment is absolutely essential. since 1997, public and private investment has been increasing steadily. public and private investment should reach 21% of gross domestic product in 2001 and 23% in 2004, bringing us closer to the 24% target mentioned at the time in the commission's white paper on competitiveness, growth and employment. i would like to raise a point here which i consider essential: in my view there is no contradiction between an increase in investment and an increase in public investment and the stability pact; on the contrary, i believe that the stability pact, insofar as it has helped to consolidate public finances, will allow us to increase public investment in the future. i agree with those who believe that, in these new conditions, improving the quality of public finances must involve more public investment. this is a point which the commission has raised in the various stability and convergence programmes and it is obviously a point which we will continue to insist on. some speakers also commented on the importance of r & d and the new economy. this is one of the fundamental elements of the broad guidelines, but i would like to recall - as i always do - that the fundamental point of introducing the new economy is the improvement of productivity, which is clearly the element that will facilitate future growth. i would like to make a comment on two points. firstly, on the interinstitutional agreement, which has been a matter of concern to the commission, and secondly, on the problems of better coordination in the face of better subsidiarity. as for the interinstitutional agreement, it is true that this is a recurrent request from parliament. the implementation of the programme raises legal problems and even problems of the size of the participants, but i think that in any case we should be satisfied with the progress made this year. i promised you a few months ago, when we first discussed this subject in the committee on economic and monetary affairs, that the commission would try to make as much progress as possible in its cooperation with parliament. although it does not take the form of an interinstitutional agreement, the presentation of the document on the results of the broad economic policy guidelines, which contains elements allowing for a preliminary debate in parliament, seems to me positive. i also believe that other, more profound elements, such as the launching of the idea of wider economic debates, with the participation of parliament, the famous economic talks, will in future have to offer us new possibilities and ideas for our political debate. in my view, the idea of the portuguese presidency - which we support - to engage in a debate with parliament on these issues, not at the institutional level as parliament suggests, but of a different nature, is also positive. i believe that this is a good way in which we should continue to cooperate. finally, i would like to point out a point which might seem contradictory to those who advocate better coordination of economic policies and those who advocate better subsidiarity in their implementation. as you know, economic policies are the responsibility of the member states and subsidiarity is guaranteed in this respect. i think that better coordination is essential. i therefore support the view that coordination of economic policies must be maintained, even referring to what the member states must do. i understand that for some of you this may seem to be an interference by the commission in the responsibilities of the member states, but that is what the treaty establishes, that is what the legislation we have adopted establishes, and that is the mandate given to the commission: to make specific recommendations. i said that coordination is necessary, but i think there is no reason why this should be in conflict with subsidiarity. better coordination and better definition of overall policies do not, however, exclude the existence of a margin of manoeuvre at the head of the member states. i would like to conclude by thanking all of you for your contribution, for your participation in the debate and for your majority support for the document presented.

in writing. - the gonzaléz álvarez report concerns the reduction of co2 emissions, a necessary objective, particularly in the fight against global warming. such an objective would require europe to devise effective means of limiting these emissions, either by binding standards, as is the case for other pollutants, or by incentives, with controls and penalties. in addition, the increase in the number of vehicles plays a major role in the increase in co2 emissions. this aspect of the problem must also be tackled by developing a policy of rail and water transport, combined transport and a public service which can offer an effective alternative to the private car. however, in the light of the explanatory memorandum, the commission is 'attempting to monitor', i.e. to collect statistics, but without undertaking an effective control, and apparently excluding light commercial vehicles (trucks) and heavy goods vehicles (heavy goods vehicles). it's better than nothing... but it's close to nothing! nevertheless, despite its limitations, we voted in favour of the gonzález álvarez report.
in writing. - i can only recommend that this text, which is the result of a long and difficult conciliation process involving the council, the commission and parliament, be approved. this positive vote is crucial because it concerns the safety and health of some 7 million workers in europe. transport workers and offshore workers, fishermen at sea and doctors in training will finally be entitled to benefit from european provisions on working time. as a french member of the ep's committee on employment and social affairs, i supported parliament's position at second reading, in particular that a four-year transition period for doctors in training should be provided, with a maximum of 54 hours of work per week over a four-month reference period. the agreement reached in the conciliation on this point provides that doctors in training will be covered by the directive in terms of scope (maximum 48 hours of work per week over a reference period of four months) after a period of nine years. the nine-year period will be divided as follows: four-year transposition period and five-year transitional period. during the first three years of the transitional period, the number of hours worked per week will not exceed 58 hours, and during the last two years, 56 hours. for some member states, however, such a nine-year period will not be sufficient to make the necessary adjustments. therefore, such a state may have an additional period of two years. the commission will decide on the notification by the member state concerned after consulting employers and workers at european level and the representatives of the member states. the notification, the commission's opinion and, if this opinion is not followed, the justification of the member state, will be published in the oj and forwarded to the european parliament. in the event of specific difficulties, the two-year period may be extended by one year, but the member state must resume the whole procedure from the beginning. the maximum number of hours worked per week may not then exceed 52 hours.
in writing. - the text which has been submitted to you, after years of negotiations, which aims to define limit values for the weekly duration of working time is emblematic in more than one way of the ambiguities and inadequacies of european social policy. firstly, as regards the very principle of a european social policy, the maastricht treaty limits it to minimum social standards, and again, as long as they do not impose "excessive constraints on smes". these limits are no longer acceptable today. this is already an urgent question for the next revision of the treaty. but the ambiguity and the shortcomings are also clear in the project itself which is submitted to us. it is well known that in 1994, when the member states agreed on a maximum of 48 hours for the weekly working time, they excluded several million workers, whether road workers, oil rig workers or internal medicine trainees. mrs smet's proposal reintegrates some of them into the common law of 48 hours. but it still does not solve the question of long-distance road transport employees and, as far as interns are concerned, it proposes a deadline for implementation that is frankly exaggerated! the situation of these medical trainees is similar in many countries: 70, 80 hours a week of work in conditions that are sometimes undignified and dangerous for the sick. the recent strike by the inmates in france has shown that such a situation is unacceptable, both for doctors and for the sick and for the public health service. but whereas last november the european parliament proposed - almost unanimously - that the 48-hour rule should be applied within four years, now we are being asked to change our position radically. we should adopt the joint proposal of the ministers and the parliament's delegation which accepts that the member states have up to 12 years to apply the 48-hour directive to doctors in training. let us understand that this means that the first doctors in training who will benefit from these provisions have just entered secondary school! i do not know of any other area - the euro, the free movement of persons, goods or capital - where such a time limit applies. how can we expect to take the european union's social policy seriously in such circumstances? the proposal divides this 12-year period into several periods with the maximum working hours attached to them: - until 2004: no change, the working time is not limited; - from 2004 to 2007: the maximum working time will be 58 hours; - from 2007 to 2009: it will be 56 hours; - from 2009 to 2012: it will be 52 hours. we are sending a worrying signal by adopting this text. it is the first social directive to be adopted after the lisbon summit on employment: let me hope that the commission, parliament and council will finally take european social policy more seriously. it is not with such projects that social europe will move forward and convince the citizens of our countries.
in writing. - i want to express my satisfaction with the contents of this report. i would remind you that by presenting this proposal for a regulation the commission is fulfilling the commitment it made to the temporary committee of inquiry of the european parliament in 1997 to present measures for the effective surveillance of transmissible spongiform encephalopathies (tses). the proposal aims to create a uniform legal basis for the control and prevention of tses of all types and for all products of animal origin. it incorporates all the community rules in force in the field of tse. like the rapporteur, i agree with the general strategy adopted by the european commission, but i think that the text proposed to us needs to be strengthened to ensure maximum consumer safety. that is why i supported the amendments tabled by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection. the amendments were intended to introduce the possibility of systematic use of rapid diagnostic tests, to reintroduce the request made by the european parliament in the context of the follow-up to the bse recommendations, namely to remove the entire herd from the food chain, to prohibit any movement of animals defined as being at risk, and to advocate their slaughter and destruction, with the exception of animals intended for scientific research. it was also necessary to complete the proposal by inviting the commission to submit proposals concerning the inclusion of certain cosmetic products and medicinal products, to establish a procedure for determining the epidemiological status of countries or regions with regard to bse (i.e. a classification of countries according to their level of contamination). i would like to conclude by stressing that the european parliament must remain involved, through the codecision procedure, in the fundamental decisions on the prevention of tse.
the problem we are dealing with this morning has been identified for a long time. the concern today to prevent the risks of bse at community level is commendable, but it is now almost 15 years since our researchers have clearly established that one of the origins of mad cow disease was the consumption of animal meal containing carcases of sheep affected by scrapie. this is why we emphasized strongly, when we helped launch the parliament's committee of inquiry into bse, that any regulatory framework must necessarily incorporate all transmissible spongiform encephalopathies. why has it taken so long to make the necessary regulatory adjustments? why such a gap between community proposals and scientific findings? fortunately, for the protection of the population, the responses at national level and in a number of member states were otherwise quick and effective, compared with the incredibly slow and usual paradoxes of the community bureaucracy. i would remind you that some countries, in order to guarantee the food safety of their consumers, have to deliberately infringe the community rules. it is quite good to generalize rapid diagnostic tests. these will be a significant element for the surveillance of bse at community level. but we must not make it a panacea. these tests can detect the altered prion protein only after a certain threshold. they should therefore not replace, in particular, the removal of specified risk material. and above all, it would be absurd if member states which have put in place a screening programme based on tests which are much more rigorous than the community programme were to be penalized in terms of classification in relation to the risk of bse compared to those which would have settled for the community minimum programme. community legislation must not in any case constitute a brake or an obstacle for member states wishing to provide their populations with more stringent protection. it has become clear since the beginning of the bse crisis that the most adequate and effective level of protection for our people is directly linked to the vigilance of the national authorities, and community procedures, when they are finally formulated, can naturally play a useful complementary role.

in writing. - first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on his excellent work on the commission's report on the implementation and effects of directive 96/48/ec on the interoperability of the trans-european high-speed rail system. creating the technical conditions for interoperability of the european rail networks means harmonising the many systems and components that ensure the movement of trains between the different networks. the objective is, in fact, threefold. the aim is to gradually create the conditions for the uninterrupted movement of convoys on the 15 national networks: free movement objective; to eliminate the current additional costs and delays in order to improve the competitiveness and reliability of the railway in relation to its competitors: the objective of sustainable mobility; the aim is to create, through the harmonization of railway components, the conditions for a single european market in railway equipment: an economic and technological objective. the purpose of the directive under discussion today was to publish technical specifications for interoperability (tsis) for six subsystems (maintenance, infrastructure, energy, rolling stock, operation, control and command), to start work on component standardisation in collaboration with cen, cenelec and etsi, and to establish in each member state a list of notified bodies responsible for assessing the conformity of components produced by industry. this report, prepared in accordance with directive 96/48/ec, provides an initial assessment of the progress made. it is clear that four years after the adoption of the directive, not a single technical specification for interoperability (tsi) has been drawn up, while interoperability is considered fundamental for the mobility of people and the efficiency of trans-european rail systems. to date, the majority of member states have not transposed the provisions of the directive into their national law. we're a long way from talking about railway priority! however, it would be unfair to say that no progress has been made. a tripartite body, aeif (european association for railway interoperability), has been set up and is engaged in identifying and specifying existing technologies, components and processes, which should lead to two tsis in the near future. moreover, the latest investments in the high-speed network, such as the thalys, have for the first time experienced an effort at convergence and technical coherence. however, these advances are still insufficient in view of the challenges. national differences are a major handicap to the development of rail transport in europe, despite the many advantages of this mode of transport in terms of sustainable development, pollution and safety. the figures do not require comment: in 1970 the railway had 21% of the freight traffic market share, today it has only 8.5%. the trend is the same for travellers, with market shares falling from 10% in 1970 to 6%. as far as freight is concerned, iron may well disappear altogether from large segments of the freight traffic market. there is no doubt that the closure of large parts of the european network would result in considerable job losses. a new impetus for interoperability is therefore needed.

it's one of the greatest embarrassments of humanity in the year 2000. we made commitments in 1995, commitments which have been fulfilled to a certain extent, and we are going to analyse them in full. the question is whether we have the necessary elements at the level of the european union. i would like to inform you that the commission has been trying for a long time to gather information from the member states, to receive answers to questionnaires that have been sent and returned, to collect answers to all the various questions concerning legislation, infrastructure, actions, statistics. after a lot of hard work, i have to admit, we have come up with a set of concrete elements which will be published as soon as possible - within two weeks, i hope - with the data for 1999. and that is the reason for the considerable delay that has occurred. i would like to mention three points in relation to the report which, according to the questionnaires sent back by the countries of europe, are of the highest priority in their concerns. first, the new changes brought about by the information society in the economy, society and the work model, are creating both great challenges and serious problems, especially in the poorer strata, serious problems among women who are participating at much lower rates in this new world of technologies and, of course, have higher levels of unemployment. in this respect, we must insist on the new focus on education, lifelong learning, retraining, specialised programmes for women's participation in the information society and, therefore, women's participation in the labour market. the second point concerns democracy; it is linked to the information society, which opens up a new way of communicating between citizens and politicians, but also a new way that must be known by equipping oneself with the appropriate means. and then, of course, there is the classic problem of women's representation, which all the speakers have touched on. thirdly, and as it turned out, it is also one to which the member states attach importance, violence against women, with the most serious manifestation being trafficking in women, in other words the modern form of human trafficking. unfortunately, ladies and gentlemen, we must admit that the new era puts women and children at the forefront of the agenda, in addition to electronic commerce as defined in economics. and of course, these are issues that require new solutions, that require new approaches that we cannot simply regard as the ransom of the new age. i think these are the fundamental elements of what we call a review and, above all, a renewal of our commitments. i would like to stress that there will be a problem of negotiation at beijing + 5. i agree that there will be centres and organised forces which will want to challenge all this progress and reopen the action programme we approved. and how we are going to organise ourselves and how our pressure groups at all levels are going to function, so that there is no reexamination of the programme of action, no return to the past, but renewing our commitments and creating a driving force to achieve what we have committed ourselves to in the new era. as each negotiation depends on preparation but also on a good knowledge of our own data as well as the data of those we have in front of us, we will need close cooperation with the portuguese presidency, both from parliament and the commission. i think it is superfluous to assure you that the commission - including myself - is at the disposal of the portuguese presidency to prepare this negotiation as well as possible.
- as president of the european parliament, i have the honour and the great pleasure of welcoming mr milan kuçan, president of the republic of slovenia. it is the first time, mr president, that we have had the opportunity to welcome you to our group, and i am delighted. just ten years ago, on 8 april 1990, the first free and democratic elections took place, the culmination of the slovenian spring. this spring was the beginning of the clashes and tensions of the summer of 1991, when slovenia gained its independence. of course, we all still remember the images of those ten dramatic days in the summer of 1991. at that time, the courage, the love of freedom and the determination of the slovenian people and their president prevailed over the threats of violence. thus was born the free and democratic slovenia. this event marked simultaneously the return to the common european values of freedom and peace, democracy and respect for human rights. these essential achievements of our european civilization are the indelible foundation of our common action today and tomorrow. the european union is first and foremost a community of values. i am pleased to see that after decades of communist dictatorship, slovenia has elevated these values to the status of a foundation of the state. and today slovenia is part of the great european family which we hope to reunite soon. in 1996, the association agreement enabled us to set up a joint parliamentary committee between the european parliament and the slovenian parliament. on 10 june 1996 your country submitted its formal application for membership of the european union. in march 1998 negotiations were launched and i know that they are actively proceeding under the auspices of the president of the commission, mr romano prodi, and commissioner verheugen. we know that as president of slovenia you have played a decisive role in the positive development of your country over the last ten years. that is why i am particularly pleased to have you here with us today. mr president, you are welcome, and i give you the floor without further ado. president of slovenia. transcript of the interpretation, original speech delivered in slovenian - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is an honour for me to be able to speak in this honourable house. i am particularly pleased that this was made possible on the occasion of the 50th anniversary of robert schuman's call for france, germany and other countries to commit themselves to a common economic policy in the coal and steel sectors. this was the day on which the process of european integration began. it is your day, our common european day of celebration, and i offer you my sincere congratulations. i congratulate you, full of confidence and faith in the idea of european association. my faith is confirmed by the recent visit to slovenia of the honourable president of the european parliament, mrs fontaine. in her speech to the slovenian parliament, mrs fontaine expressed her unwavering commitment to the pursuit of the project of a united europe, stating in essence that it was important to support the will to strengthen the specificities of each of our countries, that we therefore needed to consolidate the foundations of the european union and prepare it for enlargement in such a way that it remained able to function in the future in order to respond to both internal and external challenges, which would only be possible if we maintained the balance between small and large countries and continued on the road to a europe of the citizens. this idea seems to me particularly important because it emphasizes the idea of coexistence. coexistence is the only real alternative for the future of mankind, including that of europe. the question is, though, what will that coexistence be based on? i am firmly convinced that it should be based above all on the experience we have acquired, which has given rise to the values which we have made the quintessence of european democracy and which we have set up as principles weaving the very fabric of the new europe. the experience we have at the dawn of the third millennium is one of the rise and fall of colonial powers and ideological, political and social totalitarianism. in return for this - and yet an integral part of our experience - we must pursue the final establishment of the rule of law and human rights, the freedom of individuals and nations, democracy as the criterion of political power, social justice and stability as the objectives we must pursue relentlessly. in addition to this experience, our coexistence should be based on a set of laws which will define human existence on the threshold of the third millennium and will constitute the implementation and confirmation of these values. these are the laws of the international community. for the time being, this community seems to be limited to markets, economics and information and communication technologies. politics is a long way off. however, the solid foundations of coexistence in the world require a globalised policy capable of establishing social cohesion that counterbalances the effects of an already globalised capital. the globalisation of politics presupposes that national policies and interests based on the sovereignty of the nation state are linked to an overall policy of shared responsibility. it would be, as it were, a world of "domestic affairs" to which all nations would be bound. on the one hand, it would be based on the following elements: the globalisation of political and economic democracy, binding standards of individual and collective rights, dialogue between different cultures, religions and civilizations, opposition to nationalism and xenophobia, a new balance between economically developed and developing regions, the globalisation of learning, knowledge, research and information, the development of international and interregional cooperation, the building of a social order based on the model of social justice and solidarity, security and common defence and the fight against organised crime. such policies could help us to avoid the old ideological, political and military confrontations of the cold war being replaced by clashes of cultures, religions and civilizations. if we are to move towards a global political responsibility, we should move as quickly as possible towards a policy of common responsibility within europe; the european union is not a mere institution, but a europe which is at present consolidating the foundations of future coexistence. all this is announced by common european policies - not just monetary ones; there is also talk of foreign policy, defence and security - by the european charter of human rights and, perhaps, by a future european constitution. it is also announced by the efforts in crisis management, which would prevent internal or external crises in countries in the region from degenerating into armed conflicts and aggressions that could threaten common peace, security and prosperity. a comprehensive policy of shared responsibility requires not only that we anticipate the actions of third parties which may threaten the community but also, and this is very important, that we guard against taking such actions. in an open, multipolar world free of eurocentrism, europe can only be one of the models of civilized development if it is internally globalised, if all its parts are integrated and no part is excluded from the common future or marginalised. but the ruins of the berlin wall are showing signs of new divisions in europe. in reality, several europeans coexist. we have here the countries of the european union and the members of nato, which are moving forward on the basis of a long tradition of european democracy, respect for human rights and the prospect of an economic re-start, completed by the european common currency. this group also includes a few small countries which have undergone major developments within the eu while preserving their specificities. the second europe is made up of countries negotiating with the european union: countries which are therefore in the waiting room of first or second class, hoping to board the european train. the third europe is made up of the countries of central and eastern europe (ukraine, croatia, bosnia and herzegovina, albania, macedonia and moldova) which have not yet reached the station although they aspire to do so. some of them can't do it without help. there is also a group of countries which do not wish to join the eu at present. they would rather cherish the project of a new ideological division of europe. we could call it the fourth europe. serbia, which was on the verge of tipping the balance of stability in south-eastern europe, was pushed into this fourth europe by its aggressive political elite, which occasionally enjoyed the support of the nationalist ambitions of political elites from other balkan nations. european unity is once again facing a major test as it decides on the lasting foundations of peace and the future of kosovo and montenegro, following the horrors of the balkan war. the possibility of bloody military confrontations remains real. this unity will be all the more vital when serbia needs help in its democratic transition process, when it is confronted with the truth and its own responsibility. this change will pave the way for a democratic, pluralist policy and for efforts to re-implant the european system of values in the consciousness of the serbian people. it will then be necessary to offer serbia - and other balkan countries - the difficult but realistic prospect of joining european integration on equal terms, without preferential treatment - which will require all the more assistance to these countries. none of these "europees" is immune from political or cultural drift which could distort their democratic image, not even the first europe. i am thinking of the brutal forms of xenophobia and xenophobic hatred, of resistance to the free movement of workers and of anti-semitism which are all forms of political populism at the present time. it puts pressure on the fundamental values and threatens coexistence and our common future. to be insensitive to these phenomena would create new barriers between us. the experience we have is a reminder of this. i believe that this experience is what motivates the reservations of some european countries about the position of the austrian freedom party and that the response will be consistent, whatever the entity that will be affected. new divisions are emerging alongside all the old ones and they affect europe in an even more radical way as the information society that characterizes our world today challenges every facet of our existence. there are increasingly clear signs of the emergence of two classes in society. the world is beginning to divide in a new way. on the one hand, there are the unemployed and those who, for lack of adequate knowledge, do not have access to modern information technologies. they are threatened with social exclusion, stagnation and marginalisation. on the other hand, there are those who have the necessary training and thus have a secure future. this is a new phenomenon recently identified at the eu lisbon conference on social cohesion. it is clear that today everyone in europe is facing the same problems and we are all responding to them. of course, we don't respond to it in exactly the same way. nevertheless, it is essential that we draw the answers to these problems from the same value system. the cornerstones of coexistence have been laid. everyone must now be given the opportunity to live by these values. in this respect, perhaps the new sense of commitment to europe, which i conceive as a european system of human bonds, cooperation, solidarity, respect and other values, could be given decisive importance. this implies not only the free movement of ideas, workers, goods and capital but also values such as respect for diversity, tolerance, equality before the law of all 'citizens of europe', irrespective of their national, ethnic and cultural background or opinions. this will allow a high degree of identification with the same values across europe, which could be the fundamental fabric of european cohesion. this attitude is the best guarantee that intolerance and hostility will remain marginal phenomena. at the same time, this would imply that in no european country would those in power dare, in the name of sovereignty or the principle of non-interference in internal affairs, to systematically flout or restrict individual or collective rights. to achieve this would require joint action without any hesitation or compromise. the nato intervention in kosovo may be the first step in this direction. fundamental rights have been placed above traditional national sovereignty. in future, systematic and widespread violations of human rights should no longer be a matter of national concern. it becomes the responsibility of the international community. time will tell whether this marks the beginning of a new chapter in international relations and international law. europe, and the eu in particular, should not be indecisive on this issue. for europe, the real path of globalisation is the enlargement of the european union to include all european countries. this is an exciting undertaking as we enter a period of enlargement of the european union to countries with a different political pedigree from the current members. the countries which, in the great division of the world, belonged to the former ideological orient of europe have now been called upon to do so. the turn came from countries whose economic development was delayed by this division. but the fact is that only this enlargement will bring about the real integration and globalisation of europe, put an end to the past for east and west europe and mark the beginning of a comprehensive european future for both. for countries which, like slovenia, have been forcibly integrated into another culture by the bloc system, inclusion in european integration would also be proof that they have finally returned to the european civilization that is their own. in any case, we should not forget that these countries, including slovenia, have shown that they were able, in a relatively short time, to adopt the rules that took a relatively long time to establish in the eu and western europe. the major efforts in reform could ensure that enlargement will benefit both current and prospective members. delaying enlargement would indicate that europe has not yet buried the past, that it has not learned enough from history and that globalisation is not yet an internal requirement. it would also mean that europe is giving up its influence and presence in the world. this new qualitative step forward is being questioned by eu members. they go from the fully known to the partially known. the decision on enlargement involves entirely new risks and the eu's dilemma must be understood. i am thinking above all of the implementation of serious internal, institutional and substantive reforms within the eu, the eu's willingness to accept new members and the postponement of the date of enlargement. could it be that the special interests of the member states are once again coming to the fore? does not the change from accepting new members as soon as they are ready to be integrated to integrating the applicants in two waves mean that enlargement will be postponed again to the end of the first decade of this century? dilemmas, doubts and uncertainties also emerge among the candidate countries. there is a growing sense of a "moving target" that, by moving, dampens the enthusiasm of the more prepared candidates and makes them feel that they will have to wait for the less prepared candidates. clearness and transparency in this area would of course be encouraging and it would be particularly helpful if each side would stop trying to make excuses for the other. the eu should not use problems among candidate countries to justify the delay of its own reforms and candidate countries should not use the difficulties encountered by internal eu reforms to delay the reforms necessary for their full membership. such excuses would slow down the prospects for the emergence of the future europe and would have no less effect if enlargement were to be conditioned on bilateral requirements and specific national interests. this includes conditions that stand out from ancient history and constitute an attempt to revise history, especially world war ii. such demands seem to be motivated by the position of strength held by those in the european union against the powerlessness of those who are merely exercising their right to be accepted into the european union. at this point i would like to recall the speech i made in november 1995 to the former foreign affairs, security and defence committee of your parliament. i denounced at the time the discriminatory treatment of slovenia because the italian government was preventing us from signing the association agreement by exercising its right of veto and by making it conditional on the resolution of what italy called disputes arising from the treaties establishing the borders between italy and the former yugoslavia. slovenia had signed the so-called spanish compromise. i am not mentioning this episode to bring back old memories but because in the current negotiations there have also been tendencies to elevate allegedly justified interests in slovenia to the level of community demands. i am thinking here of the demand for the restitution of property expropriated as part of the sanctions imposed after the second world war on those who collaborated with the nazi and fascist occupation regime. in the former yugoslavia, slovenia did nothing that was not in the spirit of the allied resolutions at potsdam, with which the slovenes had fought nazism and fascism. this time slovenia does not wish to accept such conditions and is looking for the european union's understanding and sympathy. i believe that if european integration and its future are to be based on clear and open foundations, bilateral issues should in no way be a condition for full acceptance into the eu, nor should they be a condition for gaining the pragmatic support of eu members. slovenia is a small nation. for many centuries we lived in a multinational political community, in the austro-hungarian empire and in two yugoslavs. we have experienced the anguish of the lack of respect for national identity, the attempts to erase our national identity and the dire consequences of inequality in society and before the law. the worst of all was the aggression during the nazi and fascist occupation. our right to exist as a nation has been taken away from us. for this reason, we hold in high esteem those who support the project of a european home based on the concept of autonomy of national and other entities of society. the european union is committed to the principle of subsidiarity and the principle of subsidiarity is a fundamental principle of the union. our historical experience and the future of our citizens mean that we cannot go back to a voluntary or forced isolation of the euro-atlantic institutions. slovenia wants to be part of it and is ready to contribute to the common existence of the european nations but is not ready to pay an unfair price for this. slovenia will be ready for membership by the end of 2002 and believes it will be welcomed into the club of eu member states. we also welcome the fact that in helsinki the eu member states committed themselves to enlargement to the most prepared candidate countries on the same date. in order to achieve the current objectives, the negotiations should be concluded next year. we are convinced that the pace at which they are now progressing should allow this. finally, i would like to emphasize that i do not equate globalisation and european integration with unification. the positive effects of these processes depend on the simultaneous establishment of freedom of individuation and fragmentation. it is not only the freedom and autonomy of the individual but also the freedom of social groups to express their ethnic, cultural, religious, political and spiritual beliefs and affiliations. these freedoms have a special meaning in people's lives and it is through them that they express their attachment to specific values. only respect for these freedoms can be the basis of european coexistence. this involves establishing the principle of 'unity in diversity'. the alternative is clear. if we fail in this new millennium to lay the foundations for coexistence, which cannot be reduced to the negation of the past but must also be the active acceptance of the future and include the formulation of a european universal policy of shared responsibility within an open european union, europe will be committed to the past rather than the future. in the first decade of this new century, of this new millennium, europe is also facing new challenges. i am firmly convinced that united europeans will rise to the challenge.

from pity to stigma, from victimization to contempt, to exclusion from public debate, there's only one step. in fact, the only solution for prostitutes is to be integrated into a common law system, to take care of themselves, to live a decent life, to defend themselves against the violence they are subjected to by pimps as clients or institutions; the only solution is to recognize them as such and, above all, to give them a voice. they are asking for recognition of their professional activity, for open social rights, for police protection to protect them from all forms of violence. let's hear them. whether they are abolitionist, as in france, prohibitionist, as in sweden, or sometimes even regulatory, laws that imply the non-recognition of an entire population can only reinforce discrimination against people in forced immigration, but also against hired prostitutes, immigrant or non-immigrant. the ineffectiveness of the law reinforces the enslavement of some to pimps, the impossibility of living with dignity or getting out of it for others, breaking fragile solidarities and further deteriorating self-image. mrs roure is right in her analysis of the problem, but we admit that different solutions must be considered and that different proposals must be made and taken into account. it is essential that the commission considers all forms of common legislation on prostitution giving real status to prostitutes, in order to protect women and men from pimping, violence and exclusion.

in writing. - the report by mr ferber, which we are debating today, expresses the concern for a more rigorous budgetary policy for our institution, and we welcome it. the limited increase of some 2.28% of parliament's budget proposed for the financial year 2001, or some eur 987.8 million, seems acceptable to us, especially since this proposal takes account of an inflation rate of around 2%, which seems realistic. the amount proposed is 20% of the appropriations for heading 5 and thus respects the ceiling which the european parliament itself set for 2001. however, in view of the need to deal with the consequences, including linguistic ones, of future enlargements, this limited increase in the budget of our institution requires, more than ever, a rational and responsible management of the budget of our assembly. in the field of staff policy, therefore, as requested in the report, an analysis of the current staff profiles of the institution should be carried out, in the light of the obviously evolving needs of parliament, in order to prepare as far as possible for the necessary structural adjustments. as regards the court of auditors' observations on the expenditure of the political groups, the resolution seems to be moving in the right direction when it calls on the bureau of parliament and the secretary-general of the institution to ensure full transparency in the use of appropriations. however, the french delegation of the union for a europe of nations group cannot accept the idea of allocating funds for european political parties to a separate budget line, because, we do not doubt for a moment, this would ultimately only serve to enhance the alliances, associations and groupings of european political parties with a federalist and integrationist vocation. in the field of languages - in writing. - the katiforis report is a hallucinatory exposé of the unconscious of european capital. it is based on a complete misunderstanding of the reasons for the current recovery: it is not the result of neoliberal policies favouring wage austerity and hard currency. the current job creation is taking place in a context characterised by an increase in consumption by employees and a weak euro which is favourable to exports. despite this practical denial, the report proposes to go a little deeper into social regression. it proposes greater flexibility in markets, starting with the labour market. it calls for "wage stability" and urges trade unions to adopt "reasonable positions" in wage negotiations. in order not to appear as the direct spokesman of the employers, the report introduces social clauses. but the contradictions are obvious: how, for example, to propose to reform ("modernize") social protection, which in practice means replacing solidarity with financial products, and invoking a "spirit of social cohesion"? how can wages be held "in a spirit of fairness" when profits are showing an insolent exuberance? the only remaining argument in the report is that new technologies should be used to 'make it modern'. but why should they automatically call into question the european social model? this vulgar materialism, sometimes attributed to the marxists, is today that of a cynical capitalism whose only project is to extend the reign of the commodity in disregard of social needs. we therefore voted against a text which is both stupid and repugnant.

ensuring the transition to the information society. there is still a long way to go, but we must also remember that the jobs created must be sustainable and of good quality.
in writing. - the report by mrs gröner and mrs smet allows me to return to a questionable programme of action. in addition to the malthusian ideology it covers, the beijing programme uses ways of implementation which we denounce. the un already claims to rule the world by imposing a uniform vision, based on the western model, on all regions of the planet, regardless of their cultures and existing legislation. moreover, to circumvent the rules of its intergovernmental nature and thus subject to the approval of states, the un uses ngos financed by it, but which can implement un programmes everywhere and with much less constraints. secondly, in the case of reluctant countries, it uses blackmail to obtain financial aid in order to obtain the application, for example, of birth control measures. while it is essential that the specific role of women be recognised in any society, it is equally essential that this be done in accordance with local traditions and regulations accepted by all and which do not in any way prejudice respect for the dignity of women. such an approach requires that the populations concerned better understand international texts of general application. we also discussed and voted on mrs sörensen's report on trafficking in women. these two debates should make us reflect on the real scope and purpose of these major international programmes. if they succeeded in making the demographics of western countries even more vulnerable, they obviously did not answer the more urgent question of protecting women who are really in difficulty. once again, it was the ideology and selfishness of a few that prevailed over concern for the common good, it was the culture of death that took precedence over the defense of life.
in writing. - the uen group has chosen to vote against the gröner-smet report for several reasons. one of them is the ideology that motivates beijing plus 5. we do not wish to reject the content of this report as a whole, but we reject the ideological vision of women which is being imposed on the world. the vision of the woman we reject includes empirical presuppositions: first of all, we do not agree with the principle of the woman who brings peace, with the image of the dove which overlaps with that of the woman to form one. man would be that hairy, belligerent creature, the source of all the world's disorder. on the other hand, it cannot be considered that women, by nature, can be a factor in economic development. it is true that she can contribute to this and that she should be given the means to do so. however, we believe that education should be given the highest priority in this debate. nor can we accept the segmentation of human rights which is found in this report. the uen group, committed to the integral european tradition of human rights, cannot accept a segmentation of these rights when they represent only specific needs to which appropriate responses must be given. we cannot, of course, base a binding international instrument on erroneous assumptions.
in writing. - the report on the follow-up to the beijing action programme notes that the situation of women, although improved, still involves great inequalities. in terms of work, it seems important to do more than "assess the impact of parttime and non-standard jobs . . . on female poverty". indeed, women often have little choice in choosing a full-time job with a decent salary. however, 85% of them would like to work full-time. the consequences of such parttime work are, of course, poverty. that is why we are opposed to it. the gender pay gap of around 30% remains. on this point, the report should have introduced coercive measures to remove this situation. that would require political will. finally, over a thousand women's organizations in 140 countries are organizing a world march this year to fight the ongoing violence and for equality. it is our duty to support them. we voted in favour of this report despite its limitations and we will be demonstrating in paris on 17 june with all those who are campaigning for equality and women's rights.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, three years after the treaty of amsterdam and the introduction of the famous article 13, which has been the subject of so much debate, the council is proposing two directives to implement the principles of this treaty. we can only welcome the council's willingness to do so, especially at a time when some parties on the traditional right are no longer hesitant to reach agreements with far-right movements; it was the case yesterday in france, it is the case today in austria and it may be the case tomorrow in italy. the definition of a minimum european framework for the fight against discrimination is therefore an urgent necessity. the directive on combating racial and ethnic discrimination goes in this direction by providing for the reversal of the burden of proof, the gradual introduction of positive discrimination - more effective than mere theoretical equality - and the recognition of indirect discrimination. all these aspects show a real desire to move forward. however, some shortcomings should be noted. our rapporteur has mentioned some of them. it therefore raises the question of free procedures for complainants and the necessary extension of the right to bring legal proceedings against groups or associations. but there are two other shortcomings i would like to raise. the first is general. how is it that the council has merely dealt with ethnic and racial discrimination, without seeking to create a comprehensive legislative framework for all forms of discrimination? pointing to one type of discrimination among others suggests that some discriminations are less reprehensible than others. which is unacceptable. a second directive on discrimination at work is due to be examined in the near future. the council must therefore move quickly to propose a draft directive to include all forms of discrimination. this is imperative, because the most excluded are those who experience several types of discrimination. protecting them from one type of discrimination only helps them very partially. the second shortcoming is the exclusion of discrimination on grounds of religion from the directive. personally, i find it extremely regrettable that religious discrimination has not been dealt with alongside racial and ethnic discrimination, because these different types of discrimination are, in my view, closely linked. for example, how do you define jewish identity? is not the hatred of jews, which is still very strong in many countries, as much rooted in anti-semitism, and therefore in ethnic origin, as in religious aspects? discrimination against the maghreb communities in europe is also twofold. it can even be said that fear of islam is often a catalyst for racism against these communities. the court of justice has already held that the principle of equal treatment for men and women is not a fundamental principle of community law. in conclusion, i think it is essential that the council adopts an integrated approach to the legal instruments to be put in place to transcribe article 13 into our daily lives. i believe that dividing the fight against discrimination into multiple texts is dangerous for the overall coherence of the antidiscrimination system and thus weakens it.
- mr president, this resolution is positive and we will vote for it, but it will only be credible if the member states start by sweeping up their own backs. what credibility does belgium claim to have when it is rounding up and deporting gypsy asylum seekers en masse to slovakia and bulgaria, despite the recommendations of parliament and the express request of the european court of human rights? what credibility do the member states have in imposing discrimination in the recruitment of non-eu nationals in their public service, condemning the immigrants they employ to perpetual precariousness? what credibility does france have when a constitutional bill, which advocates the right of non-eu immigrants to vote in local elections, was voted on in the national assembly on 3 may and is now blocked by the hostility of the senate, the president and the ill will of the government? how can we claim to protect those who are denied citizenship from discrimination? the only way to combat discrimination effectively is to put an end to the double-talk of governments. but this text is already a step which will have to be clarified.

the underlying racism, the more subtle racism that is insidiously taking root in the heart of our countries. these daily humiliations and harassments can have serious consequences and, in any case, younger brothers and sisters who are denied entry to schools, denied access to internships, denied access to housing, denied access to health care. it was therefore, and still is, very important to the economic interests of rich countries, but that it is based on the values of freedom, tolerance and solidarity. for all these reasons, we must vote in favour of this report. we know, ladies and constitutions. however, discrimination continues. what is often lacking, it must be admitted, is the genuine political will to actually apply the texts. in france last year there were only 14 important than improving the lot and the daily lives of individuals, of human beings. the extension of the power of associations, as mrs buitenweg's report rightly advocates, is a good thing, but the states must not offload their responsibilities onto the associations. equal rights are indeed a responsibility of the states. today, associations are at the forefront of the fight against discrimination. often they have to collect complaints, find a lawyer, find adequate legal aid and sometimes go to the bailiffs to see for themselves what discrimination is. mrs buitenweg's report calls for giving financial resources to associations, but i find it hard to believe that the member states will do so, when at the same time the economic criteria of the stability pact require member states to reduce their budgets. i would also like to see the commission's proposals for the introduction of a european social security system in the member states, which is a very important one, and the commission's proposals for the introduction of a european social security system in the member states. there is another problem, and this is my last point: the differentiated application of the nationality code. today, a young person born to immigrant parents in a country of the european union faces two situations. if the young person was born in france and is covered by the nationality code, he may indeed benefit from the protection of the circular in the event of being refused access to employment on discriminatory terms. on the other hand, many second- or third-generation youths born in a country such as germany or austria where the right of blood prevails will remain there forever as foreigners with no legal protection. i know that this was not the subject of mrs buitenweg's report, but i wanted to emphasize this because it seems to me to be highly regrettable that, in the face of an identical situation, such different treatment can exist within the union. parliament and the commission should call on the council to take action on this issue in order to move towards greater consistency in the legislation as a whole. in any case, congratulations to mrs buitenweg and i applaud this report with both hands.
