in writing. - the commission's proposal for a directive to implement the principle of equal treatment of persons irrespective of race or ethnic origin at european level, and even more so the buitenweg report of the european parliament, clearly show that the best is the enemy of the good. the proposal, however, seemed well-intentioned at first. the aim was to improve protection for victims of racism in the european union. but in reality the text which has just been presented to us is so obsessed with the hunt for discrimination that it completely loses sight of the elementary principles of the rule of law and even, to top it off, the principle of equal treatment between persons. of course, it should not be forgotten that, as usual, the proposal for a directive ignores all respect for subsidiarity and the necessary margin of appreciation for the member states. in particular, on the chapter on the rule of law, it is astonishing to read in the commission's own text that if, in a given situation, there is a mere presumption of discrimination, it is for the respondent to prove that there has been no violation of equal treatment (article 8). this would be a violation of the traditional principle of our law that it is the prosecution that must prove the guilt of the accused, not the accused who must prove his innocence. the effect of such a provision would be all the more destructive as the alleged discrimination could be mere 'indirect discrimination', which occurs, according to article 2b, 'when an apparently neutral provision, criterion or practice is likely to produce an adverse effect on a person or group of persons of a given race or ethnic origin'. but this anti-discrimination drive soon finds its limits, again in the commission's own text, when it comes to taking special measures to compensate for the handicaps of a supposedly disadvantaged ethnic group (article 5). this is the famous american policy, now very much contested in the united states itself, of 'positive discrimination'. and again, this is only the commission's text, which is the most moderate. the european parliament's report adds to this in all areas. however, some in the commission seem to have had their doubts, since they took the trouble to add to the proposal for a directive an explanatory note on its possible impact on businesses. this unusual procedure shows that the question is not clear. in this fact sheet, the commission states simply that 'the directive will strengthen the competitiveness of european businesses by ensuring that they have a greater volume of skills and resources than they currently have, and that these skills are used without distinction of race or ethnic origin'. unfortunately, this statement, which is only intended to give the authors a good conscience, is completely false. it is clear that business owners may be harassed, particularly in the area of recruitment, by threats from people whose applications have been rejected. it cannot be denied, however, that the majority of immigrants in european countries today are unskilled people from countries where the experience of working in companies as we do here is particularly poor. threatened by this new legislation, and in order to have peace of mind, the employer may be led to engage in unjustified hiring which will hinder the competitiveness of his company. for all these reasons, we reject the buitenweg report and hope that the council, which must act unanimously under article 13 of the ec treaty, will reject the commission's proposal.
in writing. - we voted in favour of the buitenweg report, which supports and improves on many points the proposal for a council directive on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of race or ethnic origin. however, as we were able to say when voting on amendment no 39, we would like to reiterate our complete disagreement with the wording of article 4 of the draft directive, which, by stating that 'a difference in treatment based on a characteristic linked to race or ethnic origin does not constitute discrimination where, by reason of the nature of an occupational activity or the conditions for its exercise, the characteristic in question constitutes an essential occupational requirement', is in total contradiction with the provisions of the international and european conventions on human rights and the elimination of all forms of social discrimination which bind the european union and the member states which have ratified them, as well as with the laws and constitutions of several member states of the european union. this article cannot be transposed into french law, for example, and the constitutional council is rightly opposed to it. this article, if retained in the final version of the directive, would for the first time provide a legal basis for discrimination based on 'a characteristic related to race or ethnic origin in labour law'. we wanted to accompany our vote with this reservation which also applies to the use, in the french version at any rate, of the word 'race' in a totally inappropriate way in several articles. article 2, for example, where it is used as a descriptive element of 'a group of persons' and not as an element characterising unacceptable discrimination, which amounts to considering this concept as well-founded and as being capable of being used to describe a person or group in a real and valid way. the fight against racism, properly understood, is based precisely on the rejection of the concept of race, on its denunciation, on the refusal to lock men or women in this category, to divide humanity according to this so-called concept.
mr president, the karamanou report we are considering today asks the european parliament to give a negative opinion on the finnish proposal to set up within the european union a kind of system for returning illegally staying persons to the responsible state. the initiative provides that a member state which apprehends illegal immigrants on its territory could return them to the member state through which they entered, pending the latter's possible return to the third country from which they originated. i find this idea interesting for three reasons. firstly, it responds to a real problem caused by the abolition of internal borders in europe and therefore fills a legal vacuum by imagining a system for the return of illegal immigrants based on the schengen acquis and displaced from the 1990 dublin convention on asylum seekers. secondly, it obliges the member state which has been negligent in its border control to take back illegal immigrants who have infiltrated into neighbouring countries from its own territory. thirdly, it shows the usefulness - whatever the previous speakers have said - of the right of initiative of the states, which the treaty of amsterdam has provisionally retained in matters relating to immigration and the movement of persons. in these areas it is important that national governments, which remain closer to the people than the commission, retain full power of proposal and, of course, decision. the commission's proposal is not a new one, but it is a new one, and it is a new one. it is taking legal imperfections as a pretext for rejecting everything altogether, when it could very well have proposed corrections in a more positive spirit. but this initiative is not to the liking of federalists who would prefer a procedure which is less intergovernmental and more community-based, i.e. giving more power to the commission and the european parliament. it is also displeasing to the pro-immigration pressure groups, who are barely hiding in the explanatory statement, where it is about the positive contribution of immigration and the rejection of an initiative supposedly repressive a priori. these reasons are, of course, diametrically opposed to ours.

the next item is the report (a5-0151/2000) by mr maccormick, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the request for waiver of mr andreas brie's immunity.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there is one figure which you must bear in mind in this debate and especially in your votes: 500 000 deaths a year in the european community are caused by tobacco. more than aids, tuberculosis, or any other infectious disease. and if we were to make a directive on social costs or public health, we should discuss the outright ban on this deadly poison. but that's not the case. we are indeed in the context of a directive which aims to facilitate the free movement of goods in the european union by approximating the laws, regulations and administrative provisions of the member states concerning the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco products. we must therefore not ban it, but inform consumers in the same terms throughout the european union about the content and the potential dangers to which they are exposed by consuming this product. we must think particularly of young people who do not have the necessary distance and who only see young smokers and not the view i may have as a doctor in a pulmonary or oncology ward where smokers die in great suffering from lung cancer. this is not the future we want for our own children. think of others too. in this respect, we should welcome the report by mr maaten and the votes on amendments by the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection which improve the draft directive. however, this is still below the level of information needed by the consumer and the will to compromise has often prevailed. amendments coming directly from the tobacco industry should not distort the text. we must therefore remain vigilant about the content, size and presentation of these warnings, which must not be changed. there are still a few questions. the labelling of tobacco products other than cigarettes must be carried out in the same way as for cigarettes. the difficulty of measuring or the fact that these products are not intended for young people should not be used as an excuse to forget that these products, like cigars or cigarette or snuff, are harmful and should be labelled as such, especially since, like cigars or pipes, they can sometimes be more attractive to young people. the maximum tar content - 10 mg - is too high and does not take into account the actual amount inhaled and the habits acquired. the tar content will have to be further limited. more worrying is the establishment of a technical committee which would include experts from the tobacco industry. how can we imagine a neutral instrument, comprising so-called experts who have spent their time lying to the public and who would become impartial judges of the harmfulness and toxicity of products sold by those who employ them? i think it takes a lot of naivety, hoping that it is not perversity, to believe in the objectivity of such an organization. the same experts who advise the industry allow the introduction of ingredients to increase consumption but also to increase addiction. in conclusion, in the face of 500,000 deaths a year, in the face of the money poured into this parliament by the tobacco lobbies, we must, ladies and gentlemen, choose life together.
mr president, it is paradoxical that today we are discussing the desire to harmonize tobacco products and at the same time the desire to facilitate the free movement of what we all agree is a very dangerous substance for health. is it not absurd that the european union believes in good conscience that it can protect public health by covering cigarette packs with ever larger labels with significant advertising effects such as 'smoking kills' or 'smoking causes cancer'? is it credible to harmonize these warnings when these toxic products are circulating freely in the union, with the approval of the union? let us leave it to the states to deal with tobacco, with their own structures and cultural messages; let them have their own dialogues with producers and consumers. i refuse to believe that the union, by harmonizing warnings and labels, is acting for the common good. i do not want europeans to feel safe in a tobacco office in lisbon or paris simply because the europeanised and standardised product they will recognise will seem familiar. we know that warnings are useless, whether they are in helvetica or not. is it not our duty to empower the consumer rather than infantilize him by telling him what is good or bad for him? although smokers have a choice, we have a duty to prevent, especially towards the younger generation. we will therefore support amendments which give priority to public health, and in particular those which prohibit descriptors such as 'light', 'mild' or 'mild' tobacco, cigarettes, cigars or chewing tobacco, which are seriously harmful to health. the pneumologists, no doubt, but also the cardiologists know very well - and they see it every day - that smoking is seriously damaging to health.
mr president, in the debate in this parliament we have great classics that come up again and again: human rights, bananas, mad cow and now tobacco. the aim is to reform three directives on the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco, cigarettes, snuff and other tobacco products. and at this stage we are also faced with another classic debate, that of the legal basis: is it the market that is concerned, in which case it must be article 95 of the community treaty, or are the operating rules, or health policy? the case was brought before the court of justice of the european communities. the rapporteur for the legal affairs committee proposes that we should put the matter to the vote by postponing the debate. either way, we're caught at the bottom. so we make a statement on the substance, which is correct, the rapporteur makes reasonable proposals, but in the end we slip up. the truth of the matter is that tobacco makes people sick and eventually kills them, just as the poverty brought about by ultra-liberalism also endangers health. cigarettes contain tar, nicotine, carbon monoxide, additives, citrates, tartrates, acetates, nitrates, sorbates, phosphates, even fungicides, and all of these eventually lead to lung cancer, cardiovascular disease, sudden infant death: there are 500,000 people who die every year. and there are many more who die too. based on these facts, therefore, reasonable proposals are made. the tar content should be limited to 10 mg per cigarette and the nicotine content to 1 mg per cigarette. there are even smart amendments to ban ammonia, which increases nicotine intake and addiction, and to devote 2 percent of the profits of the tobacco multinationals to scientific research. it's smart and it's reasonable. we also want to educate people about the dangers of smoking, and to protect children and even infants who are at risk of sudden death. but that is when we start to drift towards unrealism, pharisaism and fundamentalism. in other words, if we start with good evidence and good proposals, we end up with a harm worse than tobacco. what are these slips? first, the bureaucratic slip with the history of etiquette. we put labels on everything. the ecologist's neurosis is recognized by the fact that he says the word 'etiquette'. we put labels on meat, on wine, on gmo, on chocolate. he's the jocker of liberties. and now we're putting it on tobacco. but be careful, with tobacco, the label is serious. the label must cover 30% of the surface of the package, 35% if the labelling is in two languages and 12,5% of the outer surface of the package if it is pipe tobacco. the label shall be black on a white background and the edges shall be at least 3 mm and at most 4 mm thick, i.e. on average 3,5 mm. the labels must bear signs, but not just any signs: in bold helvetica, with a texture of 100% intensity. this proves that smoking not only attacks the lungs, but also the brain. the label must also include the telephone number of an organisation to which you can call: 'hello, i smoke, am i in danger?' the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. so when you look at the impotence of our governments in dealing with immigration, insecurity, taxation, unemployment, it's safe to say they must be smoking a lot. but none of this is very reasonable. for example, tobacco was introduced into europe at the same time as the potato. we grew tobacco immediately, but it took centuries to grow potatoes: that is how irrational things can be. even if there was a label on the apple saying that if you eat it, you're banished from heaven, the woman would have eaten it! what does that prove? well, that proves that slogans are ineffective, just as a price increase would be ineffective, because it would only increase smuggling and crime. and that is the drift into pharisaism, into hypocrisy. they say there are social costs. but the smoker pays excise duty: 75-85% of the price of tobacco. in my country, the revenue from excise duties is greater than that from registration fees. it is whether smoking pays for the cost of cancer treatment. it is said that it is inconsistent to spend a billion on tobacco cultivation and then pay for tobacco control. it is just as incoherent to bomb kosovo and then pay for its reconstruction as it is to abolish the borders and thus lose customs duties and then create olaf to defend the financial interests of the european union. is it not demographically inconsistent, my friends, to cause a demographic gap of 5 million europeans a year through abortions and then mourn the deaths of 500 000 people caused by smoking? puritan drift: the rapporteur is giving me the cold shoulder ! he's talking about social deviants, social instincts. i'm talking about the social democratic sweden of the 1960s, which sterilized 15-year-olds because they were deviants. i hear the moral order, the witches of salem. i hear the puritanism of northern europe, those reformers who want to reform everything, including the conditions of drinking and eating. i am referring to northern europe, which bans wine on the grounds that it is harmful to health, but which does not prohibit the injection of lots of things. it's the same puritanism that links robespierre, pol pot, the greens and the quakers. our rapporteur is a liberal. let him not forget the lessons of liberalism: let them live, let them be born, let them drink, let them smoke.
- mr president, when ideology goes beyond the law and treads lightly on individual freedoms to the point of advocating a tobacco-free europe, there is cause for concern. you don't make people happy against their will, except in totalitarian regimes. the purpose of this directive, which proposes to harmonize the legislation on tobacco products, is to oppose tobacco by all means, including those which are most legally questionable. the commission is misusing article 95 of the ec treaty, which requires that the objective of the internal market be taken as a reference point for the initiation of harmonisation. the commission justifies its action in the name of public health and consumer protection, which it refers to in article 152 of the ec treaty and states that only incentives and not harmonisation are possible. what can be said about this crude manoeuvre to divert articles 95 and 152 from their purpose? what about the negative opinion of the legal affairs committee? what will the usefulness of this committee now be, like that of the union's legal services? what about the unemployment which will inevitably result from the adoption of this directive which, by removing all production subsidies, will deal a fatal blow to the tobacco sector? this is 1 million jobs in europe. in france, 40 000 small producers are barely surviving thanks to this complementary activity, which is very labour-intensive. what can we say about this europe which, at the behest of the power of lobbies and special interests, allows the addition of vegetable fats in chocolate, allows the use of gmos and imposes such constraints that it calls into question the sale of our products on the markets and now threatens the production of tobacco, which is perfectly legal? you have understood, we will vote against this directive. is it too much to ask that we demand compliance with articles 95 and 152? a minimum of subsidiarity and a tiny bit of tolerance.
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i do not think that the proposal for a directive on the harmonization of the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco products is in doubt. the proposal to tighten up the standards for maximum levels of nicotine, tar and carbon monoxide in cigarettes must naturally be seen as one of the ways of ensuring better protection of public health. as a member of parliament's committee on agriculture, i would like to stress in particular that tobacco producers are not opposed to the changes proposed by the commission, as they are justified on grounds of public health. i am, however, with them in regret that the commission has not carried out an impact study of its proposal on the manufacturing sector, as it has done on certain enterprises, particularly smes. the fact that european producers as a whole will not even be able to produce the required quality in 2003 has thus been neglected. this is why i am in favour of delaying the date of entry into force of these new provisions. i would remind you that the tobacco sector, which involves 130 000 producers and 400 000 seasonal workers, is most often located in regions which offer few agricultural alternatives. this social reality cannot be ignored, especially since, from an economic point of view, its production covers less than 25% of european tobacco consumption. under these conditions, weakening our european producers would risk making the multinationals benefit from import-export. i don't want to believe that that could be our goal.
mr president, today's debate reminds me, line by line, of the debate we had on the second reading of the directive on tobacco advertising. the same legal arguments are being used as scapegoats by the same members who, under the guise of a sacrosanct legal consistency, are in reality defending colossal financial interests. i regret that in the course of these years their arguments have not changed. i regret this all the more as the tobacco industry itself is now beginning to recognise that this debate should no longer be taking place. those who today hypocritically present us with the legal arguments of yesterday are participating in an outdated back-room debate. from a legal point of view, the debate for the future is that concerning the trials which are beginning to emerge in europe. how can we balance the financial interests of certain industrialists with the devastating health consequences of tobacco use? smoking kills more people every year. and if we compare the constraints we have to bear in the context of mad cow disease, how can we conceive of doing nothing about the 500,000 deaths caused by smoking in europe each year? how can we not shudder at the thought of our young people, our young women, our young mothers? as regards the specific issue of agricultural subsidies for tobacco production, i hope that the european union will finally pursue a coherent policy. we cannot, on the one hand, give these products a large subsidy and, on the other, allocate funds which are still insufficient to combat smoking and cancer. the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection has been denouncing these budgetary choices for years. in the area of the common agricultural policy, much remains to be done to find alternative solutions for farmers. i would like to see all tobacco products subject to this directive, not only cigarettes but also cigars, rolling tobacco and pipe tobacco, because if their use does not cause the same diseases, oral tobacco also wreaks havoc. unfortunately, this directive will not solve all the problems associated with tobacco consumption, but it will at least attempt to inform the consumer.
- mr president, i will not repeat what our colleagues have said, but i believe that all members of parliament agree that we must find global and cultural solutions for consumer health. we have a duty to act. however, taking a puritanical stance and removing subsidies to producers will not solve the problem. ladies and gentlemen, we must defend the consumer and his health, but we must do so with logic, not by abolishing the premium for producers, but by putting in place coordinated policies. if we reduce consumption, we reduce production. it is not by 100% tobacco tomorrow that we will have solved the health problem. i ask parliament, as a responsible body, on behalf of the producers, to propose tomorrow a comprehensive alternative to protect the health of consumers.
the commission is therefore proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. the valverde lopez report, which parliament adopted in 1997, called on the commission to submit this proposal as a matter of urgency - a repeated call from the 'healthy' council. the proposal consolidates existing internal market rules on product regulation, including tar content of cigarettes and the use of labels with health warnings. it proposes reducing the level of tar, the most carcinogenic component, in cigarettes. it also proposes to increase substantially the size of health warnings and to update them in line with scientific advice. it introduces harmonisation rules for nicotine, the addictive agent in cigarettes, and for carbon monoxide, the agent linked to cardiovascular disease. it also limits the use of misleading descriptions that might lead people to believe that light cigarettes are healthier, when it would appear that they are not. i am aware that some in this house would prefer to ban such descriptions immediately. however, i do not think that is appropriate. instead, in the future, these terms should be subject to the approval of the member states and the commission could act to correct any distortion of the internal market. the proposal requires the declaration of additives in tobacco products which make the products easier to smoke or which may enhance the effect of nicotine by increasing dependence. the commission has decided in this proposal, as in the existing directives of 1989, 1990 and 1992, that the appropriate legal basis for action is article 95 of the treaty. the reason for this is clearly that differences between the national rules of the member states concerning a product as widely traded as tobacco can cause serious problems in the internal market and endanger the protection of public health. even if national rules were fully applied, economic operators would benefit from unequal treatment, given that the content of the current national legislation is very different. by adopting community rules, as we have done since the late 1980s, we ensure that certain basic standards are set and respected for the benefit of all european citizens. i now turn to the report on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection. the amendments proposed in this report are of very high quality. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr maaten, on his positive and constructive contribution to the preparation of these amendments. i should now like to explain the commission's position on these amendments. in total, 48 amendments were proposed in this report. i am pleased to inform you that of these 48 amendments, the commission accepts 38 in whole or in part. however, it cannot accept amendments nos 9, 17, 20, 21, 34, 36, 37, 40, 42 and 46. the amendments accepted include the proposal to increase the size of labels. however, we must be careful to continue to inform the consumer and avoid harassing him, which would produce the opposite of the desired effect. the ban on certain additives is premature until we have more information on their use and effects. in fact, the industry has not provided all the relevant information to the member states and i think the first step would be to adopt legislation which would allow member states to require the tobacco industry and individual companies to provide this information. we would have achieved the result we wanted this morning, with the establishment of a positive list, but first we must have the precise information that will enable us to act. in this respect, the cooperation of the tobacco industry will be essential. we need to put their experience and knowledge of the tobacco products sector to work in the regulatory and control process. it is no more appropriate to deal with the question of the common agricultural policy in a text on the internal market than to mention the warnings on vending machines which are not covered by this proposal. the majority of the amendments which the commission has accepted will therefore greatly improve this text, while several rejected amendments can also be taken into account outside this text but in the context of other initiatives. i now turn to the other 71 amendments tabled last thursday. the commission accepts 34 of them - either in whole or in part. however, it considers that amendments nos 49 and 50, 52, 54, 56, 59 61, 64, 65, 68 73, 77, 79, 80, 82 85, 89, 93, 94, 96, 99, 101, 104 106, 110 112, 114 and 117 are not compatible with the scope, intention and legal basis of the proposal and must be rejected. i would mention in particular that this proposal is a recast of three existing directives on the internal market. amendments undermining this legal basis, which has been considered valid for more than ten years, would not be constructive and would ignore the opinions of the legal services of the three legislative institutions of the european union, namely the commission, the council and, of course, the european parliament itself. similarly, amendments to exclude exports from the scope of the directive altogether are not acceptable because we have to cover all products manufactured in the european union in order to ensure that products ultimately consumed within the eu comply with the rules. however, a transitional period for exports may be justified in order to allow companies to change the brand formulas in the appropriate way and to modify their marketing strategies. this extension should also be seen in the light of the forthcoming negotiations with the who on a framework convention on tobacco control. the aim of the convention is to establish global standards for tobacco products. if we succeed, there will be no need to distinguish between tobacco products for domestic consumption and those for export. as regards additives, the commission will refer to article 10 of the proposal concerning the use of additives in tobacco products, a subject of great concern to consumers. unfortunately, it is impossible to introduce immediate harmonization on additives as some members of parliament would like. to ensure a full and detailed report, the proposal envisages that producers and importers should declare additives. it's a necessary first step before we can proceed. it would be premature at this stage to ban specific substances. i hope that a constructive dialogue can be established with the experts in the tobacco industry to develop community legislation in full knowledge of the technical data. the commission recognises the complexity of the issues covered by the proposed directive; in particular, the need to ensure that the drafting of the reports provided for in article 10 and any other explanatory proposals take full account of scientific, technical and other data. to provide long-term advice, the commission intends to set up a multidisciplinary group on tobacco, the first meeting of which will take place before the end of this year. finally, the commission considers that cigars and smoking tobacco should not be treated as if they were not tobacco-based. consumers of tobacco products, regardless of age or social class, must be adequately informed. i would like to thank the members for their positive contribution and the rapporteur, mr maaten, for his excellent work and to stress that this is another example of close cooperation between our two institutions to achieve a good result.
thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.
the agenda calls for the recommendation for second reading (a5-0148/2000) on the council's common position with a view to adopting a european parliament and council decision establishing a community framework for cooperation in the field of accidental or intentional marine pollution (12612/1/1999/rev1 - c5-0101/2000 - 1998/0350 (cod)) (committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy) (rapporteur: mrs mckenna).
- mr president, i agree with you that i will welcome the work done by our colleague, mrs mckenna, on this framework for community cooperation on marine pollution, which should be an interesting tool, as the recent maritime disaster off the french coast has shown us. our parliament adopted a resolution last january following the oil spill on the erika. where are we today ? the fuel continues to leak from the hull, which is lying about 100 metres down, and contrary to what was stated six months ago, this oil continues to pollute our coasts and poison the marine environment. the consequences for the environment and wildlife have been dramatic and the threats still exist. the social consequences are still to come: fishermen, hoteliers and the tourist industry as a whole will suffer from this black tide for years to come. the international fund for compensation, that is to say fipol, seems reluctant to compensate the victims and, in any case, the sums it agrees to release would not be enough. this again proves that the polluter pays principle is not applied. i hope that real cooperation can be established to ensure that the damage is repaired on the basis of this principle. this cooperation framework will therefore improve existing local or national capacities, in particular by creating better conditions for response, not only in the event of accidental pollution but also in the event of intentional pollution. this allows for the inclusion of wild gas discharges and any other source of pollution. the importance of research must also be stressed. this winter, on our french atlantic coast, the effective techniques for controlling the black tide in brittany were sorely lacking. cooperation and the exchange of know-how in this highly technological field must be encouraged and supported. as regards the opening up of this cooperation to the mediterranean countries and the countries of central and eastern europe as well as to the countries benefiting from the tacis programme, i would say to mrs mckenna that i do not entirely agree with her - and that is perhaps one of the only points on which i disagree. there are international conventions on the mediterranean and the baltic. they are already doing that. mrs mckenna's idea may seem quite generous, but the appropriations and the staff allocated to this cooperation framework, the appropriations being eur 7 million for a period of 7 years, seem to me far too modest. for the same reasons, i do not think it is necessary to set up a management committee. in its resolution of last january on the black tide, our parliament called for this framework of cooperation to be put into effect as soon as possible. let me stress today that the five compromise amendments must be adopted and that we must not delay the establishment of community cooperation, which will be an excellent tool and which the european citizens are eagerly awaiting, concerned about the protection of our marine environment.
mr president, it is more necessary than ever to discuss today the question of a community framework for cooperation in the field of accidental or intentional marine pollution, at a time when the preparatory work for pumping the oil off the coast of brittany is just beginning. whether intentional or accidental, even if we cannot equate the uncontrolled discharges with the use of obsolete ships and flags of convenience, it is still the same logic of immediate and maximum profit that oil groups such as total, elf or fina use. that is why we must support at all levels, french, european and international, any binding legislation on the liability of any contractor, civil or military, by enforcing the polluter-pays principle. it is scandalous that no sanctions are being seriously considered today in the wake of the sinking of the erika. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the safety of ships is not compromised by the fact that the ships are not designed to be used for the purpose of transporting dangerous goods. this also means the establishment of an independent system of classification societies, an increase in the number of inspectors in union ports, and also a ban on sailing for oil tankers over 20 years old. the dumping of harmful substances from the coast must of course be prohibited and, of course, radioactive substances, which must be named, must be included in the list of toxic substances. finally, the acceptance by many states of more than a hundred flags of complacency with more than dubious guarantees seriously endangers the safety, working conditions and even the lives of many seafarers. the european union will also have to address this problem and work towards the establishment of international standards. the mckenna report is a step in the right direction and that is why we shall vote for it. we must, however, remain vigilant so that the good resolutions of the european parliament and the council are rapidly translated into directives and binding regulations.
- mr president, i can assure you that the victims of the erika disaster were expecting something other than the extremely pale text on which we voted at second reading. it is true that the commission's proposal for a decision dates back to december 1998 and that the erika shipwreck occurred in december 1999. but the very fact that this proposal is not consistent, despite repeated adverse tides long before erika's, shows a very worrying lack of determination. in such an obvious area of common interest, doing everything possible to avoid the recurrence of such disasters and developing an effective and dissuasive prevention system as a matter of urgency should have been the priority of the priorities. the few measures which are presented to us today as a community framework for cooperation concern only the management of the consequences of pollution, mainly in the field of information, and are silent on prevention. the fact that the text is so thin also reflects the rigidity and inertia of community procedures, which are incapable of taking account of the consequences of new events of such importance as the erika. it has nevertheless highlighted the very serious consequences of the opacity of the chain of operators, the absence of responsibility on the part of the polluter, the absence of dissuasive sanctions and insufficient compensation mechanisms. the text before us does not address any of these essential questions and is still inspired by a philosophy which places freedom of movement above all other considerations, and in particular that of the security of our territories, our maritime areas and the people who live and work there. six months after the erika disaster, with the entire atlantic coast in turmoil, nothing has really moved forward. if a disaster similar to the erika happened today, everything would happen under the same conditions because nothing has changed, and it is not this benign text that will significantly help the victims who are struggling today in intractable problems. we are hearing proposals for legislation, perhaps by the end of the year. it's about time. when will this parliament finally be informed? at the moment, mr president, some amendments are trying to introduce the polluter pays principle into the common position. we will naturally support them.
mr president, the erika disaster has at least served to underline the importance of european cooperation in the field of accidental marine pollution. france did not have enough anti-pollution ships to deal with this black tide. fortunately, the british, the germans, the dutch and the norwegians were all willing to help. the evidence is that it is time to establish a new regulatory framework to optimise this cooperation and allow mutual assistance. we therefore agree with the philosophy of this report. the exchange of information and know-how between member states will make it possible to take decisions quickly and perhaps better, especially in the case of cleaning operations where there is a certain degree of anarchy. the emphasis should be on transparency towards the public, particularly in the case of health risks linked to the nature of the polluting product. it is inconceivable to conceal the risk of cancer from volunteers, as was the case with the erika disaster. we are also in favour of a broad definition of accidental marine pollution including radioactive pollution, munitions and outgassing. the extension of cooperation to the neighbouring coastal countries seems to us to be a good thing. the sea is a world heritage whose preservation calls for international responsibility. the recognition of the polluter pays principle is essential. today, the owner of the potentially polluting product is not held responsible for its pollution. in fact, only the carrier is to blame. this is unacceptable and we hope that the member states will ensure that the principle of extended economic responsibility for cargo owners is applied. however, the proposed budget of eur 7 million for the period 2000-2006 seems to us to be too low to achieve these objectives.
- madam commissioner, mr president, unfortunately, something is wrong. mrs mckenna's report is timely, even though her work began before the erika disaster. how many times have we not been moved by the consequences of this disaster in this house and how many times have we not wondered about the inability of the union and the member states to respond quickly to the expectations of the victims and to respond to the ecological damage? today, parliament cannot but respond to public opinion, which is constantly asking us to send a strong and positive message. we must not miss the opportunity this report offers. the problems caused by, say, the erika six months ago are still intact. nothing, it seems, is settled yet, and that is the lesson we must learn from this disaster. we know that containers of radioactive material are sailing the seas from the hague to japan. we cannot wait for another disaster, this time nuclear, to do something about it, because we know how oil reacts, but we do not yet know how radioactive waste dumped on the seabed would react. the report by mrs mckenna gives us the opportunity to incorporate radioactive substances. i ask you, my dear colleagues, not to hesitate for a moment. let's avoid a catastrophe and vote for the amendment that aims to incorporate nuclear substances.
commission. - (sv) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, and in particular mrs mckenna, for the work they have done on this important question: how can we combat marine pollution, both accidental and intentional, better within the european union? the aim of the commission's proposal is to strengthen and develop further the various community measures which have been taken in this field over the last twenty years and to bring them together in a sound legal framework. since the first reading of this proposal by the european parliament, the erika disaster has occurred in france, which has probably caused the most serious damage to the marine environment in europe. i myself went there in january and saw the dramatic effects of this pollution on people, animals and the environment. i have also seen the tremendous efforts of the hundreds of volunteers who have come to help clean up the coast, and i think they deserve our special appreciation. as regards preventive measures, the commission reacted immediately through my colleague mr de palacio and adopted on 21 march a communication on safety in the transport of oil by sea. the text proposes a series of measures to improve safety in this area. even with the best precautions, the risk of accidents is never zero. that is why we also need to improve cooperation within the eu in the event of such accidents. we need an effective cooperation framework to support, complement and further improve the measures taken at national level. the lessons we have learned from the erika disaster show that there is much to be learned about how to deal with major pollution accidents. at first reading, parliament adopted or reformulated 20 of the 29 amendments we had proposed. the council has introduced most of these amendments in its common position. these amendments improved the text and in particular defined better the type of accidental pollution covered by the decision, in particular pollution from fuel discharges. the need for proper coordination between the international conventions and agreements in force concerning european waters is also highlighted. as for the amendments tabled up to second reading, the commission can accept seven of them, either in full or in part. amendment no 16 recognises the important role of environmental non-governmental organisations in this area. here again, the erika accident has raised awareness of the importance of their involvement, as was seen in the case of the treatment of birds affected by the black tide. parts of amendments nos 6, 24 and 25 are intended to clarify the scope of the directive. parts of amendments nos 17 and 19 are in full agreement with the commission's text as regards the most appropriate committee procedure. amendment no 22 introduces an important reference to the polluter pays principle. the other amendments are problematic for the following reasons: amendment no 2 and parts of amendments nos 6, 10 and 24 introduce a specific reference to pollution caused by radioactive substances. radioactive materials are of course included and covered by the area of cooperation defined in this text. however, the commission considers that there is no need to add a relative mention of the specific materials. this has not been done in the other existing international conventions protecting the mediterranean, the baltic and the north sea, to which the eu is a signatory. a specific reference to radioactive materials would also complicate the legal situation, because of the relationship between the directive and the euratom treaty, and would therefore delay the adoption of the decision. the commission cannot therefore accept these amendments. what protection do we have? there are two directives and an information system for accidents involving radioactive materials. there is directive 96/29/euratom on the definition of basic safety standards. this text contains formulations on community measures to be taken in the event of an accident involving ionising radiation pollution, according to which member states must draw up action plans and develop forms of cooperation and networks. the purpose of the ecurie system is to enable rapid exchange of information in the event of such an accident. it's a 24-hour operating system. in addition, there is directive 89/618/euratom on the information of the public concerning health protection measures in the event of an accident involving ionising radiation. we have therefore a number of instruments and regulations which come into play in the event of possible marine pollution by radioactive materials. the introduction of a specific reference in this proposal for a text is not only unnecessary, but would in effect create an ambiguous legal situation - why should we delay the adoption of this text which should already be in force? several amendments, namely amendments nos 5, 6, 9, 10, 12, 23, 24, 25, 26 and 27, deal with the issue of munitions dumped at sea. the commission supported the european parliament's position at first reading on this point. however, it considers that the text of the common position is an appropriate solution. several members of the council were not prepared to accept a reference to this subject in any form other than a reasoned opinion. it is only because i insisted that this should finally appear in article 1 (2) (b) of the common position. amendments nos 5 and 9 contain a definition of the concept of accidental marine pollution. this issue was discussed at length in the council, where it was finally concluded that the proposed decision would not apply to continuous flows from sources of pollution located inland. the commission has taken this view, because it was never its intention to include this type of pollution in the text. this is a subject which we are dealing with in various other proposals. amendments nos 5 and 9 cannot therefore be accepted. amendment no 14 and parts of amendment no 17 are aimed at improving cooperation with countries participating in the phare, tacis and meda programmes. a certain degree of coordination already exists with the countries concerned in the framework of the international agreements for the protection of the mediterranean and the baltic. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of the information provided by the member states. amendments nos 11, 20 and 21 go far beyond the scope of the text presented: the commission therefore prefers to support amendment no 22 rather than these three other amendments as regards the reference to the polluter pays principle. the second amendment seeks to involve the institutions concerned more closely, as does proposal 15, or stresses the need to take account of international conventions for the protection of certain regional seas, as does proposal 1. the commission considers that the common position constitutes an acceptable solution to these justified objectives. in summary, the commission adopts in full amendments nos 16, 19 and 22 and in part amendments nos 6, 17, 24 and 25. the other amendments cannot be accepted. finally, i would like to thank the european parliament for the two resolutions it adopted within the year following the study of the consequences of the sinking of the erika, in which parliament calls for this decision to be taken swiftly. i hope that your contribution and support today will confirm this position and that we can therefore reach a decision on this crucial issue for the marine environment soon.

mr president, we all know that the words communication, information, networking and connection lead to the following two expressions: the information market, on the one hand, and the communication society, on the other. market or company. it is a market, that's for sure, everything points to it. but let's look at society for a moment. even if mr van velzen's report is entirely technical, purely technical questions end up crossing two problems of a different technical nature and which are also found in the amendments: access for all, democratic access to this market of the information society, and the definition of a public service which is now called universal service, not to mention the development of content for these information and communication channels, content which i am continually surprised that so few people are interested in. on the subject of democratic access first, i am told that other reports, other programmes, e-learning for example, are being developed to support the efforts of european countries to provide access to the internet and new technologies. but the programmes must not be a patchwork of existing infrastructures, of those we are in the process of putting in place. could we be consistent ? today, 94 of the 106 most visited websites in the world are american. europe is ahead of the united states in mobile communications, but it is particularly behind in content. the reminder is perhaps enchanting: it is what i tell myself every time that, in the face of the new economy, our only concern is networks. but maybe there 's an emergency today ? - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, with the report by our colleague mr van velzen, a review of the current regulatory framework for communications is being launched. the european commission's aim is to provide the european union with a world-class communications infrastructure at the best possible price-quality ratio, if not at the lowest possible prices. no one can, of course, disagree with this objective - and i personally agree. the means of achieving this are very different, however, and i personally refuse to accept the rapporteur's overly liberal options, which go beyond the text presented by the commission, which is intended to encourage a competitive european single market. i would like to add four points to the debate which are important to me. firstly, as regards the principle of competition, i could never accept that it should be regarded as an end in itself. secondly, as regards control, i am not in favour of putting national regulatory authorities under the control of the commission. thirdly, as regards the frequency allocations required for umts licences, i think that this should remain a matter for the member states. fourthly, and finally, on universal service, i am in favour of the rapid establishment of a review mechanism which is transparent, proportionate and non-discriminatory and i support the call for internet access to be included in universal service. in conclusion, and while i thank the rapporteur for his work, i feel closer to the commission than to the rapporteur on this matter, whose liberal if not ultra-liberal options somewhat worry me.
in writing. - i emphasized during the debate the shocking discrepancy between the very benign nature of the text on which we were called upon to vote and the particularly difficult reality facing the victims of the erika disaster, whose losses appear to be absolutely considerable. this tragedy should have brought about a major change in the community procedure. unfortunately, this has not been the case and the war continues unabated. it merely proposes exchanges of information, which are certainly very useful, for the period 2000-06. the essential questions will have to wait. the victims, on the other hand, found that the polluter pays principle was still not really recognised and that the compensation system put in place in 1992 was very unsatisfactory and that it curiously exempted the ship's operator. the fipol, in 6 months, has not paid 2 million in compensation. the mechanism of fipol itself appears to be particularly perverse. it is a system of compensation without liability, the ceiling of which is irrelevant to the extent of the actual damage. it is not normal that the state and local authorities should be forced to substitute themselves for a large part of the polluter. this system is advantageous to the oil companies and, as we have just seen, it puts unacceptable pressure on the victims, whether they are professionals or local authorities, who are anxious to go to court to have their damage recognised. this arrangement must therefore be renegotiated and supplemented by a strict legal framework, of the same type as that which the united states has long been able to provide. the necessary debates and the necessary measures must not be postponed this time. the erika victims hope that their experiences will be used to prevent such disasters from happening again. it is good that the amendment affirming the polluter pays principle has been adopted by our assembly. it's a small step in the right direction.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, during the portuguese presidency of the european union, the development of the common security and defence policy was a priority, and this was also expressed in the document we presented at the beginning of this presidency. the report which the portuguese presidency will submit to the european council in santa maria da feira will report on the progress made in the various mandates received in helsinki, particularly with regard to: the development of european military capabilities, the headline goal; the institutional development of the permanent political and military bodies; relations between the european union and third countries in this field; relations between the european union and nato; whether or not the treaty on european union needs to be revised and the problem of non-military instruments for crisis management. in the framework of its external policy and its common security and defence policy, the union has decided to develop its military and non-military dimensions in parallel. it is clear that these two dimensions must be coordinated, especially the military and non-military crisis management actions that the union decides to undertake. this coordination will take place through the new structures of the common foreign and security policy, in particular through the political and security committee, the future military committee and the crisis management committee. i would like to point out that the interim bodies started functioning in march 2000 and that the committee on civil crisis management was formally established under the portuguese presidency. as the presidency's report to the feira european council will show, there is a concomitant effort to develop civilian and military crisis management capabilities. beyond the development of the headline target by member states (a general affairs council meeting with defence ministers was held yesterday and this issue was discussed), member states will commit themselves at the feira european council to developing their civilian policy capacity (up to 5 000 elements) by 2003 for crisis management operations. member states are also making a major effort to develop these two dimensions, which are fundamental to security and stability, in a sustainable and parallel way. as regards the other issue raised by mr elmar brok in his speech, i would like to say that the strengthening of the common foreign and security policy through the development of a common european security and defence policy, which will enable the european union to acquire military capability and also to strengthen the effectiveness of its civilian crisis management instruments, does not necessarily imply an increase in the defence budgets of the member states. the fundamental objective is to make better use of and to rationalise the military resources and capabilities of states. in this context, it is important to recall that the european union will use nato's defence planning, the planning and review process for non-alliance countries and the alliance defence capabilities initiative in the development of the headline goal. every effort shall be made to use all means and capabilities more efficiently, avoiding duplication which could lead to additional defence expenditure. again in relation to the community budget, no increase is foreseen as these efforts are implemented by the member states in the framework of voluntary cooperation. however, the final answer on the budgetary impact of this policy can only come after the commitment capability conference in the autumn, which will analyse national military contributions to this joint effort and the gaps that may need to be filled. as regards the involvement of the european parliament in this process, it should be recalled and stated that the common european security and defence policy is a component of the common foreign and security policy. the union wants to give more efficiency and credibility to its external dimension, through the development of military and civilian capacities for crisis management. in accordance with article 21 of the treaty on european union, the presidency shall consult parliament on the main aspects and basic options of the common foreign and security policy. the positions expressed by parliament shall be taken into consideration by the council of the european union. parliament is also regularly informed of developments in the common foreign and security policy, can ask the council questions on matters it considers important and can make recommendations it deems most appropriate. the development of the common european security and defence policy also requires the avoidance of unnecessary duplication and the use of all existing means and capabilities. it is therefore only natural that the member states of the european union have from the outset defended the transfer of functions from the weu which could prove useful to the process currently under way within the european union. in its presidency of the weu, portugal has tried to advance the process of transferring functions from the weu to the european union.

amsterdam, the decision taken in helsinki - all these decisions are a sign of progress, a proof that we have not done enough to make europe's voice heard adequately in the world and to ensure that europe's capacity to prevent and manage crises is used with sufficient competence and vigour to exert any influence. this time, we have to make a difference. this time we must ensure that europe implements a common foreign and security policy capable of responding effectively to events and, i think, to the demands of our citizens. the commission wants to play its full role and ensure the resounding success of a common foreign and security policy. an intergovernmental process with variable geometry, whereby all the states that wish to commit can do so and thus pool their assets, without any of those who wish to abstain being able to be dragged into involuntary participation in an action that they would not approve of. the organization of such a capacity for intervention must not be conceived in an ideological way, as a compelling factor for in writing. - when voting on the calendar of the 2001 part-sessions, the majority of members of the european parliament considered that they were entitled to remove friday from the monthly part-sessions in strasbourg. this is just one more episode in the perpetual guerrilla war waged by the anti-strasbourg forces against the letter of the treaties. the anti-strasbourg group had already suffered a crushing defeat at the court of justice in 1997 when it tried to abolish one of the 12 normal monthly partsession periods altogether. this time they wanted to make progress in a more subtle way, shortening the duration of each normal session without affecting their numbers. the court of justice, in its judgment of 1 october 1997, had rightly pointed out that the decision of the edinburgh council of 12 december 1992, taken pursuant to article 216 of the treaty (and subsequently raised to the status of protocol by the treaty of amsterdam), had the same value as the treaty and was therefore binding on the european parliament. in passing, the parliament had thus been subjected to the supreme humiliation of being reminded that it was not a sovereign parliament, like a national parliament, but only an assembly created by a treaty and subject to the conditions and limits laid down by that treaty. the edinburgh decision, which was taken over by the amsterdam protocol, states that 'the european parliament shall have its seat in strasbourg, where the twelve monthly plenary sessions shall be held ...'. in 1997, advocate general lenz pointed out that if the text contains the phrase 'where the twelve plenary sessions are held' (and not, for example, 'the number of plenary sessions to be held at this place is fixed at twelve'), this means that 'the representatives of the governments of the member states have referred to a practice followed by parliament as regards its functioning'. this practice, as far as we are concerned today, is that of normal sessions in strasbourg lasting a full week. this practice, on which the treaty is based, must be respected. if it were accepted that the normal plenary sessions could be cut by one day, this would be likely to be pushed further, so that gradually strasbourg would no longer be the centre of the work of the plenary. the letter of the treaty would thus be violated, in small steps. i would like to take this opportunity to point out that i do not think that the setting of additional brussels sessions more than a year in advance is a practice in conformity with the treaty either. the 1997 decision states that 'additional plenary sessions may be held at another place of work only if parliament holds the 12 ordinary sessions in strasbourg, the seat of the institution'. the court therefore considered very logically that there could be an 'additional' part-session only if the normal part-sessions had been held and if they had indeed proved insufficient to deal with all the cases pending. i conclude that the european parliament has no right to set the holding of additional partsession more than one year in advance, as it does today. it should be able to know whether the normal sessions in strasbourg were sufficient, or insufficient, to deal with the pending cases. but he can't know that long in advance. moreover, it might be seen as contradictory that it reduces the normal plenary weeks in strasbourg, while maintaining additional sessions in brussels. if he thinks we are spending too much time sitting, the first thing to do is to abolish the additional partsession in brussels. i very much hope that the french government will refer the matter to the court of justice again, as it did in 1995. i also hope that he will make a real effort to facilitate the coming to strasbourg of our foreign colleagues. it is no wonder that those who travel for 10 to 12 hours because of poor rail or air services end up getting tired and catching the flu in strasbourg.
in writing. - as regards the calendar of the 2001 sessions of the european parliament, i want to say very clearly, i who have never been absent even once since the renewal of 12 june 1999, that i have opposed, i oppose and i will oppose any decision to empty our strasbourg plenary session of its substance with the more or less avowed aim of contesting the seat of the european parliament in strasbourg. such a decision not only calls into question an institutional balance accepted by all states, but, more seriously, it calls into question a 'certain idea of europe' which strasbourg symbolises: that of a political europe reconciled and peaceful. finally, who can deny the absurdity of creating a single capital for a federal europe which, in 10 years' time, will have more than 500 million inhabitants? it would be an urban, environmental and therefore human disaster! to be modern in the 21st century means to want a multipolar capital in the heart of which strasbourg will always have a special place. for all these reasons, i denounce the ideological and mercantile maneuvers of the anti-strasbourgeois who never miss an opportunity to strike!
- mr president, as regards the revision of the directive on the manufacture, presentation and sale of tobacco products, we have followed the rapporteur in his most severe amendments, because we are convinced that tobacco represents a huge cost to society and a far greater danger to consumers than they themselves imagine. however, at the same time we are convinced that article 95 of the treaty on the approximation of the rules on the internal market, on which this project is based, represents a wrong legal basis. the proposed measures are designed to protect public health and not to remove obstacles to the movement of products. article 152 of the treaty on public health authorizes the community to encourage cooperation between member states but not to take binding harmonization measures itself, which are expressly excluded by paragraph 3 (c). in these circumstances, we are well aware that the commission is, as so often, using a laudable cause - in this case, the fight against smoking - to give itself new powers, in defiance of the letter of the treaties and in defiance of subsidiarity. we therefore voted for the amendments to show that we wanted to be strict on the substance, but at the same time we call on the council to transform the draft directive, in accordance with article 152, into a recommendation encouraging the member states to take their responsibilities. they are perfectly capable of doing so, and even if this national competence resulted in different consumer information rules for different countries, depending on their own culture, the tobacco industry would have to adapt to them. if we do not do this, it could be said that subsidiarity would no longer make sense in the community.
- mr president, i share this explanation of vote with mrs cauquil and mrs bordes. by voting for this report, despite its shortcomings and above all despite the hypocrisy of the states in their efforts to curb smoking, we intend to oppose, within the limits of the possibilities afforded to us, the right of tobacco trusts to poison the population for private profit. the measures should also impose the same restrictions, at least on european tobacco trusts, when they license the manufacture or sale of their poison in eastern european countries, in africa or elsewhere. the behaviour of tobacco companies, so contrary to the interests of society, is similar to the behaviour of all the big oil, asbestos, arms and food companies, which are willing to risk harm to the population or the environment in order to make a little more profit. we have rejected all the amendments which seek to mitigate the already limited scope of the proposed measures, or to curb the information indicating the deadly harmfulness of smoking, because they all meet the wishes of the tobacco trust lobby. on the other hand, we stand in solidarity with the workers in this sector and with the small farmers who produce tobacco, whose income and their conversion to useful production should be financed by levies on the enormous profits of the tobacco trusts.
in writing. - the commission proposal for a directive is essentially designed to revise existing directives concerning, in particular, the tar content of cigarettes and the labelling of tobacco products. it also aims to complement existing provisions to take account of scientific findings and to improve the level of protection of public health. the directive has the merit of clarifying existing law, of bringing regulations closer together, of improving consumer protection and of combating smoking. i am in favour of this directive and find the indecent press campaign by the multinational tobacco companies, which make a mockery of the health of the population and are only concerned with their market shares and profits, scandalous. it would also be essential to take measures at international level to stop the offensive of these firms towards developing countries where they multiply, without restraint or control, advertising and propaganda campaigns. i am in favour of the commission's proposal and also of the amendments to the report by the committee on the environment which improve the protection of public health. we are also not hiding the problems we are facing with the decision to call into question the aid to community tobacco production. we must take account of the socioeconomic aspects of this production. it is also a question of facing these problems, of engaging in a process, of taking into account that the european union imports almost 80% of its tobacco consumption. that is why i co-signed an amendment calling for 'respect for community preference in order to reduce the share of american multinational firms in tobacco consumption'.
in writing. - as a representative of a tobacco-producing region, i should like to express my reservations about the proposal for a tobacco directive. the validity of its objectives will be beyond doubt: tobacco kills 500,000 people a year in the european union alone. so we must fight tobacco as firmly as we fight drugs, alcoholism and all other dangerous addictions, whether of natural or chemical origin. in this respect, the proposals in this report which aim to improve prevention, awareness and information of the risks to which the consumer is exposed by excessive tobacco consumption cannot but be shared. let us go even further than labelling or limiting toxic substances by making better use of the special fund set up under the common organization of the tobacco market and funded by the producers to finance research and development of less harmful varieties. but we must also be careful not to destabilise too abruptly, without giving it time to recover, an agricultural sector which still has 135 000 producers and employs 400 000 seasonal workers in agricultural regions which are often fragile. in this case, i think we should be guided by a few simple principles: to act fairly against all the risks of addiction, including the advertising and excessive consumption - which is also financed by social security - of dangerous pharmacological substances; ensure that the restriction of domestic tobacco production is accompanied by control and restriction of imports in order not to negate the effects on consumption; allowing growers an appropriate period to adapt their production to the new tar content standards; we are not going to accept any limitation of subsidies to tobacco production without replacing them with incentive aid for conversion. in other words, the producers of the european union alone - who supply only 25% of the raw tobacco consumed in europe - must not bear, without compensation or delay, the costs of a regulation which is certainly laudable but too caricatural in the form in which it is proposed to us.
in writing. - the programme we have discussed today is aimed at organizing the dismantling of the nuclear installations of the joint research centre and the management of waste arising from its nuclear activities. i do not have a major disagreement on the substance of the proposal, but i do have questions about the budgetary dimension of this programme. the rapporteur has refrained from making any concrete proposals. it is true that he rejected the european commission's proposal. it is worth recalling that the commission has proposed to us that this operation be financed by using, at the end of each year, unspent appropriations from heading 3. it would use a hotline in the current subsection b4 (energy, nuclear safety control, environment) for this purpose. this solution is satisfactory in that it places funding outside the framework research programmes, a point which our european parliament had stressed, but it is not up to the challenge. in the long term, it is unacceptable to finance the dismantling of nuclear activities by means of a "pick-up" line whose importance is left to chance. i take this opportunity to say that i disapprove of the increasing use of this type of line! i imagine that is what led the rapporteur to 'take note of the commission's proposal' without however following it up. the report proposes that we set up a trilogue between the institutions to find a solution. he remains silent on the other funding possibilities that have been considered. the most illusory solution would be to have the member states finance the dismantling of these nuclear activities in ways that have yet to be found. it is obvious that this would not fail to stir up trouble in the member states which are not particularly concerned by this problem. the solution is to finance the programme through an autonomous budget line. i am well aware that it is not the easy way out, because it implies voting for additional appropriations when the budgetary perspective is revised. but we must be prepared to meet its ambitions, especially when it comes to nuclear energy. in the long term, therefore, pressure will have to be put on the council to accept the creation of this autonomous budget line. in the short term, and out of pragmatism, i think that we should not block the rapid implementation of this programme. the compromise i support is therefore the following: the introduction of the commission's proposed 'mixing' line in the very short term and the trialogue's prompt commitment to vote on an autonomous budget line in the medium term.

counsel. - (pt) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i think that at the beginning of a question like this, we should recall the general attitude of the european union regarding its framework of external relations. the european union has a set of values and principles which it naturally wishes to express in its relations and which it seeks to assert in all dimensions of its association with third countries. contrary to what one member's speech might suggest, the european union is not engaged in a kind of geographical approximation, which would be more demanding of what is closer to it and less demanding of what is further away. that is not our view of things. we normally work on the basis of uniform criteria and we have, in particular, the notion that it is better to open up spaces the opportunity to take stock of the human rights situation in tunisia at ministerial level at the two association councils held so far. the union has made it a point to address the issue of human russia to the mediterranean. strong men are sometimes needed to ensure that institutions are robust and operate within the rule of law. the third instrument is more radical. it consists of the the problem of trade union freedoms. the great wave of repression that has hit the opposition, all tendencies combined since the 1990s, has allowed the general union of tunisian workers, the ugtt, to mr president, i too would like to express my deep concern at the deterioration of the human rights situation in tunisia, a concern which is shared by all the friends of that country. for several years now, human rights defenders and their families have been subjected to constant harassment by the tunisian authorities. some of them are sentenced to prison terms; they are all regularly followed by members of the police; their passports and those of their relatives are confiscated; their communications are cut off or tapped; campaigns of defamation or physical and verbal threats are launched against them; finally, their relatives are regularly questioned. in the face of such a drift, the european parliament today reiterates its conviction that respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms cannot be subject to any exception and cannot be ignored without damage, since tunisia is the first european partner to have concluded an association agreement with the european union in 1995. the agreement contains a clause on respect for human rights, which has a suspensive effect, and provides for political dialogue. i am certainly in favour of political dialogue rather than unilateral sanctions, but it is precisely in this context that we have the duty to tell our partners that we are very concerned about the situation in tunisia. we have a duty to ask the tunisian authorities to take all the necessary steps to establish a genuine multiparty system and to guarantee freedom of the press and of association. but, mr patten, what is this dialogue about?
