in writing. - first of all, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur and my colleagues who took part in the conciliation meetings and who had to fight hard against a council of ministers that is more than reluctant to move forward with legislation on late payments, which is absolutely scandalous in view of the economic challenges facing smes. it must be borne in mind that late payment is the main cause of insolvencies that threaten the survival of companies and lead to many bankruptcies resulting in redundancies. national regulations to deal with this problem differ considerably from one member state to another. it is therefore important to adopt legislation as soon as possible to harmonise the provisions on payment deadlines, due dates and the statutory interest rate at european level. the aim is to establish a legal framework to discourage late payments and to give creditors the right to fair compensation in the event of late payment. this is the subject of the directive we are discussing today. the negotiations on this text were difficult. a common position was finally adopted on 29 may. the european parliament has emerged victorious on several key points from these long negotiations. the points of divergence between parliament and the council have been particularly crystallised on the difference in treatment between the public and private sectors, which have finally been placed on an equal footing. as regards the retention of title, parliament succeeded in requiring that this provision be included in the text of the directive. member states will thus have to ensure that the seller retains ownership of the goods until full settlement, in compliance with the applicable national provisions. as regards the anti-abuse clause, the european parliament refused to give priority to contractual freedom to the detriment of the creditor. the directive therefore provides that where the main purpose of an agreement is to provide the debtor with additional liquidity at the expense of the creditor or where the main contractor imposes on his suppliers and subcontractors payment conditions which are not justified by the conditions imposed on him, such provisions may be regarded as constituting factors of abuse. as regards compensation, except where the debtor is not responsible for the delay, the creditor is entitled to claim from the debtor, as a result of the agreement, reasonable compensation for all recovery costs incurred. such compensation may include the borrowing or overdraft costs of the creditor, the administrative costs of recovery incurred by the creditor company, the costs of debt collection agencies and the costs of legal proceedings. as regards interest, parliament and the council agreed on a rate of 7%, plus the rate applied by the european central bank, which gives a total of 10.5% at present. the european parliament wanted to reduce the period for payment of interest to 21 days instead of 30 days from the date of receipt of the invoice as provided for by the council. finally, the 30-day time limit was maintained, but it was provided that this could give rise to an action for damages where it constituted a manifest abuse of the creditor. in conclusion, i would say that the result of the conciliation is satisfactory, since many of the european parliament's wishes have been granted. i therefore voted in favour of this text.
mr president, the preparations for the feira european council next week seem to be giving rise, behind the scenes, to a tug of war between those who want to lengthen the agenda of the intergovernmental conference and those who want to reduce it. behind this divide lies another: between the former, who are in favour of a federalist leap forward, and the realists, who are beginning to wonder whether a fully integrated europe - economically and politically - is the right solution to enlargement and the democratic deficit. i am pleased to say that the second category seems to be winning, which is perfectly acceptable to us. the only point that could be added seems to us quite acceptable, since it is a question of opening up the possibility of so-called 'enhanced' cooperation. we prefer to call them 'differentiated cooperation' to show that we are not trying to lock europe into a one-way street towards federalism, but rather to allow the member states to explore freely, in formations with variable geometry, the forms of cooperation which seem to them to be most in line with their vision of the future and their interests. in any case, whatever the name chosen: 'enhanced' or 'differentiated' cooperation, the main thing in our view is to take the first step and open the discussion by unblocking a european system which is now completely out of order. i would add that we believe that the new differentiated cooperation should be applied to security policy, so that it can develop while remaining based on voluntary action and respect for national sovereignty. finally, if the feira council is to consider the question of the charter of fundamental rights, we ask it not to put it on the igc agenda, so that it can now proceed to a declaratory document which is not part of the treaty. as i have already said in this house and in the chamber responsible for drawing up the charter, it would be interesting to proclaim our common values - if we did it well - but we must not deprive our peoples of the freedom to define for themselves the rights of their citizens.
in writing. - as we vote on the joint resolution for the feira summit, i would like to pay tribute to the important work of the portuguese presidency, its attentiveness, its dynamism and its availability. i also want to say that although everything i would have liked is unfortunately not in the joint resolution - in particular the need for a framework directive on public services - many of the proposals are very pleasing, this is probably one of the best resolutions we have had to consider in the current political composition of the european parliament on all these points. unfortunately, in this resolution, a point concerning austria was introduced by the right. this is completely unacceptable to me at a time when 'several indicators are in the red' and when there is ample evidence that the alliance with the austrian far right is beginning to take its toll. more than ever, we must fight against the fascists, neo-fascists and their accomplices. it is the very future of europe that is at stake. and that is why, whatever the quality of a text devoted to feira, to the work and conclusions of the portuguese presidency, there can be no question, in my view, of validating, even in the margins, even in the water, a shameful alliance, with consequences that could be dramatic for europe. shame on the sorcerer 's apprentices ! how, 60 years after the nazi invasion of 1940 and 55 years after the end of a horrible european and world conflict, can some, for reasons of low electoral values, have "such a short memory"? ! !
- mr president, mrs cauquil and mrs bordes, who are also present, agree with this explanation. we voted against this resolution to affirm our opposition to both a common european army and national armies. the past half century has shown that the armies of the great imperialist powers of europe, allied with each other or each in its own hunt, have not served to defend the population but to wage wars of banditry. in particular, the french army was used in colonial wars: madagascar, indochina, algeria. once these colonies became independent, it intervened to support infamous dictatorships, especially in its former colonies in africa. the same was true of other former colonial powers in europe in the same situation. the european armies which have recently intervened against serbia and kosovo certainly have no reason to boast of this. the author of the report is careful not to specify against which enemy the future european army would be directed. so what will it be used for and against, if not to be able to continue, in the name of the whole european union, the political and communitarian game of the great powers of europe in africa, the west indies or elsewhere? hence, we not only refuse to vote for this army by any means, human or financial, but we even oppose its existence.
in writing. - for the past few months, the european union has been following an extremely complicated path, marked by the councils of cologne, helsinki, lisbon and tomorrow by the feira council, in an attempt to establish what it calls a 'common european security and defence policy'. the exercise is complicated, firstly because we have to try to clarify relations with nato, and the united states, but also other nato countries that are not members of the european union, such as turkey, do not make it easy for us. everything is made more difficult by the desire of the institutions of the union to extend the scope of this new policy, presenting it as 'a new step towards the political integration of europe', in the words of the resolution we have just voted, that is to say, a new step towards supranationality. as regards the scope of this security policy, ambiguity is purposely maintained. strictly speaking, these are only 'petersberg' missions (crisis prevention and peacekeeping in third countries, excluding the defence of national territories or vital external interests), but the european parliament insists on referring to a much broader objective, that of a common security and defence policy in the broad sense - this is the very title of the resolution voted today. the ambiguity is fuelled by the decision to set up common military means to prevent crises (for example the european rapid action force, of 50 000 to 60 000 men, decided in helsinki), which allows the 'integrationists' to continually play on words, and to make it appear that there is a question of implementing a defence policy in the full sense of the term. as regards both the method and the objective, political integration or cooperation, we believe that the ever-shaky prospect of a supranational, unitary and integrated power is counterproductive. to be effective, the instruments of voluntary cooperation, with variable geometry, must be put in place, involving the member states of the union which are interested in this or that action - and also, if necessary, non-member states, why not? in summary, the europe of nations group believes that it is desirable to move towards common security actions, provided that we do not lock ourselves into a rigid institutional system, but instead put in place flexible procedures based on voluntary action and respect for national sovereignty. we are open to the idea of joint action on security, which we believe europe badly needs. but at the same time we must be very clear about their conditions: it is impossible to hand over military decision-making power (even if we are told at first that it will be only petersberg missions) to european institutions which are very imperfectly democratic - and which will remain so from a human point of view, because there is no european people. this has three consequences: the last word must always be left to national democracies, so the operations concerned must remain within an interstate framework; decisions may in no circumstances be taken by majority vote on matters of principle; the system must be based on the possibility of 'differentiated actions', allowing each people to exercise its freedom of choice without interruption. i hope that the feira council will decide to add this subject to the agenda of the intergovernmental conference.
in writing. - we are against the proposal for a european army which, in the name of stability, democracy and humanity, will in fact defend the eu's sphere of influence and protect the interests of multinational companies worldwide. the resumption of the local and regional arms race, together with the increase in military budgets, will give a new impetus to the militarization of the world. we are also opposed to a 'high-tech army' for the eu, just as we are opposed to nato. together, europe and the united states are seeking to impose this army as the armed arm of the imf-world bank-wto triangle. it is not an army that the people need, but a social policy that guarantees their well-being. this will not happen without a radical break with neoliberalism. the military intervention in kosovo has exacerbated the misery of the people and exacerbated xenophobic sentiments, thus proving that stability and democracy were certainly not the goal of this war.
in writing. - the outcome of the beijing+5 conference which just ended in new york is a victory for women. after very bitter negotiations, realism in the appreciation of women's needs and respect for their dignity won out. yet we know how strong the pressures have been, whether political, from the united states, japan or the european union, or ideological, from feminist ngos generously funded by western countries. how can we justify, for example, the pressure exerted by the european union on nicaragua or poland? how can we balance the so-called "sexual and reproductive rights" on the one hand, with development aid or delays in eu integration on the other? the pressure exerted on the poorest countries was such that dozens of members of the us congress and national or european parliamentarians formally withdrew from their delegation, expressly condemning their positions. in the same vein, it is instructive to note that, although all of them were officially specialised in the 'situation of women', the ngos with the largest financial means of political communication systematically advocated the notions of 'reproductive health' to the detriment of more serious and urgent needs, thus offering unfailing support to the european and american delegations. however, if this conference was ultimately a success for women around the world, it was mainly thanks to the realism and resilience of the poorest countries, which were able to overcome western ideological polemics on sexuality to promote concrete measures against poverty - such as "micro-credit" - against international trafficking of women or against the lack of education and medical assistance. if the voice of the poor countries was finally heard last saturday at about 4 a.m. despite all kinds of pressure, we owe it to respect for the essential principles which alone guarantee a realistic and measured international policy, namely the principles of national sovereignty and equality between states. the un, after having ignored them for a long time, is now returning to respecting the rules of consensus, which has allowed the negotiations to focus on the real needs of women. we are pleased that the european union has thus celebrated this victory of women with respect for national sovereignty by adopting the final document.

in writing. - the number of asylum applications fell from 660,000 in 1993 to 227,000 in 1997, not because persecution has decreased but because it is more difficult to apply for a visa. the dublin convention allows asylum to be sought only in the country to which the refugee first entered. the aim of the schmitt report is clear: 'to restore the genuine right of asylum, the admission procedure must be clarified and abuses seriously repressed'. in addition, the states on the periphery of the schengen area are considered to be 'safe'. they then become the border guards of fortress europe. in the name of what are countries which practice severe discrimination against roma (romania and slovakia) considered safe enough for belgium to expel the populations it considers undesirable en masse? finally, the current definition of a refugee falls far short of what the 1951 geneva convention states: "a refugee is any person who, for fear of persecution, . . . cannot claim the protection of his country". in fact, today more and more evidence is needed that his life is in danger. which is obviously difficult, if not impossible. for the european union to finally apply the right of asylum, it would have to break with the obsessive practices of immigration control. the more freedom of movement is respected, the more europe will be worthy of those who come to seek refuge in it.

substance. on the substance, ladies and gentlemen, as regards investment in transport, your rapporteur calls for a better balance in favour of sustainable transport, in particular rail. the commissioner for regional policy, who was once his country's minister for the environment, is certainly very much in favour of this approach and will personally ensure that it is followed, particularly in the programming of the cohesion fund for the next six years. i share that concern. it was also stressed by mrs schörling and mrs damião, and you can be sure that i will be working on increasing the focus on sustainable transport, particularly rail, which has been evident for several years now. but this is not enough: i want to give it even more emphasis in the next six years. as regards other investments which can contribute to the objective of sustainable transport, i am talking about ports and airports, the commission wishes to observe - let me say this frankly - a certain degree of caution with regard to air transport and certain forms of maritime transport. in any case, we want to look at things closely and adjust the cofinancing rate to take account, to say the least, of the commercial nature of the activities and the revenue they generate. the commission will, however, support the approach to sustainable transport with all its strength. as regards the environment, your rapporteur stresses the need to take better account - as mr mastorakis has also said very strongly - of the serious problem of the treatment of solid waste and household waste. the fund has so far focused on three sectors which are the subject of community directives: drinking water treatment, waste water treatment and solid waste treatment. the priority was to enable the member states to meet the deadlines set under the waste water directive, and we know that the problems i have just mentioned, particularly the question of waste or water treatment, are difficult in the countries concerned. i have seen this firsthand in the azores and i know that the same is true of the greek islands, to take these two examples: these problems are particularly difficult when there is peripheral, ultra-peripheral or geographical isolation due to insularity. as regards the specific problems of the environment, i would like to say, particularly with regard to the islands, that i am very keen to support investment in renewable energy sources, and i have made this known to the member states. with regard more specifically to the issue of solid waste, 14% of the budgetary envelope was allocated to its treatment, which represents a significant increase compared to the period 1993-1997. however, i share your rapporteur's concern to use the most modern and environmentally friendly technologies for this purpose. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this is no coincidence, madam deputy. i have deliberately wanted to give the commission's consent to the use - not just any way or for any purpose - but to the use of the cohesion fund for biodiversity and nature protection. you have the concrete expression of this in the approval of this amendment. you will also see that i will continue to be concerned, in the context of objective 2, objective 1 and the cohesion fund, that part of the appropriations should be used for the benefit of biodiversity. after speaking of substance, i want to say a word of form, and first to respond to the comments of your rapporteur on the study commissioned by the commission on the socioeconomic effects of the cohesion fund. i believe that these remarks are based on a misunderstanding which i should like to correct. the five years mentioned by your rapporteur refer to the time elapsed between the start of the projects assessed and the final evaluation. the consultants selected by the commission first developed an evaluation methodology and then evaluated the projects concerned. a five-year period is not unusual for the completion of a major project and the ex-post evaluation of its results. the commission has just received this study and is analysing it. in any event, it will be sent to you as soon as possible. i would then like to turn to the question of the coherence between the cohesion fund and the structural funds, as raised by your rapporteur. i am particularly attentive to this question. for this reason, the structural fund programmes currently being negotiated by the commission with the cohesion member states include indicative amounts for both cohesion fund and european investment bank aid. the information requested by your parliament is thus available in the individual programming documents. i would also point out that the recent restructuring of the regional action directorate brings together the geographical teams and the competences within the same units for the structural funds and the cohesion fund, so that the cohesion countries, which are eligible for the structural funds in most cases, will have the same interlocutors within this directorate-general. i think that is a more coherent approach for these countries. but the coherence between the structural funds and the cohesion fund also implies respect for the specific nature of these two instruments, in accordance with the general regulation on the structural funds. it would be inappropriate to intervene under the cohesion fund for the same purposes and in the same way as we do with the structural funds. from the point of view of sound financial management, it is not appropriate to abandon the specificity of each instrument. in any event, i am not in a position to change the powers of the cohesion fund which derive directly from the treaty. mrs schörling, you mentioned the question of additionality. i would like to make a few comments on the report by mr turco. i have made it clear that i am concerned about checking additionality and what is true of mr turco's report is also true of the cohesion fund. i have even said that the fact of this additionality will be one of the points which will enable me to validate or approve programmes and projects. i would like to conclude by emphasizing that the annual report is a particularly useful instrument for the analysis, evaluation and reflection we regularly carry out on the implementation of regional policy. this report is all the more useful because it is comprehensive. i agree with the need to receive the annual report as soon as possible and i can assure you that my services will make every effort to expedite its publication in the future as much as possible. it is clear, ladies and gentlemen, that our reflection is not confined to these annual reports. i can assure you that, beyond our regular contacts, the report on cohesion which i will present to you at the end of this year will largely answer the questions, the criticisms and the proposals raised by your rapporteur on the continuation of solidarity with the countries benefiting from the cohesion fund, particularly in the great prospect which confronts us all: enlargement.
the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow morning at 9 a.m.

the next item is the joint debate on the report (a5-0147/2000) by mr sousa pinto, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council regulation supplementing regulation (eec) no 302/93 on the establishment of a european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction (emcdda) (com (1999) 430 - c5-0304/1999 - 1999/0187 (cns)) - report (a5-0157/2000) by mr turco, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the proposal for a council decision on the conclusion of an agreement between the european community and the kingdom of norway concerning the participation of norway in the work of the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction (com (99) 496 - c5-0054/2000 - 1999/0203 (cns)).
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, at a time when phrases such as 'bringing the european union closer to the citizens' and 'good governance' are on everyone's lips, the examination of the operation and scientific production of the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction leaves no room for doubt, as the results are close to nothing. like the many observatories set up to better mask our differences, this observatory, in its five years of existence, has produced nothing that justifies the millions of euros allocated to it each year. when the amounts allocated to the agency are compared with the resources available to the national agencies, one might expect in-depth studies to provide objective, reliable and comparable information in the field of drugs and drug addiction, as specified in the definition of its mission in article 2. the observatory should be able to develop uniform definitions and indicators to assess the different drug control policies in the member states from both a health and socioeconomic and a public policy perspective. for example, when will we finally know what the consequences of the prohibitionist policy of france or the regulatory policy of the netherlands have been? the independent evaluation of the activities of the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction, the conclusions of which were made public in march 2000, is very explicit about the serious dysfunction of the management board and the reitox network for the collection of information on drugs and drug addiction. the reports we are considering today are intended to extend the observatory to norway and the 13 candidate countries. we can only agree on this point, but would it not be better to reform the institution first so that it can finally serve a purpose? to welcome new members, yes, but with what prospects? to reproduce on a larger scale the failure of the last few years? increase the thickness of beautiful annual reports that have no use? it is time for the european union to realise that, far from the splendid premises of the observatory in lisbon, thousands of people are directly confronted with the health and social problems caused by drug addiction. we are not asking him to tackle these problems; we are simply asking him to decipher them. hundreds of different initiatives are being taken in europe at institutional or associative level, with a view to enforcement or, on the contrary, risk reduction. what is the observatory waiting for to evaluate these attempts? why are the member states so reluctant to cooperate in this assessment? is it to be seen as a fear of politically unflattering results? i therefore support the rapporteur's call for a real reform of the monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction, both in terms of its operation and in terms of the extension of its powers. this is a necessary precondition for welcoming new members.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. even if some of your amendments go further than our proposals, particularly with regard to the proposed improvements in the operation of the monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction. the commission agrees with parliament that the functioning of the emcdda needs to be improved. i would remind you that the commission requested the external evaluation of the emcdda. we will of course take into account the recommendations of this parliament and the decisions of the observatory's board of directors, which are based on the conclusions of this evaluation report. our two proposals, however, are much broader. the first is to enable an agreement to be concluded with norway. there is political unanimity on this and i am glad that the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs is also supporting this agreement. the latter is of great political importance to the norwegians. it seems that they want to gain a better understanding of the drug problem on the european continent. the agreement is also important for the union because, as everyone knows, the drug problem knows no borders. norway has received a copy of the emcdda's evaluation report and has confirmed, through a positive opinion by the norwegian parliament, that it would be happy to accede to this agreement. the commission believes that we should not send a negative signal to our norwegian partners by attaching conditions to the signing of this agreement relating to the improvement of the operation of the observatory and thus delaying the conclusion of the agreement. the commission will therefore not amend the proposal on improving the functioning of the emcdda, although it has no objection to the content of the amendments in mr turco's report. our second proposal is to facilitate the participation of candidate countries in the emcdda and to assist them in setting up national focal points and in establishing structural links with the reitox network. of the 22 amendments contained in the sousa pinto report, five have a direct link with this point. we have noted that parliament has expressly mentioned malta, cyprus and turkey as the countries for which this technical assistance is intended. our intention - and i am speaking also on behalf of the council - is to give this assistance to all the applicant countries and therefore also to malta, cyprus and turkey. we will therefore take up the clarification you have made by specifically mentioning malta, cyprus and turkey and defend it before the council. the commission, however, cannot accept the extension to third countries which are not candidates for membership. this is because we do not want to make the emcdda a global centre for technical assistance, but to enable it to pass on the available knowledge to the candidate countries for their future participation. we agree with parliament that the evaluation of the drug policy of the member states is essential. this is also part of the action plan to combat drugs for the period 2000-2004, which will be discussed at the feira european council. in our view, however, it is not for the emcdda to judge the policy of the member states in this area. this is a political issue which should not be left to the emcdda, which is more of a technical body, but to the institutions of the union. the emcdda, on the other hand, is responsible for developing methodological instruments for assessing national policies. such activities can now also be carried out and are included, for example, in the work programme for the year 2000. to this end, the emcdda's budget has been increased by half a million euro. we do not think that the time is right to propose to amend the emcdda regulation and to introduce explicitly the development of a methodological evaluation instrument, thus making this kind of activity more visible. there are two reasons for this. firstly, following the evaluation report, the emcdda's management board is currently discussing the observatory's role and tasks, and the commission considers it appropriate to await the management board's conclusions in order to make further proposals in this area. secondly, if we extend our proposal in this direction, there is a risk that we will enter into a long discussion with the council and not reach a decision before the end of the year. if that were the case, we would have to abandon a €2 million phare project to help future eastern european member states to set up or strengthen national focal points with the emcdda's technical assistance. this money will not be transferred after 31 december 2000. the other amendments, which are not directly related to our proposal, are based primarily on the emcdda's evaluation report and should lead to a fundamental revision of the basic regulation. the amendments would oblige the member states to provide the data requested by the observatory, whereas, until now, cooperation was only voluntary. the distribution of responsibilities between the director and the administrative board would also be changed, as would the way in which discharge for the budget would be given. the latter is a horizontal issue which must be the subject of a similar regulation for all the bodies and on which a commission proposal has been tabled on the council's table. the amendments also introduce a three-yearly report on the evaluation of the functioning of the emcdda. the amendments tabled by mrs ilka schröder all deal with the same subject. they all aim to add to the tasks of the observatory the evaluation of policy in the field of risk reduction. this terminology is explained in a wide variety of ways and is therefore not found in the european union's drugs strategy for 2000-04. in addition, this subject should not be approached in isolation but as part of a coherent whole which also includes prevention, treatment, rehabilitation and accompanying social measures. as i have already said, mr president, the commission agrees with the european parliament that the functioning of the emcdda must be improved. i want to stress that point. but as i said, we will not amend our proposal, and that is mainly because it is not the right time. the emcdda's administrative board, on which parliament is also represented, will take a number of decisions, on the basis of an evaluation report, at its september meeting, and we think it is more appropriate to wait for the results before proposing further amendments to the emcdda regulation, such as those relating to evaluation. at this meeting of the emcdda's administrative board, the commission will advocate the need to review the functioning of the emcdda and to clarify its objectives and tasks. depending on the action taken by the administrative board, the commission may be able to introduce a proposal for amendment of the emcdda regulation, which would also respond to the wish of the parliament to carry out a periodic evaluation of the functioning of the emcdda. in that case, we shall take due account of the opinion of your parliament when drawing up this proposal.

the next item is the report (a5-0150/2000) by mr ferri, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a council regulation (ec) on community designs (com (99) 310 - c5-0129/1999 - 1993/0463 (cns)).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community design is not used in the manufacture of goods. the commission therefore welcomes the very detailed and thoughtful report by mr ferri. as i announced at the internal market council on 16 march, i intend to submit a new amended proposal for a regulation to the commission very shortly for approval. we will be addressing the problems that have been identified since the commission tabled its proposal last june. in this respect, the recommendations of mr ferri's report are particularly useful and important. i am pleased to inform you that the commission supports the recommendations contained in the following amendments: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 7, 8, 9, 13, 14, 16, 18 and 20. some amendments, however, and especially amendments nos 10, 11, 21, 22 and 23, do not entirely correspond to what was agreed in the 1998 community design directive and therefore unfortunately cannot be accepted by the commission. i would like to point out that the commission is very much attached to the principle that the regulation cannot depart from the concepts laid down in the directive. i would also like to mention briefly the issue of the protection of designs when parts of complex products are used for repair purposes, which is dealt with in amendments nos 6 and 12. this question, which was the subject of long and complicated negotiations in the conciliation procedure for the directive, found its echo in the directive and in the approval of the so-called 'reparation clause' compromise. in this context, and in accordance with the compromise reached when the directive was approved, the commission promised to examine this issue further and to put forward a proposal within the framework of the directive. in order not to prejudge the solution which will ultimately be adopted, the commission's proposal for a regulation determines that the parts are not protected under the community system, at least as long as no agreement is reached on a definitive solution. the commission is open to parliament's proposal to bring the text of the regulation closer to that of the directive and i can assure the house that the commission will continue its reflections in this direction. i would like to continue with amendments nos 15 and 19 on counterfeiting. as regards amendment no 15, the commission agrees with parliament that a right to information is necessary. however, the commission prefers to deal with this issue in the context of the fight against counterfeiting and piracy. in this connection, i should like to point out that the commission is dealing with this issue in the green paper on the fight against counterfeiting and piracy in the internal market. as regards the obligation to transfer ownership to the right holder of counterfeit products, proposed in amendment no 19, the commission is of the opinion that this may not be an appropriate solution in all cases and that it may, in some cases, be embarrassing for the right holder. for this reason, and in view of the fact that article 93 (1) (d) of the regulation gives the member state's courts the possibility of taking such measures if necessary, the commission does not agree with the proposed amendment. finally, i would like to thank the members of your assembly for their support and cooperation in this important regulation. i hope and am convinced that european companies will be delighted to have a single, simple and inexpensive procedure for the protection of industrial designs in the european union.

the next item is the report (a5-0132/2000) by mrs grossetête, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the 16th annual report of the commission on monitoring the application of community law (1998) (com (1999) 301 - c5-0213/1999 - 1999/2168 (cos)).
the rapporteur. mr president, just because this report is the last item on the agenda this week does not mean that it is not important, on the contrary, because we are all concerned with the europe of the citizens, the europe for the citizens. it is our duty to think of the interests of the european citizen, to ensure that community law is applied in the member states and that the european commission, as guardian of the treaties, follows this process with the greatest attention. the figures in the report drawn up by the european commission for 1998 unfortunately do not show much improvement and are an encouragement to be vigilant from the outset. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. i am convinced, however, that in the future we will have to be more vigilant in other areas of activity. the european parliament must also reiterate its request for information on the application of international standards. all member states are to some extent concerned by these problems of application of community law. that is why i wanted to stress how important it is that they should be exemplary in their behaviour on the eve of several successive enlargements. how can we expect new countries entering the european union to apply community law if the member states themselves are not able to comply with it? if additional information is needed, it is in the interest of the citizen himself, who is increasingly involved in the process of monitoring community law. this is where the whole question of the infringement procedure comes in. the european commission should not advocate greater selectivity in the handling of cases which could give rise to infringement proceedings, a proposal whereby the commission, in cases of limited scope - take for example the mutual recognition of diplomas - could refrain from intervening. we must oppose this approach very strongly, which cannot be justified on the grounds of cost or efficiency. in doing so, the european commission would be turning away from its role as guardian of the treaties and would be closing access to justice to european citizens. as for the arrangements, i think we can improve them. as the european ombudsman has repeatedly stated, it is important to protect the rights of individuals by improving confidentiality, access to documents and the reasons for the european commission's classification decisions. similarly, more data should be obtained on the liability of member states for damage caused to individuals. no one is thinking of calling into question the importance of petitions, which go a long way towards pointing out that community law is occasionally not applied in the member states. in this context, it is requested that all complaints be given special publicity to give greater visibility to the actions undertaken. but in view of the approach adopted, which is primarily aimed at defending the working methods of the committee on petitions, i do not wish to support amendment no 2. the attention paid to the celex and eur-lex databases, i.e. better access and continuous optimisation, is in my view beneficial for the citizen. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i therefore support this amendment. finally, there is the problem of the question referred for a preliminary ruling. i do not think that the principle of the directive should be called into question, but we can ask questions about the way in which it is applied. poorly drafted questions for a preliminary ruling may have the opposite effect to the objective of clarifying the law. i therefore suggest that the court of justice reconsider the operation of this procedure. i believe that, in order to understand the text of recital g, which says: 'considering that it is primarily for the national courts to apply community law' it would be better to say 'to monitor the application of community law'. finally, there is the question of relations with public administrations which have to deal with new community standards. the current state of european integration places the emphasis on the principle of subsidiarity. i am opposed to amendment no 3 because of this key principle. the creation of a european administrative law does not seem to me to be appropriate. in conclusion, the objective of a control system is nevertheless to punish failure to apply the law. i would stress the importance of the procedure under article 228 (2) of the treaty, which is a new procedure, undoubtedly a deterrent, and which the commission should consider with less timidity in future. so by voting for this resolution we will be sending a positive signal, that of a european parliament that listens to the citizens.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, this community law which we are helping to develop is causing serious difficulties in its application in our member states. the european citizens have used this last resort to express their anger and indignation at the disruption, even destruction, of their daily lives imposed by bureaucrats for an aim that sometimes escapes us and for reasons that do not justify it. while this report should be an opportunity for us elected representatives to take stock of the many texts we are voting on and to draw lessons for the future, we are limiting ourselves to a control/sanction approach. this europe of restrictions and over-regulation is certainly not the europe our fellow citizens want. the way in which this report was adopted is appalling. the rapporteur for the legal affairs committee showed a profound contempt for the committee on petitions by not even considering it useful to put its conclusions to the vote. the plenary yesterday showed the same contempt by ignoring the opinion of the legal affairs committee on the maaten report. i fear that the commission is not giving much more importance to the text we are about to vote on in a virtually empty chamber, because of the contagion. rather than unnecessary amendments, i should like to have an answer to the following question. the 1998 statistics show that the number of reasoned opinions doubled, cases of non-compliance or misapplication detected ex officio increased by more than 50%, complaints by 18% and formal notice by 12%. at this stage, this is not proof of effective control, but rather of the existence of an overabundance of texts which, left to the judges, threaten our national assemblies, which legitimately and democratically express the will of the people, with sentences and fines. does the commission and our rapporteur not think that the number of texts should be reduced and especially those which clearly raise essential political, legal and practical issues which do not appear with the same clarity or acuteness at the time of their drafting should be amended, or do they prefer to continue to punish our states by making our fellow citizens the real victims?
the rapporteur. mr president, i would not like to see a problem between the legal affairs committee and the committee on petitions. however, the main points made by the committee on petitions are reflected in the text of the report i have drawn up. we simply do not agree with your amendments, as mrs palacio has explained, because they should not be inserted here. if you look at the report in depth, you'll see that most of your conclusions are restated.
the debate is closed. we'll move on to the vote. (parliament adopted the resolution)
mr president, my group abstained on the grossetête report because, in the midst of very acceptable general considerations on the application of community law, the resolution contained a paragraph which we cannot accept. it is paragraph 11 which calls on the commission, and i quote: 'to show less timidity in the use of the procedure for the withdrawal of the application provided for in the third subparagraph of article 228 (2) tec'. this article provides for the court of justice to impose fines or penalties, sometimes very high, on a member state which, for whatever reason, does not apply community law as it wishes. we believe that the legal problem is not so simple and that it is too much to impose such penalties on the member states. there can be contradictions between community law and national law which are perfectly legitimate: for example, a contradiction which would appear as a result of a qualified majority vote in the council - and you know that these votes are increasing - or a contradiction which would appear between a national constitution and community law, or a contradiction which would appear between community law and a law deliberately voted by the people of a member state. these contradictions are very serious and have not been resolved, and that is why we consider the existence of article 228 which was introduced by the maastricht treaty to be totally questionable. i would like to remind you in particular that france could be faced with very high constraints today in the case of the 1998 law, for example, on hunting periods which are contrary to community law, or in the case of the british beef embargo, or in the case of the conflict which is now emerging, mr president, on the patentability of human genes which authorizes a european directive which is contrary to french law. that is why we could not accept this report at all. it is a matter of respect for national sovereignty.
in writing. - i welcome the adoption in strasbourg of the motion for a resolution contained in the report drawn up on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and citizens' rights on monitoring the application of community law in 1998, for which i am the rapporteur. the european parliament is thus sending a positive signal to the european citizen, who is entitled to expect a good level of protection from community law. the house has thus shown its vigilance in the face of the difficulties of implementation which exist in several member states and in many fields of activity. it stressed the importance of the infringement procedure, which should not be subject to any opportunistic reform by the commission. it stressed the place of the question of the right to a preliminary ruling in our european system and the need to intensify training in community law in the member states. if no one is going to deny the importance of petitions, i did not want to follow the amendments tabled by the members of the committee on petitions, and in particular the request to create a 'european administrative law'. the current state of european integration and the principle of subsidiarity must be taken into account. but i would stress that it is intended to ask the commission to intensify its relations with the national administrations, when a problem exists, to solve it upstream. the resolution adopted in this way is aimed at greater transparency and efficiency for the benefit of the european citizen.

ladies and gentlemen, it was with great sadness that we learned last tuesday of the death of president pierre pflimlin, former president of the european parliament. pierre pflimlin was a true statesman. his public career had begun the day after the war. it led him to the posts of president of the council, head of government, where, in 1958, when france was going through one of the most troubled periods in its history, he facilitated the transition with general de gaulle. he took an active part in the drafting of the constitution of the fifth republic and became minister of state, a position he held until 1962. pierre pflimlin was one of those historic europeans who, since the end of the war, as a parliamentarian, minister and political activist, has been involved in all the struggles for the construction of a strong and reunified europe. a native of alsace and strasbourg, he was a friend and companion of robert schuman, one of the most active promoters of reconciliation between france and germany and a strong symbol of franco-german friendship. this reconciliation, for which he had worked so hard, he perceived, as he entrusted it to the bishop of strasbourg, as a true miracle. but he knew that this miracle was not the result of chance but of a voluntary and constructive commitment based on common goals and effective institutions. pierre pflimlin was a member of the parliamentary assembly of the council of europe from 1959 and then chaired it for three years from 1963. at the same time he became a member of the european parliament, serving from 1962 to 1967, before returning to it for the first elections by universal suffrage in 1979. he was elected first vice-president in 1982 and was president of our assembly from 1984 to 1987. during its presidency, the european parliament will prove to be an indispensable partner, particularly in budgetary matters. he will become better known in europe itself and internationally, as pierre pflimlin had the privilege of welcoming president of the united states ronald reagan to the european parliament. building on altiero spinelli's draft treaty on european union, he strongly encouraged the reform of the treaties by the single european act, but denounced its shortcomings in view of the insufficient powers given to the european parliament. in friendly collaboration with president delors, he urged parliament to make the most of the situation by calling for tripartite meetings with the council and the commission, a form of early conciliation. because pierre pflimlin was also a man of dialogue. he was firm on his options, respectful of the opinions of his political opponents, and always put the best interests of europe before ideological considerations. for him, strasbourg, the city where he was mayor for 24 years, was the symbol of this openness, the visible sign of franco-german reconciliation and a sign of confidence and hope in the future of europe. he had therefore invested himself with energy and sincerity in the development of his city and its status as a european capital, by creating the real estate infrastructure and developing a genuine policy of welcoming. pierre pflimlin left the european parliament in 1989, but for many europeans, and especially for young people, he remained an authoritative reference point, a voice that raised enthusiasm, a reminder of the political purpose of european integration. until the end, we were impressed by the strength and clarity of president pflimlin's message, which remains very timely for all of us. i would like to express once again our deepest sympathy and condolences to the family of pierre pflimlin, and in particular to his daughter, who is present at this moment. it was under the presidency of pierre pflimlin that the flag and anthem were adopted as emblems of the european union in 1986. so if you will, in memory of president pflimlin, i would ask you to accept the european anthem. (the sitting was suspended at 7.30 p.m. and resumed at 9.30 p.m.)
a few days ago, ladies and gentlemen, 58 illegal immigrants died tragically in a lorry on the british border. it was june 18th. the tragic disappearance of men and women who, like the two young guineans who died last summer in the landing gear of a european plane, had placed all their hopes in europe, can only stir up the most intense emotion. i am sure that each of us has been shocked by this tragedy and i am sure that we all agree that the european union must step up its fight against modern slavery. everything must be done to dismantle this chain of death. the european union's response must be immediate, including a genuine common immigration policy and the redefinition of relations between the north and the south, which is to be achieved first and foremost by supporting economic development and access to knowledge. the treaty of amsterdam has been in force for one year and the tampere european council was held six months ago. the legal basis for action is therefore there, but it requires real political will. we must act now. that is why the presidency of the council and the european commission, at your request, will raise this matter before the european parliament tomorrow afternoon. counsel. - (pt) madam president, ladies and gentlemen, it is particularly significant for me to be able, at the beginning of this speech, to associate the portuguese government with the tributes paid to president pflimlin and also to send our most sincere condolences to his family and his people. now that we are no longer holding the presidency of the council of the union, i would like to express my warm thanks on behalf of the portuguese government for the extraordinary cooperation which has always existed between parliament and the council, a cooperation which has been made possible thanks to the strong commitment of this institution. i would like to emphasize the essential contribution which parliament has made from the beginning so that we can start the intergovernmental conference on time and which lasted until the last moment, until the last conciliation, the conciliation on the framework directive on water policy, which we can successfully conclude thanks to your understanding. at the end of those six months, i think we can say quite simply that we have fulfilled our mission. we have fulfilled our mission in the name of a european ideal and inspired by our vision of the world today and its problems, a world which is not politically structured and therefore incapable of fully ensuring peace, stability, human rights and democracy within itself, a world which has become globalised in terms of economy and market, but which has not yet been able to regulate this market and this world economy; the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. that is why we have defined a strategy during these six months. the first element of this strategy is to work towards creating the conditions to make the european union the most dynamic and competitive knowledge-based economic area in the world within ten years, achieving high levels of employment, economic growth and social cohesion. the second element is nothing less than the consolidation of our european political union: on the basis of our universalist values, the strengthening of europe's role in order to realize our desire to occupy the top of a new architecture of international relations, more multipolar, more balanced and more just. the third and final element is to take greater care of the citizens, of the european citizenship area, because, in the end, a strategy only makes sense if it is developed and implemented in the interests of the citizens. i now turn to the first element, namely our desire to make the european union the most dynamic and competitive knowledge-based economic area in the world in the coming decade. this is the main subject of the lisbon summit, the objectives of which i have had the opportunity to present in this house. i think i can say that we have fully achieved these objectives. we have defined a strategy which we believe will create the conditions for europe to achieve sustained growth of at least 3% and an employment rate of almost 70% within ten years. this is an essential basis for our social protection systems, which are based on the following four fundamental pillars: first, preparing the european union for a knowledge-based economy through action instruments in the fields of the information society, science and technology, training and education; secondly, the achievement of the economic reforms essential to our competitiveness and innovation, by deepening the process of economic reforms necessary for the creation of a fully integrated internal market or by adopting new innovation and enterprise policies; thirdly, the affirmation of social cohesion, based on employment, on reforms to ensure the sustainability of our social protection models, on the fight against exclusion; and finally, fourthly, the coordination of macroeconomic policies with a view to guaranteeing at the same time the stability we have achieved and which has been the basis for the euro, through a reduced rate of inflation, the reduction of public deficits, but also by establishing a macroeconomic framework more favourable to growth, employment, innovation and entrepreneurship. the four elements of this strategy have already produced tangible results. thanks to the excellent cooperation established with the commission, the santa maria da feira european council has already produced the action plan for the information society, the first set of decisions on the european science area, some decisive elements in the affirmation of our policy towards enterprises (the charter for small enterprises), the multiannual programme, a set of measures foreseen for the reform of markets, in particular financial markets, the 2000 initiative of the european investment bank for innovation, entrepreneurship and the information society, the reports of the high-level group on the sustainability of our social protection and the fight against social exclusion, which led to the creation of a social protection committee already in operation and finally the commission's initiative on the fight against exclusion. the lisbon strategy is therefore not an isolated event, but will soon become a reality. in this connection, we must emphasize the extremely important role that the commission is playing at the moment. this is because we have developed, in addition to a strategy, an open method of coordination, which ranges from information society, science, education, training and poverty reduction policies to those of enterprise, innovation, economic reforms, and the revision of our social protection, employment and cohesion schemes and systems. in all these areas we have defined an open method of coordination which will enable guidelines to be drawn up at european level, providing for benchmarking indicators which will shortly be selected, national initiatives which can be compared and coordinated and the possibility, therefore, of converging economic and social policies at community level in the form of open coordination, which represents a fundamental innovation in the functioning of the union. secondly, because the strategy is backed by a strong political will at the highest level to bring about economic and social reforms. hence the decision to hold a european council every spring at which, on the basis of a set of structural change indicators set by the commission and a report from the commission itself, the council will be able to set the main economic and social policy priorities for the year, thus giving the political direction needed for the work of all the other council formations and the various committees. this semester will also be the one in which greece joins the euro and the decision on the fiscal package is taken at the feira european council. this is not a final decision, this is only the beginning of the end, but the beginning of the end we have been waiting for for twelve years. it was incomprehensible that europe, which has been able to establish a single market and a single currency for the majority of its members, should still be totally incapable of reaching any agreement on taxation, an essential element of any political and economic system. a europe which is able to ensure its competitiveness with cohesion, but also a stronger and more united political europe. in this connection, i would like to stress the extremely important progress that has been made in terms of the credibility of our common european security and defence policy. the interim political and security committees and the interim military committee are now functioning. the military staff has taken over. the preparatory work will allow a conference on force building to be held in october. the rules for coordination between the european union and nato have been defined, as have the institutionalised consultation arrangements with the six eu countries which are members of nato and with the group of 15 countries which includes all the countries applying for membership. these reforms make it possible to implement all the decisions taken in helsinki, accompanied by the creation of the committee for civil crisis management, which has already started its work, and by a programme also for civil crisis management which we want to establish for the union's police forces, with the aim of seconding five thousand officers by 2003, including 1000 within a month. the common european security and defence policy is therefore a pillar of the credibility of our political union, which obviously requires institutional reform, which was on the agenda of the intergovernmental conference. during these six months, one of the objectives of the council presidency was to work hard to ensure that the work of the conference could be concluded before the end of the year, as this is an indispensable instrument for ensuring the viability of the first enlargement. in this connection, we have mainly worked on a detailed report on the amsterdam issues, and we have also had the opportunity to put enhanced cooperation on the agenda, on which the fifteen have finally agreed. we have worked hard to achieve this agreement, which we consider to be of the utmost importance in order to allow the deepening of european integration within the framework of a wider and more heterogeneous europe. it is obvious that a fundamental debate on the future of europe should be held at the same time. it was the aim of the presidency to devote the work of the igc to ensuring its success, to allow enlargement, but it goes without saying that this debate cannot leave any of us indifferent, either those who can - and i am speaking here only as a portuguese - understand that our institutional model must be refined without fundamentally altering it, or those who might possibly wish for an intergovernmental drift away from the european union - personally i will oppose this as much as possible - ... (applause)... or those who believe that a new leap forward must be made in restructuring and that we must move clearly along the road to european federalism. we will always be open to this debate, but i would like to draw parliament's attention to one essential point: no federal system in the world can be strictly political. no federal political authority can do without a strong federal budget and strong powers at the federal level. (applause) i would like to thank we therefore believe that a vague and abstract discussion of the institutional aspects, without taking account of all the financial and fiscal implications of this federal model, would be a discussion in a vacuum. we are quite prepared to take part in this debate, but only if we address all its components, otherwise we think it will be meaningless. but, in addition, at the institutional level, the presidency of the council was able to concentrate during this six-month period on creating the conditions necessary for enlargement. the pace of work on enlargement was maintained during the six months. we were able to conclude 78 negotiating files with the candidates and open 52 of them. it should be stressed that to open a negotiating file the 15 states must reach a common position on it. at present, all the negotiating dossiers are open with all the countries of the luxembourg group, with the exception of institutional affairs and miscellaneous subjects. even in the countries of the helsinki group, a large number of cases have already been opened or closed. i would like to stress here the extremely dynamic and important role played by the commission in the steady pace of the negotiations. it is clear that in our worldview, in which we want europe to be at the forefront of a new, more balanced and fairer architecture of international relations, it is very important to give the union's external relations a great deal of vitality and dynamism. that is what we have tried to do, with the close cooperation of the commission - and i would like to welcome the presence of vice-president christopher patten - that is what we have tried to do during this semester. two new things: the euro-african summit and the summit at the highest level with india, the world's most populous democracy, which will now have regular relations at the highest level with the european union. we should also mention the work which has enabled the negotiations to be concluded with a view to renewing the lomé convention and the agreements with mexico and south africa, the opening of negotiations with mercosur and intensive action on the euro-mediterranean and middle east fronts, on the fronts linked to the countries of asia and the pacific, on transatlantic relations, on relations with russia and other countries of central and eastern europe and central asia, and on the adoption of a common strategy for the mediterranean and an action plan for the northern dimension of the european union, two aspects which, in my view, complement each other very well because they are linked to the south and north of the european union, which shows that our vocation is not a geographical one-sided orientation, which is not really our vocation in any universal direction, being a geographical one. the balkans will of course have been at the heart of our concerns. our concern was acute when we began our work, beyond the magnitude of the problems we had to overcome, we had the bitter taste of those who felt that the international community itself was suffering from a balkanization of how to solve the balkan problem. in this respect, i would like to pay tribute to the excellent cooperation work of the high representative, mr javier solana, and the vice-president of the commission, mr christopher patten, because thanks to them the european union has not suffered from balkanization. on the contrary, it was able to carry out coordinated and integrated action in the balkans during this period, particularly with the stability pact, which finally saw the creation of the funds necessary to be able to support the countries and carry out coherent action in relation to all the extremely complex situations which, for lack of time, i will not describe here. we know that we still have a lot of work to do. we are aware of the enormous obstacles to be overcome, starting with the absence of a democratic state in serbia, a key problem which makes the implementation of any strategy for the balkans extremely difficult. but we also know that the european union is not balkanized and that it is now acting in an integrated manner. i would also like to thank parliament for its efforts to resolve the problem of financial support for montenegro, which we felt was essential to send a very clear message to all those who are committed to democracy in that region. i should also mention the issue of citizenship in the third pillar, following the tampere summit, with regard to the strategy to combat drugs, the external dimension of the third pillar - these are issues of the utmost importance, such as immigration, which is a fundamental pillar of the development of our relations with the outside world and of our analysis of our societies in the years to come -; but if you will allow me, i will emphasize the work being done on the charter of fundamental rights, since this charter is a key milestone in the affirmation of european citizenship, a citizenship which i would like us all to see in the light of the values of the enlightenment, that is to say the values of political rationalism against all forms of political populism, of exacerbated nationalism, of religious fundamentalism or of manifestations of xenophobia or racism. it is in the light of these values that the emergence of european citizenship makes sense, and it is in this light that the affirmation of the european project of civilisation makes sense. in conclusion, madam president, i would like to extend to president jacques chirac - who will be in this chamber tomorrow, i suppose - and to the french government my best wishes for success in the leadership of the council over the next six months, and i would like to assure them of the full cooperation of the portuguese government.
