in writing. - i will speak on my own behalf on the report on the forests. i know that the committee on agriculture is telling us that we are misunderstanding the debate by advocating an increase in the budget in the context of these reports. i believe that we have a political responsibility to send strong political signals to the commission, the council and the citizens. in december 1999, parts of the union were hit by terrible storms which devastated large parts of the forests of southern and eastern france and caused despair among the victims, especially among smallholders. i also know that you don't dress peter by undressing paul. in voting for the rapporteur's proposals, i wanted to contribute to the establishment of a genuine forestry policy for the union. because despite the colossal budget of the cap, the forest, which is an integral part of agriculture, is largely forgotten.
in writing. - (fr) we are dealing here with two council regulations which establish a systematic monitoring of forest ecosystems, unique in the world. regulation no 3582/86 concerns the protection of forests against air pollution and regulation no 2158/92 has established a framework for combating forest fires. the rapporteur proposes to increase the amounts allocated to these two programmes, whereas the commission's proposal aims to reduce them sharply. it is the rapporteur's approach that is relevant. it is logical to take account of the almost doubling of the community's forest area since 1998, the date of the last enlargement, and to meet the requirements of the european union's forestry strategy. it is true that there is no legal basis in the treaty for a common forestry policy. the report is not intended to re-launch the debate but merely to recall that the union's forestry strategy is based on subsidiarity. in other words, an action is proposed only if it has added value compared to the national action. the question is whether there is added value. subsidiarity is in favour of community action in this specific context. it is true that the issues are not the same in the forests of the fifteen. the nordic countries, which provided the bulk of the troops during the 1998 enlargement, are particularly affected by air pollution, the stress of climate tensions and acidification of the soil, while the southern states suffer more from the effects of desertification, drought and fires. but these differences should not undermine the need to manage such monitoring at community level, given the acknowledged interdependence of stressors affecting forest ecosystems in general and as a whole. the increase in funding is also timely. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's forestry sector is not affected by the fires. the prevention of such disasters requires improved fire safety. while the commission, in its communication of 2 february 2000, advocates the use of the precautionary principle in all directions and a community action programme for civil protection, established by council decision of 9 december 1999, expects only one thing, that is, that it be used, it is not appropriate to amputate regulation no 2158/92 financially. the fight against air pollution is taking on a new dimension in the light of the guidelines adopted by the commission on climate change, biodiversity and sustainable management. monitoring of ecosystems is expected to be multidisciplinary. while air pollution has lost its burning relevance in the face of these new priorities, it is a coherent part of global challenges. the root of the problem is political. doubts have sometimes been raised by member states about the importance of forests, when the forestry industry employs 2.2 million people in europe and forests cover 36% of the union's area! in this case, the devil is biting his own tail: the regulations in question need political support. but for this to be granted, networks must have the capacity to detect changes, even risks. but to prove scientifically that such risks exist, adequate financial support is needed! pending the question of whether these programmes should be extended beyond 2001, it is our political responsibility to support them financially. the data collected are supposed to provide technical support for policy decisions in areas where 'no report, no action'.
in writing. - the toy safety issue is particularly close to my heart. i was rapporteur on this subject in 1992 and i have been following legislative developments in this area with the greatest attention. as regards phthalates, the chemicals used to soften pvc, i have always advocated voluntary measures to protect properly this particularly vulnerable group of consumers, children. experiments on animals have demonstrated the toxicity and carcinogenicity of certain phthalates. these substances can cause liver, kidney, and testicular problems in children who suck or chew on nipples, chewing gum, or rings. this list of risks raised legitimate concerns among parents, which should have led to firm measures meeting the requirements of the precautionary principle. the commission's reaction, at least, was relatively swift (request for an opinion from the scientific committee, toxicity, ecotoxicity and environmental impact studies, emergency ban decision and proposal to amend the relevant directives), but it was very lax in relation to the issues at stake and the objectives of ensuring a high level of consumer protection and human health protection. what has the european commission proposed? it proposed to ban toys containing one of the six phthalates listed in the indictment intended to be placed in the mouth by children under three years of age; the commission has also proposed that the directive be amended to include a warning on toys containing one of the six phthalates that may be put into the mouth by children under three years of age and to revise the directive within four years. of course, that's not enough! it is ridiculous to ban only toys or childcare articles intended to be placed in the mouth. because every parent knows that babies put everything in their mouths. toys and articles which are liable to be placed in the mouth, wholly or partially, and which contain phthalates should therefore be prohibited. the lack of reliable scientific information on the migration of these chemicals into the body should lead us to apply the precautionary principle. i would also like to stress that we will have to be particularly vigilant about the substances that will be used to replace phthalates. it is also essential to make the labelling of toys and childcare articles containing phthalates that can be placed in the mouth more general. to avoid encouraging children to chew or suck on their toys, a provision should be added prohibiting the addition of flavouring substances. provision should be made for revising the directive in order to update it in the light of progress in scientific knowledge. i am convinced that in the present state of our information we must exercise the utmost caution. i supported the amendments tabled by the socialist members of the committee on the environment. i would like to conclude by recalling that, as regards the safety of toys, the rules on ce marking are too ambiguous and should be clarified quickly.
in writing. - we abstained on this proposal even though we are convinced that a policy of exchanges and cooperation between the different countries in the field of education would help to improve its quality by promoting the blending of cultures and exchanges between the peoples living in europe. but such a policy will only be a factor of progress if it is based on a national education policy aimed at providing more resources for public education, accessible to all. this priority is not stated anywhere in the texts, but, above all, it is not applied in any of the countries of the european union. we are concerned that various formulations reflect a limited and utilitarian conception of cooperation whose objectives are dictated by market requirements and the initiatives of private companies or organizations looking for a workforce which they intend to train and qualify according to their needs. but to introduce the laws of the market into education is to reserve the quality of education for a minority and to deteriorate it for the majority. that is why we voted for the amendments which warn against too much market involvement in education.
in writing. - in substance, as in each of its formulations, this report is a panegyric on competition and the market economy. the author's exclusive concern is, under the guise of unifying the energy markets in europe, to turn the whole sector over to private profit. or, more precisely, by separating the production of electricity from the management of the distribution network, the author is willing to allow the states to take care of what requires a lot of investment and brings little return, provided they leave the private sector what brings a lot. the unification of energy production and distribution throughout the european union, the planning and rationalisation of both, could be progress, but on the condition that the whole remains a public service exclusively concerned with meeting needs, and not with maximising private profit. the author of the report is doing exactly the opposite. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover all the activities of the public authorities. we have therefore voted against this report.
in writing. - as a new member of this parliament, i am shocked! i did not participate in the previous legislature, which saw the great flourish of the notion of a public service "in the french style". i am talking about the sale of goods, as has been done in the transport, postal and telecommunications sectors. by proposing to take stock of the transposition of the december 1996 directives on electricity and the june 1998 directives on gas, the mombaur report clearly betrays the ultra-liberal philosophy of the commission, which, under the guise of achieving the internal energy market to the greatest benefit of consumers, calls for the complete opening of these markets to full competition. the process is unchanged: the commission proposes a minimalist directive arguing that liberalisation can only be profitable in a deregulatory context; the commission has also been asked to take a number of measures to ensure that the directive is implemented in a uniform manner. this is all the more unacceptable as the problems remain! why create a single energy market when electricity and gas are not comparable (in terms of production/distribution, market development, concept of public service)? how can a provider be asked to ensure continuity and fairness of public service when it is not economically viable? at the same time, how can we ask the former monopolies to assume full competition today when they have to continue to pay back heavy investments which are the product of political choices of yesterday? how can we demand ever lower prices in the name of a sacrosanct competition without calling into question the current requirements for nuclear safety? how can the national concept of public service be replaced by the much more restrictive community concept of a mission of general interest? i could go on like this for pages. know that it took decades of republican tradition to allow the gradual construction of our public services; only four years of transition will be enough to wipe them out ! we have therefore not been able to vote in favour of this report, which expresses the will of the all-powerful commission to go further and faster in liberalization. liberalism may be desirable, but it must be pursued gradually, in moderation, and without definitively excluding public interventionism, or else we shall have to bear the financial consequences of such a renunciation tomorrow!
- mr president, the european central bank's 1999 annual report does not say much about the big question that all observers are asking: why is the euro, which was announced as a strong currency, in the end a weak currency? the bank devotes one page out of almost two hundred to this subject, with a very small graph, in which only the weakening of the euro is noted. as for the explanations, the only one provided is the difference in economic health and structures between europe and the united states. that's true, but it's not enough. it should be mentioned, first, that europe is not a country, with a people, a state, an economic government, and that consequently the euro is generally considered to be more fragile than a national currency. moreover, it was originally launched at too high a level, precisely because it was valued on the basis of the existing exchange rate of genuine national currencies, while lacking their intrinsic qualities. how do european officials intend to combat this depreciation? first, indirectly, through pro-growth policies, and we can only approve of this type of action. but at the same time, we see the european central bank raising interest rates, officially to fight against inflation... which does not exist, in reality to support the parity of the euro. it is a double-edged sword, for if used at the wrong time in the cycle, it can break the growth that is being worked on elsewhere. another dubious solution is to run forwards by strengthening the euro, which should lead gradually to an economic government of europe. it won't change much in the short term. to get to the bottom of the problem, we would have to take away the autonomy of the nations of europe, but that is obviously impossible. at any rate, a system lock is set up at the same time. as i explained at a recent colloquium in the french national assembly, the charter of fundamental rights will have the function, among other things, of binding the peoples even more closely to community law and therefore also to the single currency. this adventure is contributing to the loss of our freedoms.
mr president, this is the report by the european parliament on the communication strategy to be adopted in the last phase of monetary union, a report which i voted against, so that mrs peijs can understand it. this report reflects the concern of many officials at the almost total lack of public interest in the introduction of the euro. however, we are only a year and a half away from a crucial deadline: the withdrawal of national currencies and the introduction of physical euro banknotes and coins. so far, the euro has proved relatively easy, since the first phase has mainly involved technicians, bankers, investors and stock exchange users, all of whom are already well informed and generally convinced in advance. in these circumstances, the ease with which the euro is being introduced at this stage is not surprising. but now the difficult part begins: the meeting with the citizen, who often does not yet understand the effort required of him and is trapped by the decisions already taken. the european parliament calls for the communication policy to be stepped up by increasing the appropriations by about 30%, to eur 38 million per year. to ease the minds of those who might have doubts, he adds with a certain naivety, and i quote the resolution that was adopted, that 'in accordance with article 37 (a) of the interinstitutional agreement of 6 may 1999, information policy is an autonomous activity requiring no legal basis'. in these circumstances, why deprive oneself? i would point out in passing that we have always contested the possibility for the commission to incur expenditure without a legal basis, and we have contested this interinstitutional agreement which the council had the weakness to accept in contradiction with the usual principles of sound management of public money.
in writing. - i reject the karas report as a whole. while the aim of familiarizing europeans with their future currency is perfectly legitimate, since the choice to abandon national currencies has been made (under conditions which i condemn), i strongly reject the propaganda that this text organizes in favour of what mr karas calls 'an essential element of the european integration process' which 'contributes to forging european identity'. this text at least has the merit of exposing the enormous lie to which the supporters of a federal europe resorted when they asked the french to ratify the maastricht treaty in 1992: the single currency was then presented as a purely technical instrument aimed at a better functioning of the economy compared to the dollar and the yen and as a completely neutral operation in matters of national sovereignty. how far we were then from the essential element of the integration process! this text will undoubtedly be an essential weapon for all those in britain, sweden and denmark who are fighting to preserve their national democracies: the euro is good, even if its supporters deny it today in these countries, the war machine of a federal europe that the overwhelming majority of their populations reject. so when my colleagues reject the amendment tabled by william abitbol which simply asks that this integrationist objective be clearly stated in the commission's communication programmes, they are contributing to a false propaganda operation which their voters will certainly sanction. the resolution of the karas report claims that women, for unexplained reasons, do not share in the general enthusiasm that should have accompanied the introduction of the euro. here we find the unpleasant accents of revolutionary propagandists of all times, who see in every home a reactionary plot of the petticoats and the cap to refuse the singing tomorrows. it seems to have never occurred to anyone that it might be because of their experience of the day-to-day economy that women are more than reluctant to switch to the euro. this is despicable and betrays the dictatorship of the single-mindedness which consists in taxing opponents, opponents, or "reluctant" to the euro as ignorant, illiterate, underdeveloped. look where the federalist blindness leads !
in writing. - the annual activity reports of the ombudsman and the committee on petitions are part of the traditions of this house. the parliament responds to the accounts of these two bodies with two reports which are fairly similar from one year to the next. however, there is a new element: the thors report, based in particular on the work of the constitutional committee and on the request of mr söderman, claims to give the ombudsman a right of general access to all documents which are necessary for the examination of complaints. we oppose this proposal not because we would refuse any control over the administration, but because such powers go beyond the powers of an ombudsman to reach those of a judge. it is obvious, and we are certainly not the ones to say otherwise, that the community's insane administration and the evils it causes can only create growing dissatisfaction among our fellow citizens and, therefore, more and more appeals. the multiplication of powers, the diversification of areas of intervention, the legislative bulimia of the commission and of our assembly will probably not correct this phenomenon. but it is not the ombudsman and his few collaborators who will be able to respond properly to these challenges. it is our political responsibility to dry up the very sources of these disputes, by preferring the quality of our work to a textual activism that would justify our existence, by really respecting the principle of subsidiarity which will prevent the union from taking a position on matters which do not concern it, by exercising ourselves, where appropriate, the powers we have in the area of control of the community bodies. we have seen too often our assembly take refuge behind committees of experts, because it refused to assume its own political responsibilities. if we leave the ombudsman in control of the administrative problems, we must learn to control, upstream and downstream, the mad community machine launched into a deadly leap forward. the excesses to be combated are often the result of the very nature of the current european construction and must therefore be combated at the root.
in writing. - this partsession is rich in reports on transport. unfortunately, i must say that this sector is only considered from a liberal point of view. mr atkins' report, which deals with the european commission's proposal for a single sky, is part of this logic of full liberalisation. this is what caused the french air traffic controllers to strike last week. they expressed their concern at a purely commercial conception of their profession. i understand their motivation, which is certainly not the case for mr atkins, who in his report 'invites the commission to urge the governments of the member states which currently tolerate national labour disputes disrupting air traffic to tackle this problem as a matter of urgency'. this is ridiculous ! no one denies the reality of the deteriorating air traffic situation. indeed, air corridors and airports are crowded, delays are commonplace with one in three planes not arriving on time, and all this is accompanied by a cortege of noise and environmental nuisance. i therefore welcome the willingness of mrs de palacio, the commissioner responsible for transport, to tackle the problem head on in order to achieve the creation of a single european sky as quickly as possible. however, i totally disagree with the arguments it puts forward, just as i disagree with the proposals in the report. the aim is to put air traffic control centres in competition by separating the regulatory authorities from the operators. the control function could be exercised within separate companies whose capital would be open to airlines or private partners. this would lead to a weakening of air transport safety, which is of course unacceptable and contrary to the ec treaty, which states that improving transport safety is one of the main objectives of the common transport policy. france certainly appears to be an isolated case in europe, where air traffic control in most countries is managed by agencies under the auspices of the state but open to private capital. france is keen to maintain these activities in the public service. the principle of subsidiarity must be applied here and each member state must be left in charge of the organisation of air traffic control. this is a requirement, especially since the problem of delays does not come from air traffic control, which is responsible for less than 25% of delays! in conclusion, i support the proposals to strengthen the role of eurocontrol, the pan-european agency responsible for the management of the airspace of european states, both eu and non-eu, as a regulatory authority. the report wrongly underestimates the potential of this agency, and i voted against a report which is completely unacceptable.
in writing. - i voted against mr atkins' report because it is totally out of step with reality and is based on an ideological a priori view rather than on the real needs of our citizens and air transport users. of course, this is not to deny the need to improve the situation of air traffic control and regulation in europe in the spirit of the single european sky. it is clear that aircraft flying through our airspace cannot be subject to inconsistent, uncoordinated, complicated processing of their passage. and it is true that while progress has been made with eurocontrol, the time has already come to take a new step and improve the system, with a major imperative that must take precedence over everything else: safety, regulation and air traffic control must not be a matter of competition law, but of the concept of a service of general interest. in fact, the united states has never liberalized its air traffic control since it is a state agency that manages it. that's what i'm talking about! the whole atkins report is aimed at this objective of competing with a service which we can hardly see how it could be a source of private profit and which would find its performance criteria in the profits generated! the pretext for speeding up this liberalization is the delay in flights. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat this problem, but the real reasons for it and the real solutions to it must be analysed if it is to be effective. first of all, there are positive developments this year, as delays have decreased substantially in france. this shows first that a distinction must be made between cyclical (use of space by the military for kosovo, change of control system, etc.) and structural dysfunctions. we must also take account of the airlines and the narrowness of the european civil space, in terms of the number of overflights. the share of air traffic control in these delays is not huge, after all, and in any case the improvement of the system requires a better organization of the coordination of the various control systems in the member states, by strengthening eurocontrol in this role. this should be the priority and the guidelines of the single european sky. unfortunately, the commission does not seem to be on this line, and the atkins report seems even worse.
in writing. - on 26 june 2000, french air traffic controllers went on strike to protest against the european union's plans to liberalize air traffic control: i would like to express my solidarity with this strike and with the demands of the air traffic control unions. the response to the saturation of european airspace is a leakage forward, with more airports and runways, worse working conditions for workers in the sector and more nuisance. we are, on the contrary, in favour of a harmonized development of transport at european level, which gives priority to the satisfaction of real social needs and which, for example, chooses the railway for the needs of the greatest number, especially for distances of less than 500 kilometres. liberalising air traffic control will not solve the problem of delays, since only 20 to 30% of delays are attributable to air traffic control. we know that the military now occupies, for example, in france, 80 per cent of the airspace. why is this not questioned? the commission is using delays as a pretext to move towards a separation between a european regulatory office and the establishment of a privatised internal market for the provision of air traffic services. such measures, taken under pressure from airline lobbyists, can only be carried out at the expense of safety, especially since the airlines themselves can apply for such services. that is why i voted against this report.
in writing. - we voted in favour of the paragraphs in this report which go in the direction of protecting women workers, both from the point of view of their health and their wages and from the point of view of the health of their children. it is regrettable, however, that the report does not even propose to align benefits and rights in all areas with those countries which are most favourable to pregnant women in employment. we also do not want our vote in favour of specific protection for pregnant women working at night to be interpreted as a recognition of the legitimacy of women's night work. we want to reaffirm our opposition to night work, which is not socially useful, not only for women but also for men. the prohibition of night work for women was an achievement of the workers' movement in france. to go back on that is a social regression. calling for equality between men and women adds to the hypocrisy. this is a hypocritical attempt to hide the fact that the legislator is more concerned with ensuring that employers use their equipment profitably than with ensuring the health and safety of their employees.
in writing. - we are in favour of all amendments to the directive aimed at improving the protection of pregnant workers before, during and after maternity leave. the resolution proposes to close the gaps in the current directive and to harmonise european legislation to align it with those that guarantee the most rights. we support such proposals in the name of guaranteeing the right of workers to health. this is all the more so as the proposed amendments to the ilo convention on the protection of the motherhood (convention 103) suggest many setbacks, such as the exclusion of certain women from the benefit of maternity leave, the minimum duration of this leave, and the possibility of dismissing a woman during her leave. a strong european framework is needed to protect pregnant women against discrimination in employment, working conditions, access to and duration of maternity leave: 20 weeks, including 8 weeks of compulsory leave after childbirth. they must be protected against unfair dismissal and their previous salary must be guaranteed. finally, night work for women and men should be prohibited in sectors where it is not essential, rather than attempting to make it available to pregnant women.

- mr president, armonia bordes, chantal cauquil and i, although we regard the prospects for the development of short sea shipping in europe, as well as inland waterway transport, as positive, have nevertheless chosen to abstain on this proposal. the report states that the large and costly investments required for the construction of the infrastructure will be financed by public money, while its operation will primarily take account of the requirements of profitability and competitiveness of private companies, which, according to the project, should be the first users.
in writing. - short sea shipping is, as we know, an integral part of the european transport system. moreover, as the commission's report and the report of the committee on regional policy and transport point out, short sea shipping has a poor image in terms of cost, slowness and inefficiency. however, this image no longer corresponds to reality and this mode of transport is able to provide solutions to the global problems in this field in europe. i am thinking of the problems of traffic congestion, the high cost of infrastructure and the environmental cost. in recent years, progress has been made and there has been a real growth in short sea shipping: from 1990 to 1997, tonnes transported (+ 17%) tonnes per kilometre (+ 23%). while this success is undeniable, it is not yet up to the potential and advantages of this mode of transport: cost advantages: it is the most economical mode of transport; benefits in terms of energy consumption per tonne/kilometre; efficiency advantages: it is the most efficient mode of transport in terms of investment in transport capacity; advantages in terms of regional cohesion: it is the mode best suited to serving europe's peripheral regions; environmental benefits: it is a less polluting mode of transport than land transport; advantages in terms of intermodality: it is an ideal means of implementing multimodal transport . measures must therefore be taken rapidly to contribute to its development. this will include the development of joint investment programmes. one of the priorities should be to increase the efficiency of port operations and to reduce waiting times in ports. it stresses that public authorities have a major role to play at regional, national and european level. however, i have a problem with two points in my colleague's report. the proposal is to establish a list of ports particularly suited to short sea shipping. the establishment of such a list does not seem to me to be necessary and, above all, it would be dangerous to penalise ports which are not yet fully adapted but are undertaking transformations to that end. it is also suggested that the supply of transport logistics services to end users be brought together under a single point. while i agree that we must find a way to set up an information system, i do not want a major port which already has a strong market position to centralise this service. finally, i would have liked to have found in the report the proposal made by the committee on industry that short sea shipping should not be seen as an alternative to road transport or as a competing system. the european commission should then draw up an intermodal strategy establishing complementarity between transport modes. in this context and in this spirit, member states should harmonise existing regulations to avoid that they constitute obstacles to the continuity between short sea shipping and land transport, in particular in the area of gross vehicle weight. what is proposed today is therefore an important step in the right direction in the field of short sea shipping. the commission has not yet done so.

the rapporteur, mr president, is the concrete implementation, the instrument of our euro-mediterranean policy, which was defined by the barcelona convention in november 1995, followed by several forums, notably those in malta, naples and stuttgart. we are presenting here the first activity report, called the 1998 annual report, but which in fact takes stock of the entire first implementation period 1996 to 1999 and prepares the implementation of the actions for the second period 2000 to 2006, the regulation for which is proposed by our colleague mr valdivielso de cué. the report is submitted to the hughes procedure, and we have fully incorporated the proposals adopted unanimously not only by our committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, which is the committee responsible for the subject, but also by the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy and the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. background: around €4 billion over the last four years, plus substantial eib loans, have been allocated. the barcelona agreements signed by 27 countries, the european union and the 12 countries of the southern mediterranean: algeria, the palestinian authority, cyprus, egypt, israel, jordan, lebanon, malta, morocco, syria, tunisia and turkey. the objectives are embodied in a political and security dimension, an economic and financial dimension and a social, cultural and human dimension. the conclusion is that this is a young programme which has had difficulty in getting off the ground and has suffered from various malfunctions identified by the european court of auditors and the committee on budgetary control. criticism was directed in particular at subcontracting associations such as the rtm. in the end, implementation was semi-paralysed and, despite committing almost 100% of the appropriations, only 26% have now been paid, and this is very difficult to achieve over an average period of four years. we have presented the ins and outs in detail in our report to summarise the conclusions. we conclude. firstly, there is a need to simplify the regulation in order to allow the process to be speeded up and made more transparent by providing the means for the commission to examine the case and for the council to monitor it. and above all, the european parliament must be involved in the process and be more regularly informed, particularly through the euro-mediterranean forum. it would be appropriate to speed up the signing of association agreements, which is only done today with seven countries. this applies in particular to lebanon, algeria, syria, etc. secondly, the choice of projects must be made more democratically, with greater participation by civil society, ngos, who have constantly expressed this wish, in particular at a symposium held on 29 june in brussels entitled 'towards a sustainable meda'. thirdly, to pay close attention to the respect for human rights, since this cooperation is not only aimed at economic progress but also, and fundamentally, at democracy, freedom, peace, the elimination of inequalities and sustainable development. we therefore ask that a report on the respect of human rights by the signatory or candidate countries be presented to parliament every year so that this can be taken into account in the choice of projects. fourthly, we believe that the appropriations allocated to regional cooperation (10%) are insufficient compared with those allocated to bilateral cooperation (90%). the volume of regional action, which we admit is more difficult to negotiate and implement but which is consistent with an objective of efficiency, in particular to improve south-south relations and above all to preserve a larger action of decentralized cooperation to which we are all very attached, must therefore be commented on. fifthly, with regard to the six priorities of the partnership: environment, water policy, industry, energy, transport and the information society, we believe that it is necessary to revive the smap programmes on the environment, which were too much neglected until now. at least 10 million euros a year would have to be allocated to water. efforts should be made to promote renewable energy, to help smes and to promote transport. we must support the sustainable development plans of each country. we therefore consider it imperative to implement the proposals for regulations made by mr valdivielso de cué, in particular those concerning the simplification of procedures for more transparency, efficiency and speed in payments and those concerning the establishment of more staff in the commission for a better control of the programme which must not remain a poor relative in comparison with those of cooperation with asian or acp countries. i would like to thank not only the many contributions, particularly from the countries concerned and the ngos, which have enabled me to optimise this report, but also our european commissioner, mr patten, who has a clear view of the situation and whose external relations services should now contribute to improving this mediterranean action. i also thank his collaborators, particularly mr patrick laurent. i would also like to stress the interest we have in commissioner busquin's relaunching mediterranean cooperation in the field of research, particularly at the informal summit in capri on 29 september. i also thank all our colleagues in parliament, in particular mrs terrón and mrs mcnally and mr sami naïr, who are working on this matter. the implementation of our proposals is fundamental to the necessary revival of the euro-mediterranean process, which should not be penalized at the level of the 2000-2006 appropriations because of the problems encountered in its early years and which should be the spearhead of our policy, which will be discussed at the marseille conference in november. we wish the french presidency, which i know is very conciliatory and determined to achieve its objectives, every success. mr president, the meda programme is an essential instrument for the gradual establishment of a genuine area of shared prosperity, as proclaimed in the barcelona declaration. the difficulties in implementing it, the impatience and even the disappointment it has aroused in our partners in the south should, however, encourage us to ask ourselves more about the state of the euro-mediterranean partnership as a whole. the countries of the southern mediterranean need europe's help, solidarity aid which contributes to the development of their societies and to the reduction of disparities between the two shores by putting an end to the economic domination relations which are currently prevailing and whose debt system is perhaps the most obvious and unjust. what about meda? with over eur 3 billion in commitment appropriations for 1995-99, meda i has resulted in a real commitment of just over eur 2 billion in the first four years and an actual payment of eur 553 million, a payment which represents barely a quarter of the committed appropriations. what a gap between promised help and actual help! it is true that this lag is due in part to the fact that, as mr patten has often told us, the commission lacks the human resources to carry out all the tasks entrusted to it. i will not be the last to call for more human resources if this will enable the european union to meet its responsibilities. the commission's proposals are also aimed at simplifying and speeding up the procedures of the new regulation, even if removing the ability of the member states to control projects from the outset would not necessarily be the best solution to achieve greater transparency. more credit should be given to small-scale projects. i have met far too often people who are well versed in the local voluntary movement who are disillusioned by the procedures for obtaining grants. the euro-mediterranean partnership will only be built by and for its citizens, who are themselves willing to promote a partnership that benefits the people. the meda programme also raises fundamental questions about euro-mediterranean policy in general. firstly, cooperation is mainly focused on the economic and financial aspects, leaving social and cultural aspects to the margins. secondly, it is time to take greater account of the growing opposition to free trade at all levels. the social consequences of the free trade area raise serious concerns which cannot be ignored. the budgetary resources from customs duties are in danger of being dangerously cut off from the social budgets of the countries of the south. the increase in competition could erode the industrial fabric of these countries, some of which are fragile small and medium-sized enterprises. rather than so-called 'accompanying' measures, the economic systems of the south need genuine technological support. in addition, the aid should not only be designed to adapt firms to the criteria of profitability but also to meet the employment needs of the population. while the development of the private sector is strongly supported by meda, the public sector, for example, is relatively neglected, even though it meets real needs. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the galeote report is of two kinds: firstly, because it clearly reveals the real aims of this house, and secondly, because no one pays any attention to it. what is it, exactly? the aim is nothing less than to give the european union, which is now reduced to the commission, the last attributes of a sovereign state which it still lacked, namely a diplomatic service and its condition, legal personality. because, after all, let's be a little logical. if this school is to serve any purpose, it is to create a common diplomatic corps, following a process which is only too clear, as outlined in the galeote report. if those who support this report succeed in their aims, the dispatch of nations will have reached its logical conclusion, once again using the old technique of monnet, schuman and delors, which consists in creating an organ in the hope that this will eventually create the function and the content. but then again, you leave out so many prerequisites that you feel like you're making a little joke out of the world. the creation of a diplomatic instrument without regard to the first precondition, common diplomacy, presupposes itself another precondition, namely that we first define the interests common to the member states, and this precondition itself presupposes another, which is to define a common relationship of europe with the rest of the world. but even between the three major powers - germany, great britain and france - we cannot, we cannot see what these common interests and diplomacy could be based on, neither with regard to the west in relations with the united states and the role of nato, with which we are absolutely not in agreement and are not prepared to be, nor with regard to the east - here the thorny question of russia and our relations with all the countries of central europe arises - nor with regard to the south, and perhaps even less so with regard to the south, especially in the political context of the mediterranean. so it is a scam, the worst of all, namely an intellectual scam. unless we take for granted that the diplomacy of the major power - the central power - is de facto required of all, which would indeed be to solve the problem. our polish friends recently had the opportunity to discover the flexibility of common diplomacy at a un conference - women 2000 - when they were asked to align themselves with the position advocated by the union, or else their country's accession process would be delayed. we can only hope that the experience of our friends in central europe in resisting totalitarianism will one day be useful to us, a totalitarianism which has recently been given a new illustration in the inadmissible quarrel with one of our colleagues, mr daniel hannan. we are not mistaken, because through a common representation at the united nations, it is the permanent seat, which some member states have, that is being attacked and also the idea that there may be dissenting voices in this world, such as the one that france very often tries to make heard, vis-à-vis the united states. in the end, europe can only speak with one voice if it says nothing. the evidence is once again given, and the evidence is also given that this europe does not simply deny nations through nations; it is itself that it denies and annihilates.
- mr president, the study of the ecip development programme gives us a good caricature of the dysfunctions of the european commission. while this programme is rather moving in the right direction - that is, a transfer of technology to developing countries - the commission has, perhaps unintentionally, put a brake on it. the programme has been in existence for 12 years now and the commission has waited for its expiry to consider whether it would be renewed. as in the case of other programmes, it did not consider the consequences of the possible termination of the programme, the continuity of the measures taken and the situation of the partner enterprises and jobs. it seems that last year the budgeted €90 million for this programme was not even used, because there were no human resources to study the files piled up in an office in brussels. the administrative procedures also became more cumbersome year by year, while the staff in charge of the programme did not see any progress in its staffing. at the same time, the partners were not informed of the possible termination of the programme. finally, the criteria for allocating funds between the different pillars of the programme, in particular the social rights of workers, remained very vague. in view of the above, we ask the commission to examine the means, first, of rapidly evaluating the programme and, second, of extending it while promoting its transparency and maintaining its budget.
mr president, i shall vote against the dell'alba report and more generally against the ecip and meda programmes, which are essentially intended to finance grants and loans to private companies investing in latin america, asia, the mediterranean and south africa. i am opposed to public money being used - in any form - to produce private profit. the project, which is supposed to be primarily aimed at smes, often involves subsidiaries of large multinational companies, such as banks, which participate in the operation and benefit from it. the stated political objective of these programmes is to promote the opening up of these countries' markets to capital from europe. in the past these poor countries have been plundered and exploited by the capital of the great competing powers of europe. the only change is that the programmes now call for coordinated action on these funds. the capital invested is not, as in the past, directed towards developing the poor countries; they are subordinated to european capital. they're not meant to make life easier for the working classes, but to exploit cheap labor over there to enrich the landlords and stockholders here. i therefore reject these programmes as a whole because, despite the hypocritical phrases about the fight against poverty, they are all designed to provide the imperialism of the great european powers with additional instruments for penetration and domination over the poor countries.
- mr president, all over the world, humanitarian aid is taking precedence over development aid. even here, the external relations dg is gradually taking over the subjects that were the responsibility of the development dg, with humanitarian aid filling in the gaps in foreign policy. it is not just a matter of helping, but of rebalancing the use of natural resources among all the inhabitants of the planet. unfortunately, humanitarian aid cannot play this role and must not be the guarantor of a liberal policy which also kills the populations of the countries receiving aid. sustainable development is almost absent from the european union's humanitarian policy, little preparation for natural disasters, no prevention of conflicts. regular training in earthquake and flood management and non-violence would be welcome in many parts of the world. instead, the european union always reacts too late, when the catastrophe is confirmed. this lack of planning is reflected in the health and nutrition assistance programmes, and the gender issue is also forgotten. there is a consistent lack of link between humanitarian policy and development. it is essential. we are not just trying to provide the bare necessities, but to prevent the effects of these disasters, and above all their amplifying effect, poverty. we want cross-functional posts to be created to link echo and dg development. they could also manage collaboration with other global humanitarian aid agencies, starting with those of the member states, as their coordination is largely lacking. we also think it is important that the operating and evaluation costs do not exceed 20% of echo's budget. we also need to make payments faster. venezuela has been waiting since last december for the promised aid. although we are generally satisfied with the european union's humanitarian policy, and we generally support mr imbeni's report, it should be more broadly integrated into a framework of sustainable development.

the community's humanitarian activities. many congratulations to the honourable member. humanitarian aid, as a number of honourable members have said, is an extremely important facet of the european union's external identity. i am the first to acknowledge that we have a great deal to do to improve our performance. but, it is also important that we should acknowledge the enormous amount of good that our help does, day-in day-out, often in extremely difficult circumstances, often in very difficult situations right across the world. whatever the faults – and it is our responsibility to try to put them right – let me pay tribute to what has been achieved and is being achieved by european union aid and by the generous support of europe's taxpayers. we are the biggest providers of this humanitarian assistance in the world and it is important, occasionally, that we remember that. we very much appreciate parliament's support for the reforms we are seeking. much of the strategy which honourable members urge on us tallies, marches very closely, with what we anyway wanted to do. i would stress that however much we might all like to do more we have to focus our action, given the very limited human resources at our disposal, on getting right what we are trying to do already. in this context, the commission has decided to focus echo's interventions based on a definition of the term "humanitarian" which is, in my judgement, generous and flexible but is not infinitely elastic. we believe it would be wrong to overload echo with an ever-growing number of tasks simply for reasons of administrative ease. both commissioner nielson and i want to help countries and peoples in emergencies. but we also want to help them out of emergencies so that they can stand on their own feet again as quickly as possible. we will address this through country strategies which bring together the various types of assistance, emergency, developmental and so on, as quickly as it is feasible to do so. that in my view is the best kind of assistance and it is the wisest use of our taxpayers' money. let me add that we do not intend to make echo into an operational department which delivers aid from contingency planning to distribution in the field. that is not, and never has been, where echo's strengths lie. such an approach would be ineffective and it would detract from the many advantages of echo's partnership approach which allows it, as has been said, to make funds quickly available to those who need them most. the partnership approach also allows for real involvement of civil society at the outset of aid operations, and the value of that has been proven time and time again. we will continue to choose partners on the basis of their efficiency and the availability of partners for the task in hand and bearing in mind, of course, their different comparative strengths and the roles they can play. the ngo sector is an extremely important channel, but the united nations and the red cross movement are also valued partners. thanks to this mixed approach to partnership when necessary, we will be able to send specific messages to the different political fora. mr imbeni mentioned the important issue of visibility. that is important. we want europe's voters and taxpayers to know what is being done with their money and in their name. we have planned a eurobarometer survey to gauge the current levels of awareness of echo in member states and on the basis of that survey, which of course we will want to discuss with the honourable member and others, we will be able to develop appropriate ways of increasing the awareness to which the honourable member referred. the humanitarian aid we give will continue to be governed by the principles of impartiality and non-discrimination laid down in our regulation and accepted by the humanitarian community worldwide. it is an element of our external identity demonstrating that europe can act worldwide with one voice and that it can make a difference on the ground. as the biggest single source of humanitarian aid funding worldwide, as i said earlier, the european union has a responsibility to be not just the biggest in terms of quantity but the best in terms of delivery. that is our clear and ambitious goal. i should like to end with just one reflection. i do not come entirely new to the debate on these issues. over ten years ago i was the development minister in the country i know best, as we learn to say, and was responsible among other things for humanitarian assistance. what has most depressed me about the international scene over the years is that, in practice, our ability to deliver humanitarian relief rapidly in the most unpromising circumstances has increased a great deal more than our ability to prevent that humanitarian assistance being necessary in the first place. that raises serious political and environmental questions about issues such as humanitarian intervention which are going to dominate much of the foreign policy agenda in the years ahead. but in the meantime we must make what we do in terms of humanitarian aid more effective. the honourable member's report will make a sympathy and emotion in condemning terrorism. this was a subject we discussed at our informal meeting of foreign ministers in evian on saturday and sunday. in turn, i would like to turn to the people of malaga, to the widow of mr carpena, and assure them of the european union's intention to take action on their behalf against the scourge of terrorism, which is a real threat to our democracies. you have very rightly chosen, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, to refer to the situation in the middle east. this is all the more timely as the region, which has been the scene of particularly significant events in recent months, is approaching a turning point which may be historic. we are indeed on the eve of decisive moments for the peoples of the region, with the first real possibility of seeing the half-century of israeli-palestinian conflict come to an end, but also with the risk, if this hope is disappointed, of seeing violence reappear. the fact that the presidents of the knesset, mr avraham burg, and of the palestinian legislative council, mr ahmed qurie, have agreed to come together to speak to the european parliament today, at your invitation, madam president, is an indication of the will for peace and dialogue which is now driving both sides. i also see in this, unprecedented to my knowledge, a sign of appreciation for the continuing efforts of the european union to promote the emergence of peace, a recognition which is also accompanied by a strong expectation of europe. this expectation should not be disappointed. this is an exceptional gesture, which i see as a sign of confidence and hope, and it deserves to be welcomed. i shall now try to share with you our analysis of the latest developments in the region and the prospects for the peace process. in recent months we have seen major events in the middle east, from the camp david summit to the israeli withdrawal from southern lebanon. the disappearance of syrian president hafez el assad, who made his country a major player in the regional arena, occurred at the same time. this accelerated development of events concerns first and foremost the israeli-palestinian negotiations. the accession to power in israel of ehud barak, elected on a peace programme, and yasser arafat's unwavering determination to continue the dialogue, helped to revive the negotiations and thus to break the deadlock which had been building for several years. the charm el-sheikh agreement, signed on 4 september 1999, opened a new phase in the peace process, breaking a long period of stagnation and even retreat. it defined the modalities for implementing the provisions of the wye river agreement, which had not been implemented until then. it set a new timetable for the conclusion of the final status negotiations by setting their new terms at a very close deadline now, 13 september 2000, thus de facto extending the interim period by one year. as this deadline approaches, it is possible to draw up a preliminary, necessarily provisional, assessment of this revival of the peace process. i would first say that the charm el-sheikh agreement has been able to be implemented in its main provisions, although often with a delay in the timetable. the second redeployment was completed on 24 march 2000, just over two months after the planned deadline. several hundred prisoners have been released, but the balance is still not entirely satisfactory. other provisions have been applied only in part. thus, the third redeployment did not take place. only one of the two planned corridors between gaza and the west bank has actually been opened. the settlement activities and land expropriation in the west bank continued in violation of the sharm el-sheikh agreement which prohibited any unilateral measures aimed at changing the situation on the ground. these difficulties, combined with a depressed economic and social situation, have contributed significantly to the maintenance of high tension in the territories, which has repeatedly escalated into violent incidents. the negotiations on the final status, which were to go through the intermediate stage of a framework agreement, have been stalled for a long time. the divergence of the parties' initial positions may have given the impression that it was too early to hope for compromises, and this is what prompted the recent camp david summit which, although it did not lead to the desired agreement, opened up new perspectives on all final status issues and, as such, cannot be considered a failure in our view. on the contrary, we believe that it has created a new dynamic. this result, unthinkable only a few months ago, would probably not have been possible, i say, without the personal commitment of president clinton and mrs albright. the progress achieved is largely due to their determination to bring views together and to advance the negotiations. of course, they are also, and above all, due to the political courage, the sense of responsibility and the commitment to peace which the president of the palestinian authority and the israeli prime minister have shown. for the first time, they discussed, without taboos, all the questions relating to the permanent status, not hesitating, both of them, to make progress, to relax positions of principle which had hitherto been presented as intangible. the discussions have certainly not been successful, as we know, and none of the progress achieved can, of course, be considered definitive in the absence of a global agreement, in accordance with the diplomatic rule that there is no agreement on anything until there is agreement on everything. peace in the middle east is now in sight, but it is not yet achieved. the progress made at camp david will have to be consolidated and further progress is needed, particularly on the question of jerusalem, the refugees and, above all, the holy places. prospects were opened up at camp david. we have no doubt that a solution which takes into account the legitimate expectations of each part and the rest of the world is possible, including in regard to the holy places. so there is a historic opportunity. we are still in an exceptionally favourable situation. the israeli prime minister, who was elected on a peace programme, wants an agreement, which he has every interest in obtaining, just as does president arafat, who remains faithful to the choice he has made to engage in the oslo process. president clinton, on the other hand, is more determined than ever to use all his influence and that of his country to promote a positive outcome to the negotiations before the end of his term of office - that is, by the end of the year. this window of opportunity, which is quite exceptional, could, however - and we must be careful - soon close. the us elections are coming up, as is the israeli parliamentary term, which we know can be tricky. as for the deadline of 13 september, set by the charm el-sheikh agreement for the conclusion of the final status negotiations, it cannot be indefinitely postponed unless tangible progress and prospects of a close conclusion are made in the negotiations. this is a unique opportunity that should not be hidden. for the hope raised by camp david to come true, it is important first of all that the parties remain mobilized and that they continue to show the same commitment and the same willingness as they have shown so far. their leaders have to make tough decisions for them and take courage. in this context, every effort must be made to encourage the parties to persevere unremittingly in the process they have begun with a view to the conclusion of a comprehensive and definitive agreement. the european union is ready to make every effort to ensure the success of these efforts. its role, which it intends to pursue actively and usefully, is divided into several areas: encouragement of the parties, contribution to the search for solutions, support for the implementation of the agreements. through its close and regular political dialogue with all the regional parties, the union never fails to recall international law, the concern to see the un resolutions and the fundamental principles guiding the peace process implemented, and its willingness to encourage the parties to progress along the path of peace. you have seen, madam president, on your visit to the middle east earlier this year, how european positions are heard and expected, scrutinized, dissected, sometimes considered too timid, sometimes, on the contrary, too lax or inappropriate, but, in general, constructive and balanced. you have also noticed how much the expectations of europe remained high. it was this concern to assert europe's role and to meet the expectations of the parties that led to the appointment of a special envoy of the european union as early as 1996. ambassador moratinos - whom i welcome and who has been in office for four years - has succeeded in giving europe a face in the middle east by developing daily contacts with all the leaders of the region. this role of support, facilitation and intermediation, complementary to that of the united states, is also a contribution to collective thinking in order to devise new solutions, break taboos or propose compromises. the berlin declaration of 1999, like the venice declaration of 1980, reflects a remarkable unity of view among the european partners and is a reference text which has helped - i am sure - to pave the way for historic compromises between israelis and palestinians. europe has developed a policy of cooperation with all the countries of the middle east aimed at creating the conditions for harmonious economic and social development while strengthening regional integration, which is the condition for the lasting anchoring of peace. it is thus responsible - as we know - for almost half of the financial commitments for international aid to the palestinian territories since 1993. it is of course still available, and i stress this point, to help, when the time comes, to implement fully the agreements reached. it is probably too early to talk about what an agreement on the permanent status of the palestinian territories might be, which will in any case be decided by the parties alone through negotiation, which is the only acceptable method. the camp david discussions, however, give a first idea of what the outlines of a future agreement might be. in this context, i would like to say that we believe that the establishment of a palestinian state is inevitable, provided that it is viable, peaceful and democratic. it is the inalienable right of the palestinians to self-determination, and i am convinced that it is also the best guarantee of security for israel. this right to have a state and, therefore, to proclaim it, cannot be vetoed. however, as the european union has already stated, its preference would clearly be for the creation of a palestinian state following a successful negotiation process. but it does not make this a condition, as you know. its position on this issue remains that expressed in the berlin declaration of march 1999. but all the efforts made at this stage, starting of course with those of the parties, must be directed towards the conclusion of an agreement which is - i repeat - within reach. as you have noted, the palestinians are now asking themselves whether, under what conditions and, above all, when they should proclaim their state in the light of the developments under way. the exchange of views between the foreign ministers of the fifteen at the recent informal meeting in evian, to which i referred earlier, confirmed the validity of the european approach to date in support of the peace process. the urgency of achieving a decisive breakthrough on the israeli-palestinian front must not, however, distract us from the other parts of the peace process, which form a coherent whole. it requires a comprehensive and lasting solution. an israeli-palestinian agreement is essential. it is vital, but it cannot, on its own, ensure peace and stability in the middle east. it is therefore time, as the president of the french republic has recently stressed, for the thread of discussion to be renewed between syria and israel, the status quo being in the interest of neither country. all efforts should therefore be made to promote the conclusion of an agreement as soon as possible between israel and syria and between israel and lebanon. the situation in this respect, although it seems to be mixed today, is nevertheless promising. the israeli withdrawal from southern lebanon on 24 may brought an end to 22 years of occupation and thereby created what i would call a 'new situation'. this withdrawal, which was certified by the secretary-general of the united nations on 16 june, is a positive element in more than one way. it marked first the late but full and unconditional implementation of security council resolution 425. it was therefore a definite advance in this respect. it was then held under less favourable conditions than might have been feared and was not accompanied - and this is very important - by the escalation of violence that might have been feared. the sense of responsibility shown by all the parties must be emphasized here. so far, the difficulties have been overcome and the provisions of resolution 425 have been implemented. the question of israeli encroachments along the blue line was thus resolved after two months of difficulty. on 27 july the security council adopted resolution 1310 extending the mandate of unifil for a further period of six months. the lebanese government gave its consent on 5 august to the redeployment of the force to the former occupied zone, and since then unifil has established a number of fixed posts in the area and has also taken up positions along the israeli-lebanese border. at the same time, on 9 august the lebanese government deployed a joint force of 1,000 men, 500 soldiers and 500 police officers to the former occupied zone, with the task of maintaining public order within lebanese territory, but excluding any border surveillance, which was its responsibility. the redeployment of unifil and the lebanese government's deployment of a joint security force to the south are positive developments in our view. but the situation on the border with israel remains fragile. so far relatively minor incidents occur from time to time along the blue line. it is therefore in the interest of all parties to avoid any incident that could lead to an escalation. in this regard, it is important that the lebanese government assume all its responsibilities in order to create the necessary conditions for the full exercise of the mandate of unifil. stabilisation of the situation in southern lebanon also requires the rehabilitation of this region, which, as we know, has suffered greatly from the occupation and the war, and its reintegration into lebanon's economic and social area. the european union is naturally ready to take part in the reconstruction of southern lebanon as soon as the conditions on the ground are met. it intends to give a very concrete demonstration of its support for lebanon at the donor conference for the reconstruction of south lebanon, which is to be held in the autumn under our presidency. the withdrawal of israel from southern lebanon and the gradual restoration of lebanese sovereignty in the area are also moving in the right direction. the changes taking place in the region also suggest the possibility, as we hope, of a gradual development of syrian-lebanese relations; the situation is still fragile. we are convinced that only an israeli-syrian agreement, in accordance with security council resolution 242 and the principle of exchanging territory for peace, can bring about a just and lasting peace in the region. the context may not, admittedly, appear very favourable - let us admit it - to a resumption of the israeli-syrian negotiations, at least in the short term. the positions of the two sides, as we know them, remain at this stage irreconcilable, even if the differences appear less profound than on many aspects of the israeli-palestinian conflict. moreover, the internal agendas of the israeli and syrian leaderships seem to be immediately overwhelmed by other political issues. yet the strategic choice of peace remains on both sides and has recently been reaffirmed at the highest level. president bashar al assad, in his inaugural speech on 7 july, expressed his readiness to conclude an agreement with israel, recalling that everything was negotiable except the 4 june 1967 line. ehud barak, for his part, called on syria to conclude what he called - a phrase which resonates with us - the "peace of the brave". it is therefore to be hoped that in the coming months the negotiating lines can be united. the recent developments in the region, i conclude, are not only linked to the peace process, even though it plays a central role. regional integration, although still very weak, is progressing slowly but steadily. it is particularly relevant to the wider context of the barcelona euro-mediterranean process, which reflects the european union's concern to develop a comprehensive strategy for this region which is so close to us and so closely linked to us. a free trade area is being built with the union, which includes all the countries of the middle east and which should - we are convinced of this - promote the opening up and modernisation of economies and their integration into the world economy. association agreements have already been signed with jordan, israel and the palestinian authority. a deal with egypt should be in the offing. negotiations are under way with lebanon and syria. there is no doubt that the euro-mediterranean process, in its political dimension, with the draft charter for peace and stability, economic but also social and human stability, will help to build the middle east of the 'after-peace' which we wish to see, because there is no alternative to the peace process which is now under way in a phase which we hope and believe will be decisive. europe, like the rest of the international community, particularly the united states - and i will end here, madam president - intends to do everything possible to facilitate the decisions which are the responsibility of the primary actors, the israelis and the palestinians, who are responsible to their peoples and to history, in order to promote the emergence of that long awaited, long desired and now within reach peace.
