- madam president, my group had asked for a major debate on the situation in the middle east to be held at this part-session. he also suggested that senior israeli and palestinian leaders be invited to the european parliament together. we therefore welcome the initiatives taken in this direction and i warmly welcome the presidents of both houses who have honoured us with their presence. in this period which everyone feels is decisive, what useful message for peace can we europeans send today? i agree with much of what the president-in-office said on this subject. the first of these messages, i think, touches on the central issue of the whole process, the palestinian state. i think it is time to reaffirm in all clarity the content of the unambiguous declaration adopted by the berlin european council in march 1999 in which the fifteen declared their willingness to recognize a palestinian state. has the recognition by europe of this inalienable right led the palestinians to proclaim their state without any other consideration? no, it's the opposite. it has supported the sovereign and responsible decision of the palestinian leadership to postpone the deadline, and i am convinced that it is ready to postpone it for a few more weeks to give the negotiations a chance if, by 13 september, it feels that we are moving towards a comprehensive peace agreement. the european union must therefore reaffirm its position in berlin in all clarity and i believe that it will facilitate such a move by the palestinians. the second message from europe should be, in my view, to recall the principles on which the negotiations can and must be based, namely the relevant un resolutions, in particular those on the israeli withdrawal from all the occupied territories, including east jerusalem, or on the right of return or compensation for refugees. such a reminder would in no way close the door to the necessary compromises. it would, however, leave it to the sovereign palestinians to seek out with the sovereign israeli negotiators, on the basis of these basic facts recognized by the entire international community, original mutually acceptable legal formulae. the third message from europe, i think, is to ensure that the future global agreement will be implemented to the end, unlike all the partial agreements that have followed since oslo. the united states alone cannot provide this guarantee. no one knows today what their next leaders will be like. the european union is therefore an irreplaceable guarantor, alongside the united states and egypt, representing the arab world, of a faithful and rigorous follow-up of the commitments made. this is the triple wish of my group, with the hope that thus, yerushalayim, which means in hebrew: peace, will appear.
mr president, on the middle east and the israeli-palestinian peace process, i have always said that it is up to the peoples of the region and their leaders to define the conditions for their peaceful coexistence, and that they must make the necessary efforts and make the necessary sacrifices. as a european who is committed to the euro-mediterranean balance, i have, like many others, regretted the european union's lack of political weight in this process, but i have also always refused, in this parliament, to play what i would call the role of the lecturer. today, with only a few days to go before a peace agreement is reached or a major crisis can lead to dramatic violence, we must, in order to give peace its best chance, help those on both sides who are taking major collective and personal risks to achieve peace. that is why i am in full agreement with the position expressed by pierre moscovici and i say today that we will not advance peace by taking sides in the difficult debate and negotiations under way. so for me, in the very short time that we have left, our message to the israelis and the palestinians must be simple and clear. it is based on three points: we want a peace agreement in the middle east, we will support and guarantee this peace agreement, once it is signed, we will help its implementation by all means, including financial, but not only financial. in conclusion, as we all know, peace is always a difficult act. europe, so torn throughout its history, knows this better than anyone. it is also easier said than done to eradicate divisions and terrorism, as we know very well with the balkans, the division in nicosia and the bombings in the basque country. the european union is not only a political force, but also a political force, and we must not forget that the european union is a political force, and that it is the european union which is the political force.
in writing. - the meda programme is the main element of financial cooperation within the framework of the euro-mediterranean partnership established in 1995. but the procedures are too complex, not transparent enough, the project implementation data too long... reform is urgently needed because these difficulties are discrediting the whole process and have been perceived as negative signs by the peoples of the mediterranean who had welcomed the barcelona process with a certain enthusiasm. the commission's text is a good thing because it is part of a logic of simplification of the current regulation. but we must wait for more if we are to give our mediterranean policy a new start: involving the people more by supporting decentralized cooperation, integrating the cultural and human aspects more fully, opening up the free trade area to agricultural products, monitoring and supporting fundamental freedoms. i fully support the rapporteur's proposal that an annual report be drawn up on the respect for human rights in the mediterranean countries.
in writing. - mr galeote's report has the peculiarity of actually indicating quite clearly its real objective and logic, the creation of a single community diplomatic service, while formally claiming the opposite. the whole of the proposed scheme contradicts recital o, according to which it is not intended to replace national diplomatic services by a single european service. i welcome the frankness and consistency of mr dupuis' amendments, which at least have the merit of clarifying matters. the subtle internal balances of the epp probably explain the baroque character of the building we are dealing with. these seemingly rather ridiculous precautions and counter-phrases are in fact in line with the monnet-delors method, of which mr galeote is only proposing a new version, this time on diplomacy. it is the method which requires the organ to create the function, the container to secrete the content, the technique to give rise to the policy. but now we have the reading grid and we know how to decode. when mr galeote proposes to set up a training school to train community super-diplomats and to retrain national diplomats, to give the european union international legal personality and to 'coordinate' representations, particularly to the un, we know that what we really need to read is: merging embassies, creating a single community diplomatic corps and communitizing the french and british permanent seats on the un security council. and of course, as always, the question of the object, the content, the only one that counts, is omitted. why are we creating this new organ? in this case, what foreign policy would this community diplomatic service serve? what common interests should he defend ? this is a typical marxist approach. the 'sudden qualitative leap' is expected, which will hopefully change from a certain threshold, the quantitative into the qualitative. the common instrument is supposed to produce a common conscience, a common will, a common responsibility. this cult of the quantitative culminates in the grotesque comparison between the number of american and "european" diplomats, the latter being obtained by adding the number of professional diplomats working in the foreign services of our various states. it is important to remember that the united states is one and the same nation and that the member states of the european union each have special links in the world, different and sometimes divergent experiences and affinities, which are the richness of european diplomacy. it is the complementarity of these expertise that can be put to the service of a common, clearly defined objective, thus truly serving european interests. with the single diplomacy that is being proposed to us, it is precisely these assets that will be devalued. in reality, national wills, which are europe's diplomatic engine, are being eroded, and it is at the same time surprising that the multiplicity of instruments and declarations is matched only by a lack of content and a general lack of interest. the only positive aspect of this report could be its desire to streamline the organisation and improve the professionalism of the european commission's delegations in third countries. experience shows that these bodies are not always up to their real task, which is the implementation and monitoring of community programmes and agreements on the ground. it seems that this mission has been relegated to the background of the concerns of commission representatives who are too busy officially obtaining a usurped title of ambassador to ensure rigorously the proper execution of the programmes for which they are responsible. apart from this last point, it will nevertheless be clear that we obviously did not vote in favour of the other proposals, which are quite surreal, in this own-initiative report. today we see the absurdity and the inherent weakness of a single currency without the support of any sovereign state. and we would like to see a single diplomacy, designed in the same way, working, or rather not working, in reverse.
mr president, one example from the explanatory statement shows the ridiculousness of the report on the humanitarian activities of the european community. the report mentions the absence of operational tools, in particular helicopters, to explain the lack of international aid in general, and that of the european institutions in particular, in response to the floods in mozambique, whereas - who does not remember? - there was no shortage of helicopters, planes, transport equipment of any kind, or even means of destruction, to intervene in yugoslavia or iraq? the only conclusion that can be drawn is that the great powers, who are capable of mobilizing considerable resources to impose their hegemony on the rest of the world, are not willing to make the slightest effort to save human lives. in these circumstances, the european institutions' lecherous statements on humanitarian aid are an indecent hypocrisy and we have no intention of endorsing them, which is why we abstained on this question.
in writing. - i would first like to congratulate mr imbeni on the quality of his report. the report is in line with the position of our institution, which has always been strongly representative of the most deprived countries, through its opinions, resolutions and practical measures to improve and develop humanitarian aid. since the early 1990s and the creation of the european union humanitarian office (echo), europe has established itself as the largest donor in the world. however, despite our legitimate efforts, in view of the historical links between some european countries and some developing countries, it is clear that poverty is increasing worldwide. today, half the population lives on less than two dollars a day. this is intolerable! was the money you gave me wasted? i don't think he is. without echo's emergency response to natural disasters or serious crises that regularly affect the most vulnerable on our planet, i cannot imagine what we would be facing today. however, an effort to rationalize humanitarian aid is needed. i therefore welcome the call by this house for greater coherence and coordination in aid and for greater collaboration between the various partners, such as the commission, the member states, associations and the united nations. in addition to strict humanitarian aid, we must work on better conflict prevention, as 25% of africa's territory is still "gangrenous" by war. finally, although the problem of development is multi-dimensional and the european union is not the only remedy, we must continue and intensify our action in order to lay the foundations for sustainable global development and contribute to the eradication of poverty. in any case, this idea was the inspiration for the work of the committee on development and cooperation. that is why i voted in favour of the report presented today by our colleague.

counsel. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i shall try to follow your recommendation and talk to you about aids. as you know, the aids pandemic currently affects 33.6 million people, the majority of whom live in developing countries. in 1999, the un aids agency reported 5.6 million new cases and 2.6 million deaths, 50 percent of them among women. this epidemic has already destroyed the achievements of thirty years of development aid in the most affected countries. africa is suffering the most dramatic consequences. the african continent finally had the cadres and experts it lacked so much at the time of independence. but these educated, active adults have paid a heavy price for the disease. we cannot ignore the enormous loss of human capital that this first generation of victims represents, a loss that adds to the personal tragedy experienced by the patients and their families. we also do not forget the poorest and most deprived who are even more excluded from care. no one can forget the testimony of edwin cameron, a white, gay, hiv-positive judge on the supreme court of south africa, who bravely presented himself at the opening of the plenary session of the international aids congress in durban last july. only his social status, his income, allows him to have access to care that is unfortunately unavailable to the majority of his compatriots. his confession illustrates the injustice of africa. for the past decade or so, africa has courageously embarked on a difficult process of structural reform and adjustment. however, by placing a heavy burden on the healthcare system, the epidemic has made it even more difficult to modernise the healthcare sector. at a time when efforts are being made to establish financing systems that guarantee the sustainability and improvement of services, the burden of aids appears disproportionate for communities already heavily burdened by the economic crisis, the backwardness of development, the lack of health structures and the absence of a system of collective social protection. the question of hiv, which causes aids, is therefore at the very heart of sustainable development. it decimates societies, threatens future generations, and undermines economic growth. this issue is now considered a matter of the utmost importance by the members of the un security council. beyond africa, this pandemic is global. 35 million people are living with hiv, but fewer than 500,000 have access to antiretroviral treatment. it is clear that in this respect too the gap between rich and poor countries has widened. the inequality of access to treatment, intolerable in itself, is today all the more outrageous because information is circulating, and circulating fast, on our planet. everyone, today, knows that these treatments exist. it is humanly, morally and politically desirable to seek with developing countries solutions adapted to their situation, taking into account their potential, which will enable them to improve access to these treatments, while pursuing cooperation in the fields of education, health, prevention and training of local health personnel. the european union became aware, as early as the early 1980s, of the need to provide practical assistance to developing countries in the fight against hiv, the cause of aids, by placing respect for people with aids, especially the most vulnerable, at the centre of its concerns. it has thus helped to set up actions in the fields of transfusion safety, information campaigns, youth awareness-raising, the creation of documentation and information centres, as well as training and medical and social care. some countries, particularly france, have also undertaken initiatives to facilitate access to treatment. the first results of the two programmes for access to medicines, which were set up in 1999 in côte d'ivoire and morocco under the international therapeutic solidarity fund, are encouraging. new programmes are currently being launched in senegal, vietnam and south africa. although these are only a small number of individuals, compared to the needs of millions of people, we are convinced that they contribute to international mobilisation, increase partner involvement and promote the sharing of know-how. the effects of these are already being seen in the mother-child prevention programmes implemented by the un-aids and unicef. the international context is therefore changing. the united nations and its agencies, the world bank, are mobilizing to strengthen international solidarity in the field of health care. a major, historic agreement, we might say, has been reached between the who, un-aids and five pharmaceutical companies. this agreement makes it possible to reduce the price of aids medicines significantly. the recent decision to make available free of charge an anti-retroviral molecule, nevirapine, which is effective in preventing mother-to-child transmission, also adds credibility to the agreement, as it shows that the pharmaceutical industry can do more than just advertise. finally, many countries are becoming aware that the debt burden of developing countries is an unbearable burden on their economies and is hampering their ability to effectively combat poverty, and especially the pandemic. france has taken concrete measures to cancel these debts, while promoting development and health education. these initiatives illustrate the strengthening of the international community's commitment, which must not be slackened. however, this can only be a first step in the fight against the aids pandemic. at the international conference held last july in the african continent in durban, africa, as i have already mentioned, researchers, health professionals, activists from non-governmental organizations, political leaders, were unanimous in stressing the urgency of the situation. the contact with the poor health professionals, the resigned distress of the mothers of children who themselves have been infected, the inability of the health authorities to act, the visit to a paediatric hospital, convinced me, if necessary, of the importance of the growing gap between the inhabitants of the countries of the south and their peers that has been created by chance in our regions. new commitments are necessary. we are convinced of that. the strengthening of international aid in the fight against hiv/aids is an absolute emergency. in the context of internationally defined strategies, in partnership with national aids programmes and other donors, coordination of all resources at all levels remains a top priority for international aid. there is an urgent need to strengthen prevention programmes, improve research efforts for developing countries and provide real access to treatment for all patients. in addition to the availability of affordable antiretroviral medicines from local health systems, access to treatment requires increased training, support for structures and support for associations of people affected. while programmes to prevent mother-to-child transmission are still essential, we also need to implement massive projects to provide access to treatment for chronic infections, because otherwise who would be raising these children whom we would have prevented from being infected? access to medicines poses complex socioeconomic, ethical and medical problems, as well as political and cultural problems, which we must try to overcome by respecting our partners and considering them as partners with whom we can cooperate. there is a need for extensive consultation between donors, recipients, the pharmaceutical industry and associations to develop operational arrangements for access to treatment. several initiatives have been launched. firstly, a commission round table on aids, tuberculosis and malaria will be held in september. a japanese conference will also be held in the framework of the g8 this autumn on these three diseases. finally, a proposal for a special session of the un general assembly will be devoted to aids before may 2002. the presidency will support initiatives to find sustainable solutions to the problem of comprehensive and respectful care for sick people, through concrete projects and partnership agreements with the countries concerned. ensuring that everyone has access to quality care, information and the necessary resources must be the objective of the european community. the idea of access to treatment is not new. this path is difficult, but it is necessary. it cannot succeed without the participation of all: the pharmaceutical industry, bilateral and multilateral donors, the countries concerned. we now know that only a long-term commitment will overcome the epidemic. we must be convinced that this commitment is all the more necessary because it would be immoral, dangerous for the development and progress of mankind, and also dangerous for global balance and peace, since recent advances, particularly in health care, are only benefiting the wealthier countries. (applause) i would like to thank
commission. – the commission attended the 13th international aids conference, which took place in durban, south africa, from 7 to14 july 2000. the theme of the conference, 'breaking the silence', provided a framework which helped to strengthen national and international action against hiv/aids. the conference welcomed scientific progress in addressing aids, especially news of the first efficacy trials for an aids vaccine and the evidence that transmission of hiv from mother to infant could be largely prevented by cost-effective use of anti-retroviral drugs. also welcome was information on the many small-scale condom and safe sex empowerment education programmes that have proved their worth in stemming the spread of hiv/aids. i believe that the conference could have given more attention to the lessons of success stories as regards improving and expanding these prevention strategies because information and prevention is in fact the most important ways of fighting aids. prevention is central to a successful long-term national, international and global response to aids. at the same time a full spectrum of care from basic treatment of opportunistic infections to entry retroviral therapy for hiv infection can no longer be denied to the vast majority of the millions of people infected with the virus. the commission welcomes the new initiatives being taken against hiv/aids by some countries to produce cheaper generic drugs and would like to offer its support to help such countries provide technical assistance to other developing countries to enable them to pursue such initiatives. possibilities will be further discussed with the countries involved. we recognise that the production of generic drugs could greatly improve access to care and treatment for hiv/aids. the statistics of the epidemic are frightening and still getting worse. for example, one in four zimbabweans will die from hiv/aids, including one in three in the capital, harare. more than a million children are already orphaned by hiv/aids in zimbabwe, almost 10% of the population. more than half the pregnant women in some areas in botswana are infected with hiv, and a third of them transmit hiv to their new-born babies during delivery. the conference opened up exciting new opportunities and partnerships that will enable people who are vulnerable to hiv infection to gain access to technologies and procedures to make care more affordable for hiv/aids sufferers and invest in new technologies and products to prevent and treat hiv/aids. these opportunities must be exploited immediately, and the commission intends to play its part. it is accordingly discussing innovative approaches with its developing country partners as well as with other donors. we can and must be doing all that we should do about hiv/aids. we can and must also do everything possible to combat other major killer diseases affecting poor people. malaria and tuberculosis, both of which kill more than a million people a year, must assume new importance in our work to reduce poverty and ill-health. accelerated action on the three key communicable diseases - hiv/aids, malaria and tuberculosis - has been addressed this year by a number of high-level meetings. the commission will shortly submit a communication to the council and parliament outlining proposals for accelerated action to improve access to proven key measures and commodities to develop active and effective delivery structures and systems for drugs and increase investment in research into and development of priority drugs and vaccines. the communication points especially to the value of bringing condoms, bed nets and other preventive procedures to the poorest and most vulnerable more rapidly and on a sufficiently large scale. the european union accounted for 55% of global development aid in the social sectors in 1997 and has increased its support for health, aids and population programmes from 1% of our total assistance in 1986 to over 8% at the present time, compared to an oecd average of 5.5%. we are therefore focusing more and more on this field. total commitments of eur 3.4 billion were earmarked for health, aids and population between 1990 and 1998, none of which was offered as loans. this is in clear contrast to the recent offer from the united states to southern africa. the commission is holding wide-ranging consultations on options for accelerated national and international action and innovative approaches to address these diseases. on 28 september, in collaboration with the who and un aids, it will be hosting an international round table. the meeting will consider how a comprehensive approach at national and international level might tackle these three diseases and how we can make a difference.
- madam president, the world aids congress in durban has made it possible to take an important step which, in my view, is explained by the fact that, although we have heard that prevention remains essential to combat the scourge, the question of access to care has finally been placed at the heart of the debate. durban has opened up the crucial issues of drug pricing and the development of generic medicines, and has advanced thinking on intellectual property rights or compulsory licences. it is time, because the behaviour of the big pharmaceutical companies has too often contributed to imposing a two-speed diet in health care, one of medicine for the rich, one of despair for the poor. the pharmaceutical companies' initiative on drug prices, launched on the sidelines of the conference, is therefore an encouraging opening, if not a mere publicity stunt. the g8 summit in okinawa also sealed the commitment of the rich countries and set targets for reducing the ravages of private operators is to be held in new york to initiate and finance the action plan against aids in southern africa. we really feel like we're finally starting to address the right questions. perhaps now is the time to provide the right answers. it is clear that the european union is not on the sidelines of this mobilization, but i believe we must move up a gear, as i have heard the french tuberculosis. we are aware that the time has come not only for reflection but also for action, and we are awaiting very concrete proposals which will make it possible to move forward very quickly. i am thinking in particular of the debate on industrial property rights and the debate on compulsory licences. i am thinking of the development of the international therapeutic fund, which is being set the pharmaceutical industry, ngos and donors. perhaps the round table on 28 september, organized by the commission in conjunction with the who and the un aids, could be the first step in shaping this?
- madam president, i will not repeat what has already been said and very well said, and with very praiseworthy intentions. i'll try to talk about the facts. i think the facts today are simple. the facts are about access to care and treatment for the sick. the un-aids itself has recognized the ineffectiveness of the programme announced by the pharmaceutical companies, which were in fact only trying to change their image and are now backing down, now that it is a matter of actually negotiating a lowering of the price of care. the problem is no longer the supply of medicines, which is necessarily limited in time and subordinated to the specific interests of the laboratories, but rather the adjustment between the cost of care and the purchasing power in developing countries. the european union must encourage multinational pharmaceutical companies to grant voluntary licences, the first step towards access to care for disadvantaged populations. in the event that these are not implemented, the european union should enforce compliance with the agreements in the event of a health emergency and require the granting of compulsory licences, which would finally help to overcome the problem of the price of care. i believe that the agony of an entire continent takes precedence over the interests of individuals.
- madam president, i believe that, as our colleague mrs carlotti said, the durban conference has had the merit of clarifying the fact that the fight against aids is not being fought in the same way in europe as in africa. aids is a reflection of all the economic and social deficiencies of developing countries and is a part of the broader problem of poverty. prevention can therefore only be successful if it is accompanied by access to care. i therefore agree with the previous speaker that the pharmaceutical companies, which have a monopoly on the manufacture and marketing of trithera­pies and even azt, must sell them at cost. there wouldn't be a debate here between us if triple therapy cost a dollar. and, as the director of un-aids recommends, we must increase the amount of money we are investing tenfold if we are to even begin a genuine policy of prevention and care. and you should know that medicine is not handed out like bags of rice. we need doctors, clinics, social structures to support them. and under the dictates of the imf, poor countries are cutting public spending, especially on education and health. the european union must help to speed up the debt relief for african countries, which amounts to 15 billion a year, so that these resources can be used to set up health infrastructure and new social programmes. finally, the development of a vaccine must be the priority of research.

the agenda calls for the declaration by the council and the commission on the establishment of an observatory on industrial change. i shall now give the floor to mrs péry, on behalf of the council, who will be in the chamber for a while, as she has been vice-president of this house for a long time.
thank you, madam president.
- we will not oppose the creation of an observatory of industrial change. the unanimous opposition of the right only confirms that it refuses any transparency on the disastrous consequences for society of factory closures and layoffs which are boldly presented as inevitable in order to cope with the changes. but this observatory could be only a statistical instrument which, in this class society, would not even be objective. an observatory is no substitute for the political will to prevent large companies from laying off workers to make more profit. so, to call for social cohesion is to ask workers who have been laid off by a company that is closing down and the unemployed who have been affected by restructuring to bear their lot with patience. most mergers or restructurings are financial operations which are not even motivated by industrial change. and it's always the workers who pay the price, never the shareholders. that is why i say to the workers that they can and must defend themselves, in particular by imposing a ban on dismissals in any company that makes a profit. the accumulated profit must be used to finance the distribution of work among all, without reduction of wages, without precariousness and without flexibility.
- mr president, madam minister, madam commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to put this debate back into its proper context. as an auvergne member, i would remind you that about a year ago, in this room, there was the michelin crisis. michelin announced massive layoffs at its factories in europe, along with record profits on the stock exchange. at that time, in this very room, we had collectively committed ourselves to reviewing the european merger regulations. i would remind the commission that it would be good to review directive 94/ec and regulation 4064/89 to strengthen information and consultation of employees before major changes, which involve redundancies, whether by restructuring or merger. a year later, as a first concrete step, we were offered an observatory on industrial change. okay, but make sure he's really serving the cause of the employees. two conditions seem to be essential: the commission must be able to assess the application of the directive on collective redundancies and the closure of companies and to make proposals for effective penalties in the event of non-compliance with the regulations. the social partners must be involved in this initiative through budgetary resources allocated by the european institutions.

the agenda calls for the report (a5-0209/2000) by mr veltroni, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on the communication from the commission to the council, the european parliament, the economic and social committee and the committee of the regions - principles and guidelines for the community's audiovisual policy in the digital age (com (1999) 657 - c5-0144/2000 - 2000/2087 (cos))
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission has set itself the task of defining, within a short time, what constitutes a european audiovisual work. i am very interested in such a definition, which is a natural complement to today's discussion. the effect of the 'television without frontiers' directive has been to maintain a high percentage of national works in each country, without succeeding in stimulating the circulation of these works from one country to another. the objective of the definition of a european audiovisual work must therefore be to achieve the circulation of these works. in this context, we agree that the cultural diversity claimed today is not simply the addition of the respective identities of each member state, but rather their exchange and circulation. the circulation of works, however, and the origin of their funding, will probably not be sufficient to define a european audiovisual work. the question of the content of work is of concern to all of us. what content can define a work, if not that which is based on the pluralism of production? partnerships are necessary for the audiovisual creation of today and tomorrow, but monopolies and hegemonic strategies are contrary to the creation itself. nothing is more dangerous than the current concentration of operators, possessing both broadcasting capacities and content catalogues. in the face of the digital revolution and technological change, mr veltroni's excellent report strongly demonstrates the economic and cultural need for a european audiovisual policy. i would like to end by stressing one of the main points of this report. who better to defend diversity and pluralism than universal service? who can ensure free access to information, entertainment and knowledge? public television is not a monopoly and should not be. but public service is a matter of the general interest and must be valued as such. the public television stations of each member state develop independently, in accordance with protocol 32 of the treaty of amsterdam, but they agree to give each other similar tasks: information, innovation, places for exchanges and integration, etc. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. in short, not to die in the digital age but to perpetuate the fulfilment of its tasks, which should, i believe, be the guiding principles of the community's audiovisual policy.

however, the commission has a duty under the treaty to ensure that the financing system does not affect trading conditions and competition in the community to the detriment of the common interest. in order for the commission to be able to carry out its task and to assess whether the advantages granted to the undertakings in question correspond to the public service missions entrusted to them, the latter must be defined by the member state and their financing must be transparent. any commercial activities carried out by these undertakings must not, directly or indirectly, benefit from public service funds. transparency requires that, and i think the latest texts issued by the commission help to make these principles understandable, clear and transparent for all. the informal council on culture and audiovisual, held in lille on 20 and 21 july, discussed the future of public sector broadcasting. some ministers felt that a new stage, complementary to the amsterdam protocol, was necessary in view of the rapid technological developments in this sector, and i expressed my readiness to discuss this matter with them and with you in the near future. it should also be noted that the commission has recently adopted a revised version of the transparency directive, as i have already mentioned. this directive, which is very important, does not apply to public service broadcasting companies which do not carry on commercial activities. public services defined by the state, with public funding clearly falling within the definition of public service, are therefore not covered by the transparency directive. the concept of universal service is mentioned in the report. in this connection, it should be noted that the concept of universal service is borrowed from the telecommunications service and cannot, in my view, be automatically transposed into the audiovisual sector. the guarantee of citizens' access to certain broadcasting services and content forms is a matter of the definition of the public service broadcasting mandate and is therefore the responsibility of the member states, in accordance with the amsterdam protocol. as regards the call for a european forum to discuss issues concerning all kinds of audiovisual content, this is an interesting proposal which the commission will consider and study with the parties concerned in the context of the review of the 'television without frontiers' directive. it should be noted that under the current directive a contact committee has been set up to examine all aspects of audiovisual policy related to the directive. as far as the international trade negotiations in the audiovisual sector are concerned, i can tell you that there has been no change. the commission has clarified its position on several occasions. it should retain its freedom, acquired in the uruguay round, to develop and implement financial and regulatory arrangements in the audiovisual sector with a view to safeguarding, in particular, cultural diversity. in its conclusions of 26 october 1999, the council gave the commission a mandate to this effect for the forthcoming negotiations on services, and i can assure you that my colleague, commissioner lamy, is fully in line with this. we can be confident that it will safeguard and help the european audiovisual sector in the way we want it, in the way you want it, and if each of us does his part, we will all succeed together in safeguarding and strengthening in the future our audiovisual service, which is essential for job creation and the maintenance of cultural pluralism.
thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon.

the next item is the joint debate on the following reports: - by mr varela suanzes-carpegna (a5-0194/2000), on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation on the conclusion of the protocol setting out the fishing opportunities and financial contribution provided for in the agreement between the european economic community and the government of the republic of guinea on fishing off the guinean coast for the period 1 january 2000 to 31 december 2001. (com (2000) 304 - c5-0315/2000 - 2000/0154 (cns)) by mr varela suanzes-carpegna, on behalf of the committee on fisheries, on the proposal for a council regulation (ec) fixing for the period from 3 december 1999 to 2 december 2002 the fishing opportunities and financial contribution provided for in the agreement between the european community and the government of mauritius on fishing off mauritius (com (2000) 229 - c5-0253/2000 - 2000/0094 (cns))
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i should like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr varela suanzes-carpegna, for his two reports on the new protocol to the fisheries agreement between the european community and the republic of mauritius and the republic of guinea, which are being discussed today. as regards the first agreement with mauritius, i am pleased to hear that you support the new technical elements and the further amendments to this protocol, such as the sharing of costs, increased funding for scientific programmes, monitoring and control and follow-up funding. the agreement with mauritius is a typical tuna agreement with a small share of fishing opportunities for linenfish and forms an important component of the ec network of tuna agreements in the indian ocean. this new protocol is the fourth since the framework convention entered into force in 1990. the extension of the protocol for three years will open up fishing opportunities for 83 tuna fishermen and will incorporate for the first time the guidelines of the fisheries council of october 1997 into the agreement, namely an increase in targeted measures for the development of the fisheries sector and a redistribution of costs between the community and the shipowners. the main features of the protocol include the reduction of the reference tonnage from 7 500 tonnes to 5 500 tonnes, in view of the low catches during the three-year period covered by the last protocol, which also results in a corresponding reduction in the compensation payments, namely by 29%. i can also tell you that 50%, that is to say half of the compensation, is earmarked for specific measures to develop the local fisheries sector. the programme will finance scientific and technical measures, including monitoring and control. in this context, i would like to emphasize that the conditions for monitoring such measures have been improved by requiring the mauritanian authorities to submit a detailed report every year and by giving the commission the possibility of reviewing payments in the light of the actual implementation of the various measures. the licence fees for shipowners were raised substantially, from eur 20 to eur 25 per tonne. the protocol will result in a major redistribution of costs between the community and shipowners, since shipowners will now have to bear 23.5% of the total cost, compared with 7% in the past. this is in line with the 1997 council decision on third country agreements, which requires a balanced distribution of costs. technical improvements are also being made to catch declarations, the charging of fees and the procedures for boarding. i understand that you also welcome the technical elements we have introduced in the agreement with guinea, in particular the fact that the development of marine resources is better taken into account by means of a special premium. we have also had a framework agreement with the republic of guinea since 1983. this agreement is also important for the european union because it contains fishing opportunities for trawlers and tuna fishermen. it also provides a partial alternative to fishing during the protection periods under the agreements with various neighbouring countries, in particular senegal, mauritania and morocco, and it also provides an alternative to moroccan waters to a certain extent. i am therefore pleased to inform you that the protocol with the republic of guinea contains important innovations aimed in particular at promoting the precautionary principle and the sustainable use of resources. i should like to mention specifically that a premium is being introduced to help the guinean authorities to improve the state of fish stocks in the guinean exclusive economic zone. this premium shall only be paid if guinea demonstrates that the overall fishing effort has been reduced and that the agreed measures for enhanced surveillance and control have been applied. the aim is to help guinea to promote bilateral fisheries agreements with other countries and to reduce the private agreements that often undermine sustainable fisheries management. the financial contribution for specific measures such as scientific and technical research, monitoring and inspection of fishing activities, support for training and retraining in the artisanal fisheries sector and support for participation in the work of international organisations was also increased to 46% of the total amount of the aid. finally, the protocol provides for close cooperation between the two parties in the management of the measures. monitoring will be facilitated by a detailed annual report and by the possibility for the community to review payments in the light of the actual implementation of the measures. as regards your amendments, i would like to make it clear that the commission can accept the first two amendments in principle. the commission must reject amendment no 3 because it contradicts the conventional theory of protocols to fisheries agreements and affects the commission's negotiating powers. it goes without saying, however, that the commission, as negotiator, will ensure that the negotiating directives laid down by the council are respected. the commission must also reject the fourth amendment because it is contrary to the spirit of the council decision of 1997 which calls for a cost-sharing between ship owners and the community. thank you very much for your attention.
thank you, commissioner. the debate is closed. the vote will take place tomorrow at noon. the agenda is exhausted, as i think we all are. ladies and gentlemen, i just have to say good night. the next item is the report (doc. (the sitting was closed at 11.25 p.m.)

fraternal coexistence of the three monotheistic religions, expressed in religious freedom, respect for beliefs and the practice of worship. palestine is therefore the land of the prophets who called all monotheistic religions and be a land of love and peace. yet, despite this divine blessing, the land has been plagued by conflict throughout history. the 20th century, which saw the catastrophe that befell the jewish people in europe, also saw the catastrophe that befell the palestinian people in their own country, when everyone began to seek a solution to the jewish problem in europe in palestinian land. in 1947 the united nations proposed a plan to divide palestine into two states: a jewish state on the larger part of palestine, and an arab state on a smaller part. the jewish state was declared on 15 may 1948, immediately recognized by the western countries, led by the european countries and the united states, which gave it the necessary support, while the palestinian people continued to suffer all forms of suffering, emigration, forced displacement, deprivation of their country, their identity and their state. this situation has largely paved the way for violence and war. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the conflicts and wars in our region have caused destruction, desolation and great human and material losses. throughout the second half of the 20th century, the region experienced many wars and multiple confrontations that spread death and desolation everywhere, reducing the economies of the region to war economies, which hampered development operations in many countries and caused a scientific and cultural lag in others. our palestinian people have been the most affected in the region. it has paid the heaviest price, politically, economically and socially. the great difficulties associated with israel's isolation from its neighbours, the constant state of alert linked to the state of war in the region and the severe suffering of the palestinian people who remained on their own soil, as refugees abroad or in camps, made it necessary to take the initiative in seeking an alternative to war and deadly conflicts. peace has thus become the only option to meet the aspirations of the peoples of the region for stability and development, for living in security and peace. but for this peace to be permanent and comprehensive, it must be just. the peace process began in madrid in 1991. we have participated in this process out of our sincere desire to achieve a just and comprehensive peace in the region in general and at the palestinian-israeli level in particular. this process is based on un security council resolutions 242 and 338, which stipulate that the acquisition of another's territory by force is inadmissible. it is also based on the search for a just solution to the refugee problem and on the principle of territories in exchange for peace. in accepting these resolutions, we have agreed to have only 23% of the territory of historic palestine and this is a major concession, i repeat, a major concession that the political leadership of israel refuses to accept in the final status negotiations, on the pretext of the intransigence and lack of flexibility of the palestinian side. in accordance with these principles, we have embarked on the peace process, motivated by the conviction that a long and bloody chapter must be ended in order to achieve the just peace we so earnestly desire after a long period of hostility and painful and destructive conflict. our priority at that time was to revive long-absent or hidden hopes by preparing the regional political and economic environment and climate for the establishment of regional development and economic cooperation relationships that would allow the flow of investments and projects to our region, which had been exhausted by conflict and bled by the exorbitant cost of wars. the negotiations in washington and, in parallel, those held in oslo, resulted in an agreement on a declaration of principles, the oslo accords. the plo exchanged with the israeli government the mutual recognition documents, the most important step, in my opinion, in the history of the arab-israeli conflict in general, and the palestinian-israeli conflict in particular. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the agreement on the declaration of principles for the transitional period and for the final status negotiations was drawn up on the basis of a definite philosophy and clear political principles, in particular security council resolutions 242 and 338 and their implementation, the territories in exchange for peace and a timetable for the final status negotiations. in addition, we also agreed to complete the steps of a gradual solution which begins with the withdrawal of israeli forces from the west bank and the gaza strip, in parallel with the gradual transfer of civilian and security powers and responsibilities to the palestinian authority. during this stage, presidential and parliamentary elections would be held in the west bank, the gaza strip and the arab city of jerusalem, al-quds. it was assumed that this period would end with the transfer of all the territories of the west bank and the gaza strip to the palestinian authority, except for the issues of the final status negotiations, which are: jerusalem (al-quds), settlements, borders, refugees, relations with other actors, and what was added later, water. this would be accompanied by the progressive creation of a palestinian entity with its own executive, legislative and judicial organs. all of this was to be accomplished in less than five years, by may 4, 1999, and culminate in the creation of an independent palestinian state. we have accepted these agreements and respected their implementation, but unfortunately we have encountered serious difficulties, constant attempts to break the agreements and to abandon what has been agreed and the failure to implement speaker of the knesset. – madam president, members of parliament, abu ala, i am an optimist. i am not the kind of an optimist who, when once asked by somebody "are you an optimist or a pessimist", - mr president, as is not customary, i would like to congratulate the commission on the serious and balanced work it has done because, too often, when we deal with immigration issues, passions, excesses, political motives prevent us from thinking objectively and making progress. the text, by dealing in depth with the question of the right to family life and by defining the precise conditions for its application, makes it possible to have a real debate. far from casting a priori suspicion, as is often done with those who want to live with their spouse and children, the text on the contrary recognises the legitimacy of such a right, even if it is indeed necessary today that this right should also be valid in particular for homosexuals, without neglecting any category, as my colleague has just said, particularly with regard to asylum seekers. the text also acknowledges that there are several types of family in our societies today, including certain forms of cohabitation, and that there is therefore no reason to discriminate against immigrants who would do the same. it thus contributes to giving a true meaning to the word 'integration'. the proposal for a directive, by harmonizing the laws of the member states, will have the advantage of giving legal protection and stability to immigrants and, above all, of preventing them from being subject to national political fluctuations. i would therefore like the commission and parliament to follow this example in their future work. perhaps then we can talk more about equal rights and the often positive contribution of immigration by addressing issues that are essential for integration and the fight against unemployment, precariousness, violence and discrimination to which immigrants may be subject. immigration is not a problem. we should instead decide to talk about the real problems of imbalances between the north and the south, which often lead men and women to flee poverty. it should also be acknowledged that the flows of immigrants to the countries of the union have remained more or less constant for the past two decades. in other words, when states implemented restrictive laws, they didn't decrease the overall number of entries, they simply decreased the number of legal immigrants and increased and manufactured illegal immigrants. this draft directive, based on these values, will therefore not only have positive consequences for immigrants and their families, but will also be a real symbolic force for reception and integration. i would very much like to see the same approach followed in the work that is to follow.
mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the text which has been proposed to us, and indeed the whole of the immigration policy followed by the european institutions, shows a worrying drift. it is true that there was concern that some form of capitalism might somehow import workers by cutting them off from their families of origin with all the risks of uprooting that this might entail, but this situation has now been moved far beyond that. what were only temporary employment contracts - and even in the best of cases - tend to become permanent settlements. what was definitive for one person tends to become definitive for all those who may be around him. first, the immediate family, but also the extended family, and this extended family, we know well that it is large in view of the social structures of the countries of origin, countries in which civil status is sometimes only somewhat limited. and then, from extended family, brothers, cousins, nephews, parents, grandparents, we move on to the polygamous family. the polygamous family - why should it be given priority over family ties - is being replaced by cohabitation and, as mr sylla, the previous speaker, has just suggested, it will soon be replaced by a simple homosexual partnership. that is to say, what are the considerable risks of drifting away from this policy. we're going to end up with what we're seeing right now. it is a genuine, suicidal settlement migration, which is organized by the member states and which is also organized by the european institutions. this is europe's obvious suicide. the only solution worth having is to organise family reunification, but to organise it in the country of origin with the support of the cooperation policy to which these means should be applied. - mr president, after the recent events in dover, where 29 chinese illegal immigrants were suffocated to death, the problem of illegal immigration and the means of responding to it has become a major issue which the european union must urgently address today. this problem calls for us to work on a particularly sensitive subject, namely the elaboration and harmonization of a european immigration policy, which will be one of the major issues of the 21st century. the commission proposal for a directive on the right to family reunification is therefore very timely and i would like to thank and congratulate the commission, which, under the auspices of commissioner vitorino, has drawn up this text. the right to family reunification is an essential element in the realisation of a normal family life, and this has been stated for a long time in article 8 of the european convention on human rights, which states that everyone has the right to respect for his or her family life. but it is also a particularly sensitive issue, given the differences in legislation between the various states, because it can clash with the notions of sovereignty, but this is the particular challenge that is being put to the european parliament to overcome these differences. the draft directive on which we are asked to give our opinion today is, in my view, a very important text which must receive the firm and definitive support of the european parliament, since it offers real prospects for legal immigration, of which i would remind you that family immigration constitutes the majority. as has been said, this directive is the first example of this construction in the spirit of the treaty of amsterdam and the tampere european council, which is why it is so important. i would also like to point out that the modern world offers many advantages, but also risks of significant exclusion of certain categories of people, including foreigners, and that it is our duty as european democrats to be particularly attentive to this. the directive proposed by the commission allows, under very satisfactory conditions, but with the necessary guarantees - and all the necessary guarantees - to take a big step forward. there has never been any question, for example, as i have just heard, of allowing polygamous family reunification. that's completely inaccurate. it should be recalled that this is the first important to remember that the aim is to establish a right to family reunification and to put an end to the concept of family reunification as a privilege. the challenge for us is indeed the building - mr president, i do believe that this draft directive is a step forward. however, the family reunification procedure is still subject to restrictive conditions. i think we should insist that it is unemployment and precariousness that should be prohibited, not the right of an immigrant to live with his or her family when he or she cannot prove sufficient resources or adequate housing. while for the national population society is changing slowly, but it is changing nonetheless, as in the case of the pacs vote in france, for immigrants the concept of the family remains rigid. the legislation in force provides for the abolition of the right of residence in the event of a breakdown in the marriage, effectively prohibiting divorce, and, as mentioned earlier, homosexual couples are still not recognised. under the pretext of combating polygamy, second wives or concubines and their children are condemned to live in hiding and to a greater dependence. the family reunification must therefore be freed from the archaism which still exists and which is the result of a forced control of immigration. but in conclusion i would say that fortunately mr watson's report is a real step forward from the work done in committee on mrs klamt's original report. i must say that when i hear mr gollnisch's racist, reactionary and unacceptable remarks, i feel the need to vote for this report, because it is a matter of dignity.
the rapporteur. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking all those who have contributed their thoughts to the debate. before i go into the explanation of my report, i would like to begin with a question that has been haunting me ever since. i think that is the heart of the problem in my report and will determine the direction of our vote. the question is: what does european citizenship really mean ? is this merely a phrase to sell europe, or do we really want to put a substance under the word? today, for the majority of europeans, european citizenship is still a meaningless concept. if we are to make europe more than a vast free trade area, we must act to make it more than a concept and to make it part of the daily lives of the inhabitants of europe. i would like to put our debate in that perspective. the directives under consideration concern community nationals, but adjustments are necessary for third country nationals. the report aims to take stock of the situation regarding the free movement of persons and their right to reside in the union. from the point of view of the treaties, i am in the double frame of article 14 on the free movement of persons and articles 17 and 18 on european citizenship. the member states have made enormous progress in the free movement of goods, services and capital, but it is clear that we are still a long way from achieving this for people. a brief history and content of the directives: the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to grant exemptions from the general rules on freedom of movement for workers. in june 1990 the council adopted three commission proposals for directives to extend this right to all nationals of the member states, even if they are not engaged in an economic activity. i shall merely recall the broad lines of these directives. for pensioners and other inactive persons, the right of residence is open to those who have health insurance and sufficient resources. for students, the conditions are enrolment in an approved institution and health insurance. in both cases, the spouse and dependent children may accompany the holder and possibly work. the transposition of these directives has been doubly problematic. firstly, the member states have transposed these directives very late. on the other hand, almost all the member states have adopted a poor transposition of these directives. the commission has had to initiate 14 infringement procedures. the commission notes that 'the incorrect transposition of directives has resulted in the deprivation of certain rights of eu citizens or unjustified administrative difficulties'. let's make a practical assessment of the situation. this right to freedom of movement and residence, which is confirmed in the maastricht treaty, is being violated on economic grounds. the concept of sufficient resources is misinterpreted by the administrations. what income should be taken into account when judging resources? what kind of proof ? how to report a changing financial situation which may depend on the support provided by the spouse. due to lengthy and difficult recognition procedures, it is often necessary to take out a second health insurance in the host country. when you are not in paid employment, it is difficult to obtain a right of residence, and the precariousness of the residence permit is added to the instability of the employment situation. as regards special measures justified on grounds of public policy, the commission notes that many misinterpretations, such as criminal convictions, justify systematic removal and expulsion. finally, administrative procedures are too long - more than six months - and remain costly when frequent renewal is required: often a validity period of two years instead of the normal five. to overcome these problems, i present the main measures recommended. our first proposal is to ask the commission to prepare a framework directive which would take a position on the basis of the fundamental right to move and reside freely in order to organise it rather than starting from a categorical approach which necessarily leaves room for ambiguities. afterwards, it will always be possible to put in place a whole range of specific measures to help citizens according to their own situation. this revision of the existing directives must dissociate the fundamental right to move and reside from any economic considerations. these measures must be accompanied by a real simplification of administrative procedures and the free provision of documents. a transitional measure to the introduction of these arrangements may be the introduction of a one-year residence card for all applicants. the harmonization of social protection and pension systems is essential. finally, as regards special measures justified by the notions of public order, we can only appeal to the states to restrict their interpretation and to put an end to double punishment and to protect certain categories from expulsion. finally, a few points. rights must be attached to the person and move with him. third country nationals living and working legally in a member state must enjoy the same rights as european citizens. it is a pity that the council has not followed up this proposal on citizenship and residence. in conclusion, i hope i have convinced you to support a strongly citizen-led approach to freedom of movement and residence, which is a fundamental issue for the creation of a european conscience. at a time when discussions on the future of europe are in full swing and we are considering a future charter of fundamental rights, we must support any project for an area of freedom, justice and equality where all residents and citizens who contribute to the construction of europe should have the same rights. finally, goods, capital and services now move freely within the union. perhaps it is time that men acquired the same rights as the products they consume.

in writing. - i had already had the opportunity to speak at the march plenary session on this subject, which was very heated at the time, since the debate on maritime safety after the sinking of the erika was very heated. today, discussions are more discreet, but they are still important. european citizens are deeply concerned about the pollution of the seas and coasts of the member states. the european parliament echoed these legitimate concerns and amended the directive proposed by the european commission on the management of waste from ships in order to hold member states accountable. it suggested, as an alternative to the polluter-pays principle, which can only be seen to be ineffective, the introduction of a system of fees paid by all ships at each passage through a port, whether or not they use waste disposal facilities. the levy would be used to finance 90% of such installations. this system would encourage ships to discharge their operating residues or other waste in ports rather than off-shore. it was obvious that the council would not accept such a proposal. the discussions within the conciliation committee therefore naturally continued. the agreement reached by the negotiators of the european parliament and the council is that all ships calling at a community port make a significant contribution (the commission, in an annexed statement, considers that this means at least 30% of the costs), whether the facilities are used or not. the part of the costs not covered by the fee, if any, will be covered on the basis of the types and quantities of operational waste actually deposited by the ship. in addition, within three years of the implementation of the directive, the commission shall submit an assessment report on the impact of the diversity of cost recovery on the marine environment. in the light of that assessment, it shall, if necessary, submit a proposal to amend this directive by introducing a system providing for the payment by all ships calling at a community port, whether or not they use reception facilities, of an appropriate percentage covering at least one third of the costs of port reception facilities. i am satisfied with the compromise we have reached. this directive is a significant step towards a more effective strategy for the protection of marine areas.
in writing. - we are now at the final stage of the drafting of this proposal for a directive and, although i am not entirely satisfied with the result of the conciliation, i can only approve this compromise, which, it must be admitted, is entirely in the interest of the european parliament, its control and its relative maturity in the legislative process of the european union. the european commission, aware of the untimely nature of uncontrolled discharges at sea, and even of the unacceptable behaviour of certain crews who take advantage of a tragic accident to dump their extra waste with impunity, thus aggravating marine pollution, proposes to concentrate its action on installation in european ports. all ports must be equipped with facilities capable of treating ship's waste and at the same time every ship calling at one of these ports must be made to bear the costs of receiving and treating waste (up to 90% for parliament but, finally, following the compromise with the council, up to at least 30%), whether or not it uses the facilities. this is a first step, the recognition of the polluter pays principle. no, how necessary, but not yet enough. let's not hide our faces. if we are to have a genuine ambition to clean up the oceans and preserve the natural balance for future generations, then we will have to consider more radical measures, particularly in terms of the financial support for these facilities, the need to avoid distortions of competition between ports; in short, we will have to consider the establishment of a genuine public waste disposal service. i can only recommend to parliament that it approve the results of this conciliation.

family reunification which, legally, does not yet exist at this level and which, in our view, should not exist as a right. the host state does not oblige the immigrant to come. this is a decision made by the immigrant himself, and if he is accepted, he does not have to claim as a right to bring others. it should be noted that the explanatory memorandum to the proposal for a directive makes a good reunification, but is no longer valid when it could be used to support european families. the proposal for a directive approved by the watson report does not simply proclaim that this right does not exist. it gives the status of 'grouping' not only to legal immigrants but also to persons enjoying refugee status. furthermore, the beneficiaries of family reunification are not simply the spouse and the legislation of the member state. the directive also adds adult children who "are objectively unable to support themselves" and the ascendants of the parent, spouse or even unmarried partner. we in writing. - as early as 1957, the treaty establishing the european economic community contained provisions to ensure the free movement of workers within the community. various community instruments have helped to make this right a reality. in 1990, two directives (90/364/eec and 90/365/eec) extended the right of residence by defining general principles and rules for workers who have ceased their activity. a third directive (93/96/ec), adopted in 1993, contains specific provisions for students. since 1993 and the maastricht treaty, any national of a member state can move and reside freely within the european union (article 14 of the ec treaty), this right being linked to european citizenship (article 18). the report under discussion today is intended to report on the application of the directives on the right of residence of students, pensioners and others who are not in employment and to examine special measures concerning the movement and residence of union citizens justified on grounds of public policy, public security and public health (directive 64/221/eec). as regards the first aspect, it must be admitted that although the directives in question have been transposed into national legal systems, sometimes with great effort, many obstacles remain which will have to be removed by adopting a range of targeted measures. to mention a problem i am familiar with, that of students, i think it is essential to inform them better about their rights if they wish to continue their studies in another member state. the problem of the recognition of diplomas, which is a crucial issue for certain professions, should also be addressed. as regards the second part, there are many difficulties in the application of directive 64/221/eec. the treaty allows member states to impose restrictions on the free movement of persons on grounds of public policy, public security or public health. the commission notes, however, that the member states interpret these concepts in a totally different and often extensive way. it stresses that they must be applied in accordance with the principle of proportionality and be motivated by a real and sufficiently serious threat affecting a fundamental interest of society. in any event, these concepts must be in accordance with the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms. to overcome these difficulties, it seems necessary to adopt a framework directive organising and guaranteeing the fundamental exercise of the freedom of movement and residence. this will be made possible by a comprehensive revision of existing texts, which would have the effect of putting an end to the inequalities of treatment which currently exist in the various member states. only then will the citizens of the member states be able to become aware of and give substance to the concept of european citizenship, which for many remains an empty shell.
