commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, recent scientific advances in the field of life sciences offer very important prospects for application, but they also raise ethical questions which affect the majority of our fellow citizens. it is becoming increasingly important to anticipate such ethical issues in order to integrate them into a wider dialogue between science and society. in its communication of january 2000, the commission highlighted the fact that a genuine european research area can only be achieved if we also promote a european area of shared ethical values in europe. to this end, the commission intends to take initiatives such as strengthening links between ethics committees in europe and exchanging good practice in ethical evaluation of research projects. therapeutic cloning, or more specifically the use of embryonic stem cells obtained by cloning techniques for therapeutic purposes, is an example of ethical issues raised by rapid scientific advances in the life sciences. this technique of therapeutic cloning is particularly sensitive for obvious cultural, religious or ethical reasons. the report of the british panel, published on 16 august, acknowledges the major interest of research into human embryonic stem cells and their therapeutic applications. the report advocates authorizing research in this area, including the use of cloned embryos using the technique of nuclear replacement, while recommending a clear legal and ethical framework. the publication of this report has generated a great deal of discussion across europe and has opened up a genuine debate at european level, beyond the scientific circles concerned. as president prodi recently announced in a press release, the commission is far from silent and wants an informed debate to continue, in close association with the european parliament. respect for the national identity of the member states has led the treaty on european union to leave the states their prerogatives to legislate on ethical matters. in fact, there is a very wide diversity of legislation or legislative gaps which reflect a very different range of sensitivities in the countries of the union. however, community action in the field of biotechnology research is increasingly based on the most rigorous fundamental ethical principles, while respecting national sensitivities. this is the case with community legislation on the patentability of biotechnological inventions, which is expressly based on respect for the fundamental principles guaranteeing the dignity and integrity of the human person and which reaffirms the principle that the human body, at all stages of its constitution or development, including germ cells, and the mere discovery of one of these elements or products, including the partial sequencing of a human gene, are not patentable. this legislation excludes from patentability reproductive human cloning and the commercialisation of embryos or parts of the human body. while regulating the conditions under which an invention based on biological material may be protected by patent, the directive does not, however, aim to fix the conditions under which research itself may be carried out. as far as research is concerned, the european commission has been supporting the biomedical field for many years. the fifth framework programme, adopted under the co-decision procedure, respects the fundamental ethical principles and is based on the opinion delivered by the european ethics group before the adoption of the framework programme. research on cloning techniques for reproductive or therapeutic purposes is thus explicitly excluded. similarly, animal cloning is limited to ethically justified purposes, provided that the operations are carried out without causing unnecessary suffering. the framework programme, which also has an anticipatory role, is currently supporting bioethical studies on the potential risks and benefits of cloning technologies. in addition, complementary approaches to therapeutic cloning are under way to develop new cell therapy techniques, including through very large-scale work using adult stem cells. such research shall be conducted in compliance with fundamental ethical principles and applicable national rules. i would like to emphasise that ethical aspects are systematically taken into account when proposals are evaluated and that a thorough ethical review is carried out for proposals that touch on more sensitive ethical issues. the commission is looking forward with great interest to the opinion on the use of human stem cells to be given by the european ethics group in november this year. this group has demonstrated its independence and its great competence in highly sensitive and highly technical matters. this opinion, like the previous ones, will of course be very important for the framework of community research policy. more generally, the high-level panel on life sciences, recently set up on my initiative, should help us to build a genuine dialogue between the research world and society in the field of life sciences. the discussion forum which will be organized by this group on 6 and 7 november in brussels, to which i of course invite all interested members of your assembly, is an important step in the establishment of this dialogue. so, although it is not its intention to legislate or harmonize in the field of ethics, the commission wants to contribute to the debate, while respecting the diversity of our cultures and our sensitivities in europe. this is also one of the objectives of the european research area which is being built up step by step.

- the report contains some positive elements, in particular the assertion of the binding nature of the measures envisaged to protect water quality. but by granting time limits, including a 20-year time limit, for the prohibition of the discharge of dangerous substances, the report is destroying its own resolution. this is equivalent to 20 years of permission for companies to dump their toxic substances. in addition, it is not clear that the polluting companies are the ones who have to pay for the damage they have caused. as for water pricing, the only decision that would be in the public interest would be to prohibit any private profit from the supply and distribution of water. but this is not even mentioned in this report, which, by putting ireland on the back burner because of its practice of public financing of water, is on the contrary seeking to accentuate the commercial nature of this vital substance. therefore, we abstained.
in writing. - the water framework directive is finally adopted and i can only rejoice. since 1997, the european parliament has been calling for an end to the fragmentation of water legislation in europe. after almost four years, this rationalization work has finally been completed. the conciliation between parliament and the council of ministers, the final stage of the legislative procedure, has led to a compromise which i consider to be balanced and satisfactory. the discussions were difficult, but i am glad that the council finally agreed to make the main objectives of this new regulation binding. our parliament could not have supported a purely declaratory text. the epp-ed group has always taken an ambitious and realistic position. it was essential to me that this new framework text should guarantee an improvement in the quality of european waters for the future and for future generations. water management in europe will now be based on the water district. this entity, which goes beyond the administrative framework of the member states, takes account of the hydrological realities of the european territory. the objective is to phase out discharges of hazardous substances no later than 20 years after they have been identified. this is a realistic compromise between mrs lienemann's initial position, which was in favour of zero discharge to water, and the council's position, which was against any binding objective. a list of so-called 'priority' substances will shortly be submitted to the european parliament. this will be a crucial step, and i hope that our parliament will follow the same line as today. in line with the polluter pays principle, member states will have to integrate environmental costs into the price of water. that is real progress. water is a fragile natural resource of inestimable importance. the issues involved are as much public health and a long-term supply of clean drinking water as biodiversity and the preservation of landscapes. for all these reasons i voted in favour of this text. i regret, however, that the article on the possibility for member states to carry out water transfers could not be maintained as we had voted on at second reading. this type of project is in keeping with the principle of regional cohesion and solidarity which we have always defended. in this spirit, it should benefit from the european union's generous support in promoting transeuropean networks and regional policy.
in writing. - all proposals for improving the environment in europe are welcome. attempting to bring together the disparate water policies in a framework directive is a considerable challenge. the binding commitment of the european union, through its member states, to eliminate the discharge of dangerous products into water within 20 years is a sure step forward, even if for some chemicals 3 years is enough. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a natural disaster is a good one. in this case, water management and the water savings that can be made will have to be considered first before proposing gigantic projects to transfer water from one basin to another. the european union must now also consider the price of water. it is unacceptable that multinational companies alone set the price of water, under the pretext that they provide a technical water management service. this directive is a step in the right direction, but it will require more precise rules to reduce pollution of upstream water.
in writing. - i have already had the opportunity to speak on several occasions on this complex issue, where not only important economic interests but also and above all environmental protection are at stake. the proposal for a directive on end-of-life vehicles, presented in 1997, aims to prevent the creation of waste from vehicles and to promote the reuse, recycling and recovery of vehicles and their components in order to reduce the amount of waste from end-of-life vehicles that is landfilled or incinerated without energy recovery. the european commission's strategy is based on measures such as increasing the percentage of recyclable components, providing a sufficient number of collection centres for used vehicles, implementing a set of objectives on the reuse and recovery of used vehicles, controlling the use of certain heavy metals at the stage of vehicle manufacture and ensuring that the costs of disposing of used vehicles are not borne by the last owner. the negotiations have been hampered on several points. the difficulties have been concentrated on producer responsibility and the disposal of heavy metals. after several hours of conciliation, the negotiators reached an agreement. as regards the responsibility of producers, the directive provided that the return of the used vehicle should be possible at no cost to the last owner and that the producer should bear a significant part of the costs of the treatment of old vehicles. the compromise reached provides that for new vehicles, i.e. those placed on the market from 1 july 2002, producer liability will come into effect from 1 july 2002. for the existing car fleet, i.e. vehicles put on the market before 1 july 2002, the producer's liability will be deferred from 2006 to 2007. the text of the directive also states that member states have the possibility of implementing the relevant provisions before the dates set. as regards heavy metals, the council and parliament agreed that all vehicles marketed after 1 july 2003 should no longer contain heavy metals such as cadmium, lead and hexavalent chromium. the two delegations agreed on the derogations set out in annex ii to the directive. i am also pleased that the european parliament's request to exclude collector vehicles from the scope of the directive has been welcomed.
in writing. - the compromise reached in the conciliation procedure, the final legislative phase, is the result of laborious negotiations between the european parliament and the council of ministers. i am not satisfied with it, but i think it is a first step, but in some respects it is a step in the right direction. while we should welcome the numerical targets that have been set (85 per cent of the weight of vehicles produced after 1980 will have to be recycled, reused or recovered by 2006, and 95 per cent by 2015), i nevertheless regret the hypocrisy of certain provisions advocated by the pse and supported by the socialist and social democratic governments. the council of ministers has remained adamant about the fact that the owner is not charged for the return of his vehicle after it has been taken out of use. this is a demagogic arrangement. it is based on a good feeling for consumers, but it is totally unrealistic. the directive provides that the cost of treatment will be borne entirely by the producers. the latter will have no choice but to pass on at least part of these costs to the purchase of new vehicles. so far from encouraging the purchase of new generation vehicles that are less polluting, this measure is a disguised bonus to those who own the most polluting older cars. the council of ministers finally agreed with the wishes of the meps, who had been calling since the first reading for vintage vehicles to be expressly excluded from the scope of this directive. the amendment which i tabled and defended was in fact incorporated in its entirety in the final text. more generally, this directive lacks ambition. for example, it completely ignores the problem of abandoned car bodies that disfigure the landscape. despite the polluter-pays principle, the costs of removing them remain the responsibility of all taxpayers. it is regrettable that neither this directive nor the directive on the landfill of waste has addressed this problem, which has disastrous consequences for the environment in large parts of europe.

in writing. - once again, communication is seen as a commodity from which to extract maximum benefits. we object to this logic, which ignores the question of the social needs of the population. the ever-increasing introduction of private capital into public operators which have become multinational companies is leading these operators to wage a ruthless economic war. it involves a division of world markets that favours the most profitable areas and introduces unequal pricing, not to mention job losses and the precariousness of hundreds of thousands of employees. this requires that national and european political authorities impose public service obligations on all operators, regardless of their origin, for example: - for fixed telecommunications: a reduction in subscriptions and local communications, which account for 83% of the average bill of private individuals; - for mobile communications: in addition to the reduction in rates, a total coverage of the territory, even if satellite links are used in places that are difficult to reach; - for fast internet access: in addition to a radical reduction in rates, a timetable for the complete coverage of the territory. in this era of undignified record profits, this is how we make communication a fundamental right that must be respected by a quality public service.
in writing. - therapeutic cloning is the creation of an embryo by cloning and then destroying it in order to extract cells for medical research and, later, perhaps for the cure of certain incurable diseases. so we can't say that the intention is bad. but the method is highly questionable for at least two reasons: first, it creates a life (either by using a surplus embryo, which was originally intended to give birth to a new human being, or by using a cloned embryo), and then it destroys it to save another. is it right to create a class of sub-beings who can be manipulated at will? i obviously don't think so. secondly, while everyone agrees that human cloning in general is wrong, some would like to introduce a distinction between 'reproductive cloning' (aimed at reproducing the whole of a being), which would be prohibited, and 'therapeutic cloning', which could be allowed under supervision, within certain limits, and provided that it is not commercially available. but this distinction is artificial, since it is based on the intention of cloning, whereas the act itself is identical in both cases: therapeutic cloning is also based, at its core, on the reproduction of embryos by cloning. all cloning is by definition reproductive. the cloning of embryos for research purposes, or even the mere use of surplus embryos for such purposes, would push us over an invisible threshold beyond which it would be permissible to exploit human life. we would enter another society, contrary to our values. one way out of this dilemma would be to accelerate research into the possibility of obtaining stem cells from adult organs that are differentiable for therapeutic purposes, as requested in the resolution tabled by our colleagues elisabeth montfort and nicole thomas-mauro. this operation would be acceptable, since it is similar to organ donation. such a perspective allows us to see that our current questions may be related only to a transitional stage of research. at least we hope so. unfortunately, the working group, which calls itself the convention and is preparing a first draft of a charter of fundamental rights of the european union, is taking the wrong direction on this point. article 3 of the draft, as it stands, merely prohibits 'the reproductive cloning of human beings', i.e. it gives full expression to the false distinction we denounce. i tabled an amendment on this point, together with a few members, but although our proposal is very moderate, it has not been accepted so far. indeed, no matter how one looks at the charter, one cannot find a single quality in it.
in writing. - at all times, mankind has had to evaluate how to orient scientific developments in accordance with its ethical and social choices. the issue is all the more delicate when it comes to humans and the genetic basis of life. so extreme caution is needed, not to fall into obscurantism. in the present state of our knowledge and ethical debate, and in view of the unacceptable authorization given by the british government for human cloning, the first thing to be achieved is a total and absolute moratorium on all human cloning experiments. the second is to define, after consulting the european ethics council, a clear guideline guaranteeing human dignity. as the texts stand, i do not agree with any of the resolutions tabled by the groups. the socialist group is not demanding enough for an immediate halt to all human cloning. the epp group seems to have finally settled some delicate debates such as the distinction between reproductive and other cloning. i think that the analysis of the european ethics committee on this point would be useful in clarifying the arbitration. the urgency of the situation would have required an effective attitude: - immediate and absolute moratorium; - thorough reflection and a broad debate on the substance before a directive setting out the rule adopted. that is not the vote that was taken today. i shall therefore abstain on these motions for resolutions.
in writing. - there are some subjects on which political differences should remain silent, not to give the appearance of a possible consensus, but because they are imposed on all in a horizontal way. and if there were only one, it would be the defence and promotion of human life and dignity. scientific research has made tremendous progress in recent decades and has brought hope to those suffering from illness or disability and to their families. however, at the same time, some of this research and the scientists who are doing it seem to have lost what i would call a fair and healthy scale of values. and it is then the duty of those responsible for the common good, particularly moral and political, to correct certain deviations. the uk and us decisions allow cloning on the one hand and the use of so-called "overcrowded" and "non-parental" embryos on the other, both for therapeutic purposes. the problems raised here are many but closely interrelated. there are not two kinds of cloning, reproductive and therapeutic: the creation of human embryos with the same genetic constitution as another human being remains prohibited, whatever the purpose. no human law can ever deny the fact that the embryo is the beginning of life without being criminal. thus, the destruction of an embryo is in any case unjustifiable, even for the treatment of a sick person; how could we decently justify destroying one life to heal another? similarly, and more generally, life is an indivisible whole, present from conception and hence no longer conditioned by any human will. does the recognition of life depend on a "parenting project"? certainly, before conception, the prospective parents have to think, as responsible persons, about the coming of a child; but once it is conceived, it is present and any manipulation of it, and even more so the programming of its disappearance, for whatever reasons, constitute violations of its fundamental rights, and in the worst cases crimes. it was good that our parliament made a clear statement on these deviations and thus made the choice of life, against the wishes of some of its members.
in writing. - i welcome the commission communication which stresses that the environmental impact of air transport is increasing rapidly at local, regional and global levels. it is clear that this trend cannot be allowed to continue and that urgent action is needed to reverse it. the preservation of the environment, the quality of life and the health of europeans are at stake. the commission's limits. there are also too few concrete measures to make aviation more environmentally friendly. it is therefore essential to set targets and to meet deadlines to allow the aviation industry, airlines and users to adapt to the legislative measures in a timely manner. this is what the european parliament has been doing. the report addresses several problems arising from air transport. it deals with the noise problem in particular. this problem is of growing concern to european citizens. according to a study carried out under the eu's fifth environment action programme, 80 million people in europe are exposed to noise levels that scientists consider intolerable, while another 170 million people are exposed to disturbing noise levels. recent studies also show a link between aircraft noise and sleep disturbances, health and learning capacity. people living near airports are particularly affected by the noise of aircraft at night. the oaci has initiated a process of reviewing noise levels. the european union must support this process. the commission will also have to implement additional measures if necessary if the icao does not reach a satisfactory agreement. aircraft noise can be reduced in two ways: at the source, through stricter certification standards, through phasing-out programmes for non-compliant aircraft, and through land-use planning measures at airports. there is also the problem of gas emissions. it is therefore accepted that air transport emissions contribute about 3.5% to global warming caused by human activity. these emissions are projected to increase by 3% per year over the period 1992 to 2015. it is therefore both urgent and essential to take initiatives to reduce aircraft emissions. the list of nuisances caused by aviation is long. this alarming fact should lead us to take immediate action. this requires that the member states give the commission a clear negotiating mandate so that it can pursue the environmental and transport policy objectives vigorously at the 33rd session of the icao assembly in 2001.

commission. – the commission has been following the political debate on the temelín nuclear power plant with great attention. it has repeatedly stressed the importance of candidate countries adhering to a high level of nuclear safety in line with relevant council resolutions. the commission is actively participating in the deliberations of the council aimed at assessing and ensuring a high level of nuclear safety in candidate countries as a key requirement for accession to the european union. the responsibility for licensing nuclear installations lies with the czech nuclear regulatory authority. the commission has cooperated with the czech authorities in order to reinforce the authority's capacities. the czech authorities have ensured that the operating licence for unit 1 of the temelín nuclear power plant will not be issued until all outstanding problems are solved to the satisfaction of the nuclear regulatory authority. according to current czech legislation, an environmental impact assessment is required before the operating licence is issued. the commission expects this provision to be enforced by the czech authorities. mr adams asks whether the czechs took account of the iaea's inspections and views. the answer is ‘yes’. the iaea has reviewed the modifications made to the safety systems by the czechs following the iaea's programmes. the iaea concluded that the issues were properly addressed by the czechs. that is the information i am able to supply on this subject.

- mr president, as if it were a chronic and seasonal disease, the summer of 2000 will have been further affected by the ravages of the fire, whose wounds for our country and our continent extend over thousands of hectares, including some cemeteries for the firefighters and the residents who were tragically killed. this evil has criminal origins: it is the fault of irresponsible arsonists, who should be given dissuasive penalties, or of unscrupulous developers, ready to do anything to seize areas where construction is prohibited, for whom the panoply of repressive legal instruments must be a nightmare. but this problem also has its own causes: on the one hand, the lack of a record of economic activities, such as agro-pastoral farming in corsica, for example, or the lack of real approaches, based on geographical databases, to the development of rural areas that enhance natural resources and reduce the spread of fires. finally, and most importantly, the lack of real environmental education that goes far beyond the necessary prevention and awareness campaigns. so this summer pandemic is curable, mr. president. it is imperative to rebalance the orientations of certain land-use policies, such as that of livestock farming in corsica, and to break down the allocations of premiums according to the economic and preventive contexts. these upstream measures do not replace the necessary downstream investments in adequate firefighting equipment in sufficient numbers to be deployed in all countries of the union located in the risk areas. the citizens concerned are counting on the commission to take concrete action.
commission. – the commission deeply regrets the loss of human life as well as the ecological and economic damage caused by the recent forest fires in europe. the principle of subsidiarity has been mentioned in this debate. we have to avoid raising too many expectations and overloading the commission with tasks. we must be careful not to promise things we cannot deliver. frankly, there has been enough of that in the past. we should be careful, when entering into discussions such as this, not to automatically assume that the commission will solve the problem. we can and should do something, but i wanted to make that cautionary remark. to get to the core of this discussion, the question of an emergency aid budget line, the commission is considering proposing a legal basis for such a line at the moment. however, the commission might consider financial support for the restoration of the forestry production potential on the basis of the rural development regulation, no 1257/1999. according to the greek authorities, the financial contributions from the agricultural funds are not sufficient for a substantial contribution to be made to the restoration work. the commission therefore invites the greek authorities to present proposals for the amendment of the development programme so that the necessary appropriations can be considered. i should like to draw your attention to ec regulation no 2158/1992, under which preventive action in relation to forest fires may be financed. each member state should verify that all the necessary steps have been taken to reduce the risk of fires to a minimum. new commission initiatives are already in effect, or will shortly become effective. a proposal for a council decision establishing a community mechanism for the coordination of emergency civil protection action will be considered by the college in the near future. this will aim to improve the mutual assistance between member states. it will also have an important side effect in that it will help third countries to manage unexpected emergencies or disasters they would not be able to handle by themselves. through this coordination mechanism member states will be invited to identify groups which can intervene at short notice at the scene. the commission recently initiated a satellite-based project to improve information on operational fire fighting centres in the mediterranean region, with the aim of determining the levels of risk from day to day. we will consider whether this could lead to a system for early detection of forest fires. the commission is also encouraging member states to reinforce their intervention capacities. the regional fund and the cohesion fund have already contributed substantially in the period 1994-99. the national authorities should provide for the necessary financial resources to consolidate this action for the period 2000-06. in general, the decision on the acquisition of such fire-fighting equipment will remain the responsibility of the member states. self-tuition workshops on fighting forest fires are also planned. however the commission does not have enough resources to extend its activities beyond that. the structural funds can be used for restoration after natural disasters and advantage has been taken of this possibility in recent years.

- the agenda calls for the commission's statement on the measures to be taken in response to the oil crisis and the increase in oil prices.
- mr president, madam vice-president of the commission, i have the impression that this so-called oil crisis is indicative of several structural problems on which the union and the fifteen should reflect without blinders and without taboos. the first of these problems concerns our relationship with the south, in this case the producing countries. at the beginning of last year, was europe concerned about the catastrophic consequences for the economy and the people of some of them of a barrel of oil under $10? we heard good news, but it was just as worrying as a $34 barrel. we need to establish a real long-term partnership between them and us. and then, you have to look at all the other causes of the current situation, speculation, the shortage of stocks in the united states, and the fall of the euro. the second problem that this crisis reveals, in my view, is the lack of coherence in our policy choices within the union. today we are talking about giving priority to rail over road and about railroading. this is fundamental. it is a genuine choice of society, an act of ecological responsibility in the strongest sense of the word. but how long has it been doing the exact opposite, pushing road transport against rail? europe is so unprepared for this change that today we still have to change locomotives between france and italy, because the electric currents of the two countries are not compatible. the third fundamental problem that this crisis has dramatically illustrated is the extreme difficulty many european leaders have in gauging the rising demands of our societies. they did not see or did not want to see the serious problems that this increase in fuel caused to people who were forced to use their cars or to use domestic fuel. our citizens do not accept the burden of this economic shock and they are protesting against the leniency of the states towards the oil companies, even though they are showing insolent profits. the pressure will grow stronger for a lighter tax on fuel and a corresponding taxation of company profits. the majority of my group is of the opinion that the fifteen should undertake radical measures on the ecological front, with the effective promotion of rail, while at the same time responding, in the present context, to this legitimate social expectation. in doing so, mr president, they would also be doing a service to europe, which i believe is in great need of it at the moment.
mr president, there are reasons for the excessive rise in oil prices, but it is to be feared that europe is not taking this into account because it has a great responsibility. the first of these is the increase in producer prices due to the carefully organized oligopoly of the producing countries. the shortage of supply is aggravated by the iraqi blockade, the immoral and unjust pursuit of which may be in line with the interests of american oil tankers, but contrary to those of europe. the second reason is the depreciation of the euro, and therefore of all the european currencies that are part of it. it was $1.18 when it was created. it's down to $0.85. we promised a strong currency. we lied and the bill went up by that much. the third reason is the excessive, even insane, taxation by the states, and this socialising policy has been pursued, if not initiated, by the conservative governments. it is maintained under pressure from environmental groups, hostile to the car, because the car is individual freedom. it is this taxation that multiplies by a coefficient of 3, 4 or 5 the increase in producer prices. the alignment of our foreign policy with that of the united states, the monetary depreciation of the euro, and the increased taxation under pressure from the environmental movements are the three causes of the increase, which we deplore but for which our institutions bear a very heavy responsibility.
- mr president, madam commissioner, in the last fortnight we have been experiencing a real 'europe-wide' transport crisis: shortages of petrol, roadblocks, social protests, paralysed governments. it was like 1973 after the first oil shock. this is not to mention the explosion of the barrel of crude oil and the free fall of the euro, despite the past oracles of the so-called european experts. this crisis, though largely predictable, is as much the responsibility of the oil producers as of the government. many different solutions have been proposed, as the situations and reasons for them vary from one country to another. these solutions are often obvious or rational, sometimes ideological, such as vehicle bridging or eco-taxation, but none of them is the panacea - as you have pointed out - and will not solve the situation by itself. it should be remembered that the relevance of the fuel question is based mainly on currency and taxation, but also has an impact on land use planning. the crisis is affecting both professionals and private individuals, particularly in rural areas where the car is too often the only means of communication and transport. this situation is the result of the gradual disengagement of public services, not compensated by private providers, far too concerned with the search for maximum profitability. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. in conclusion, we want the tax on fuel to be less severe, because it is too onerous for our fellow citizens, individuals or professionals, but there are complementary avenues open to our states. the union must leave them free to choose their policy independently and with relevance. this is the case for energy savings, complementary renewable energy sources, the rebalancing of freight to rail and river transport, the development of public transport and the opening up of rural areas.

mr president, i would like to ask the commissioner whether he is aware that the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. annex 1 to the treaty sets out the list of products which are to be covered by a common organization of the market under the cap. these are basic agricultural products and products resulting from primary processing. products not included in annex 1 are those of secondary processing. the problem which is now coming to the fore and which the community will have to face from this year onwards is that the amount of refunds is not sufficient in relation to needs, because of the consolidations agreed by the community in the framework of the marrakesh agreements. in seeking solutions to this difficult problem, which is a major challenge for our producers and processors of agricultural products, the commission has not shown any great imagination. apart from the mere removal of certain products from the list of products eligible for refunds, which poses difficult management problems for the sectors concerned, we are presented with a single solution, as usual: that of extending the inward processing arrangements which allow the import of agricultural raw materials at the world price, provided that the processed products in which they are incorporated are re-exported. no alternative to rpa has been seriously considered. the prospects opened up by certain member states, such as germany or austria, were immediately closed, any alternative proposal being declared a priori incompatible with the constraints in which we have enclosed ourselves in gatt. in these circumstances, we must of course give priority to the importance of the sector concerned and the weight of exports. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. for these products, additional access to rpa is at least a partial solution, which can be used quickly and which makes it possible, in the short term, to guarantee the competitiveness of products not included in annex 1, in the absence of alternative proposals. our committee on agriculture and rural development considered that the detailed rules for applying the additional rpa should be determined in such a way as to allow companies to make use of it effectively within the limits of the possibilities provided for in the forecast balance sheets, so as to be able to maintain a sufficient amount of refunds for companies that cannot make use of it, either to avoid gmos, or because of the lack of raw materials available on the world market, or because of the lack of staff or appropriate infrastructure. however, rpa has a number of disadvantages and risks. first, there is a problem of principle: the rpa is in itself a circumvention of the community preference. the european agri-food industry must be encouraged to give preference to community raw materials. this means that the rpa, despite the extension proposed to us, must absolutely remain a residual scheme, not become a structural instrument, remain a solution of last resort, to be implemented only when there is a real deficit of refunds. we therefore propose a series of amendments which must be taken as a whole and which are intended to reinforce the residual nature of the rpa. we believe that any extension of the rpa must be subject to very strict supervision and monitoring. that is why we are in favour of a quota system. that is why we are also proposing that the commission submits a precise interim report to the european parliament after the first year of implementation of the new system, including an update for each of the cmos concerned. we will thus have a monitoring and control instrument which will enable us to ensure that the opening of the rpa remains limited, that it covers only the quantities really needed, that it does not have a negative effect on our raw material producers and that it does not concentrate on certain coms, at the risk of upsetting them. a second disadvantage of the rpa is its particular complexity and the burden of procedures, especially on smes. the commission will therefore have to promote access for these farmers to refunds, which are less burdensome to manage, and, in this context, exempt them from the presentation of certificates up to a ceiling of eur 50 000 per year, which can be adjusted. it should be remembered that refunds, particularly for processed food products, are far from being reserved for large companies. they play a vital role for smes. these are the building blocks of a genuine monitoring mechanism, which we believe is essential to ensure that the opening of the rpa is working well in accordance with the objectives for which we accept it. however, in the long run, the question which we must deal with today in an urgent way will only be solved in a lasting way if the community negotiators, at the next wto meetings, receive clear instructions to ensure that the interests of our non-annex 1 products are adequately taken into account and that the close links established by our processors with our producers of agricultural raw materials and their territories can be preserved and developed.

anti-semitism in germany in 1999. the renowned german newspaper der tagesspiegel lists 93 murders with a right-wing extremist background in the last ten years. the development in east germany is of course particularly bitter for me, who come from the gdr. there are undoubtedly reasons for this which lie in the society of the gdr, in particular the repercussions of authoritarian structures and the weakness of civil society in eastern germany. but there are many other reasons for the development of the last ten years: the decoupling of economic and social development in east germany from that in the old länder, the disregard for east german life histories and experiences, the lack of consistency in dealing with the history and present of right-wing extremism. infrastructure, organisation and money are being brought massively into the new länder by long-standing far-right parties and organisations from the old federal states. the social polarization of society, the withdrawal of the state from social and educational institutions and the increasingly fierce competition in the labour market are fertile ground for racism and xenophobia. the sense of helplessness that many people feel in the face of the socially and culturally destructive race to globalization, the repression of politics and democracy against corporate profit interests, offers good starting points for the far right. a rhetorical policy based on nationalism, making immigration and immigration the starting point of election campaigns, paves the way for racism and xenophobia. the restrictive asylum and immigration policies of the european union, the lack of transparency and the involvement of citizens in decision-making do the rest. but we need firstly, a consistent stigmatisation of racist and right-wing extremist views; secondly, a change in the asylum and immigration policies of the eu and its member states towards acceptance and integration of immigrants and asylum seekers; thirdly, active employment and social policies, especially for young people; fourthly, a humanistic education policy that teaches tolerance and considers cultural and ethnic diversity as an enrichment.
the council. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to answer mrs ludford's question point by point. the council and the presidency attach great importance to the european regional conference 'all different, all equal' to be held in strasbourg from 11 to 13 october 2000 in preparation for the world conference against racism in 2001. in this context, the presidency is making every effort to ensure the greatest possible cooperation and coordination between the member states of the union in preparation for the strasbourg conference. there is already very active coordination between the member states, in the margins of the many preparatory meetings that have taken place. at this stage the council does not intend to present a common position to the 15 member states at the strasbourg regional conference under article 34 (2). however, coordination - and i think this is important - between the member states of the european union will continue to prevent them from expressing differing views on the various issues that are being discussed. on the other hand, the council intends - and i stress this point - to present a common position at the world conference to be held in south africa next year, and work to develop this common position has already begun. in coordinating their positions for the regional conference, the member states will of course take account of the very useful recommendations contained in the commission staff document of 17 april. as regards the means to be used, in order to ensure greater synergy, the work carried out in this field by the united nations high commissioner for human rights, the council of europe's european commission against racism and intolerance and the european observatory on racism and xenophobia are also important. i would remind mrs ludford that the council adopted a decision on 21 december 1998 on the conclusion of an agreement to establish closer cooperation between the european observatory and the council of europe, and that the cooperation between these two institutions has in fact been quite fruitful. in addition, work is continuing to examine how to establish closer links between the high commission and the european observatory on racism and xenophobia. i would also like to recall that on 21 june 2000 the council directive on the implementation of the principle of equal treatment between persons irrespective of race or ethnic origin was adopted. because of the duplication of work thus created between this directive and the proposal for a directive establishing a general framework for equal treatment in employment and occupation - the discrimination directive - racial discrimination has been removed from the scope of the latter, but i would remind you that the scope of this proposal for a directive is much narrower than that of the previously adopted directive, which covers not only the employment and labour sectors but also social protection, social benefits, education, as well as access to goods and services and the provision of goods and services. as regards the community action programme to combat discrimination, work is well under way in the council - i can confirm this today - if the european parliament delivers its opinion at its first part-session in october, the council will be able to adopt a political agreement on this text on 17 october, a text which could be adopted before the end of the french presidency, so that the programme can be launched as planned on 1 january 2001. finally, as regards the 1996 joint action on action against racism and xenophobia, the council examined in may 1998 a report on the member states' compliance with their obligations under the joint action and decided that the implementation of this joint action should be reviewed in 2000. i would point out that the presidency is currently making arrangements to enable this review to take place, which will help the council to assess the overall effectiveness of the joint action and to see whether it is appropriate to strengthen certain elements of it. i hope, madam member, that i have answered your question as completely as possible.
the commission. your honor, in ancient greek mythology, there were two monsters, scylla and charybdis, who killed and swallowed people. the two monsters in europe today are terrorism and racism. and unfortunately, those are the issues we're discussing today. ulysses was the one who defeated the two monsters, and it took intelligence, persistence and courage. the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to play its full part in the development of the union. 60 years ago we lived through one of the most brutal wars in human history. the idea of the european union was based on creating institutions to ensure peace. the years that have passed have made important strides. the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe in the past, and it is a great help to the people of europe today. the fight against racism at european level has many dimensions. the first is the basic policies of the european union, which are concerned with deepening its policies, i.e. strengthening social europe and reducing differences, and its enlargement policy, i.e. supporting countries in difficulty. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. since 1996, the council has adopted a joint action on judicial cooperation between countries on matters of racism. we shall soon be moving to a second phase of this joint action. the amsterdam treaty is indeed an important weapon in europe's institutional arsenal. articles 29 and 13 allow for very specific policies. article 29 makes it possible to combat racism and xenophobia through cooperation in the area of justice and security, in order to create this single area of freedom and justice. the policy covering measures in this area was evaluated and decided at tampere, and we are moving more towards measures concerning such crimes also via the internet. secondly, two directives were proposed under article 13, the directive on racial discrimination was adopted in record time by the european parliament and the council, within six months, and is now part of european legislation. the second directive concerns the possibility of combating all forms of discrimination at work and is the subject of discussion during the french presidency. of course, laws are never enough on their own. the commission has therefore proposed an anti-discrimination programme which enables governments, non-governmental organisations and local authorities to work together to develop innovative policies and exchange experiences on effective ways of combating racism. the european observatory in vienna is an important institution whose aim is to present objective, reliable and comparable data on the phenomena of racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism and to be a key planning tool not only at european level but also at national level. the observatory has already produced studies on the extent of racism, on manifestations of racism, xenophobia and anti-semitism in various member states, on the analysis of their causes, consequences and effects, and has examined examples of good practice that have had an impact in some member states. the observatory is also working towards the creation of a coordinated network of non-governmental organisations and bodies which can cooperate at european level and tackle xenophobia issues. it can also make recommendations to the community and the member states on policies to be pursued and there has already been cooperation with the german government. the european parliament has already made a number of proposals to the council and the commission. the commission also participates in the formulation of theoretical and policy proposals. we have already tabled two documents in which we incorporate all the experience and proposals of combating racism at community level, as well as our experience in education, training, research, youth policy to deal with these issues. there is a financial backing of the conference in terms of ngos, because we believe they can play a very important role, beyond the role of governments, and of course we are negotiating to support the participation of ngos in the regional conferences planned for chile, senegal and iran. ladies and gentlemen, we must never forget that the european union was built to prevent the repetition of the racist atrocities we experienced 60 years ago. the policy is based, at european level, on an institutional arsenal that was strengthened by the treaty of amsterdam, but where there is still room for further efforts, on the creation of structures that study, analyse the phenomenon and support governments, on the support of a network, at european level, of various organisations to be able to awaken public opinion and, of course, on the exchange and support of national policies concerning education, the media, youth policies, information at national level. but it is important to say that all policies, all logic, are based on one principle: no tolerance in europe of racism and no acceptance of any justification for any action based on racism.
- mr president, racism is indeed a scourge of our society. it is one of the most terrible human vices, and no one has a monopoly on it. it is often the result of fear, ignorance, stupidity, selfishness, but also of the cowardice of the institutions. a civilized society, if it is to deserve this adjective, must hunt it down, banish it, punish it and eradicate it through education and repression. europe wants to be a civilized society and it has the opportunity to show this in its daily life. our parliament has to express its opinion on the european union's position at the world conference on racism. our position must be clear, intelligible and specific. it must be clear, without unnecessary length. i, for one, am a big fan of short texts. it must be modern, that is to say, it must take account of the new means of communication which also serve as a medium for racist expressions. it must be intelligible, that is to say, articulated around the big ideas and forces that set up a method: identification, with the help of our ngo partners or our own observatories; sanction, with the idea of zero tolerance and prevention, of course. it must be specific, that is to say, beyond the universal value of the fight against racism, there must be a specifically european message. because, let us be clear, europe has often been the hotbed of racism. we are even seeing a resurgence of this in some countries of the european union. we have a duty to remember and a duty to be vigilant. we need to have an ambitious message. we have to set an example. the commissioner said that there was no shortage of panoply, whether it was the fight against discrimination or the whole panoply on racism. we have a charter of fundamental rights in the making, where article 1 puts human dignity first. that is why i believe the epp has been involved in drafting this text. we want it to be free of all the economic scum, unnecessarily controversial, and free of any additions that will not bring anything back to the expression of the text. we have a common responsibility here, the commission, the council of ministers and parliament, and we are very attentive to this common approach, because the credibility of europe, at this world conference on racism, will depend above all on our state of affairs and on our credibility on our own territory.
mr president, from the witch hunts in el ejido, spain, to the murders of mozambicans in east germany, racist violence is inflaming the heart of europe. we often denounce those who do. i think it's high time we identified what we are arming them with, ideologically, in a few sentences. the extreme right-wing parties are structured using social problems, we know, precariousness, unemployment, and this is what we have to tackle. sometimes also, the soft consensus between the mainstream political parties, left and right, which helps them to expand their audience. the extreme right only comes to power, you must know, by relying on our weaknesses, our abandonments. so those who take their speeches and themes give them credibility, and those who think they can tame them by associating them with public affairs trivialize them. you can't understand the strategy of the far-right parties just by looking at their xenophobia, but by looking at their overall project in society, by looking at their homophobic speeches, their attitude against culture. we see, then, that there is a homophobic discourse, attacks on culture, on the rights of employees, on the right to strike, against their will. we must also avoid sending women back to the home by introducing a maternity wage, as we have seen recently. a rigid attitude is the only answer. in france, if we have been able to fight effectively against the national front, it is because there has never been a government alliance. in europe we must invest heavily in education, prevention, the fight against poverty and reaffirm the equal rights of foreign and european residents. i would like to end by thanking commissioner diamantopoulou for drawing a parallel between terrorism and racism, because i believe that this is an attack on the physical integrity of individuals, and that is intolerable. the europe of tolerance against hatred, against the europe of violence and indifference: this is the challenge of the conference.

in writing. - while i fully support mr wijkman's report, and in particular the budgetary effort made in the conciliation, i am concerned first of all that we have not understood what sustainable development means, but also that the environment may not necessarily be taken into account in all development projects for the disadvantaged countries. how can we think of the term or the development strategy without designing it in the context of environmental protection? how can we even separate development from the environment? and what applies to the development strategies of the third world countries should also apply to the growth strategies of the developed countries. the advocates of unrestrained liberalism will certainly want to see these environmental safeguards as additional constraints or obstacles to the difficult economic emergence of these deprived countries. but what would be the value of an economic take-off that would destroy a country's environmental framework, that would sacrifice its ecological potential? the cure would be worse than the disease. the deceptive balms of a purely economic recovery would soon disappear, caught up by the gangrene of environmental convulsions, hence health convulsions, and ultimately social convulsions. the first is that the community's economic policy is not only a matter of the economic policy of the member states, but also of the community's economic policy. the antinomy is clear, and its lessons and illustrations are inflicted on us every day: economic development alone cannot be sustainable. straw fire, it would devour its own roots. the very concept of development refers to the concept of duration, of the long term. and this concept of time itself contains that of a natural environment, a preserved living environment. respected by such a way of thinking and civilization today, it will guarantee the future of future generations.
in writing. - the green group, on behalf of which i speak, has given its full support to this report by mr fernández martín on the conservation and sustainable management of tropical and other forests in developing countries. the greens/efa group welcomes the increase in the budget for the protection of tropical forests. in view of their continuing and alarming deterioration, this eu surge appears to be an honourable start, but nevertheless modest in the face of the restoration requirements. in fact, the only attention paid to tropical forests has so far been a selfish reflex of westerners concerned with preserving these green lungs, the last refuge of our industrialized societies, with no regard for the indigenous peoples living in and through these forested areas, and doomed to lose out to the profits of industrial groups exploiting their resources. the appalling but continuing example of gold mining in french guiana, which is destroying entire areas of forest and killing flora, fauna and indigenous peoples, is mercury in their soil, their sap and their blood. the argument that the 'economic package' is the ultimate and hopeless springboard for development in third world countries that cannot afford the luxury of environmental safeguards is just an argument. sustainable development can only be achieved within a framework of responsible use of the environment. the same applies to the commercial charm of cutting down forests in the name of combating the greenhouse effect. under the same noble pretext of environmental preservation, these theories are aimed only at the preservation of the interests of these few large industrial groups. in the hague, the european union must refuse to fall into this trap which would allow the shameless exploitation of tropical forests, which are regarded as carbon sinks, and which would allow states to pay off their debts in terms of combating the greenhouse effect.
in writing. - i will begin by reminding you that the creation of the eurodac system for comparing the fingerprints of asylum seekers and certain other foreigners is intended to facilitate the application of the dublin convention, a text which makes it possible to determine the state responsible for examining asylum applications lodged in one of the member states of the union. this convention was signed on 15 june 1990. the report under discussion concerns this eurodac system and its operating procedures, which the council is proposing to modify in a way that is not at all in the interests of our parliament. the council has therefore proposed to remove the commission from the implementation of the eurodac system for the collection and comparison of asylum seekers' fingerprints (the eurodac database is used to determine the country which was the point of entry of an asylum seeker and which is therefore responsible for examining the asylum application) and to entrust it to the council in order to regain this competence. the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs has of course rejected this proposal from the council. the rapporteur rightly pointed out that under the ec treaty the council in principle confers implementing powers on the european commission. it is only in 'specific cases' that the council can reserve the right to exercise these powers itself and, obviously, that is not the case in the present case. the council has not yet taken a decision on the matter, and the commission has not yet taken a decision on the matter. of course, that is totally unacceptable! the new wording proposed for articles 22 and 23 of the eurodac regulation, on which parliament is now being consulted, was therefore rejected by the committee, which instead proposed an amendment conferring unreservedly on the commission the exercise of implementing powers. i support that position without reservation.
- mr president, this report claims to combat undeclared work. but the rapporteur's only concern is the conditions of competition between employers, not the situation of workers forced to work in the dark. it's your economy, it's unemployment, it's poverty that forces more and more workers to accept any job. these workers are the first and main victims of undeclared work, in their flesh and in their lives, because they are overworked, subjected to the worst working conditions, wages, and deprived of any legal protection against illness and accidents. so to blame them for their own misery, even partially, is outrageous. in the report's explanatory statement, the author even indecently asks whether it is not the too low retirement age, the too short working day or the "rigid nature of certain provisions of labour law" that are responsible for undeclared work. this suggests that if the legal working conditions were made as abject as those of black-collar work, employers would be less inclined to use them. if parliament really wanted to fight undeclared work, it should start by proposing that any employer guilty of employing a undeclared worker should be obliged to hire him on a permanent contract. we have obviously not voted for this report which, while pretending to protect the victims, in fact absolves the slave owners, including some large companies which have nothing to do but to make vague threats of economic sanctions.
in writing. - everyone agrees that undeclared work is to be condemned, that is, undeclared work, as it is commonly called. at the same time, many people are using this cheap labour. the figures speak for themselves, since underground work, as it is commonly called, represents a percentage of between 7% and 16% of the european union's gdp. this is of course intolerable in our member states, which are faced with unemployment rates that remain high, despite a clear decline in recent years. and i agree with the rapporteur when she insists that the fight against undeclared work contributes to a very large extent and directly to the fight against unemployment. i am well aware that the solutions are not easy to find. but it is obvious that it is in the best interests of the member states to coordinate their efforts to put in place a voluntary strategy to combat this scourge. the first step is to draw up an inventory of the sectors most affected and the main categories concerned in each member state. the study will have to be followed up by practical measures to be implemented in each situation, which will be incorporated in an action programme. these programmes will have to be integrated into the national action plans linked to the employment guidelines in order to establish mutual transparency and to assess the effectiveness of the measures taken. there is also a clear link between the level of taxes and levies and the extent and growth of undeclared work. the member states must therefore make efforts to reduce taxes and levies on labour. the reduction in the vat rate for services with a high labour input, a sector where undeclared work is very common, which the member states may apply pursuant to the council decision of 28 february 2000, will most certainly have a positive effect on the fight against undeclared work. i hope, as does the committee on employment and social affairs, that those member states which do not yet have this option will reconsider their decisions. that is why i voted for this report, which is a further step towards the achievement of a social europe.
in writing. - the extension of undeclared work is not a choice of the workers which would allow them to increase their incomes. this is the will of the companies which deal directly only with the most profitable sectors. the others, those where the profit is considered less important and less rapid, are subcontracted. this subcontracting is in fact developing the outsourcing of work. it is not 'increased flexibility of the labour market' (point 11 of the motion for a resolution), 'reduced taxes and levies' (point 11), 'increased flexibility of working time' (point 26) which will reduce undeclared work. it is not the workers who are to blame, it is the capitalist economic logic that must be fought, because it always aims to reduce labour costs, in particular by abolishing employers' financial contributions to social protection.
in writing. - mrs glase's report does not measure up to her statement of reasons, which i found, once not customary in this chamber, of a rare lucidity. yes, we agree with the rapporteur that one of the causes of undeclared work is the insane level of taxation on labour, the bureaucracy, the red tape imposed on businesses, the disappearance of internal border controls in the european union, and so on. but we regret that not once in his report is there any clear link between the massive illegal immigration that our continent is suffering from and the explosion of undeclared work. nor is there any mention of the very heavy responsibilities of brussels-based europe in the establishment and aggravation of the causes of undeclared work. that is why we abstained on this report.

- the next item is the recommendation for second reading (a5-0230/2000) on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the common position of the council with a view to adopting a european parliament and council regulation (ec) amending the common principles of the european system of national and regional accounts in the community (esa 95) as regards taxes and social security contributions and council regulation (ec) no 2223/96 [8276/2/2000 - c5-0328/2000 - 1999/0200 cod (cns)) (rapporteur: mr knörr borràs).
mr president, i welcome the present report on venture capital, because i share the view that it offers the opportunity to acquire funds which are absolutely necessary for research, development, production and market entry of new products, which can then of course also create additional jobs. there is agreement on many points, such as the provision of public and private risk capital, facilitation of access conditions, priority for risk capital for smes, tax incentives for reinvestment of profits in risk capital funds, simplification and minimisation of patent applications. the overall concept is also open to criticism. firstly, if it is particularly the case for smes in underdeveloped regions, why the absolute focus on innovative services? i would also like to see investment in new products from the innovative manufacturing sector to promote regional development. secondly, what good is the genuine willingness to invest in the creation of new businesses, in research and development and in venture capital if it is not accompanied by the market development which is very costly for smes? because that is where the smes have their biggest problems, once they have the product, then also putting it on the market. thirdly, why should public venture capital be used only where private ones are not? the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect, and i am sure that the commission will be able to support them. this distorts competition to the detriment of public venture capital. fourthly, how will you ensure that the greater involvement of pension funds in venture capital, as called for in the report, does not lead to possible losses of the sums deposited and thus run counter to the objective of contributors to secure a secure end to their lives? fifthly, it is not clear why mergers on the capital market should have a positive effect on the provision of risk capital. experience shows the opposite. the fewer the suppliers, the less competition and the higher the cost!
- (inaudible) ...which will only benefit the minority of the population with capital to invest and move. the proposals are yet another illustration of the fact that the european union was built with the sole concern of promoting the movement and investment of large and, incidentally, small capital. the majority of the population is concerned, however, because it is with their money that the european institutions intend to finance the measures facilitating private investment. those who do not have capital but pay most of the taxes, particularly indirect taxes, including vat, will therefore have to finance the subsidies and tax deductions for investors and the tax benefits granted to stock options. the plan is to promote pension funds, but this inevitably means promoting the system of divided pensions. the money that should be used to provide a decent retirement for all will thus be used to enable a minority to make more private profit. we therefore reject the whole approach of increasingly emptying the pockets of the working majority of the population in order to drain the money taken from the holders of capital.
- mr president, mr commissioner, first of all, a tribute to the active rapporteur, mr hatzidakis, for his report. the european dimensions of buses seem trivial, but they are far from it. the dynamic internal market we are striving for can only be achieved if all players follow the same rules. competition, which is the real engine of development, arises when operators can offer their services across borders. we do not yet have greek drivers in finland, but the scots have already gained a firm foothold. it's worth the sleep. in order to ensure that positive competition continues to spread, we need to coordinate the standards for buses. the single dimension also means cost savings for the manufacturer, reflected in the price of the ticket and in the eu citizen's pocket. the current directive is flawed because it leads to a high level of bus literacy in different member states, which makes it difficult to develop safety standards. the tragic news of the last few days in greece requires us to take a firm stand on the creation and observance of safety rules. the commission is right to propose that buses be allowed to be 15 metres long. the more people on the bus, the cheaper the trip gets. not to mention the mood, which is going to rise exponentially as the number of passengers increases. it is also advisable to use long buses for environmental reasons. the preference for mass transportation reduces congestion in the city centre, with a few half-carriages taking up the space of a 60-passenger bus. the rapporteur, mr hatzidakis, is right in saying that it would be unreasonable to demand that the transitional period for buses in domestic use should end as early as 2009. we will not win friends for the eu by scrapping buses that are still in good condition before their time. at the same time, we are also easily destroying the faith of the entrepreneur and the man on the street in the common sense of eu decision-makers.
the commission is aware of the fact that the commission has not yet adopted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. the commission is pleased that the report points out the need to strike a balance between commercial and competition aspects, while ensuring technical progress and safety. these objectives are obviously our objectives too. the aim of the text is clear, as has already been mentioned here: to establish a uniform standard for the size of rigid buses in transport services. the current legislation is very varied, very disparate, and the need for this harmonization seems obvious. in order to understand what i am going to say next about the commission's reaction to the various amendments, it should be clear that the proposal, in accordance with our view, is intended to authorize a maximum length of fifteen metres throughout the european union provided that two conditions are met: firstly, that between twelve and fifteen metres there is a three-axle bus - an important subject which i will discuss later, which has raised some points of debate - and secondly, that the buses are manoeuvrable, that is to say, that they have manoeuvrability in accordance with the community legislation itself. let's go in with the first requirement: the three axes. the three-axis problem, according to the commission's thesis, is fundamental to ensure that, despite the size of these buses, the weight is distributed evenly and does not cause problems in road infrastructure. this is the fundamental point. we can understand that there is a debate about whether all buses are the same or not, but we believe that a proliferation of specific solutions would be a worse formula in the end. we think that the three axles for buses over 12 metres is the simplest formula that best solves the problems. the commission has therefore decided to amend amendments nos 2 and 4, which seek to relax this requirement by making the third axle compulsory only for buses over 13 and a half metres or up to 15 metres in length, and which we consider unacceptable, as we have said before, because they would have a negative impact on infrastructure. the second requirement of our proposal is that a certain test of manoeuvrability be passed. what maneuverability test? the same conditions are now laid down in directive 97/27 which also links this test to the manufacturing standards. we think that is a key point and that is also why it is impossible for the commission to accept amendment no 3 in so far as it seeks to establish different, less stringent manoeuvrability rules than those which currently exist. it is obvious that they would be easier to comply with, but they would introduce risks from the point of view of safety for this type of car. amendments nos 5 and 7 are also unacceptable to the commission. in both cases, the intention is that the directive will enter into force at a later date. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. and it also raises some difficulties in accepting amendment no 6 insofar as we consider that it does not have sufficient technical justification. however, it seems reasonable to us that buses which are currently authorized at 15 metres and which do not meet the requirements mentioned above, i.e. the three axles and manoeuvrability, should nevertheless have a transitional period and that this transitional period should be longer than initially planned. at the time, a period until 2009 was proposed. the commission considers that this exemption is perhaps too restrictive and we could accept that the directive could allow them to continue to circulate until 2015.
