the council. - madam president, mr president of the european commission, ladies and gentlemen, you have asked us to devote today's work to the next european council in biarritz, and this will be an important stage in this six-month presidency of the council. you all know that the european council has now become accustomed to meeting, at any rate almost always, twice a semester, and i believe that this pace corresponds to a real need even if this additional meeting, i should rather say especially if this additional meeting, is, and will be, of an informal nature. far from diminishing its importance, the informal nature of such a summit allows sensitive issues to be discussed very freely at the highest level. the biarritz agenda will therefore be dominated by two major issues which i know are of interest to the european parliament: the intergovernmental conference on institutional reform and the charter of fundamental rights. the date has been chosen in such a way as to ensure that the summit will be of the greatest possible use. we shall be in biarritz on 13 and 14 october, about halfway through our presidency. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. so, as you can see, it is not a question of discussing every subject, which would not make much sense. however, i would say that the french presidency has now entered a cruising phase, and that the work is progressing, i think i can say, in a satisfactory way; i know that some observers have been critical, but they have certainly placed too high hopes on this presidency, which is flattering to us, but at the same time it is not good for us, because it is always too short - four useful months, i would remind you - and we have forgotten that, like any presidency, we have to take account of many and very heavy constraints. the work of the last few weeks has thus been overshadowed by certain events which have been widely reported in the press. i am thinking in particular of the soaring oil prices - and i would also point out that the members of the european council will also be discussing this - i am thinking of fluctuations in the euro exchange rate and the danish referendum. what i can assure you is that we are continuing our efforts on schedule and i believe that the results are quite right. i take the example of the last general affairs council, with the beginning of agreement on meda ii, the continuation of the debate on improving the union's external aid, the declaration to the serbian people which we have seen weighing on the present situation and the first state of play on the enlargement process, which we will discuss again this afternoon, right here. progress was also made at the last justice and home affairs council, which saw the adoption of the regulation on the european refugee fund, the extension of europol's powers in the field of money laundering and finally a political agreement to create eurojust, a decision we took at the tampere summit. similarly, the informal council of defence ministers held on 22 september indicated that there would be very satisfactory results by the end of the six-month period in terms of capacity commitments. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very important one. but here again, things are under way and the presidency, in full agreement with the commission and parliament, is at work. i now come back to the actual agenda of the european council in biarritz, that is to say, first of all, the intergovernmental conference. as i said in the debate held on 11 july at the invitation of president napolitano, whom i welcome, our concern from the outset has been to resume the discussions on a more open basis so as to give us every chance of reaching a satisfactory agreement in nice. we have thus been keen, on the one hand, to stress the link between the three questions not settled in amsterdam, which for us form a whole, a package, and, on the other hand, to undertake a thorough reflection on the major issue, in the context of an enlarged europe, of enhanced cooperation. these are very difficult questions and that is why we felt at first, i admit, that we could not move forward as quickly as we wanted. i think you've got it right, too; the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. your participation is always very important. you have repeatedly stressed the importance of mobilizing efforts to ensure that these negotiations progress and conclude on schedule. the presidency, like the commission, emphasized forcefully at the gymnich in evian, the informal meeting of foreign ministers at the beginning of september, that there was a real risk of failure in nice and that france, as the incumbent presidency, would rather accept such a failure than a bad agreement. i would like to emphasize once again that no one should think that this is a tactical approach on our part. we do not prefer a treaty in nice to a bad treaty in nice. this message seems to have been understood, but i could see at the general affairs council on 18 september and at the small meeting i chaired that evening in brussels the signs of a beginning to awaken. so, how are we doing on this negotiation? as regards the commission, we feel that the difficulty is that a majority of member states are reluctant to both cap the number of commissioners and to a genuine restructuring of the college in the long term, even though we all agree on the need for a strong and efficient commission. i think there is a paradox here which we must get out of. this is essential for the future of the union because the commission is, i repeat emphatically, the pivot of the community system. each of us has been able to put forward his arguments in a precise way, but i believe that there is a time when we must be able to overcome certain contradictions. it seems to me impossible that we, as twenty, twenty-five or thirty member states, can continue with the present system without reforming it. on the question of re-weighting, i believe that there are developments and that a large number of member states see the advantage of this formula, the strict re-weighting of votes, over that of a double majority in any form. but this question of the reweighting is closely linked to the previous one and it can only be settled, of course, at the end of the negotiations. rest assured, we are not waiting for biarritz, let alone nice, to deal with it. the necessary preparatory work is under way. i believe, however, that - and this is my personal feeling - more substantial progress will not be made for some time. but it is important that the heads of state and government meeting in biarritz at the european council should speak about this. the large amount of work done on the skilled majority, however, is beginning to bear fruit. the commission, and i thank it, has made very constructive proposals to enable us to move forward while taking account of the main difficulties of each delegation. the list of items which could be moved to qualified majority voting is therefore becoming substantial and i believe that, overall, the results will be in line with the requirements because this is a vital subject, as we all know. perhaps it is even the main one in this igc, as is the question of the concomitant extension of our codecision procedures for parliament. i believe that the discussion is progressing well within the igc and that the principle of the correspondence between codecision and legislation is gaining ground, if not all the ground. finally, as you know, the difficulty with enhanced cooperation was and remains, to a certain extent, that many member states saw in it a priori the risk of creating a two-speed europe, or even of trying to save real progress by the 15 on the qualified majority. but i would like to say that enhanced cooperation is neither the way to a stable and closed hard core nor a substitute for advancing on the qualified majority. we have had several in-depth exchanges at ministerial level on this issue and i believe that they have helped to clarify the concept of enhanced cooperation and to overcome the reluctance of the most sceptical. the parallel debate on the future of enlarged europe has contributed in its own way, i would say both positively and perhaps also sometimes a little negatively. indeed, since a majority of member states do not seem to be considering radical reform towards an institutional model of another type, let us say a much more federal one, it must be admitted that enhanced cooperation is a good tool which responds to the realistic observation that in the enlarged europe, not all member states will always be able or willing to move forward at the same pace. a certain degree of flexibility is therefore essential so that those who want to go faster can do so while still allowing others the opportunity to join those who are more advanced, because it is clear that enhanced cooperation only makes sense if it is always open. of course, there is still work to be done, particularly to clarify the conditions under which the principles could be simplified and the conditions for triggering this mechanism relaxed, while of course maintaining a number of guarantees. it will also be necessary to examine the specific provisions to be taken in the field of the cfsp. finally, the presidency will examine, in agreement with the member states, the possibility of supplementing article 7 of the treaty on european union, in particular on the basis of the proposals already tabled by the member states and the commission: it is clear that in order to better guarantee respect for the union's values and fundamental rights in the future, a system of prevention, surveillance and alert will be necessary. i now turn to the second fundamental subject of the biarritz declaration, the charter of fundamental rights. as you know, the draft charter was solemnly adopted by the convention yesterday, 2 october, with the valuable and very effective support of the representatives of your assembly. your committee on constitutional affairs, through its chairman, giorgio napolitano, is nevertheless wondering about the future of this draft charter and the possibilities of incorporating it into the treaties at the european council in nice. i therefore conclude from this question that parliament, or at least its constitutional committee, approves the text of the convention, of course with the benefit of hindsight, which i can only welcome. we shall probably have the opportunity to discuss this again in greater detail at the debate here in november on the proclamation of the text by the three institutions. but before i answer the question of the constitutional committee specifically, let me say how i think the work of the convention is a double success. firstly, we must reflect on the success of the procedure adopted, namely the procedure of a body, the convention, composed of members of the european parliament, national parliamentarians, the european commission and personal representatives of the heads of state or government. we have broken with the traditional method of diplomatic conferences or intergovernmental conferences, which, it must be said, is now proving to be somewhat complex. (applause) i would add that the quality and diversity of the members appointed by their education, their origin and their political convictions have undoubtedly been a factor of wealth. i also find it quite remarkable that the convention has taken the double approach of working in full transparency and in full interaction with citizens via the internet. in the interests of openness, it has therefore consulted the major non-governmental organisations, the social partners and the candidate countries. this transparency and openness have actively contributed to the progressive improvement of the various versions of the draft charter. you know there's been, i don't know, 48 or 49.
the commission - madam president, mr minister, ladies and gentlemen, the biarritz summit will be a decisive stage because we will have to deal with the issues which are of fundamental importance for enlargement and institutional reforms. but trying to solve our own problems does not exempt us today from turning a thought to our neighbors and friends who are facing crucial trials. in serbia, community. however, in the candidate countries there is an equally strong sense of growing anxiety about the lack of a precise and demanding timetable. their efforts and anxieties must be answered. summit and, subsequently, of the nice summit. a treaty of nice adopted in december and fully implementing the above would allow the union, taking due account of the time needed for national ratification, to be ready for enlargement at the beginning of 2003. the stakes are known - we heard it from minister moscovici - and so is the commission's position. the aim is to make the mechanism from the single market to the euro, and through four successive enlargements - has developed through a system that is absolutely original, based on the delicate balance between the union's institutions. this system, revolving around the institutional triangle - council, parliament, commission - has proved to be a tremendous success. its originality lies first and foremost in the commission and its role as initiator. the commission is the crucible in which the various tensions and national interests converge, and from which proposals emerge which seek to reconcile these interests, which are often in conflict with each other. in this way, the commission not only provides the analysis and summary of the problems on the table but also forms the starting point for negotiations which, once national differences have been expressed, make it possible to identify the common european interest. this independent executive body, which is attentive to the interests and balances of all the member states, large and small, is the necessary condition for the pooling of sovereignty within the community. however, the role of the commission is a necessary but not sufficient condition for the construction of europe. the european interest is the product of an institutional system in which the parliament, the council and the court of justice play an equally decisive role. it is from this system, from the whole of these institutions that the synthesis arises. on the other hand, there are those who believe that they can see the positive aspects of any confrontation between the council and the commission, as if this confrontation were to turn into a benefit for parliament. nothing is more wrong: a strong council strengthens the commission's action, and this is also true of parliament. the european system is a balanced system in which the good functioning of each institution ensures the common interest. weakening any one of these institutions weakens the whole. nevertheless, ladies and gentlemen, i feel a worrying tendency to believe that the construction of europe can be further developed by methods based mainly on direct cooperation between governments. (applause) i would like to thank this is very worrying because the intergovernmental method could only produce two consequences, both negative: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. that 's what a government of bureaucrats is ! (applause) i would like to thank the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a step in the right direction. it is misleading to claim, as is sometimes done, that the legitimacy of the individual participating governments is a sufficient guarantee of the democratic accountability of the intergovernmental model. the democratic nature of the european process can only be based on two legitimations: the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. it is you, the european parliament, as the direct expression of universal european suffrage, who are specifically entitled to represent the union of the peoples of europe. and it is from the vote you, the members of the european parliament, give to the commission that it derives its democratic legitimacy. this is in addition to the other source of legitimacy, which is the member states represented in the council. the strengthening of the intergovernmental model, at the expense not only of the commission but ultimately also of the council, would therefore weaken the democratic character of the whole european construction and, in this case, would be a major step backwards. (applause) there are also great dangers if we call into question the principle of a community based on law, whose respect is guaranteed by courts to which all citizens can turn. we must, once and for all, escape the paradox of the present situation, where even the work of the 15 ministers of justice, in such sensitive areas as criminal law and cooperation between law enforcement agencies, escapes the control of parliament and the court. (applause) this is a model which, based on a confusion of roles between the council and the commission, risks weakening both pillars of the institutional system and excluding parliament from any effective power. the present situation must be seen as a transitional phase, useful for launching european action in a new area but destined to fall within the ordinary institutional framework, as has happened in similar experiences, such as that of schengen. i am therefore firmly convinced that the function of high representative should be integrated into the commission, with a special status adapted to the needs of security and defence. in writing. - the national accounts are magic. in a few aggregates, gdp, gnp, consumption, income, capital formation, etc., it gives a reduced model of the economic life of a country. it can be used to calculate tax burdens, public deficit and debt ratios. it is a major instrument for steering economic, budgetary and fiscal policy. it is through this that the maastricht criteria find their application and it is above all through this that the european community finds its vat resources and above all its fourth resource, based on gnp. however, the procedures for drawing up these national accounts, both in the operations described and in the institutional sectors summarised, must be identical in each country. otherwise, of course, there is no comparison. hence the need for common principles for the registration of taxes and social contributions within the fifteen. that is precisely the whole purpose of the regulation here. it makes the mechanics of the economic accounts integrated in the european system of accounts uniform. this european system of accounts, which dates back to 1970, was revised in 1995. there are many problems. for example, to assess the revenue, one must start from the fact that the tax is generated or collected. for example, it is known that in france the figure for tax revenue varies according to whether the statistics are taken from the directorate-general for public accounts or from the national accounts office. this makes it all the more easy to imagine the variations from one country to another. this is all the more so since it is in the interest of the states to 'cheat' in order to underestimate their taxable base for vat or gnp. the reports of the european court of auditors keep pointing to these underestimates, from greece to portugal. in the case of the amendment of the 1996 regulation in question, the commission proposes to record taxes and contributions by first taking into account the revenue actually collected, rather than the revenue rights recognised from the event giving rise to them. the commission also proposes to apply a coefficient to the 'non-recoverable' percentage in order not to underestimate the reality of the deficit, in the light of the maastricht requirements. it all sounds purely technical, but the political consequences are significant.
in writing. - we had nothing against the report's stated intention to harmonise disparate national legislation on the maximum legal length of passenger vehicles, quite the contrary. it should be stressed, however, that the proposed measures are not justified by the safety of passengers or the rational organization of transport, but by 'commercial reasons', i.e. profit for road transport undertakings. homogenization would therefore be achieved by aligning the european legal length with the maximum of the particular legislation. the european institutions are working with the national governments to promote road transport over rail. this preference is harmful to the environment and represents a social mess. a policy of rational, efficient and safe organisation should give priority to investment in a public european railway service rather than merely leveling the playing field between road hauliers, who are primarily concerned with increasing their private profits. we have therefore not voted for this report.
in writing. - in this report we are discussing a proposal to amend directive 96/53/ec to allow the circulation of 15 metre long buses in the european union. i welcome that proposal. the maximum legal length of passenger vehicles currently differs considerably from one member state to another: in seven countries (the united kingdom, ireland, france, spain, italy, portugal and greece), the limit is 12 metres. in one country, denmark, the average is 13.7 meters. in two other countries (sweden and finland) it is 14.5 metres and in five others (luxembourg, the netherlands and austria: restricted use only, and belgium and germany: unrestricted use) it is 15 metres. this legal limit has not been explicitly harmonised at european level as it has not been included in directive 96/53/ec. at present, only 12-metre buses are allowed to travel freely throughout the community. at the request of the council of ministers, the commission has drawn up a proposal to include passenger vehicles in directive 96/53/ec in order to harmonise not only the length of rigid buses but also to clarify the situation of removable accessories for buses and trailers. even in countries where 15-metre buses are not officially allowed, in reality they are not refused or returned at the border. in this sense, it can be said that this proposal formalizes a factual situation. commercial reasons are behind the lengthening of buses. a bus of 15 metres can accommodate some 67 passengers, 16 more than a bus of 12 metres. it is clearly competition which is driving some operators to use longer buses. however, it should be noted that another way to increase the number of seats is to operate double-decker buses and coaches. at the same time, the introduction of larger buses would reduce the number of buses in circulation, which would be less harmful to the environment. in order to ensure the safety of vulnerable road users and to avoid as far as possible problems with existing road infrastructure, the proposal provides for limits, applicable to all buses, for the permissible overflows at a bend. of course, such adjustments will take time. i therefore believe that it is appropriate to provide for reasonable transitional periods to enable the production facilities of the 15 member states to adapt to the new criteria and thus avoid distortions of competition. i therefore voted in an attempt to reconcile respect for the environment, the necessary completion of the internal market and the new constraints imposed on manufacturers.
- we did not vote against this resolution in order not to confuse our votes with those of the extreme right, which is opposed to a number of fundamental rights being even affirmed or opposed to the sovereignty of states. but we have no intention of endorsing the charter itself, which remains vague on such basic human rights as the right to work, a decent wage or housing, rights which concern the majority of the population, as it remains vague on social protection, freedom of movement and residence for third country nationals. it is, however, specific about the right of property, about freedom of enterprise, which concern above all the minority who own capital, the right to use and abuse it. the recognition of human rights and freedoms is only a recommendation in principle and is not legally binding, i.e. it is not binding on the member states. the european institutions are nevertheless able to take binding decisions, such as on the authorization of night work for women, when these decisions are harmful or when they lead to unnecessary hassle. but this is not the case with basic rights such as the right of all employees to strike or to join a trade union. the charter will therefore serve more to consolidate the current practices, including regressive ones, of the national states than to represent progress.

months on this subject, i have to say that the charter of fundamental rights could indeed have represented added value for europe, but that, as things stand, we cannot be satisfied with its content or the working methods which led to its elaboration. as i stated in my proposal to the bureau of this house, from the very beginning of the work, the rights of individuals are already well protected in europe, both by national legal systems and by the european convention for the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms, which is an extension of it. we do not need an additional instrument, which would mainly strengthen the supranational power of the community institutions. on the other hand, we would need a charter of the rights of nations which would recall the fundamental attachment of citizens to the democratic will expressed in the national framework, and which would affirm that the union is an association of nations. such a text would be very useful not only for restoring the true sense of democracy but also for preparing the institutions of the future enlarged europe. but that is not at all the way the authors have gone. since the beginning of the work, the draft has been riddled with a fundamental contradiction which has never been resolved: on the one hand, it states that its provisions are 'addressed to the institutions and bodies of the union', but on the other hand, many articles refer to purely national competences, which have nothing to do with those of the union. the actual scope of application does not correspond to the stated intentions, with a fearful ambiguity about the nature of the charter. this text may seem painless at first, since it essentially takes over existing rights. but if it were incorporated into the treaty with binding force, as the european parliament is asking for, it would mechanically tend, over time, to the 'uniformisation of national rights in europe'; it would confer disproportionate power on the court of justice; it would foster greater centralisation around the european institutions; it would limit the scope for autonomous decision-making by each people. it would therefore push for a uniform europe, the very one that most politicians say they reject. even if we assume that this project will be merely a political declaration, we cannot accept it as such. we cannot imagine a political declaration at european level which makes no reference to the central role of national democracies, the rights which flow from them and the consequences for the european institutions. this controversial project, which was deliberately skewed in the federalist direction, is the result of a poor working method which has encouraged confusion at all levels. the drafting body was no doubt composed in an original way, but it represented, from a legal point of view, only a simple working group of the council. from the beginning, however, it called itself the convention, despite my protests, and it has always acted as if it were a sovereign assembly, superior to the institutions that appointed it, and even to the nations. it then worked by a method known as 'consensus', i.e. without ever voting, even by way of indication, without ever knowing who was really for or against this or that provision, and without understanding who had finally decided to retain it, to delete it, or to amend it. finally, the auditions were arbitrarily determined by the candidates who presented themselves (or were invited to do so?), and it would be impossible to say that they provided a fair and honest picture of the companies of the member countries. the convention was thus a confusing system, a generator of irresponsibility, and not conducive to an orderly democracy. the final adoption of the draft charter to be submitted to the council on 2 october itself was a monument of ambiguity, since apparently some members said yes on condition that it was a political declaration, others said yes on condition that it was a binding text, and this crucial divergence was ignored, along with the existence of an opposition of which i was myself a member. the federalists have so well taken advantage of this confusion that it is not surprising to hear the european parliament today calling for the establishment, after nice, of another identical body to draft a european constitution. my group is opposed to the idea of a european constitution, which would aim to abolish the sovereignty of nations, but it is also opposed to the reproduction, on this or any other subject, of a system of negotiations as disorderly as that of the convention.
in writing. - the convention responsible for drawing up the charter of fundamental rights of the european union concluded its work yesterday in brussels, following a solemn meeting at which all delegations (european parliament, commission, national parliaments and representatives of governments) expressed their approval. president roman herzog was thus able to officially convey the final draft to the french presidency in preparation for the biarritz summit. our european parliament will vote on this text later by way of assent. today, the two oral questions put by the president of the committee on constitutional affairs, mr napolitano, to the european commission and the council give us the opportunity to discuss the legal status of this charter and, above all, to reaffirm our desire to see it given binding force and incorporated into a treaty. we had already expressed this wish when we voted on the last resolution on this subject on 16 march 2000. we are well aware that there are many reluctance and that there is a great risk of adopting a declarative charter! to avoid this and to avoid disappointing the legitimate expectations of the european citizens, we had to consider an alternative solution. that is why i voted for this resolution and supported the amendment tabled by our french socialist delegation chair, pervenche berès, calling on the biarritz summit to ask the igc to consider all the ways of incorporating the charter into the treaty: preamble, protocol or reference to the charter in article 6, which states that the union is based on the principles of liberty, democracy and respect for human rights and fundamental freedoms, as well as the notion of the rule of law. this last formula makes it possible to give the text a binding force while avoiding for the time being the debate on the constituent character of the formula of the preamble. this would be a transitional solution which would eventually lead to a binding charter. in the end, it is clear that this charter does not go as far as i would have wished. the european socialists have also won a number of important victories. i am thinking of the inclusion of rights such as the right to strike, the right to work, the implicit reference to european trade unions, the right to housing allowances. the content of this charter must certainly be enriched. that is why we must follow the debate all the way to the nice summit. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. i would like to conclude by stressing that the charter of fundamental rights must be seen as the central element of the process necessary to give the european union a real constitution, which remains for me a priority objective for the next three to four years.
in writing. - a convention, composed of 62 delegates from the governments of the 15 member states and of european and national parliamentarians, drew up a charter of fundamental rights for more than 380 million europeans. this charter is far below the european convention on human rights, far below national conventions or treaties. it is the image of the liberal europe that is being built. on such fundamental issues as women's rights, immigrant rights, the right to education, the right to housing, the right to work or to a decent income, the charter is often inadequate, sometimes regressive. because social rights are fundamental rights for a europe which respects democratic and social rights and freedoms, we support the idea of another charter which protects workers, women, foreigners, the excluded and national minorities. this charter must be drawn up by the social movement and not by a select group of elected officials. because we believe that the process of european integration deserves a genuine public and democratic debate, there can be no political construction of europe without social rights and democracy. that is why i did not vote for this draft charter. i will vote for another charter by participating in the demonstrations in biarritz on 13 and 14 october and in nice on 7 december 2000.

the commission has already submitted a proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, we would like to make our contribution to this debate. there is a debate, often fuelled here and there, about whether we should examine the accession process of the candidate countries to the union in the light of the criteria of real convergence or nominal convergence. our committee on economic and monetary affairs thinks that this is a false debate. we want to observe both real convergence and nominal convergence. when we look at the copenhagen criteria and the maastricht criteria, it seems to us that this is the essence of what we need for the accession of the applicant countries to take place under good conditions, that is to say in the name of respect for the mutual interest, the interest of the applicant countries, the interest of the countries currently members of the union. but if we want things to go well, we must first give priority to real convergence. and to that end, it seems to us that the european union must also contribute to the gradual adaptation of the productive tool of the applicant countries. when you look at the numbers, they're impressive. the latest available estimates suggest that €200 billion will be needed to put the infrastructure and environment of the candidate countries in a position to achieve real convergence, i.e. to encourage a higher level of investment to enable the economies of these countries to meet the copenhagen criteria. we also believe that a certain flexibility will have to be exercised when it comes to examining the criteria for reducing the rate of inflation or anchoring exchange rates. these are the elements of nominal convergence, and we have seen, we have experience of this within the european union, that convergence can also help to promote real convergence. we are obviously thinking of the italian or portuguese experiences, and we are seeing the same phenomenon in the candidate countries, but this requires a certain amount of flexibility to allow for the necessary adjustments in the catching-up process. this is of course particularly true of the question of prices. in this context, we believe that the establishment of a genuine macroeconomic dialogue between peers, between colleagues, at the level of finance ministers and central banks is essential before accession. and i am sure that this is not just about monetary issues, but also about what we call within the union the coordination of economic policies. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy has also stressed the need to improve the banking and prudential supervision systems, which are still in their infancy and which pose a potential risk to access to finance for small and medium-sized enterprises. finally, in mr brok's report, your parliament calls for the liberalization of capital to be gradual, particularly in the short term, in order to prevent speculation on the foreign exchange markets. one last point, mr president, on the consequences of joining the euro. we feel that membership is both a right and a duty. once the conditions are met, there is no reason for the candidate countries, or for the countries currently in the euro area, to oppose entry into the third phase of the economic and monetary union of the candidate countries. moreover, this accession will enshrine a commitment to a political project and to close coordination of economic and social policies. monetary union is not a currency area. it is also an economic and monetary union. the mutual interest is that these countries do not have a derogation, but for us too there is no exclusive membership of the euro, provided that the criteria we have defined between us are respected. these countries are destined to join the union on the basis of criteria which we have collectively defined.

- doc. a5-0257/2000 by mrs paulsen, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on undesirable substances and products in animal feed (com ((1999) 654 - c5-0344/1999 - 1999/0259 ((cod)) - doc. a5-0256/2000 by mrs paulsen, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive amending council directive 1995/53/ec laying down the principles governing the organisation of official controls on feedingstuffs and council directive 1999/29/ec on undesirable substances and products in animal feed (com (2000) 162 - c5-0686/2000 (cod))
the committee on agriculture and rural development has adopted a number of amendments to the proposal. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, it should be remembered that one of the novelties of the white paper on food safety was the farm-to-table concept, which implied direct responsibility on the part of farmers for the quality and safety of the animal and plant raw materials they produce. almost a year after the publication of this book and following the many food crises, many of which were directly linked to animal feed, mrs paulsen's report is the first foray into food safety from animal feed. we can all rejoice in that. one of the strong points of the proposal is the principle of non-dilution, which excludes any mixing of a consignment of animals contaminated, for example, with dioxin, with healthy food. that is the position of mrs paulsen, from the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy. that was also my position as rapporteur for the opinion of the committee on agriculture. the amendments tabled by my colleagues from the epp, mrs klass, mrs jeggle and mr sturdy, have made it possible to put the dilution back into the proposal voted by the committee on agriculture. i cannot sacrifice food security for the profit of the food lobby, so i have withdrawn my name from the report. what do you want, ladies and gentlemen? i cannot understand the epp which, despite successive crises, from belgian chicken to dioxin, from french sewage sludge to animal feed or other dutch waste oils to food oil, wants to continue to poison european consumers to some extent. they say that if a batch of products is contaminated with dioxin, it will not be disposed of. it is much better to add healthy products until an acceptable level of pollution is reached. my dear colleagues from the epp, at the time of the white paper, the precautionary principle, food safety, the only acceptable level of pollution in the feed of the livestock that will end up on our plate is the zero level that can be measured today, especially since dioxin is a product that accumulates in the body. if dilution were allowed, the dioxin in animal feed would be stored first by the animal, then by the consumer, who would then gradually accumulate this toxic product throughout his body. we must therefore follow mrs paulsen and the commission and adopt the principle of non-dilution to ensure the safety of animal feed and to protect european consumers. as regards controls, the commission's proposal for a directive on controls in the field of animal feed comes from the bart staes report. it summarises and clarifies the essential elements for overcoming the malfunctions such as those which emerged in the dioxin crisis of the summer of 1999. it aims to avoid any miscoordination between the national and european institutions. as rapporteur for the opinion, i agree with the main amendments proposed by the commission: the establishment of adequate national response plans, the possibility for the commission to take back provisional protective measures, the obligation for member states to inform the commission as soon as a contamination or a serious risk of contamination is detected, the creation of a legal basis. it should be stressed that controls must be carried out at three levels to enable an emergency system to be set up. the first level of control must be carried out by the feed businesses themselves and by the farmers who must be the first to ensure the quality and safety of the products they use. the second is, of course, that of the member states, which have responsibility for food safety controls. the third level - and this is the subject of this amendment - establishes the european commission as the supreme guardian of food safety. it may intervene in an emergency without consulting the member states and may take provisional measures dictated by that emergency. all this is very well, but it is still necessary to reposition parliament in this system. it will therefore be necessary to provide for a time-limit, at least at the end of the process, for the commission to inform parliament of the decisions it has taken. finally, when the european food authority envisaged in the white paper is in place, what role will it play? on the other hand, care must be taken that this process does not relieve governments, companies or producers of their responsibilities.

in writing. - i voted against the brok report on the enlargement of the european union because, although it is technically clear-sighted, it is based on wrong political views on the future of europe. this report certainly has the merit of giving an idea of the immense task that lies ahead of us if we are to bring the eastern applicant countries not even to the level of development of the west, but only to create conditions for coexistence and gradual rapprochement between the two areas that are not unbalanced for anyone. most of its technical proposals deserve to be strongly supported, for example on food security, the decommissioning of first generation nuclear power stations, environmental protection, the fight against social dumping, the indispensable code of conduct for western companies when working in the east, etc. the task is enormous, and it is also absolutely urgent. if we had to list the reasons for the existence of the european union today, we would put first this great mission of bridging the gap that communism has dug between the two parts of europe. unfortunately, from an institutional point of view, the brok report is completely in line with the brussels ready-to-think: for him, enlargement is about bringing greater europe into the institutions of lesser europe. the trouble is that they're not designed for that, and they're far too narrow. the most inadmissible statements in our view are to be found in the combination of several paragraphs of the resolution voted by the european parliament: first paragraphs 27 et seq., which state that full participation in the single currency, even if not immediate, must be a condition for accession; then paragraph 19, which 'stresses that acceptance of the provisions on economic and monetary union excludes any possibility of exemption and constitutes a commitment to a comprehensive and irreversible political project'. it is unacceptable that participation in the euro is a condition of membership, as several existing members already enjoy derogations. it is even more unacceptable to try to transform this participation into a commitment to a global and irreversible political project. this paragraph alone justifies all the fears that our danish friends have expressed in recent weeks during the referendum campaign, and which justified their 'no' vote. if they had read it in advance, they would probably have voted "no" by 80%, instead of 53%. several other passages in the european parliament's resolution are also inadmissible. for example, paragraph 45 requires that candidate countries grant freedom of acquisition of land to nationals of member countries. this provision poses a very serious problem, given the disparity in purchasing power. this is the kind of difficulty which was taken into account in 1992 in protocol no 1 to the maastricht treaty, when a derogation was granted allowing the danes to maintain their restrictions on the acquisition of second homes by non-residents. here again, it is not clear why derogations which already exist within the union could not be granted to the candidate countries, in their interests. the hegemonic and unifying will of brussels is further evidenced by paragraph 65, which declares that the non-discrimination clause in article 13 of the ec treaty is part of the community acquis, and affirms that 'legislation derived from this article must be fully implemented in the ceecs'. even if we agree with the principles of article 13, it is clear that the secondary legislation drawn up by the european union sometimes goes too far, and that there is no reason to deny the applicant countries a right to cultural differentiation. in our view, the brok report reflects a completely wrong, even dangerous, view of enlargement, which is to impose the ideas, legislation and institutions of the european union in their smallest detail on the eastern european countries unilaterally. on the contrary, we must imagine institutions for a greater europe which, while promoting the development of the east, will allow sovereignty and differences to be expressed. this excellent principle should also apply within the european union.
in writing. - in recent years, the process of european integration has been greatly accelerated. enlargement to the central and eastern european countries (ceecs), cyprus and malta, is described as a 'historic mission' for the european union. this qualification allows us to measure the challenges that are inherent in this process. the enlargement of the union, at least in a first stage, to more than 100 million new citizens will give a new impetus to the development and integration of the european economy as a whole. the accession of new member states will increase the weight and influence of the union on the international scene. at the same time, considerable difficulties remain, particularly in budgetary terms. the first wave of accession could increase the european population by more than a quarter to almost 500 million, while the total gdp of the european union would increase by a maximum of 5%. despite the enormous efforts made by these countries, their integration into existing structures and programmes will be a particularly difficult task. the report we have discussed today is intended to take stock of the progress made in the accession negotiations with all the applicant countries. it encouraged the commission and the council to ensure that the principle of differentiation, as defined in helsinki, is applied to the letter so that each country is judged on its own merits. the candidate countries, on the other hand, must continue their efforts to strengthen their administrative capacity with a view to transposing the acquis communautaire. they are also invited to improve the implementation of effective financial control and audit procedures in order to fully control the use of pre-accession funds. in addition, they could not in any case invoke an opt-out clause in the context of emu. we have many demands on the applicant countries. at the same time, the european union also has responsibilities: it must implement the reforms required by enlargement. the next intergovernmental conference must aim to strengthen the institutional framework of the european union. turning to the budgetary aspect, i think it is essential to examine the budgetary implications of the accession of such a large number of new member states before the end of the current financial framework in 2006. i would like to conclude by stressing that the enlargement process must be carried out gradually, at the same pace as the candidate countries adapt. i therefore, like many of my colleagues, do not think it is wise to set deadlines. i would also like to remind you that this process must not lead us to neglect the cooperation we have undertaken with the countries around the mediterranean!
in writing. - i would like to congratulate our colleague on her outstanding work. the report clearly sets out the challenges and objectives of enlargement in the field of regional policy, both in political and financial terms. it is a report that i would describe as forward-looking and realistic. enlargement to 13 countries not only changes the geopolitical framework of the european union, but also changes its structure, since both the total population will increase (+28%) and the number of 'less favoured' regions will also increase. we have to realize that ! the rapporteur tells us that of the 50 regions in the candidate countries, 48 have a gdp per head currently below 75% of the eu-15 average for the period 1995-97, with only the prague region (119%) and bratislava (96%) exceeding this rate. this shows us once again that the disparities between rich and poor regions are still enormous and that once accession is achieved, these disparities will still exist. it is therefore necessary to ensure that the administrative capacity to absorb appropriations from the structural funds is effective. to do this, the candidate countries need help, particularly through the phare programme. we need a sound and responsible administration, with men and women trained in community techniques and budgetary rules. the report also reminds us of the need to think about new criteria for regional policy for the period 2006-2013. once enlargement has taken place, the logic of a regional policy for 25 countries will not necessarily be the same as that for 15 countries! we must think of a new strategy based on the community development plan (sdec). a global view of the community territory thus seems essential for better regional development. this report puts us in the face of our responsibilities, which is why i voted for it.
in writing. - the european union, since its creation, has been designed to bring people together. although it is difficult to reconcile sensitivities, histories and sometimes contradictions, i believe that enlargement must be part of this logic of peace and contribute to the creation of a community that goes beyond the old geographical and ideological boundaries, guided by common values and rules. however, if europe is not to be reduced to a simple free trade area, the european union must provide a clear answer to the institutional, social and economic questions that enlargement inevitably raises. we must now consider pragmatically the consequences of a europe not of 15 but of 25 or 30. we must respond appropriately to enlargement which will considerably increase the number of disadvantaged regions, and we must think together about the risk of increasing imbalances within the european area in order to avoid europe becoming a vast and heterogeneous whole. we therefore need to use our imagination to reformulate the criteria for granting structural aid in order to ensure that the poorest regions in the candidate countries, but also in the present member states, are adequately supported. i would therefore like to see the outermost regions, six out of seven of which are still among the 10 poorest in the eu, benefiting from the structural funds, not only on the basis of gdp but also on the basis of geographical, demographic and, above all, social indicators. enlargement must not be financed by the poorest. this concept should guide institutional, economic and financial reforms throughout the accession process. only at this price will it be understood and accepted and will the principle of solidarity to strengthen economic and social cohesion within the eu become a reality. the report by mr elmar brok takes account of the concerns i have just expressed to you, and i therefore voted in favour of it.

community acquis. poland also fully respects human rights and fundamental freedoms. progress is also evident in the field of the environment with the implementation of the 'national environmental protection fund' and the application of the 'polluter pays' principle. in the field of external relations, the polish government has paid particular attention to the issue of its borders with the kaliningrad region, lithuania, belarus and ukraine by strengthening institutional and administrative capacities, in particular of the border police. problems remain: according to the commission, commitments. poland is making considerable efforts. the date and the precise terms of accession must be agreed by common accord and not 'conflict-wise'.

in writing. - since 1997, when the mad cow scandal was exposed, our parliament has been calling for the greatest possible attention to be paid to animal feedingstuffs. the commission has already proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the matter. we are particularly keen to implement food security from the barn to the table, or from the fork to the fork, at european level and in a concrete way. the three reports adopted today are a step in the right direction. the prohibition of undesirable substances in animal feed is thus a fundamental element of food safety policy. first, because it is important to set health-tolerable thresholds. secondly, because it is necessary to prohibit the possibility of diluting contaminated food in healthy food in order to make it fit for consumption. for example, hectolitres of milk contaminated with dioxin could be legally diluted in healthy milk. this derogating practice is scandalous in principle: until now, poisoning, provided it is done in homeopathic doses, was legal. in addition, the dilution opens the way to fraud throughout the european territory. the destruction of contaminated food or food compounds offers a double guarantee to limit the trafficking of this type of food. firstly, it is a guarantee of safety for the consumers who will, of course, be the first to benefit from this measure. and secondly, it is a guarantee to farmers and livestock farmers that only healthy food is available on the market. for all these reasons, i voted in favour of the ban on dilution proposed by the european commission. it was also essential to strengthen the harmonization of the conditions for carrying out controls and inspections in the field of animal feed. it's a done deal. i now hope that the council of ministers can move quickly forward and support the amendments we have adopted.

in writing. - i did not vote for the mann report because, while it is indeed necessary to seek equal treatment of persons in matters of employment and work, we should not push the zeal to the point of abandoning all protection of freedoms and all respect for the rule of law. for example, article 9 (1) of the proposed directive provides that 'a person who considers that he has been the victim of a failure to respect equal treatment in his work and who brings a complaint only needs to establish before the court a presumption of discrimination against him'; it is then up to the defendant, i.e. the employer, to prove that the accusation is false. this article has been slightly amended by an amendment of the european parliament which makes it more difficult to read, but does not alter its general orientation. if the directive were to be adopted definitively, it would therefore now be for the accused employer to prove his innocence, and not for the accuser to prove his allegations. the usual principles of the rule of law are thus gradually being changed under the influence of an extremist conception of the fight against discrimination, which the european parliament and the commission are too happy to join in and poke their noses into all national laws. once again, we cannot approve of these deviations, which the draft charter of fundamental rights of the european union will amplify, since, in its current wording, it gives an extensive version of the anti-discrimination clause that the treaty of amsterdam had already introduced into european law.
in writing. - during the negotiations of the amsterdam treaty, we welcomed the inclusion of article 13 on discrimination on grounds of sex, race or ethnic origin, religion or non-sectarian philosophical convictions, disability, age and sexual orientation. such a provision demonstrates the community's commitment to promoting a fairer and more equal society and, above all, it has opened the way for appropriate community action to contribute to the fight against discrimination in general. it complements the community's efforts to promote equality between women and men by tackling new grounds of discrimination. it gives a new and significant impetus to community action in a field where there is a certain legislative acquis and fruitful cooperation with civil society. it is on this basis that measures to combat discrimination have been adopted. the proposals consist of two draft directives (on discrimination in employment and on discrimination on grounds of race and ethnic origin) and an action programme to support member states' efforts. as regards the parallel directive on equal treatment between persons irrespective of race or ethnic origin, the council was able to reach political agreement after the european parliament had reviewed its opinion on the matter. we therefore had to vote on the directive on equal treatment in employment and on the action programme 2001/2006. in explaining my votes, i will first say that the right to equal treatment and protection against discrimination is a fundamental human right. however, this right is far from being translated into reality, hence the need for voluntary and coordinated measures at european level. as regards the mann report on equal treatment in employment, i will simply say that i am satisfied that the possibilities for derogation have been reduced to a minimum. this would open the way to abuses which would be contrary to the objective of the directive. some possibilities are maintained which, i must confess, do not suit me. this is the possibility of derogation in matters of religion. the provision according to which the concept of essential and determining professional requirements concern, as this segment of the population is particularly exposed to discrimination in the field of employment. the commission's proposal for an action programme to combat discrimination was largely satisfactory. there were several gaps or inaccuracies which had to be corrected and which i supported. it seemed to me essential to extend the scope of the programme to ensure the implementation of article 13 of the treaty. i am also very pleased that harassment is now considered a form of discrimination and that prevention of discrimination, not just combating it, has been taken into account. budget for this programme, which is 98.4 million euro, which is of course insufficient in view of the actions envisaged. in conclusion, i supported the spirit of these proposals and voted for them in in writing. - the proposal for a directive on equal treatment in employment and occupation which is before us today responds to a longstanding request from the european parliament, and in particular from our group. it is one of the three components of a package of measures to combat discrimination, based on the new article 13 introduced by the treaty of amsterdam, and is complemented by a community action programme to combat discrimination. these texts thus fill a glaring gap in the construction of europe: the taking into account of the real needs of people excluded or marginalized in our societies because of a disability, their age, their membership of a minority. in this sense, they are participating in the drafting of a europe of men, which we have been calling for too many years. i therefore enthusiastically support the proposal for a directive and the very positive amendments proposed by our rapporteur to improve the effectiveness of this text. i would like to stress in this connection the importance of the amendments which improve the protection of disabled people by clarifying the terms 'reasonable accommodation' and 'unreasonable difficulty' for the employer; which strengthen the prohibition of discrimination against older people who freely choose to continue working (63% of 55-64 year olds are not working in europe); the commission has also proposed that the social partners should be given more autonomy and that the social dialogue should play a more important role in the practical implementation of equal treatment in enterprises. at the same time, the amendment extending the exception to the principle of non-discrimination to the 'social' activities, in the broad sense, of religious organisations, in so far as this is discrimination based solely on religious beliefs and not on any other ground, helps to reinforce the specificity and original contribution of these structures in relation to public or private services. on the other hand, the amendments which provide for the exclusion from public contracts of undertakings which do not respect the principle of equal treatment seem to me to be inappropriate and subject to divergent interpretations. in addition, they open the door to distortions of competition between companies in the various countries of the european union. that is why i wish to express reservations on this point, but i shall vote in favour of the whole text.

in writing. - this third annual report on equal opportunities for women and men in the european union presents the highlights and successes of 1998. it is clear that despite the proclamation of legal equality between women and men, the facts are there to remind us that, unfortunately, discrimination and the difficulties faced by women persist. women are thus more affected by unemployment. the 1998 report looks in particular at the phenomenon of unemployment and the economic impact of women's underemployment. it also analyses the measures implemented to mainstream policies that are strictly focused on women in employment or to limit gender discrimination in employment (e.g. in terms of employment contracts, types of employment and pay). in addition, women often occupy "flexible" positions; temporary contracts or low wages are typical of sectors in which women predominate. women's careers are therefore often unstable, making it difficult for them to gain experience. this is often accompanied by low levels of social protection and precarious living conditions. women are also over-represented in typically 'female' professions but under-represented in positions of responsibility and in the liberal professions. in addition, women and men are unequally divided in sectors such as the information and communication technologies (ict), which are growing rapidly, with women occupying the bottom of the hierarchy. it is therefore imperative to introduce education and training policies specifically targeting young women, in order to restore balance. the gender pay gap is also widespread: available figures for 1995 show that, across the european union, at equal work, the hourly wage of a woman is 73% of that of a man. i therefore fully support the rapporteur's call for the commission to continue its efforts and in particular to strengthen the 'strategic' character of its annual reports by assessing the effectiveness of policy initiatives rather than simply describing them. i also think that we must insist on the implementation of the community acquis on women's rights and equal opportunities in the candidate countries even before they join. i would like to conclude by calling on the member states to continue the dual strategy advocated at community level, namely a strategy of mainstreaming and specific actions for women.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the conditions under which elections were held in peru in may of this year were unacceptable. in this context, the commission had supported the mission of the organization of american states to monitor the implementation of a number of important democratic reforms agreed between the government and the opposition. the european union has just recently issued a statement stressing that president fujimori's decision to call for new elections was an initiative. this initiative can be a significant step towards democracy, but only if he does not run in these elections, as he has announced. the commission has already taken steps to ensure that the european union's financial instruments are used effectively. these are weaknesses that have become apparent in the last elections. if these shortcomings are not eliminated, there is a danger that the next elections will also be extremely questionable. the commission is therefore assisting the organization of american states in continuing its work in accordance with the timetable agreed at the time. and it is doing so despite the difficult conditions and the many uncertainties that are plaguing these new elections. the commission is currently examining with the member states how best to provide practical assistance in the preparation of and, where appropriate, observation of pluralist and democratic elections.
- thank you, commissioner. the joint debate is closed. the vote will take place at 6 p.m.

- is afghanistan doomed to sink into the obscurantism of another age, doomed to slowly suffocate under the taliban yoke, as in the image, it has just been recalled, of its women under the weight of the imposed chadri? how many more deaths, displaced persons, will we have to count to break the veil of our political indifference? how many more tons of drugs injected into the veins of young people all over the world will we have to mourn? will we have to wait for the final installation of state terrorism, the victory of jihad, the implementation of the expansionist will of the madmen of god in the entire region, before finally accepting to involve ourselves, the members of the european union, as is expected of us? the long-running offensive by the taliban, with the open support of pakistan, has now cut off the northern alliance from a vital supply route for their survival. the international community can no longer be reduced to ostrich politics and our diplomacy to wait and see. whatever the errors of the past, i believe i speak for the majority here, in declaring that we reject a comfort neutrality which theorises passivity and justifies blindness. we oppose this neutrality, which tends to place the protagonists on the same level, putting on the same level the daily abuses of the taliban regime and the armed resistance of commander massoud. massoud has an image as a warlord, but how could he be otherwise after so many battles? but to those who know him and have seen him in action, he is also a man of dialogue and association. he wants to be the champion of a tolerant islam. he can be a man of peace. massoud says there is no military solution to the afghan problem; he's right, you know. we must urgently work towards political solutions which respect the values on which our union is founded. the resolution prepared by all the groups, which i have the honour of defending here, is in that direction. it essentially calls on the presidency of the council to use its influence to bring an end to foreign interference in that country. it called on the commission to take stock of the humanitarian aid programmes for the afghan people, so that no one is left behind. finally, and this is the main point, it insists that the european union coordinate its initiatives with those of the neighbouring countries in order to impose a solution which will restore peace, stability and respect for international law and the most basic human rights. we know that the task will not be easy, but i would like to quote the motto of a great european, william of orange: 'it is not necessary to hope to undertake, nor to succeed to persevere.'
- mr president, we are indeed concerned about the recent offensive by the taliban. the suffering associated with this conflict is terrible. so i too, of course, share the proposals in the joint resolution. but, following other colleagues, i want to stress two concerns. the first concern is the situation of women. don't get used to it. let's not trivialize it. they are still subjected to appalling conditions, with denial of access to employment, health care and education. they live in destitution, in permanent insecurity. they are regularly stoned. they're muzzled, literally. all afghan women, regardless of age, face a systematic violation of their most basic rights. i think that the commission should be able to take the necessary steps to ensure that the right of asylum is guaranteed to all those who are in need of it. the european union must renew its solidarity with all those afghan women who are fighting the taliban regime at home and abroad. secondly, because of the control they now have over almost all of afghanistan, it is clear that the taliban are seeking international recognition. so only a political solution can restore peace, stability and respect for human rights. yes, we need a greater involvement of the european union. and in this search i think it is imperative that the council reinforce the restrictive measures it has decided on. there can be no recognition by any member state as long as the policy of human rights violations, including systematic discrimination against women, is maintained. the commission should also take much more urgent humanitarian measures for the people, and should do everything possible to ensure that ngos can provide assistance to afghan women and involve them in their activities.
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the current escalation of the armed conflict between the taliban and the northern alliance is a cause for great concern. more and more people are fleeing the fighting. the number of displaced persons is estimated by some sources at 90,000. many of them are now seeking refuge in makeshift camps in the mountains of the northeast. conditions there can deteriorate dramatically as winter approaches. in view of these developments, echo, the commission's humanitarian aid office, is currently working hard to put together an emergency aid package worth €3 million to assist the displaced with medical supplies, food and wintering equipment. in addition, echo has already provided eur 5.7 million this year for the victims of drought in afghanistan, for mine clearance in the north of the country and for the resettlement of refugees. the drought victims are to receive another 3 million soon. i would like to say at this point, in relation to mrs paciotti's remarks, that i will of course ask the commission today what has happened and what should happen with the mine clearance funds. if there are, as you say, bureaucratic obstacles, i promise you that i will do everything to overcome these obstacles as quickly as possible. the commission is also committed to the long-term well-being of afghan refugees and internally displaced persons. between 1991 and 2000, the commission has provided a total of eur 400 million for refugee assistance, emergency humanitarian aid and food aid. a significant part of this was allocated to mine clearance and related intelligence activities by un agencies, european or afghan non-governmental organisations. the european union supports the un special mission in afghanistan and the peace efforts of the special representatives of the secretary-general through its common position on afghanistan. the union is determined to make an effective contribution to the restoration of peace and stability in the country, and it is clear that peace and stability in that country will only be achieved if human rights and fundamental values are fully respected. the common position also condemns the continuing discrimination against afghan women and other human rights violations in the country. as long as the taliban leadership remains as ambiguous as ever on the control of opium production, the commission will not support any anti-drug projects in afghanistan. however, it will strongly support neighbouring countries in improving their capacity to combat drugs.

high representative for the common foreign and security policy. - madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i apologize for coming a little late for reasons which are well known to the honourable members, to make a brief statement on the two items on the agenda: the situation in belgrade, and in the former yugoslav republic in general, and the situation in the middle east. unfortunately, i cannot say anything positive about either of these issues tonight. the situation in serbia: i will start with the very latest news. as you know, there are now about a million people on the streets of belgrade and the news coming in is of a rising tension. the decision taken by the constitutional court, from the point of view of the european union, seems to me to be, once again, a violation of all the basic principles of a country which must have free elections. the decision taken by the constitutional court has consisted in stealing the votes and freedom of citizens who voted freely and who obtained a majority. i want to say to you, on behalf of the european union and the council, that we regard professor kostunica as the leader of the majority of the serbian people and that it is him we will support and continue to support. we believe that he has won the elections, that his people have won the elections and that he deserves the support of all of us. (applause) i do not hide from you that the situation is not easy, and that we will experience moments of some tension in the coming days, but we must have enough cool blood, on the part of everyone, so that the situation does not turn into a serious conflict. i would also like to say that the european union is putting in place the mechanisms so that when the popular will of the serbian people is respected, that is to say, when we have a government supported by the people who voted for mr kostunica at the polls, we can have: first, an immediate lifting of sanctions and, secondly, an economic aid package that can help the serbian people to rebuild their economy. there is an important subject which i would also like to discuss with the honourable members, and on which i had the opportunity to speak with mr kofi annan, with whom i met for three hours this morning. as you know, there is still the problem of who is the successor state of the former yugoslav republic. that is a problem that is not solved and, until that problem is solved, the international financial institutions - the international monetary fund and the world bank - will not be able to help democratic serbia. we must therefore also work with the countries of the former yugoslavia within the framework of the united nations to find an agreement as soon as possible which will enable economic aid - via the international monetary fund and the world bank - to be unblocked when serbia is finally free. i want to tell you - as you know - that the presidency has organized a summit in zagreb, which we hope will be a summit with the participation of a democratic republic of the former yugoslavia, and that we want to build together a stable, prosperous, forward-looking region in the balkans with a european perspective. (applause) that's all i can tell you right now. surely, if the session lasts long, we'll have more information. but i do say to them - and i think we must stand firm on this - that president milosevic has robbed his people of their freedom. and that is what we must say and do everything possible so that it does not happen again. (applause) i have been asked by the honourable members to give them information on the latest developments in the middle east and unfortunately i cannot give them optimistic news either. i can give you news of the optimism of the will, but not really the optimism of the intelligence. the situation is not easy. we must all make an effort to reduce the tension in that area which is so dear to us and to bring the negotiations back to the table, or else the parties must return to the negotiating table. those of us who have lived it with all our intensity, participating throughout the summer in a good number of meetings which have brought about the closeness, the closeness that has never been between the two sides, we see with much greater sadness today, still, people and families broken, people suffering and dying in the streets of those beloved countries. i want to tell you that yesterday, all day long, the french presidency - (applause from the centre) i would like to make a few remarks on the dramatic, rapidly changing situation in the middle east. we feel deep sorrow and sympathy for the many victims. the majority of the victims of the newly flared conflicts in recent days have been palestinians. we condemn in the strongest terms the disproportionate and indiscriminate use of force. we condemn all acts of provocation, especially those against the holy sites in jerusalem. we welcome and support the efforts of president chirac, president mubarak and foreign minister albright and express the hope that the all-important objective of ending the violence and restoring calm and order will be achieved. the commission supports the presidency's position on the commission of inquiry. it is clear that this
