alternative for israel and the palestinian people. a just and comprehensive peace, even if it requires painful compromises on both sides. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial resources are used to the full. anything else would be a terrible tragedy. the negotiations should build on the progress made at camp david in july. the european council in brussels on 14 and 15 december adopted a resolution on the situation in the middle east. but camp david was not a failure either, as the gap between the parties was significantly reduced and some difficult taboo issues were overcome. the european union's position on the substance of the peace process has not changed. we support the parties in negotiating an agreement which is consistent with the principles and framework of the peace process launched in madrid. we are convinced that a compromise can be found on all points of dispute. we are also prepared to do our part to help. if the parties succeed, as we hope, in reaching an agreement, the european union will, in addition to the efforts being made by the other side, provide its political and financial support on the basis of fair burden-sharing and will respond to the parties' demands within a reasonable framework. we are ready to work to ensure stability in the region and, in the long term, sustainable prosperity in the region through sustained economic growth and improved living conditions, so that the dividends of peace benefit the people of the region. this philosophy is fully in line with the strengthening of the euro-mediterranean barcelona process, within which we will continue our efforts.

- mr president, on behalf of the green group, i should like to begin by congratulating and thanking mrs van lancker on the quality of her report, both in terms of its content and in terms of the way it was drafted, which she has endeavoured to make very participative. this term, which appears technical, covers the everyday realities of our citizens. the aim is both to respond to the urgency and to put into practice what is known as the european 'social model'. we cannot afford to miss this deadline, unless we are to discourage the expectations of all citizens and the collective movements they have formed, who are the most mobilized for the constitution of a european union as a community of citizens. the list of issues to be dealt with is self-evident in responding to the urgency, in conforming our actions to the speeches made at the lisbon summit. it is about giving european citizens the tools and public policies they need to build their place in europe, to ensure that their fundamental rights - including social rights - are guaranteed. the social emergency and the preservation of the european social model call for initiatives to establish rights to an income, a wage and decent pensions for all in the european union. the implementation of the social ambitions set out in lisbon calls for a community effort, an action plan for the creation of jobs in services, particularly those linked to the information society. in this respect, the directive proposed in the report is essential to guarantee the social protection of new forms of work. it is also important to guarantee quality health, an enriched social life, an improved environment for all - the third system - and fiscal and legislative measures are essential to ensure both the economic sustainability and the visibility of this emerging solidarity economy. we agree with anne van lancker and mrs péry when they propose to adopt quickly the 1998 directive on information and consultation of workers and to revise the directive on european works councils. the basic concern for the general interest should also lead us all to approve the proposal to include employment-related considerations in merger regulations and decisions, which are now dictated by competition. these three examples of fighting poverty, supporting the development of activities that create jobs, social cohesion and quality of life, and improving the rights of workers should mobilise an assembly that is concerned to make europe a dream for citizens who today too often feel that it is a machine that trades all human activities. several amendments reflect the fear of some of our colleagues who take out their erasers when they read the word 'legislation'. will they explain to the citizens that parliament considers it necessary to vote directives to protect investment, to liberalize services of general interest, but not to qualify and regulate what is called the labour market here? this refusal to legislate leads to a refusal to negotiate at all, since one amendment goes so far as to propose to abolish the objective of concluding european collective agreements between the social partners. it is in this context that we should look for the archaism blamed on those who do not expect the best of the worlds from an unhampered market.
- mr president, for almost half a century the construction of europe has been based on the economy. we were talking about the european economic community. the construction of the common market was given priority: the principle of free movement of goods, merchandise and capital, the introduction of rules governing competition between firms and state aid. the social sector acted as a corrector for the most harmful effects of economic policies. the provisions of the treaty of rome were limited to the principle of equal pay for men and women (article 141) and the free movement of workers. the with the continuation of the convergence strategy in the field of social protection. this is a genuine catalogue which is more a declaration of intent than a medium-term project. in conclusion, the mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by expressing my deep disagreement with the overly liberal, if not ultra-liberal, approach to the report by mr evans. to deny that state aid decreased during the period 1994-1998, when the commission itself acknowledges this decrease, was curious to say the least. but more serious is the fact that he is almost obsessively insisting on the exceptional nature of state aid, when the treaty itself provides for such aid when it comes to achieving objectives set by the treaties themselves, such as the environment or social cohesion, and when the european commission itself recognises that certain policies cannot be supported by market forces alone. and although i can support the demands for greater transparency in state aid and for parliament to be informed about the monitoring of aid approved by the commission, i continue to advocate the maintenance of state aid to develop social cohesion, research, innovation, environmental protection, to overcome market failures, to promote european competitiveness vis-à-vis the outside world, to counter fraudulent practices by competing countries, as is the case with korea in shipbuilding. i would add that the control of state aid must be carried out strictly within the framework of the provisions of the treaties and not according to the dominant liberal ideology. between the no-state, which no one wants any more, and the no-state at all, which is only the modern form of the law of the strongest, what many call the european social model requires us to be constantly searching for a balance between what can be regulated by the market and what the public authorities must regulate.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we have decided to postpone this report because we want the work of our parliament to be consistent in order to influence the direction of european policies. the revision of the gmo directive 90/220 is currently being conciliated. it would be perfectly consistent to wait until this procedure is completed before incorporating references to gmos in our directives and regulations. that is why, on a proposal from your rapporteur for an opinion, the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection voted unanimously to remove the references to gmos from this report. and let no one tell us that we are talking about the wrong subject, that this revision has no consequences for gmos, because such a regulation already exists for the forest. we drink wine, but we don't eat the wood from our forests yet. contrary to what the executive committee and the committee on agriculture would have us believe, this revision insinuates the irreparability of genetically modified vine plants. this clearly means that the european parliament would indirectly give its green light to experimenting with gmos in the propagation or improvement of vine plants. why the rush ? neither the vinedressers nor the merchants nor the owners of the vineyards ask for it. on 5 july, some of them launched the beaune appeal, expressing their deep concern at the introduction of gmos into their profession. the confederation of producers of wine with a controlled designation of origin replies: we support the position of the committee on the environment, because it provides assurance that the european regulation will not allow the introduction of procedures authorizing the sale of genetically modified wine-growing material which could damage the image of viticulture. who will benefit from this amended regulation incorporating gmos? - the previous directive proved its relevance and effectiveness by first allowing a standardization of products, and a substantial development of intra-community trade in wood and vine plants in recent years. it is now necessary to revise it in the light of changes in plant health regulations and scientific and technical progress, in particular in in vitro propagation. the draft text which has been presented to us by the european commission, as amended by the committee on agriculture of the european parliament, proposes some interesting developments, of which i shall mention the most significant here. the current draft thus abolishes any possibility for the fifteen to derogate unilaterally from the provisions of the directive. this provision, which was not provided for in the original version of the directive, is desirable as it will avoid barriers to trade and facilitate the movement of reproductive material within the union. the 1968 directive did not, of course, apply to material produced by the now well-established in vitro herbal breeding techniques. the new text introduces provisions recognising the specific features; if the search for more hygienically efficient propagating material is desirable for the user, it is important that this orientation does not create a barrier to trade. the amendment proposal to guarantee the free marketing throughout the union of equipment which complies with the minimum requirements of the directive should therefore be approved without reservation. finally, as regards the new provisions on genetically modified varieties, it is necessary to ensure that they are fully consistent and compatible with the existing texts or those under discussion in this field. since this regulatory framework needs to be further supplemented and clarified, it would be preferable to delete the provisions relating to this point in the draft directive. the new or updated provisions of the proposed directive can be considered to meet satisfactorily the expectations of professionals in the wine nursery and viticulture sector and should contribute to improving the quality of the equipment offered and facilitate the control of trade in wood and vine seedlings by the institutions responsible for these tasks. the rules laid down in the new rules also favour the production of a wide variety of plant material by offering the best health guarantees, which is essential if the restructuring of the community vineyard, a key point of the new wine-growing cmo, is to be effectively supported.

the commission mr president, i thank the committee on agriculture and rural development and the rapporteur, mrs klaß, for the very positive attitude they have shown towards the commission's proposal. the commission welcomes the broad agreement on its proposal. its purpose is to strengthen the internal market in the specific sector, to update the legislation in the light of technical and scientific progress in the meantime and, in the case of genetically modified varieties, to ensure that they can only be authorised after appropriate measures have been taken to avoid harmful effects on human health and the environment. as regards the third point, the proposal currently contains references both to the development of a specific procedure for the assessment of environmental risks, equivalent to that provided for in directive 90/220 for risks to man and the environment, and to the criteria and principles of assessment provided for in regulation (ec) no 258/97 on novel foods and novel food ingredients. the committee on agriculture and rural development has tabled 26 amendments. the commission can accept most of them, i.e. 24 out of 26, as they are formulated or with slight changes to the way they are drafted or presented. for example, in the case of the proposal for recognition of genotype specificity, to which amendments nos 4, 12, 15, 16 and 20 refer, the suggestion will be accepted by a different wording of the text. the genetic diversity of varieties with genotypes adapted to certain local environments will be taken into account in its entirety when discussing whether to maintain the possibility of marketing the propagating material of such varieties, in accordance with article 3 (5) (a) of the directive. as regards the other two amendments, nos 2 and 18, we can only accept them partially because some of them are unjustifiably aggressive towards other countries - amendment no 2 - or because the reference to the obligation for the commission to provide more resources in the case of the establishment of a common catalogue of varieties - amendment no 18 - is not necessary. finally, we can accept amendment no 27, which was tabled by mr lavarra and mr garot. i am pleased to inform you that we can also accept amendments nos 35 to 40 tabled by mr graefe zu baringdorf, which seek to strengthen the transposition of the safety and management requirements under directive 90/220. we cannot accept amendments nos 28 to 34 tabled by mr isler-béguin and others, because they would mean the deletion of the whole part of the directive containing references to gm varieties and the associated risk assessment. these amendments were already discussed but not accepted by the committee on agriculture. we cannot accept amendment no 41 tabled by mr schierhuber either, because it concerns an overly detailed definition in the light of the amendments proposed by the committee on agriculture. accepting this amendment would risk creating artificial barriers to trade, which would be contrary to the main purpose of the proposed directive, namely the consolidation of the internal market. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i thank you for your attention and i thank the committee on agriculture and rural development once again.

the rapporteur. - mr president, first of all i would like to thank jacques, jacques delors, altiero spinelli and fernand herman, and everyone from vaclav havel to carlo ciampi, joschka fischer to jacques chirac, michel barnier to pierre moscovici, chris patten to costa simitis, florence and the many members of the european parliament who have taken up the great movement for a european constitution since 1999. thanks from jo and giorgio to iñigo, from dany to frassoni, from richard to elmar, from bayrou to andrew. thanks to all of you, a new idea is moving forward on the european continent: that of the european constitution. a new idea for europe, an old idea at the very root of modernity, the idea of the constitution connects us to the most profound debates on democracy. on our right, joseph de maistre, the counter-revolutionary thinker, denounced and ridiculed the very idea of a constitution, because the constitution is made, horror! by men and, illusion, for man. "but man does not exist", he said, adding that he had met spaniards, frenchmen, perhaps even persians, but "man, i have never met him. if there is, it is unknown to me". on our left, karl marx, the revolutionary thinker, denounced and ridiculed the very idea of human rights, because, according to him, abstract man does not exist, and humanity cannot constitute anything. at the beginning of the 21st century, these two types of criticism are still being made and sometimes they are joined together. the crimes and barbarities committed by men are also joined in the denials of the person. but what the 20th century has taught us is that by seeing only french, germans, danes, irish, jews, arabs, hutus, tutsis, serbs, bosnians and persians everywhere, we end up forgetting their common humanity. without this fundamental benchmark, at best we don't understand each other, at worst we kill each other. the british and the irish, the serbs and the croats, the israelis and the palestinians, the citizens of here and there can only exist if there is a pre-existence of the human being. if you take away their humanity to leave them only their nationality, they are lost because they have lost the person. they don't accept the other because they see the same. they only see the enemy now. they're destroying themselves. the european community was born out of the refusal to destroy, as you know. fifty-five years without a war ! in strasbourg we know how important this record is. we want to extend this advantage to the western part of europe. enlargement will ensure that. with peace assured, western europe went about its business in search of prosperity. let us not be too critical of the market europe, and a socialist will tell you this: it has given us more wealth for all. but the european union is more than a single market. it has other aims, proclaimed in its treaties: european integration, freedom, democracy, human rights, the rule of law, fundamental social rights. peace, prosperity, democracy, justice, each in its own way, are what almost all members and groups in this parliament want, and what the majority of members and groups want is for europe and by europe. democracy is better in europe. thirty years ago, the great countries of the south were suffering under dictatorships and the east was surviving under the soviet yoke. today we have just witnessed one of the last democratic revolutions in europe: the october 2000 revolution in serbia. and we know that after tomorrow, democratic serbia will join us. what better proof of the european ideal than this link between the conquest of democracy and entry into the great community family! democracy is better off in europe, but european democracy is sick. one in two european citizens did not vote in the june 1999 elections. we're not the ones who'll forget. one in two of my students don't know who romano prodi is, while almost all of them know michael schumacher or monica lewinsky. that is to say, the decadence of politics in general and the distance between the european institutions and the citizens. some people accept it or even welcome it. we're not the ones. that is why we want a stronger european democracy, a european constitution. what's today? almost everything, but nothing at all. seven treaties, hundreds of articles, an inextricable tangle of norms, wishes, rules, procedures, the essential and the secondary. the european constitution exists, but no one has met it. it is untraceable, invisible, unreadable, unintelligible. we want a real constitution. let us at least agree on that objective, and since we do, let us say how we can achieve it. parliament proposes a two-stage path, with two stages: the reorganization of the treaties, the rapid stage, and the adoption of a constitution, the gradual stage. the report proposes these two steps. they should be hired as soon as possible, because it is possible. before it is over, there should be a european referendum, because this is the dream we need. in any case, don't kill him today. if we want to, we can, we citizens, parliamentarians, governments of the european union. today, 24 october 2000, in strasbourg, the european parliament says a simple thing and says it loudly: the european constitution, yes, you can, yes, we want it. in writing. - behind the confused wording of this text there is the outline of a series of measures all of which are detrimental to workers. what does the phrase 'the period within which member states are required to guarantee the unemployed a chance of gaining employment must not exceed two years' mean, if not a threat to unemployment benefits? what does the 'introduction of the possibility of gradual retirement through parttime work' mean, if not a threat to the already far too high retirement age in many countries? there is no ambiguity in the repeated calls for flexibility to be extended. the passage on work experience, apprenticeship and employment-training contracts is intended to extend what many states are already doing, namely, under the pretext of helping workers or unemployed young people, to make available to employers a partly or totally subsidised workforce. the report recommends what many states already do, namely "the co-financing of tax and para-tax burdens by the authorities" of "domestic work", which means in plain english that taxpayers should subsidize the maids and chauffeurs that the wealthy owners are likely to hire. such texts confirm that the role of the european institutions, including parliament, is to serve a small class of owners.
in writing. - we voted for mr maccormick's report on the maintenance of mr pacheco pereira's parliamentary immunity. not that we think that the purpose of immunity is to place the parliamentarian above the law, but because it is, in some cases, necessary to protect the institution and the independence of its members from persecution. many of us have noted in the report, page 8, section ii, paragraph d, the very important development on the autonomy of european parliamentary immunity in relation to national parliamentary immunity. it is because parliamentary immunity is autonomous that our institution has a power of assessment as to the requests that are made, and in particular as to the fumus persecutionis. but if we are competent to assess requests for waiver, how much more competent are we to assess violations of parliamentary immunity when they are violated without such a request being made! if the european parliamentary immunity is autonomous, the french authorities should have informed us of the lifting of mr le pen's immunity. we should have considered the extravagant misuse of the concept of flagrant crime by these authorities. the french cour de cassation and the conseil d'état should have referred a question to the cour de justice of luxembourg for a preliminary ruling before giving judgment. and in the absence of these essential formalities, our president would obviously have had to refuse to have any effect on the mandate of our colleague from a criminal proceeding initiated under conditions which render it absolutely null and void. this is the legal path which our parliament should follow if it is to be consistent with its principles and jurisprudence, as well as with the spirit and the letter of the treaties. many of us here would like to hear this from the luxembourg court, the guardian of the law.

in writing. - the explanatory memorandum of this report is to be credited with the unvarnished assertion that 'competition policy is unquestionably one of the most important policies of the european union'. it's actually a mild euphemism. the european institutions are only meant to try to set some rules for competition. even regulated, it remains the law of the jungle where, no matter which industrial or financial groups prevail, the consumers of the lower classes and the workers of these groups are always the victims. it is significant that in state aid to enterprises it is only the 'distortion of competition' which worries the rapporteur and not the fact that such aid always means emptying the pockets of the majority of the population to help large enterprises to produce private profit for their shareholders. as regards mergers, which the rapporteur wants the commission to take stock of, it would be useful for the balance sheet not only to describe the competitive advantages and the additional profits that companies derive from them, but also to indicate how many redundancies they have led to. all the mergers authorized by the brussels commission have resulted in restructuring, i.e. job cuts. and while they have paid the shareholders of the companies concerned, they have been paid dearly by their workers, their families and society as a whole.
in the debate last night, while i was able to commend jonathan evans for his work, i had to say at the outset that i deeply disagreed with the overly liberal, if not ultra-liberal, impregnation of his report. not only did mr evans deny that state aid decreased during the period 1994-98 when the commission itself recognised this decrease, but, more seriously, he persisted in obsessively insisting on the exceptional nature of state aid, when the treaty provides for such aid when it comes to achieving objectives which the treaties themselves set, such as the environment and social cohesion, and when the commission itself recognises that certain policies cannot be supported by market forces alone. that is why i recommended last night not to support this report as it stands. although i was able to join the european parliament's calls for greater transparency of state aid and information on the monitoring of aid approved by the commission, i argued for the maintenance of state aid to develop social cohesion, research and innovation or environmental protection, to address market failures, to promote european competitiveness vis-à-vis the rest of the world and to counter fraudulent practices by competing countries (such as korea in shipbuilding). i added that the control of state aid should be carried out strictly within the framework of the provisions of the treaties and not according to the dominant liberal ideology. in my view, between the 'any state' which no one wants any more and the 'no state at all' which is only the modern form of the 'law of the strongest', what many call the european social model requires us to be constantly seeking a balance between what can be governed by the market and what the public authorities must regulate! that is why i supported and voted for the amendments tabled by the socialist group. the right wing has beaten them to a pulp, so i did not vote for the report in question.

foreign ships entering their ports to verify that they comply with community and international legislation on maritime safety, protection of the marine environment and living and working conditions. - ladies and gentlemen, fifty years after the start of the construction of europe, it is time for the union to finally have a supervisory authority to protect citizens from the potential abuses associated with the proliferation of computer files containing personal data. the exponential growth of the union's tasks and competences, as well as the multiplication of community bodies, make it essential to define precisely the rights of citizens in law, including the flow of information between the union's institutions and bodies. it is on the basis of article 286 of the treaty that the council has proposed a draft regulation to parliament under the codecision procedure. this article states that data protection in the union was to be effective as from 1 january 1999. almost two years later, we have not succeeded, which also obliges us not to get bogged down in a long codecision procedure, which would further delay the implementation of this mechanism. that is what mrs paciotti has done, and i really think that our rapporteur has done an absolutely remarkable job. let's get to the heart of the matter. the main bone of contention between parliament and the council is the scope of the future supervisory authority. should it be limited to the first pillar, namely purely community bodies, institutions and legal standards, or should it cover all the provisions which fall within the union's remit, namely the second and third pillars, such as schengen or europol? we are clear: the risks associated with the protection of citizens' privacy and the misuse of personal data concerning them are much greater under the third pillar, which is now little or not subject to judicial and parliamentary control, than under the first pillar, which is the jurisdiction of the court of justice. it is clear to me that it would be a travesty to create such an authority for the community alone, when the main problems are, and will be in the future, also coming from the third pillar bodies. for example, is it known that the schengen system has collected more than ten million files concerning nearly one and a half million citizens, that europol is constantly expanding its powers, that it centralises information from the various police services of the fifteen member states, and that this is done under the sole control of an authority which has neither the powers nor the means to enable it to carry out any other task? the report we are about to adopt does not reflect this ambition. the scope of the resulting regulation is limited to the first pillar, namely article 286. the second and third pillars will not be covered by this regulation and will therefore remain opaque, to the detriment of the basic fundamental rights of citizens. in addition to the limited reading of article 286, it would have been possible to take article 255 of the treaty as an additional legal basis for the extension of the scope of the regulation. mrs paciotti made a good attempt to do this by including a reference to this article in article 12 of the regulation, but the council refused to consider this possibility. many other points also raise problems and deserve the judgment of practice to be assured. finally, our rapporteur is well aware of these problems and is careful not to add two more years to the delay already made. we shall therefore nevertheless support it, in the hope that the council and the commission in particular will be careful not to exploit the weaknesses of the text in an attempt to empty it of its substance. they should also seek to implement personal data protection tools in the second and third pillars as soon as possible. it is dangerous to allow bodies such as europol or the schengen system to develop without parliamentary and judicial control.
the commission is aware of the fact that the european parliament has been asked to make a statement on the subject of the protection of personal data. we are almost two years behind the deadline set in article 286 of the treaty establishing the european community, which is why it is urgent to reach agreement on this matter. the council, at the decisive instigation of the presidency, has succeeded in overcoming the difficulties raised by some delegations, so that the proposal for a regulation is likely to be the subject of unanimous agreement by the council. for its part, the european parliament has shown great determination to allow a decision at first reading, and i would like to express my appreciation and my thanks to your rapporteur, mrs paciotti, who has spared no effort, with the support of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, to facilitate this agreement. by taking the council's work as a starting point and by encouraging the emergence of a solution acceptable to the three institutions on the question of the scope of the regulation, mrs paciotti has very largely paved the way for an agreement at first reading. the commission, for its part, has also played its role of initiator and mediator between the council and parliament. it is also determined not to delay the adoption of an important instrument for the protection of citizens' personal data. while not entirely satisfied with the result achieved, it decided to adopt the text resulting from the discussions in the council and parliament as reflected in the paciotti report and will therefore reject any further amendments to its original proposal. the commission's position on the amendments contained in the paciotti report is as follows. amendments nos 1, 2, 4 to 10, 12 to 40, 42 to 54, 57, 58 and 60 to 64 take up the council's text where the commission can agree. it therefore accepts these amendments. amendments nos 55, 56 and 59 are different from the council text, but they have been the subject of political agreement between the rapporteur and the council presidency. the commission has decided not to oppose the adoption of the regulation at first reading on the basis of this compromise text and accepts the amendments. amendments nos 3 and 11 are not in line with the council's text, but they have been the subject of political agreement between the rapporteur and the council presidency. the commission decided not to prevent the adoption of the regulation at first reading on the basis of this compromise text, provided that a statement maintaining its legal position on the council's approval of the regulation was entered in the minutes. by this declaration, the commission will accept that the scope of the regulation is limited to the activities of the first pillar only. it will also stress the need to subject the processing of personal data under the second and third pillars to clear legal rules. the commission believes that these rules could be adopted on the basis of article 286. it will therefore reserve the right to submit legislative initiatives to this effect. in addition, it will reserve the right to subject the processing of personal data by it under the second and third pillars to the principles contained in the regulation until rules for such processing are established. as regards amendment no 41, the commission considers that its wording is not compatible with its right of initiative. it therefore rejects this amendment. amendment no 69 is a corrigendum to amendment no 41. it was tabled by the rapporteur, mrs paciotti, in consultation with the commission and the council presidency, with a view to preserving the commission's right of initiative. the commission supports this amendment and i would like to thank mrs paciotti for introducing it. the european data protection supervisor will play a leading role in ensuring that the community institutions comply with the provisions protecting the personal data of citizens. it is therefore clear that its opinion on legislative proposals concerning the protection of personal data will be very valuable as it will constitute an important contribution to the legislative debate between the institutions. it is also clear that the commission, when drawing up such legislative proposals, must have the freedom to make the appropriate proposal at the time it deems appropriate. amendment no 69 seems acceptable to the commission in so far as its wording does not imply a challenge to its right of initiative. the commission therefore understands this amendment as imposing the obligation to consult the controller after the adoption of its proposal. it would be helpful to clarify the text in this sense, perhaps when the language is revised. in any event, the commission will make a statement to that effect when the regulation is adopted by the council. in order to honour the political agreement it has reached with the council and the rapporteur to allow approval at first reading, the commission rejects any other amendments which would not form part of the paciotti report as approved by the parliamentary committee on civil liberties and rights, with the exception of amendment no 69 which corrects amendment no 41.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by thanking the members of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, whose reflections and amendments have enriched the report i am presenting to you this evening. the present and future fate of the seven outermost regions of europe has given our committee the opportunity to unanimously adopt a constructive, balanced and long-consulted document. the azores, the canaries, guadeloupe, french guiana, madeira, martinique and réunion form a special group whose uniqueness was recognised by the treaty of amsterdam on the basis of an innovative concept, the ultraperiphery. the treaty recognises the difficult economic and social situation of the outermost regions, aggravated by particular handicaps, the persistence and combination of which seriously hampers the development of these regions. for this reason, the existing rules should be extended as far as possible and appropriate measures adopted to solve the specific problems of the regions concerned, with the use of derogations adapted to the regional situation in question, if necessary, without this representing a threat to the community interest. the report published by the european commission on 14 march does not, strictly speaking, respond to the requests made by the national and regional authorities of the outermost regions. the commission states that it is not in a position to provide answers to all the questions; the commission's role is to provide a framework for the development of the community's action in the field of education and training. article 299 (2) expresses above all a political will, supported on several occasions by the european council and now by our parliament. my report's main objective is to remind the european commission of this political will so that it will no longer give the unpleasant impression of reluctance or inertia that it currently gives. it is therefore urgent that the inter-service group be reinforced very quickly at the heart of the general secretariat of the commission, so that all proposals for acts of general scope can be accompanied, when examined by the college on the basis of article 299 (2), by a detailed impact statement. my report calls on the commission to draw up a genuine multiannual work programme with a precise timetable, summarizing as fully as possible the measures it is planning and providing all the necessary guarantees in terms of resources to ensure the viability of the measures and the permanence of the action to combat permanent handicaps. to dispel any misunderstanding about the commission's lack of readiness to make full use of the possibilities offered by article 299 (2), i propose that a wider forum of dialogue could meet and that a report be drawn up each year. in reply to the commission, my report deals specifically with a number of areas of union competence which i shall merely review tonight. the commission has recognised that measures in the agricultural and fisheries sectors need to be adapted or improved. but the second revision of the posei regulations is taking place in an extremely difficult budgetary context which is likely to have a very heavy impact on the content of the programmes and on the level of aid. for example, the commission has proposed a scandalous reduction in the financial envelope for the posei in its draft budget for 2001, which is causing a very strong wave of concern among the many farmers in the outermost regions, whose voice i am interpreting here. in addition, coordination and optimum use of all existing instruments at community level, in particular the structural funds, state aid and fiscal and customs policies, should be strengthened. the success of the new community strategy for the outermost regions requires action geared to the strategic areas of global competition: transport, energy, the environment, the information society, research and technological development. it will thus contribute to promoting economic and social progress through a high level of employment. the geographical location and maritime space of the outermost regions must enable them to become the active frontiers of the european union. however, it is urgent to begin an analysis of the impact of the new acp-eu partnership agreement signed in cotonou last june, as well as other international trade agreements, in order to assess their impact on the outermost regions and to define compensatory measures for the outermost producers who would face additional competition which would be intolerable for them. finally, to conclude on a subject which concerns our immediate future, the enlargement process is undoubtedly an essential part of european construction, but it is urgent to undertake an assessment of its consequences now in order to prevent any change in the aid duly granted to the outermost regions and the measures resulting from the implementation of article 299 (2).
- mr president, commissioner, madam rapporteur, if we are debating today in this house the ultraperipheral regions, we must remember that this is the result of a slow maturation. although the treaty of rome already referred to the french overseas departments, it was not until 1989 and the programmes of specific options linked to remoteness and insularity, the so-called posei, that the european union finally accepted that the permanence and combination of the structural handicaps of the outermost regions justified special treatment in relation to the other regions of the community. eight years later, the treaty of amsterdam, with its article 299 (2), which we are discussing, gave rise to the hope that one day the words 'growth' and 'employment' would have the same meaning throughout the european territory. the wait has therefore been long and the hope expressed by our people is commensurate with that wait. i am therefore allowed to say that i was somewhat disappointed when i read the commission's communication. my dear colleagues, this is no longer the time for declarations of good intentions. we need concrete measures and they must come quickly. we need a specific timetable, - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, europe is regularly shaken by serious public health crises. these crises, like bse and dioxin, have become a real social problem and are leading to a loss of consumer confidence in their food. the recent news has reminded us of this. the member states have taken action, as in the case of france, which has set up a national food safety agency. the european commission is today proposing the creation of a european food safety authority to analyse any risk to public health. good scientific knowledge is certainly essential to better assess the risks associated with the food chain, from fork to fork. any initiative to increase awareness of these risks is therefore a good one. but isn't that the other way around? as is often the case, the commission proposes to regulate in order to eliminate or reduce the harmful consequences of a policy for which it is often jointly responsible, without in any way calling into question its major guidelines. the european requirements for traceability, which are good measures, are all the more necessary now that we have abandoned internal or community border controls. the european union is also trying to protect biodiversity and safeguard ecosystems through the habitats and birds directives, without calling into question agricultural productivity, which is well known to be the main cause, along with urbanisation, of imbalances in ecosystems. it is precisely this productivism that increases food risks: the specialisation of farms, the majority of which are intensive farmers, the need to align themselves with the prices of the american market and thus the search for the lowest cost, especially for animal feed, transport, sometimes long distance, the different elements of the food chain from farm to table are all risk factors for public health, but we would rather cure the disease than prevent it from occurring. the european food safety authority, in these circumstances, nevertheless has an important role to play in the field of scientific risk analysis. but let us be careful to leave it to the member states to manage these risks and to apply the precautionary principle in a reasonable and proportionate manner. it will be a guarantee of efficiency. indeed, who better than the states to carry out adequate proximity checks? who better than the states to distinguish between products which are truly dangerous and those which are part of our various food crops, even when they do not present zero health risks? this zero risk does not exist and is in any case undesirable, as asepsis is not a guarantee of food safety. finally, who better than the states can inform the public about the risks of a particular product? let us therefore entrust the european food safety authority with the sole scientific experience, in liaison with our national agencies. we demand excellence and independence from her. let us ask him to make recommendations to the political authorities in charge of risk management. and so, let's not leave it to him to take the initiative in alerting and communicating to the public. finally, we should be careful not to standardize our diet. each of our countries, and france in particular, is proud of its gastronomic culture and its products. it is also this diversity that makes europe rich and its quality of life. let's keep it jealously.
- the white paper, which is supported in its outline by mr bowis' report, does not define an imperative policy and that is a pity. however, the creation of a european food safety agency is very positive. it is still necessary, as some colleagues have said, to guarantee its independence. this is done by making financial and human resources available to the agency. we believe that a tax on the profits of agribusiness should help to provide these resources. in order to respect the principle of transparency, it should also be possible for trade unions and other associations to bring cases before the agency, both in consumer and environmental matters. a good scientific risk assessment coupled with an effective communication strategy to the public is not enough to bring food crises under control. it is, in a way, a technocratic vision that is wrong in that it ignores the cultural, social and economic dimensions of food. the resolution of some crises would require more political will. take the current mad cow crisis. it should be possible to prohibit the incorporation of animal meal in animal feed and to withdraw the approval of food manufacturers who do not comply with this regulation.

mr president, one day in december 1992 a young shepherd from mozambique forgot the danger: he thought he had gotten away with peace. that overconfidence cost him his left leg. in 1999, a small boy was found in a field two kilometers from a village in bosnia, with a sign warning of land mines. for him, it's a playground like any other. indeed, whenever a war ends, people leave the refugee camps and return to their villages, hoping to heal their wounds and gradually try to resume a normal life. but a mine does not listen to peace agreements and inevitably continues its work. even today, despite the signature of the ottawa treaty by 139 states, land mines continue to wreak havoc. twenty minutes elapses between the explosion of two mines that will kill or maim somewhere in the world. of course, progress has been made by the geneva conference, and this positive trend must be emphasized because it is really the result of the determined struggle waged by ngos for a very long time. however, progress cannot be allowed to overlook the reality that 27 people are killed and 41 others maimed every day. the reality is that there are 250 million land mines in the arsenals of 105 countries. last year alone, landmines were used in 20 conflicts, mainly in europe. so i welcome the work of my colleagues emma bonino and luisa morgantini who are putting the political debate back at the heart of this parliament. they highlight all that we still have to do. for my part, i would like to emphasize in particular the universalization of the treaty until it becomes a complete success, first by bringing the laws into conformity in the various states, so that we do not have a new example of an international agreement which is not applied. we must put pressure on the european union countries which have not signed, such as finland, or have not ratified, such as greece. why not consider sanctions, commissioner, against those who do not respect the treaties? in writing. - apart from the charter of fundamental rights, which, in an ageing europe, where the number of people in their 40s will exceed 50 million in two decades, makes no provision for the right to greater economic, social and human protection, biarritz focused in particular on the amputation of cases of unanimous voting, the only procedure capable of respecting the interests of the people, and on the curious invention of enhanced cooperation, also known as the europe of circles, pioneers, à la carte, avant-garde, variable geometry or locomotives. from 1951 to paris, to 1997 to amsterdam, to 1957 to rome, what is it? europe was created by treaties concluded, of course, between equal states. moreover, even beyond the law, europe is emotionally a great family of civilisation. a common home. the idea of enhanced cooperation means that in such crucial areas as currency, defence and taxation, some members of the european family would have more rights and obligations than others. in other words, around the table of the common european home, some would eat à la carte and others would eat the minimum menu. some would have a say on the currency and others, like denmark or sweden, would have to keep silent. as before the existence of universal suffrage, there would be active 'people's citizens' and observing 'people's citizens'. there would be, as it were, "people men", with the right to speak about war, taxation or currency, and, as in pre-1945 france, "people women" deprived, around the table, of the right to decide. moreover, as with these europe with variable geometry, the number of guests entitled to a card would change according to the subject in the european council of ministers, it would then be an additional complexity in a europe that already works well illegible. in other words, the philosophical stone of enhanced cooperation, which allows the rule of unanimity and the right of veto protecting national interests to be circumvented, would succeed in the trick of violating the equality of states, excluding minority peoples on a key issue, cracking the democratic foundation of the european construction, increasing the opacity of these european institutions and sowing confusion, if not disorder, within the council and the commission. once again, behind the smoke and mirrors of technocratic expression, there is the manoeuvre of imposing on the peoples a military and fiscal europe which they do not want and depriving them of their right to say no to the deprivation of their national liberties.
mr president, we voted against the duhamel report on the european constitution because, following the good old monnet method, it seeks to make a fundamental political change by masking it under technical considerations, without ever clearly telling people that what is really at stake is to put an end to a conception of europe in which national constitutions are the supreme rule of each people. in the explanatory statement the rapporteur goes a little further and argues that the treaty is already largely supranational, mainly because of the interpretations of the court of justice. but in our view, the interpretations of the 15 judges which go beyond the treaties as they have been ratified are clearly wrong and we are still waiting for them to be submitted to the approval of the peoples of the member states. the rapporteur also echoes the new theory in vogue in brussels, the so-called dual legitimacy of the european union: that of the citizens represented by the european parliament and that of the states represented by the council. this is not the theory of the treaty, which has only one legitimate basis, and that is 'the peoples of the states brought together in the community' in the words of articles 189 and 190 of the ec treaty. this formula means that the community is only a group of states, each of which is based on its own people. in no way do meps represent european citizens in general. they represent their respective peoples and, as such, cooperate in the european control of states, but this control is complementary, since the main control belongs to the national parliaments. in other words, the fact that the members of the european parliament represent their respective peoples does not change the nature of the community. it has no effect whatsoever of placing a phantom european citizen above national citizens, much less of placing an artificial european democracy above national democracies, or even on a par with them.

in writing. - (da) the edd group voted against the gil-robles gil-delgado report on enhanced cooperation. the report proposes to abolish the right of veto, which would give the countries most committed to integration the right to go ahead without worrying about possible popular support. the underlying desire is to be able to continue the evolution towards an 'ever closer union' without this project being hampered by the enlargement to which the eu countries have committed themselves. enhanced cooperation will mean that most community policies, including the most sensitive ones, will be centralised even more than they are today. mr gil-robles therefore proposes that the common foreign and security policy be included. on the contrary, we feel that future developments will show a greater need to diversify and to make cooperation in europe much more flexible. the desire to allow an ever-increasing number of decisions in important areas to be taken by qualified majority voting is contrary to basic democratic standards. countries which have a tradition of voting by referendum on the question of whether to give up their sovereignty may in future find themselves in a situation where a proposal rejected at national level would nevertheless be adopted at community level. the less eager countries will be reduced to copying the legislation adopted without any real power of co-decision. they will not be able to escape the legislation defined by the pioneer countries. the edd group wants a freer and more flexible europe in which participation in everything is not necessarily required. we want a europe of democracies and differences. that is why we shall vote against the report.
in writing. - i voted against the gil-robles report on enhanced cooperation, that is to say cooperation which does not concern all the members of the union, but only some of them. although this report tends to relax somewhat the very rigid regime provided for in title vii of the eu treaty of amsterdam, which is positive, the final result is still very insufficient. it manifests the conception of a far too monolithic union, where all cooperation should be expressed within the 'single institutional framework', and where all cooperation should be directed towards the goal of the superstate. the gil-robles report even proposes to include the common foreign and defence policy in the field of enhanced cooperation, which would correspond to an even more centralised situation than exists today (paragraph 4). these proposals are not acceptable, because the need for cooperation in europe, which is intense, diverse and multifaceted, can no longer be contained within a unified community framework where decisions are taken by majority vote. moreover, the report does not explain concretely - and this is a major shortcoming - how it could make cooperatives with one third of the members work within the framework of the current institutions, without changing them. in reality, the european parliament is fighting a delaying battle. it has already tried to prevent the emergence of differentiated cooperation in the amsterdam treaty, and was finally forced to give in by accepting 'enhanced cooperation'. today, it is trying to prevent the relaxation of enhanced cooperation, and it will not lose the game there either. we believe that cooperatives, which should be called 'differentiated', should not be predetermined in their objectives, limited in their creation or constrained in their operation. some could use the community framework if they so wished, others could create ad hoc institutions, linked only to the union by a liaison secretariat. finally, it is much preferable for differentiated cooperation to operate on the principle of unanimity, unless it falls back on the disadvantages of community cooperation.
in writing. - it should be remembered that the mechanism known today as enhanced cooperation existed long before the treaty of amsterdam. in fact, some member states, eager to deepen their cooperation and go beyond the integration provided for in the treaties, have developed various instruments such as the social agreement, the schengen agreements, economic and monetary union, etc. this has allowed them to progress at different rates and/or with different goals. following the entry into force of the treaty of amsterdam, the use of these instruments was formalised by the introduction of the concept of 'enhanced cooperation' in the treaty on european union (title vii) and the treaty establishing the european community (article 11). the objective of such cooperation is to enable a limited number of member states, capable and willing to go further, to pursue the deepening of european integration, while respecting the union's single institutional framework. europe is finding it increasingly difficult to move forward at the same pace. it is therefore necessary to avoid slowing down the process as a whole and thus allowing certain member states to go ahead by developing the mechanism of enhanced cooperation. the use of this instrument was subject to conditions designed to avoid turning the european union into a "europe à la carte" or a multi-speed europe. this legitimate concern is at the heart of the debate on this subject. it should be recalled that enhanced cooperation, as enshrined in the treaty of amsterdam, must in particular concern an area not falling within the exclusive competence of the community, aim to promote the achievement of the union's objectives, respect the principles of the treaties, be used only as a last resort and concern a majority of member states. enhanced cooperation could play an important role in the context of an enlarged europe. however, as these provisions currently stand, this mechanism is not in a position to function properly. the reform of the instrument has therefore been included in the igc agenda to facilitate its implementation. this report aims to give substance to the position adopted by parliament in this regard (resolution of 13 april 2000). this includes the abolition of the right of veto, the possibility of using cooperation when at least one third of the member states are involved, and the extension of enhanced cooperation to the common foreign and security policy. the rapporteur rightly insists that the commission's right of initiative, the full participation of the european parliament and the judicial review by the court of justice must be the rule for all enhanced cooperation. in the face of the union's current impasse, such a mechanism, if used intelligently, can be one of the ways out.

so in phase two of death row; mumia abu jamal had this courageous message: "phase 2 is phase 2 of the struggle. we will win". there are, of course, encouraging signs of the growing abolitionist trend worldwide. the united nations, like the european parliament, is now involved in the essential debate which is being held across all layers of society. in the united states itself, the death penalty is still more than favourable, but it is being shaken. for example, a columbia university study found that nearly 60 percent of the errors made in executions over the past 20 years were due to the fact that the execution was not carried out correctly. innocent people are being killed and racism is evident in the application of the death penalty. the residence of the texas governor and republican candidate for the white house is regularly the site of protests by opponents of the death penalty. the european union must do everything in its power to win this moratorium and impose it as an inviolable principle on all nations which still commit this state crime which traumatises the human conscience, as victor hugo said in his day. 19 years after the abolition of the death penalty in france, initiatives are now being taken to establish a national day for a universal moratorium on executions. and i agree that at european level we should put forward this proposal. on december 10th, hundreds of thousands of petitions will be presented to the united nations. the presidency of the european union could also be part of this campaign and thus give a breath of fresh air and much-needed support to those who are campaigning for abolition. the european mobilization is decisive.

- madam commissioner, madam president, ladies and gentlemen, behind the somewhat barbarous name of the draft regulation we are debating tonight, the local loop unbundling, an expression which is commission. – the night sessions are not always the greatest pleasure in the european parliament but tonight, i must say, it has been an extremely pleasant and positive debate. i share the view of of universal service. when we increase competition in the networks it will cut prices, improve quality and make the services more affordable. it will help to create an inclusive information society. one reading.

in writing. - if the european parliament were a parliament, and if europe were anything other than a free-trade monetary area, then the european budget would have to represent much more than 1% of gdp. such a budget would be responsible for harmonizing social protection systems and implementing coordinated public policies in the fields of energy and transport; it would be fuelled by a unified tax on capital. but we must not dream: today's europe is dominated by the neoliberal dogma which wants to reduce public aid and the structural funds to the strict minimum. rather than controlling erratic capital movements, priority is given to 'structural reforms' which are in fact aimed at privatising and deregulating what could still be so. the real surprise of this budget is the external actions where selfishness and meanness prevail. europe has a special responsibility towards the balkans and the southern mediterranean. while relatively small contributions to our richer countries could play a strategic role in the peace and development of these regions, the choice is made for significant cuts which resemble a dangerous ostrich policy. that is why we voted for the motion to reject this budget and against the guidelines proposed.

in writing. - we vote against this report, although it appears to be a mere formality in the process of liberalization and telecommunications. the amendments add nothing, except a few additional praises to the alleged virtues of competitiveness. the 'local loop unbundling' in fact requires public operators to make commercial offers for the leasing of public telephone lines as soon as possible. this will mean that 20 to 30% of the contracts will once again be open to private competition. many have already anticipated this directive, such as france télécom. in addition to new constraints on staff, particularly in commercial services, the inequalities in treatment for users will worsen. the regulation of the sector by the law of maximum profit implies the creation of more or less profitable zones within the territorial coverage. the commission has already taken a number of initiatives to improve the quality of public services in europe. this policy would put a stop to the general liberalism which has been quite successful under the french presidency.
in writing. - as regards the death penalty, my position today is identical to that which i took in 1981 when, courageously, the presidential candidate françois mitterrand spoke out against it, before abolishing it once he was elected president! i was against it back in 1981 ! of course i 'm still a doctor in 2000 ! i can understand the feelings and reactions of the families of the victims of often horrendous criminal acts, but a state cannot respond to barbarism with barbarism, it has no right to do so! it is also well known that the death penalty has no deterrent effect, and it is completely unacceptable that countries which claim to be civilized (such as the united states) continue to practise it on a massive and systematic basis, thereby taking on the serious risk of irreparable judicial errors. that is why i voted in favour of the request for a moratorium.
- we are in favour of any tax or levy on large industrial companies, the main polluters in general and of the atmosphere in particular. we have abstained, however, not because the proposed tax is ridiculous, but because of all the loopholes which make it likely that it will become a modest contribution to the right to pollute. to prevent pollution, we need to take binding measures, including confiscation of the polluting company, and no company should be able to escape this. but beyond the one-off measures, the problem of air pollution is a global problem affecting all human society, which can be satisfactorily solved only by a society that controls its economy and does not operate with the pursuit of private profit as its sole engine.

in writing. - the fight against the greenhouse effect is a major challenge for the industrialized countries, a duty especially towards the peoples of the third world who are already paying with their lives for the consequences of global warming. accepting the establishment of an international market for co2 emission allowances means that western countries can avoid their responsibility by buying fictitious emission allowances from russia or by financing projects in the countries of the south without any coherence with their development needs or any means of verifying the reality of emission reductions. pollution is not a commodity; to turn it into a source of profit is to open the door to all kinds of abuse. the draft resolution proposes to validate the establishment of such a system, while "the technical and legal aspects have not been studied" and "the operation and effectiveness of the system are not proven"! no control or sanction is proposed. furthermore, the development of nuclear energy and carbon sinks must be excluded from the calculation of emission reductions. the european union must, without further delay, equip itself to meet its commitments by adopting an ambitious european programme to combat the greenhouse effect - of a very different scale from the proposed resolution on policies and measures; the commission is responsible for the transport sector in particular.
in writing. - the adoption of a motion for a resolution on a community strategy on endocrine disruptors is the minimum on a complex subject where no regulations exist. identifying and studying this phenomenon of disruption of the endocrine systems of humans and animals, validating studies, demonstrating causal links between certain products and certain known abnormalities in humans or in the animal species (reduced fertility, certain malformations, certain cancers, etc.) is a necessary starting point if it respects the precautionary principle while advancing a requirement of transparency that is totally absent from the text. private and public decision-makers will not act without the constraint of public opinion. lists of products suspected of being endocrine disruptors should be made available to the public and healthcare professionals as new products are discovered. if studies are to be carried out to determine the dangers of endocrine disruptors, firms using suspect products must be required to meet the standards applicable to medicinal products, namely, above all, to provide proof of the safety of these products, as long as they are considered as suspect by the european expert groups. the urgency is therefore to propose a binding regulatory arsenal to exclude these products in the years to come.

- report (a5-0283/2000) by mrs peijs, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on retail payments in the internal market (com (2000) 0036 - c5-0103/2000 - 2000/2018 (cos)).
- madam president, mrs peijs' report on retail payments in the internal market echoes the european parliament's old claim about the high cost of crossborder transfers within the union. that's exactly right. this is a high cost, and we know why. the computer systems of the different banks in the different member countries are poorly interconnected, which means that expensive manual operations are required to transfer money from one national system to another. so this is not some diabolical move on the part of the bankers, but only a technical reality which is holding up for the moment, but which will inevitably develop in the right direction with time. so i think we have to put the problem in perspective. it is all the more necessary to put it in perspective since crossborder transfers represent a very small proportion of all transfers. according to the documents i have consulted, they occupy a share of 0.2% to 0.04%. either way, it's really microscopic. but the european parliament and the commission really do attach great importance to it. why would you do that ? firstly, because the european institutions tend to favour anything that is cross-border, and after all, that is a bit normal. but this bias in favour of crossborder travel should not end up penalizing the vast majority of citizens in favour of a very small minority. since investments which would substantially reduce the cost of cross-border transfers would not be profitable because they would be amortised on too few payers, it must be concluded that if they were made under these conditions, their cost would be passed on to all the customers of the banks which have nothing to do with this issue. i think in all fairness, that's not a very desirable outcome. politically, it is highly questionable. and we must also stop pretending that something which is expensive for technical reasons could suddenly become free because we have taken a directive to decide that. i remind you of the basic maxim we learned in our first year of economics: there's no such thing as a free lunch. there is a second reason, madam president, for the persistence of the european parliament. the peijs report itself says so in recital d of the draft resolution. i quote: 'high fees for crossborder payments are undermining consumer confidence in the euro.' but why should they undermine consumer confidence in the euro? i have just shown you precisely that these two problems are not related, at least in appearance. in fact, a few years ago, people were led to believe - and you will find out why, probably to make the euro easier to accept - that this kind of cost would disappear completely with the single currency. i have brought you a small brochure which has been distributed in millions of copies in french public places, particularly in post offices, and here is what i read in the chapter on exchange fees: "in the euro area, exchange fees will disappear". of course, strictly speaking, this is true, but the naive reader, who is not an expert on the subject, thought that all the costs of crossborder transfers would disappear, when in reality the exchange fees represented only a very small part of it, only a few percent. so now we are faced with the consequences of the forced-selling methods used to sell the euro. this brings me to a conclusion on the matter of crossborder transfers, but also, madam president, on the euro in general. you can deny reality in words, you can tell people stories, but eventually, your approximations, your lies, come back to you.
- this debate is over. the vote will take place at 6 p.m. (the sitting was suspended at 1 p.m. and resumed at 3 p.m.)
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, each of us has in mind his own list of recurring disappointments, which we cannot help but which it is necessary to deplore from time to time to prove that we are not used to it and that impotence does not always, or at least not yet, rhyme with indifference. i have heard some of my colleagues in the committee, some of whom have been here longer than i have, and i have the impression that the implementation of the multiannual programme for enterprise and entrepreneurship, to which this parliament is submitting for the fourth time, belongs to this category. i was told that all good intentions were welcome, but that we should make sure that the next report on this subject does not have to make the same findings as the previous one, as nothing really concrete has changed in the situation of european companies. the text before you today is therefore intended to transform what was a useless test of imposed figures into a promising examination of free figures, to which the european union, if it understands what its place and role in the system should be, can add its added value. the time has passed when the defence of enterprises, and in particular of small and mediumsized enterprises, was akin to a corporatist struggle, not only because there are only a handful of people left who cannot be reduced to viewing the world of business through the distorted prism of the class struggle, but above all because, on the threshold of the third millennium, everyone knows how decisive the problems of employment and social cohesion will be for our societies and that within these problems the enterprise occupies a prominent place. it is worth noting that, both economically and socially, the enterprise is the first place. the first creator of employment, the first motor of social integration, it has also gradually acquired a crucial importance in the field of training - in the case of young people - or continuing training, or in terms of spatial planning, of which it is, in the end, the most effective instrument. the fifteen adopted the charter for small businesses at the feira summit last june, which is now showing us that significant progress has been made. the charter, besides being the unquestionable basis on which we must build a policy of enterprise which is genuinely at the service of enterprises, has the immense merit of not limiting our action to small enterprises alone, but of making them the central point of our reflection, the unit of reference to which we must attach priority. parliament, made up of elected representatives who are regularly in contact with the field, has the duty to express clearly this option which reflects both an objective reality and a method which is the only one capable of properly embracing the diversity of the business world. the sme is not a miniature multinational, any more than it is sufficient to extrapolate the difficulties of a small enterprise in a quantitative way to properly understand the problems of large units. it would seem, however, to be good policy to prefer a pragmatic and pro-active approach, which puts small businesses at the heart of the system, rather than a proposal which, under the pretext of avoiding waste, would only serve to produce accurate statistics which would be completely impossible to use in practice. i therefore welcome the unanimous decision of the committee on industry to favour a sectoral approach to the problem of enterprises, an inevitable choice if we want to identify as precisely as possible the real and specific needs of enterprises whose disparity is ill-suited to a horizontal approach, which is insufficient to be effective. the notions of comparing performance and exchanging best practice are certainly interesting in their own right, but it is hard to imagine that these are the only ways of making a positive contribution to the day-to-day reality of business. so what do we do? starting with three simple ideas: first, rather than allowing a kind of renunciation to affect directly the greatest number of enterprises, use existing networks whose knowledge of the realities makes them indispensable partners in the development and effective implementation of a policy for enterprises. that is why the report stresses the need for very close cooperation between consular circles and representative bodies of companies, which have much to teach us and can help us to avoid turning a good idea into a bad decision through ignorance. secondly, to ensure that access to capital for firms, especially the smallest ones, is not made more difficult. while this is a key factor in the start-up, development, recovery, transfer and even survival of businesses, a number of decisions that have been taken or are about to be taken raise some concerns, whether it be the obscure re-design of the respective tasks of the european investment bank or the european investment fund, or the draft directive on the own funds of banks, which we will have to persuade of its painless effect on the ability of companies to obtain credit. in any case, in the face of an economy based more than ever on knowledge and technological innovation, it seems essential that the commission should ensure that the most courageous, the most innovative, the most risk-taking people are given the opportunity to take action and to see their entrepreneurial spirit translated into action. finally, since the spirit of enterprise is inseparable from the notion of responsibility, it is necessary to establish clearly what european added value can be in the field of enterprise policy. the political course is the responsibility of the states. it was the council that set the course for feira, through the charter for small enterprises. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one. i hope that the house will renew, in its vote in plenary, the unanimity which emerged in the committee on industry. it would thus send a clear and strong signal to the business world that they need it. i thank you in advance, ladies and gentlemen, for your support of my report. i know that i can count on your energy and determination to implement this programme. it is necessary to link it with the other community programmes and to take an annual assessment of it, possibly with a view to adjusting it. this is how we can meet together the twin challenges of full employment and social cohesion. on behalf of all the companies, but also on behalf of our companies, i thank you.
