commission. – mr president, i would like to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mr wuermeling, and the committee on legal affairs and the internal market for their work on better lawmaking. we are dealing with an extremely important issue. we must always ask ourselves whether we need legislation to solve a problem. the second question is, if we need legislation, should it be at european level or national level? thirdly, if we decide to legislate at european level, how can we guarantee that the legislation is simple, clear and can be transposed? fourthly, is there any way other than legislation of meeting the same objective at european level, such as soft law, a code of conduct or co-regulation? i also agree with the report and views expressed in the discussion here that enlargement will present a major challenge vis-à-vis the quality of legislation, owing to the economic, social and legal problems which the new member states will bring with them. this must be respected and taken into consideration by eu legislators. subsidiarity, proportionality, better quality legislation, simple regulation, increased codification: all must become major political issues on which we will focus. actually, this screening of the existing acquis communautaire is often a very useful exercise in showing that it is not always necessary to legislate at community level or whether a law is too detailed for legislation at the community level. i do not want to go into a deep discussion about the theological or political history of subsidiarity. what is important for the eu institutions is that we have a strong commitment to improving the quality of legislation, especially with regard to subsidiarity. the commission is making both political and internal efforts to incorporate subsidiarity into legislative proposals. the initiative to prepare a white paper on governance, for example, is an attempt to promote the principle of subsidiarity at all levels. the rapporteur mentioned the question of soft law recommendations or other agreements. i think they are extremely important issues to discuss. i see here some colleagues of yours who played a considerable part in the regulation on the information society and the internet. is it possible to regulate the issues when technology moves extremely fast? is there a risk that we will put brakes on development if we legislate? is there a risk that technology will move so fast that the problem will have changed before legislation is ready? that is the area where we must look at issues with a very open mind. i will take a very personal position by saying that there can be new types of governance here, where regulation and self-regulation can be complementary and not alternatives. but what is important for voluntary agreements or self-regulation is that they must be implemented, we must know that they are enforced, we must know how we can monitor that what has been agreed has happened. then it is important to see what the european parliament's role should be in discussions: there can perhaps be open discussions, debates, dialogue, which guarantee that the european parliament is part of the debate. however, the more we go into the details of information technology, the rapid changes on the internet, the more convinced i am personally that detailed regulation is not the solution to this problem or, if it is a solution to something, it is not the problem which is faced by information technology. there are also other areas of the internal market regulations which are very complicated. i will just mention so-called pedestrian-friendly cars, which the commission will discuss in a few weeks time. this directive could be 64 pages long, extremely detailed, mathematical, and involve a lot of engineering expertise. is that an area where we should go for detailed regulation, with guarantees that will be implemented everywhere or should we consider whether a voluntary agreement, provided that it can be enforced and controlled, as an alternative? these are the kind of debates that we need to go through in the next few years. i hope that this report, which we commissioners were given last year, will in future include subsidiarity, better regulation and assessment of alternatives, while respecting the legislative authority of the council and parliament. finally, i want to take into account the criticism which we have seen in parliament's report. it is concise and clear. i will transmit the message to my colleagues in the commission and the commission will do its best to react positively to these in the preparation of the next report. i hope that we can continue this debate so that it is not only a routine matter on thursday afternoon but part of the central debate on community legislation as a whole.

the rapporteur. - madam president, international crime has become considerably more organized and powerful in recent years. we can see that globalisation, in particular, has increased the possibilities for money laundering and the means of avoiding prosecution. the united nations has estimated that the annual amount of money laundered through money laundering is worth one trillion dollars. money laundering is a difficult crime to detect, and all the possibilities offered by the various laws are used by the big crime. therefore, only international police and judicial cooperation can effectively counteract this criminal practice. at european level, mutual legal assistance in criminal matters has already led, in general terms, to the adoption of several texts, such as the council of europe convention of 20 april 1959 and, very recently, the european convention of 29 may 2000, on which our colleague mr di pietro was rapporteur. the commission has already taken a number of measures to combat money laundering, including the recent amendment of the council directive of 10 june 1991, for which mr lehne was rapporteur. the french presidency's initiative under discussion today is aimed at improving the two general conventions on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters - which i mentioned earlier - particularly in the field of the fight against money laundering. the proposed convention improves on the previous texts, and these improvements are welcome. article 2 of the draft convention means that member states can no longer refuse to carry out searches or seizures of objects on the basis of the reservations mentioned in article 5 of the 1959 convention. article 4 requires member states to take appropriate measures to facilitate the provision and safeguarding of data on the existence, location and movements of proceeds of crime in order to facilitate investigations, and article 5 requires member states to provide information on banking matters. article 6 allows the extension of supplementary mutual assistance requests, and thanks to article 7 tax exemptions are no longer acceptable for refusing mutual legal assistance. the measures contained in this draft convention, which correspond to the concern expressed by the tampere european council regarding the fight against money laundering, which is at the very heart of organized crime and must be eradicated wherever it exists, can only be approved as a whole. it seems to me that some improvements could be proposed, and that is the subject of my report. the right to banking and commercial secrecy in respect of requests for mutual legal assistance is enshrined in article 3. it seems to me essential to extend this immunity to the commercial and financial advisory activities of lawyers or members of regulated legal professions, which by their nature are not covered by professional secrecy. secondly, article 8 of the draft convention limits the grounds for refusal of mutual assistance which the requested state may invoke to essential interests only. this is a breakthrough. however, in order to ensure that mutual legal assistance does not lose its relevance in a field where only rapid european cooperation makes sense, it seems to me useful to allow the requested state a maximum period of two months to make known its reply. article 9 calls on the member states to set up integrated, multidisciplinary teams at national level in order to increase the efficiency of research and to promote the exchange of information. i propose the creation of a cooperation unit between these multidisciplinary teams, which could facilitate the exchange of information between the relevant authorities in the member states and promote the selection and use of best practices. these proposals are aimed at making mutual legal assistance as effective as possible, in view of the challenges posed by organised crime, particularly money laundering.
- ladies and gentlemen, one of the essential issues in the construction of the european area of security, freedom and justice is judicial and police cooperation, so that this area can quickly become effective and practical for citizens. in this connection, our rapporteurs have reflected on the protocol amending the europol convention and on the improvement of mutual legal assistance. we can only commend them for this work. but the question of the extension of europol's powers is our main concern. we expressly and emphatically support the need for effective mutual legal assistance, but at the same time we denounce the drift in germ of europol, which was set up outside any parliamentary or judicial control, and more broadly the lack of democracy in a europe which the states persist in maintaining in the opaque sphere of intergovernmental procedures bypassing the obligations, duties and controls arising from universal suffrage. i see some ambiguities in europol: the diplomatic immunity of its members, no definition of the means allowed or their limits, opinions on the recording of persons, recording in areas protected by international texts and human rights declarations, the dangers to freedoms in view of the risks of abuse, especially today or tomorrow, in view of the political evolution of certain states. if the 'european police' is given the gift of self-control, it will do everything in its power to curb the european parliament's desire for democratic control, given the current structural weaknesses and lack of unity on the substance. the portuguese initiative on the europol convention is intended to encourage the european parliament to take the right security path, which would involve the discretionary recording of citizens in all areas of privacy. to identify, prosecute and condemn the money laundering of terrorists and arms and drug traffickers: yes, of course! but that will not give us any more guarantees as regards the right of defence and the protection of citizens' rights. that is why we are tabled amendments on the strengthening of these rights and freedoms, on the need to adopt an instrument, on the rights of the defence and on the recognition of the jurisdiction of the court of justice. we are aware that a provision of the council of ministers act, which has curiously gone unnoticed, states that europol shall specify whether data relating to racial origin, religious or other beliefs, political opinions, sex life or health may be entered in the analysis file. so, are we going to be further delaying the competence of europol even as democratic control is being struck off the bills? the democratic values which unite us in this house must be the ones which govern our actions and our work, so that europe is a european union of solidarity and social cohesion and not a european union of police and repression.
- mr president, commissioner, the marinho report deplores the fact that the frontiers are open to criminals but remain closed to the institutions responsible for prosecuting them. but why should we be surprised? you wanted a europe whose sole concern was to open the doors to the movement of capital and goods. dirty capital flows through the same channels as the rest, if only the operations of the companies with street vendors were not as dirty as the capital of the cali cartel. i am talking about money from corruption or profit from the exploitation of children in the third world. you are unable to take any real action to prevent money laundering, because that would require taking action against the banking and financial groups, since they are the ones laundering this money by taking refuge behind bank secrecy. and all the big banks themselves create subsidiaries in tax havens, and these havens only exist because there are banks that use them. they do so with the encouragement of the states themselves, such as france or the netherlands in st. maarten, britain in the channel islands and others. we are the only ones here who want measures that really prevent money laundering, that is to say the immediate lifting of banking secrecy, commercial secrecy, business secrecy, the opening of the books of accounts of all banking or industrial companies and the right of all employees of these companies, of all consumers, to bring to the attention of the public any movement of funds that goes against the interests of the community.
- ladies and gentlemen, although the need for a future european public prosecutor does not appear to be a long-term problem, the need to harmonize our policies on the protection of citizens' rights and a par excellence criminal procedure seems to me to be more than essential. how can a european public prosecutor's office be set up in the absence of a community civil code and, moreover, a european criminal code? even if this does not directly impede the initiative to create eurojust, it is true that there is an institution which is not yet subject to the control of the european parliament and to the judicial review of the court of justice of the european communities, in accordance with article 35 of the treaty. how can we consider the creation of eurojust when europol is already operating in free electron mode? two points must be borne in mind: we cannot consider an effective improvement in judicial cooperation between member states without making it obviously conditional on the protection of the rights of the defence in legal proceedings involving several member states. that is the point of our amendments. it follows that it is necessary to strengthen the rights of citizens by adopting an effective instrument and to recognise the jurisdiction of the court of justice, in particular as regards its right to interpretation and its power to rule or not. in addition, the shortcomings of the new research to combat organised crime relate to the division of powers between europol and eurojust, which are not clearly raised in any case or at any point. as you know, the question of jurisdiction and its limits is at the heart of this community harmonization for better justice. the clear division of areas of intervention between judicial and police cooperation is not only necessary to avoid any conflict of jurisdiction, but is also fundamental to guaranteeing the exercise of the democratic rules underlying the rule of law. the member states of the european community adhere to it on the basis of their legislative, executive and judicial systems, in accordance with the principle of fundamental rights and common values. eurojust must therefore respect the relationship between judicial cooperation and police cooperation. the european parliament is the supranational community body responsible for drawing up this report, and my speech is therefore to ask you to support its merits by supporting our rapporteur.

- madam president, ladies and gentlemen, the charter of fundamental rights - a key step in the construction of europe - has been the subject of much debate. for some it is a success; for others it is now a disappointed hope. many felt that europe had finally had the opportunity to get out of the single free trade area and the liberal rut and lay the foundations for a people's europe. this hope was reinforced by the composition of the convention, which set an original precedent for the usual intergovernmental method, by the public debates and the set of texts available on a website accessible to all, and by civil society, which was called upon to make its voice heard. but transparency did not replace the democratic deficit, as ngos were allowed to speak for only five minutes and their views were rarely taken into account. yes, some progress is being made, but it is not enough in the face of the shortcomings. it took weeks of battle to get the right to strike. the right to work has become the right to work. the right to health, social security, housing or minimum income are nonexistent or only of the order of solidarity. freedom of the press is no longer a "guarantee" it is "respected". minority rights are minimalist. discrimination between europeans and residents of third countries is entrenched, as is the case with the freedom of movement provided for in the amsterdam treaty, or the right to family life, which is recognized in international law. a number of rights, including political rights, are the subject of a european preference replacing national preference. where are our sacred principles of universality, indivisibility and the unity of law? first time in a european union document it is becoming quite clear that the rights listed in the charter are, for the most part, granted to every person, irrespective of nationality or even right of residence. this summary is important at a time when the union is called upon to define the legal status, in terms of rights and obligations, of third-country nationals who are lawfully in the european union. of course, this charter is only a start. i see it as a solid foundation on which social change can continue, even as regards its legal value. i believe that the objective of the indivisibility articles. the european council in helsinki on 13 december 1999 decided to grant turkey the status of candidate country for accession to the european union and to set up an accession partnership and a single financial framework to help turkey's application to progress in accordance with the copenhagen criteria. it is in this spirit that the work which has resulted in this report was carried out in the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, and i welcome the contribution of all my colleagues to the preparation of this report, which concludes - in agreement with the commission - that turkey does not meet the copenhagen criteria today. since the helsinki decision, turkey's efforts to develop its legal arsenal to better meet the union's requirements in respect of human rights should be welcomed. this is evidenced, among other things, by the report drawn up under the chairmanship of mr demiroc, secretary of the high coordination council for human rights in turkey, which proposes a very large package of constitutional reforms. but it is also necessary to note and understand the emotion aroused within the various political parties and in turkish public opinion by the awareness of the importance of these reforms. the turkish people feel that their accession to the union will require not only a painless revision of their institutions and the partial abandonment of a sovereignty to which they remain jealously attached, but also a radical change in their habits and mindsets. this is why our parliament has proposed the setting up of a euro-turkish forum, bringing together the qualified representatives of the turkish community and the european parliamentarians who have been given the mandate to do so, in order to conduct in-depth discussions. the decision on turkey's accession will be too important for the future of the union and of turkey itself to be taken in the hushed silence - or even in secrecy - of the cabinets. there will be long debates, both in the european parliament and in the national parliaments, and that is why everyone agrees that the road ahead will be long and difficult. the establishment of the forum proposed by our parliament should thus make it possible to overcome the first obstacles encountered on this road. our parliament will have to make it very clear to our turkish partners in this forum and during its debates that they have nothing to fear from any european interference in their internal affairs, but that we are proposing them a contract which is being defined more precisely, on the occasion of the accession partnership, commissioner, and of course the convention on the charter of fundamental rights. it will be up to the turks to accept or reject it. in the present state of affairs, it is also up to our parliament to tell the turkish people that there are three conditions for their accession today. firstly, respect for the need for identity, which is manifested all the more clearly throughout europe by our fellow citizens as they have a stronger desire to preserve their roots in the face of the inevitable progress of globalisation. europe, aware that its wealth is of the process defined in copenhagen for all the applicant countries. i have suffered too much, as have all the communities of bosnia and herzegovina, from the tragic consequences of the systematic the debate on radical reform of the political situation in the country. we are in an important historical phase for turkey, which has moved from the stage of debate to the stage of practice, that is to say, the implementation of reforms to the constitution and laws, with for example an amnesty for prisoners for crimes of opinion. turkey has this stage ahead of it. we must be clear: there can be no further phase without turkey having passed from the stage of debate to the stage of practice. that is exactly what the morillon report says. there is also the situation in cyprus. and on this point we must tell turkey that it is inconceivable that it does not accept what has been decided at the european court of justice in strasbourg. turkey has been condemned several times. it must immediately comply with the decisions of the european court of justice, as a sign of acceptance of international relations as defined by us, and not only by it. this brings us to the fundamental problem. there are several strategies in this parliament and in the member states. there are those who are in favour of turkey's candidacy and turkey's membership and who want this candidacy to involve a thoroughgoing reform of turkish society. and then there are those who are against membership and who are exploiting the necessary debate on policy and reform in turkey to push turkey away from europe. it is obvious that turkish society feels exactly this contradiction. that is why the last problem to be solved, the armenian genocide, is so important. no one here, and especially not me, denies that there was a genocide against the armenians in the last days of the ottoman empire. this is obvious, as it is obvious that turkey, like any civilized society, will have to face up to its past, as horrible as it was. it is an ideological and civilizational prerequisite for entering europe. there is another question: if we have to vote on this today, the majority of my group will vote in favour of this resolution. personally, i am not sure that this is a useful act, because i want to bring this debate inside turkey. that is to say, i propose that the european parliament itself organize a debate on the genocide in armenia, the majority will follow and we will extend the debate in turkey.
mr president, the morillon report alone is a perfect illustration of the fundamental contradictions in the european approach to turkey. the opposite is also true of this motion for a resolution. firstly, there are many illusions, many enchanting considerations, which are, fortunately, immediately overtaken by reality, and this turkish reality is obviously not in keeping with european illusions or dreams. it is both very naive and very conceited to think that the europeans are going to bring the turks, and i quote: 'to a radical change in their habits and their mentality'. what arrogance on the part of the european union to want to impose its own values, institutional principles and political culture on the turkish people! the 20th century, however, has shown us how constructivism, voluntarism, disconnection from reality, and ideologies of all kinds can lead to disaster. let us therefore leave the turkish people to their own devices, to decide their own future, to their right to be different, to their right to preserve the values of a civilization which are clearly not ours. so the only real consideration that should be imposed on all of us is a consideration of reality and of the obvious. turkey is not a european country, its culture is not european, its values are not european. turkey should therefore not be part of the european union. this would not in any way prevent europe from developing economic, diplomatic, political and peaceful relations with a free and independent turkey. this clear position would, among other things, have the merit of no longer being cold and hot towards the turkish governments, of ceasing to say to them: yes, but later, yes, but on such conditions, yes, but this or that. the contradictions of europe and its procrastination are a source of misunderstanding and humiliation. we cannot play with the dignity of the people. we shall therefore vote against this report, as we have voted against all the reports on turkey's accession to the european union.
in writing. - the paciotti report is a first step in trying to close the gap in the defence of privacy and personal data. in this sense, the creation of an 'independent monitoring body' is positive. however, none of the essential issues concerning the defence of the rights and freedoms of individuals is really explicitly addressed and the text, often technically confusing, can lend itself to divergent interpretations. moreover, it is well below the french legislation "informatics and freedoms". other proposals should have been included: making it compulsory to declare the existence of all databases; the interchange of files (in the fields of privacy, health, social situations, etc.) must be prohibited to prevent the creation of giant databases; the commission has also proposed that the european parliament should be consulted on the draft directive on the protection of employees' personal data. finally, citizens must be given the means to protect their privacy themselves by allowing all forms of encryption in data transmission. in this context, encryption techniques must be guaranteed by independent bodies. these few essential provisions must be taken into account for effective protection of personal data. that is why we abstained.
arlette laguiller, armonia bordes and chantal cauquil voted against the charter. we know that in this class society where only the balance of power counts, charters do not constitute a real protection for workers. this charter refuses to include such basic rights as the right to a decent pension, to a minimum income, to decent housing, to health care. as for the article prohibiting the employment of children before the end of compulsory schooling, it allows for exceptions, which is serious when we know that in several european countries an unacceptable number of children are working, are exploited, do not have the right to a proper education. this text does not offer additional protection and gives governments and the wealthy classes additional means to attack on these grounds. the right to strike itself is only recognised with the restriction 'in accordance with national laws and practices'. the charter therefore has no binding force for countries whose social legislation is below the minimum laid down in the charter. on the other hand, in countries where the legislation is more favourable to workers, the charter could be opposed to it. instead of dragging human and social rights upwards, it will facilitate operations designed to drag them downwards.
in writing. - the adoption of the charter of fundamental rights would be justified if a european state, based on a constitution adopted by universal suffrage, already existed. that's not the case today. the rights contained in the charter are already enshrined in national constitutions and defended by national parliaments which are close to the peoples and their cultures. the charter is also a compromise based on the lowest common denominator, which will undermine the social advantages acquired in many of our member states. the right to housing is thus reduced to the 'right to housing assistance' while the right to work is replaced by a right to 'access to employment services'. there are no restrictions on freedom of expression, which means that criminal statements (incitement to violence, racial hatred) can no longer be condemned. finally, the charter does not contain any articles on duties, which are, however, the counterpart of rights. we therefore see no reason for adopting such a text today, except to cover up the planned failure of the intergovernmental conference and the european council in nice.
in writing. - in my speech this morning i set out the reasons in principle for my opposition to the charter, which the members of the sos democracy intergroup have told me they fully support. i should now like to make a number of reservations concerning certain specific articles on which i had the opportunity to table amendments during the debate in the chamber. these reserves can be grouped into five broad categories: articles which encroach upon the powers of states. a typical case is presented by article 2-2 "no one shall be sentenced to the death penalty or executed". this statement does not correspond to any european competence. its presence in the charter, like that of many other articles of the same kind, casts doubt on the honesty of article 51-2, which states that 'this charter does not create any new competence or task for the community and the union, and does not alter the competence of the tasks defined by the treaties'. of course, if the charter became binding, so would article 2-2, with a much stronger power than the european convention on human rights, from which a country still has the right to withdraw. articles which tend to impose new unfounded obligations. several articles go beyond the existing law. for example, article 19-1, which states that 'collective expulsions are prohibited', does not specify that this prohibition may be suspended in the event of war or serious disturbances of public order. article 52-2 provides that 'in so far as this charter contains rights corresponding to those guaranteed by the european convention for the protection of human rights, their meaning and scope shall be the same as those conferred by the said convention'. but that sentence is far too vague. we have already heard that mass expulsions are prohibited in all cases. another new obligation: article 21 adds new cases of non-discrimination to those already provided for in article 13 tec. article 21-2 even provides that all discrimination on grounds of nationality is prohibited in the field of the treaty on european union, which is not provided for in any text today. third example: article 45 states that 'freedom of movement and residence may be granted to third-country nationals legally resident in the territory of a member state', whereas such a right, which is indeed envisaged by article 62 tec, is not currently in force, and may never be if the conditions are not met. articles which illegitimately freeze evolutionary situations. this is particularly the case for the economic and social rights listed in chapter iv of the charter. for example, article 29 provides that 'everyone has the right to access a free placement service'. but this is a very circumstantial statement, which another age may appreciate differently. articles that ignore the natural rules of life of societies. even though the demographic situation in the countries of europe is alarming, the charter treats family problems very lightly. nowhere is it stated, despite our demands, that the family is made up of a man and a woman raising children, and that it is the basic unit of society. article 24 on the rights of the child even fails to say, despite our requests, that every child has the right to live with his parents. at the same time, the charter is far too discreet about the existence of national communities and their right to establish their own rules. for example, the new requirement of non-discrimination on the basis of language, found in articles 21 and 22, contradicts the french constitution, which provides that the language of the republic is french. articles which obscure or distort the general framework of the charter. i have already mentioned article 51-1 which states against all evidence that the charter does not in any way alter the competences defined by the treaties. in reality, the charter contains so many contradictions that someone will have to unravel them one day. i also mentioned article 52-2, which claims that the meaning and scope of the charter's rights are the same as those of the european convention on human rights. in reality, this reconciliation is very difficult to achieve, because when reading the charter one never knows whether one is dealing with an article which has intended to respect the convention, or with an article which has intended to depart from it voluntarily. finally, it should also be recalled that article 52-1 states that restrictions may be imposed on rights if they ... 'effectively meet objectives of general interest recognised by the union ...'. if the charter were to become binding, a phrase like that would become a formidable limitation of the sovereignty of the states. more broadly, we regret that the preamble to the charter has not put this document in perspective, recalling that the european union is an association of nations and that citizens have a fundamental right to have their decisions taken democratically within the national framework respected. as i said in the debate which preceded this vote, i hope that the governments meeting in nice, if they wish to adopt this charter as a political declaration, will precede it with a preliminary declaration recalling this situation and the fundamental competence of national parliaments with regard to the rights of citizens.
in writing. - sos democracy rejects the charter of fundamental rights for three reasons. first of all, it's useless. secondly, it is undemocratic. and thirdly, it is likely to restrict, rather than strengthen, the freedom of the peoples of europe. we shall briefly explain these three objections in order. ratification of the charter of fundamental rights would be one of the most ambitious steps ever taken by the european union. before embarking on such a large-scale task, we should ask the following question: where in western europe are the monstrous human rights violations taking place to which this document would respond? after all, we are talking about 15 modern democracies, not 15 rwanda. all member states are already bound by the european convention on human rights, the un universal declaration and a whole series of smaller agreements. why does the eu as such need to intervene in this area? no one has answered that question yet. roman herzog, the president of the convention, has made it clear that the charter will not create any new rights. if so, it seems strange to decree a constitutional revolution of such importance for so few supposed benefits. human rights are probably not directly threatened within the eu. this is not the case with democratic accountability. the charter will involve the court of justice of the european communities in a number of policy decisions in areas as diverse as employment law, extradition policy, immigration and the family. in so far as the judges were not elected, this represents a step backwards in democratic governance. beyond this, the charter will oblige the ecj to override national legislation, and even provisions of state constitutions, in several new policy areas. given that the cjce, on the basis of the much more restricted text of the existing european treaties, has already shown a worrying trend towards judicial activism, it is likely that this problem will become particularly acute. even those who accept the arguments in favour of a written eu constitution should hesitate in the light of certain provisions of the charter. it is article 52 that we are most concerned about. it provides that rights mentioned elsewhere in the document may be disregarded where they conflict with 'objectives of general interest recognised by the union'. in this way, the state's reason is reintroduced, which the council has sought to eradicate during the last fifty years. the right of a government to arbitrarily set aside its constitution is the characteristic definition of tyranny. in nazi germany, for example, this provision was called the "full powers law". in a less dramatic but equally important way, the charter is badly written. i take article 21 for example, which prohibits 'any discrimination based on sex, race, colour, ethnic or social origin, genetic characteristics, language, religion or belief, political or other opinion, membership of a national minority, property, birth, disability, age or sexual orientation'. this article, if taken literally, would mean that a socialist party would not be allowed to discriminate against conservatives who would like to run as candidates for that party, or that an opera house should offer soprano roles to men. no one can guess how these provisions, so vaguely worded, will be used by an activist court. human rights are respected within the eu and protected by provisions in national constitutions, in accordance with the different traditions of the member states. the charter now provides a mechanism to limit or even trample on these rights without even giving the appearance of offering new ones. many europeans are proud of this freedom, which allows them to do everything that is not expressly prohibited by law. however, we are now being asked to "receive" these rights from the european judges. sos democracy rejects the concept that we should depend on the eu to grant us our own freedoms. in the words of aldous huxley, "freedom is not begged for, it is taken".
in writing. - the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which our european parliament adopted today, is a particularly important document. it is true that the charter still has shortcomings in both substance and form. i would have liked to see a more substantial social dimension. i would have liked to have seen it incorporated directly into our european treaties! we must not, however, 'shrink our pleasure' and deny the enormous work that has been done and the important results that have been achieved today. the charter of fundamental rights is a document and a charter common to all european citizens! we must now disseminate it widely, make it known to everyone, and get as many citizens as possible to think about its proposals. and so it will gradually permeate, through case law, all our national and european rights! this is a very positive outcome for the french presidency of the european union and for our european parliament. we shall probably have to develop and complete it tomorrow. we must incorporate it into our treaties very quickly. we must then put a european constitution in place for a democratic, transparent, efficient and citizen-led europe. but, as i say again today, we have every reason to be proud of the conditions under which we have reached this important milestone for europe.
in writing. - social democracy promised us that europe would no longer be just an economic market, a currency and a machine for liberalization. enriched by a charter of 'fundamental rights', social europe would finally become social. but it's not. this charter is a social regression in terms of democracy and freedoms, far below the existing treaties. it took a lot of pressure to finally integrate the right to unionize and strike. with a few exceptions, women are allowed to "marry and raise a family". immigrants, on the other hand, have the right not to be "collectively deported". as for social rights, they are absent. no right to work, but 'the right to work' not the right to social protection or housing, but 'the right to social assistance and housing assistance'; no right to a pension or to a minimum income; the commission has not proposed a ban on redundancies, but rather a 'protection against unjustified dismissals'. in reality, the fight against social exclusion is relegated to the level of assistance, instead of requiring basic rights binding on employers and the state. the charter, on the other hand, obviously gives the right to property and the freedom to conduct a business. for all these reasons, this charter should not be incorporated into the union's treaties, and we cannot accept it as it stands.
in writing. - the procedure chosen for the drawing up and adoption of the charter of fundamental rights leaves the european parliament with only one alternative: to accept or reject the current charter. in the face of such a binary choice, my vote is unambiguous, it approves the progress that this charter represents, a very relative progress, however, both in terms of content and in terms of the scope of this text. first, we should review the procedure followed. the convention's method of drawing up a basic text, seeking a broad compromise, is interesting and fruitful, but there is no reason why the european parliament, as the representative of the peoples of europe, should not have the opportunity to amend and enrich the text. however, when the historian looks at the way in which the declaration of the rights of man and of the citizen or similar international declarations were drawn up, he discovers how the parliamentary debate and the mechanism of amendment have been able to give these founding texts a breath, relevance and ambition, which are still full of force today. as the institutional debate is being launched at the same time as the adoption of the charter, all those who, like myself, want a european constitution and who believe that this charter can serve as the backbone of the preamble to such a constitution should demand that the european parliament be able to vote on its content, as part of its normal parliamentary intervention, which is essentially deliberative. in connection with this institutional debate, the charter's inclusion in our eu treaties is essential so that the rights it enshrines can be guaranteed for all and the public policies necessary for their implementation can be developed, either by the member states or by the union itself, without being in contradiction with existing legal texts. it is clear that the law of free competition and the single market too often takes precedence over all other requirements and in fact violates social and fundamental rights. we have seen too many declarative texts without any effect. this is the first priority: to give the charter an effective legal meaning. on the other hand, the current content is ambiguous and insufficient in some respects. firstly, the differences in translation between german and french leave open the question of the reference to "religious" or "spiritual" values. i am convinced that secularism is an emancipatory and timely value. i regret the ambiguity of the terms and the lack of a clearer reference to secularism. secondly, the right to work is not directly stated. everyone is aware of how unambitious a reference to the right of everyone to work is in this respect. there is more than one nuance between not prohibiting access to work and taking action to enable it. our charter should have clearly stated the right to work, as indeed the right to housing, also expressed in a distorted and unprotective form. this charter must be improved and our parliament must propose a strategy to update and enrich it.
in writing. - i voted against, resolutely against, the draft charter of fundamental rights which was submitted to us. i did it primarily to denounce the anti-democratic process that it is the culmination of. from start to finish, its development has been a series of strikes. semantically, from the outset, the question of the name of the body which issued this charter was a coup de force. created as a "quence" by the cologne summit, it proclaimed itself "convention", a name which is unfortunate reminiscent of 1793 and the terrorist excesses of the french revolution implemented by another convention. coup against the parliaments. this text, the final version of which was drawn up by an opaque presidium, is to be imposed by the court of justice on the citizens of our countries, even though it has not yet been ratified by our national parliaments, which have exclusive competence in the field of human rights! as for the european parliamentarians, not only were they not allowed to table amendments to the text of the charter, but they were also forced to vote on the resolution itself as a whole, in defiance of the most basic democratic rules. the council has not yet adopted the text, but it is still in the process of adopting the text. thus, the child's absolutely elementary and fundamental right to live with his father and mother, although its registration was expressly and urgently requested by a number of "conventional" parties, was not retained. the basic right to a nation, also claimed, also fundamental, has also been censored. any reference to the religious heritage of our nations, although expressly mentioned in most of the fundamental texts governing our states, including in france, with reference to the supreme being, was, while it appeared in the original text of the charter, evacuated under various pressures, exercised in particular, it seems, by the representatives, at the highest level, of some member states, in the name of an obscurantism confusing legitimate secularism and exclusion of any religious reference from the field of public activities. in the end, the bargaining that inevitably leads to this type of process has resulted in the notion of the "religious heritage" of europeans and the promotion of "free enterprise" being placed on the balance sheet. guess who won ? the limits of the rule of consensus applied in such a context are measured by the obvious choices it leads to. the text of the charter is not at all european. it could be adopted in the state by any country on the planet. it is the fate of processes of this kind to result in texts which inevitably align themselves on the lowest common denominator. such an exercise, beyond its illegitimacy, since the european union has no competence in human rights, is not even seen as being of substantive interest, whereas our freedoms in europe are remarkably protected by the founding texts of our nations and the european convention on human rights. on the other hand, the method used, the exclusions made and the ambiguity surrounding the very nature of the text throw a fairly stark light on the new totalitarian ferment at work at the very heart of the european integration process.
in writing. - we discussed last night four draft texts on the fight against organised crime, which we generally welcome, even if the reports and amendments of the european parliament are more questionable. these texts have two points in common. firstly, they complement each other by extending the powers of europol, by setting up a temporary unit for judicial cooperation, by improving the mutual legal assistance that member states can provide and by better defining the conditions for combating money laundering, which is the result, the cause or at least the point of passage for many very serious crimes. secondly, these texts are all based on member states' initiatives, since they fall either under the third pillar or under article 67 of the tec, for which the commission does not have a monopoly of initiative. i would point out in passing that during this part-session a total of seven reports originated from national initiatives, which proves that this system, where it exists, is ultimately very productive. moreover, it develops cooperation which is more respectful of national sovereignty, as is shown by the french republic's initiative on mutual judicial assistance in criminal matters, the subject of the roure report, which succeeds in reconciling mutual judicial assistance and respect for the essential interests of the member states. we have generally supported these initiatives, except when the european parliament's amendments tended to distort them too much in a federalist sense. on the other hand, we deeply regret the referral to the committee of a fifth in writing. - i have already spoken this year on the proposal to amend the 1991 directive on money laundering. the european parliament had already pointed out the shortcomings of this directive. the commission has recently put forward a proposal which takes account of parliament's comments. the council's common position is not officially known. the report we are discussing today is in line with the commitment made at the tampere european council in october 1999 to combat the scourge of money laundering, which represents between 2% and 5% of global gdp each year. the french presidency has made this a priority on its agenda. the french presidency therefore intends to create, through a set of legislative measures, a sufficiently broad legal framework to cover the crime of money laundering. on the one hand, it is proposed to extend europol's powers to money laundering (the karamanou report); the commission also proposes a series of measures to promote international cooperation in the field of mutual legal assistance in criminal matters (roure report). both reports were put to the vote today. i voted for them. the marinho report intends to extend the principle of mutual recognition of national measures for the identification, tracing, freezing or seizure and confiscation of the instruments and proceeds of crime, introduced by common position 98/6399/jha in 1998, to decisions before the trial stage, in particular those which would allow the competent authorities to act quickly to obtain evidence and seize assets which are easy to transfer. these voluntary measures are absolutely essential to combat this phenomenon, which has been steadily growing and becoming international. "he is at the very heart of organized crime. it must be eradicated wherever it exists" (tampere european council conclusion 51). that is why i voted in favour of the marinho report, thus supporting the efforts of the french presidency.

mr president, ladies and gentlemen, every day that passes is marked by the current crisis in the middle east and every day that passes shows us, if it were still necessary, that everything that is happening in the south - around the mediterranean - directly affects us, including our daily lives. when the south is well, peace is possible. there is progress in democracy, more economic development and less uncontrolled emigration: in short, there is hope. but when the south is bad, it is wars, violence, fundamentalism - including in our own neighbourhoods - and i am not talking about the risks of a new oil crisis. today, the worst is possible again. you can tell when you watch the news. all this, some of us here have been saying for years. unfortunately, in recent years too, the enlargement of europe to the east, the crises in the balkans and the wars have distanced the south from the minds of the majority of europeans, leading to many delays in mediterranean processes and policies. we are witnessing a fall in credit and, above all, difficulties in mobilising these credits. the general negotiations are stalled, the negotiations on the association agreements are lagging behind and the ratification is even further behind. this is causing very serious disappointment among our partners in the south and our political weight, the weight of europe, has been reduced, especially as we are still the main financial suppliers in the south. we must therefore - and many of us have said this afternoon - tighten up our political objectives towards the south now, strengthen the credits earmarked, speed up the association agreements with the partner countries, give priority to the charter for peace and stability, make efforts to help development and to deal with the debt burden of the poorest countries, finally open our markets to their products and harmonize our rules for the reception and asylum of people who immigrate to us. in short, we must restore confidence in europe's willingness to establish a genuine partnership with the south. everyone knows that. it is a quantitative effort, but above all a qualitative effort. the commission and the council tell us they want this. we are prepared to believe them, but the countries of the south need more than promises and speeches: it is up to us to give them that. marseille is probably the last chance for that. this is one of the great challenges of the french presidency.

the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, we are debating this evening the situation in the pig sector and its common organization of the market, which has proved inadequate in the face of the recent crisis. between 1998 and 2000, production increased dramatically, with an increase of 20 million head to reach the annual level of 205 million pigs slaughtered in the european union. we then had a 30% fall in prices, with often unsustainable consequences for producers, especially the young and the most indebted. in the event of bankruptcy, some farmers have had no choice but to change their social status to become mere employees of cooperatives or private firms, while remaining on their former farms. this is not, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the translation of the european agricultural model that the union intends to have recognised on the international scene. it is clear that, in view of the objectives set out in regulation 2759/75 as amended, the failure to adapt and the inadequacy of the pmo's pigmeat sector instruments, namely private storage and refunds, must be acknowledged: private storage, which is of less interest to operators because it is implemented in a context of structural crisis, and refunds, which are still useful but dependent on international agreements which restrict them more and more severely. new instruments should therefore be devised to guard against any serious crisis that might re-emerge, despite a very high level of domestic consumption and a good use of export opportunities. the continuous improvement in farm productivity is already generating a growth in supply and if this were to be accompanied by an unlimited extension of the production apparatus, a serious imbalance in the market would inevitably follow. the last crisis has shown us that the recovery of the markets is now taking place all the more slowly because, for the most part, specialized farms are maintaining their production while waiting for better days. in these circumstances, ladies and gentlemen, the problem is not so much the future of production as the future of the producers. it is therefore imperative to provide the union with flexible instruments for the prevention and management of crises in the pig sector. the commission proposes that a new instrument be incorporated into the cmu: the regulatory funds. the idea is certainly a good one, but since its application is optional for the member states and producers and since, in return for a required freeze on production, it does not provide any appropriate solution for farmers in times of crisis, it is ultimately of little interest. in its present state, it would probably be inoperable. the committee on agriculture and rural development, therefore, aware of the importance of the problem, has introduced amendments to make this proposal more attractive and more effective on the basis of my report. in this case, the aim is to enable reliable forecasts of the market to be made by a good knowledge of the means of production; to establish a breeding fund in all member states, with community support for its establishment, so that any breeder or fatter in the union who wishes to join can do so on condition that he commits to stabilise his production for five years; to establish the co-financing of these funds by the farmers or their groups and by the european union, in order to encourage the participation of producers; to introduce modulations in the disbursement of aid from these funds during periods of crisis; finally, the commission should encourage the member states to take, together with the commission, the measures which they consider most appropriate to restore the balance of the markets in the event of a crisis, on the understanding that this effort to restore the market must be made taking into account the development of production in each member state and must be passed on to farmers who are not members of the regulatory fund. the commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, is therefore recommending the following solutions from the committee on agriculture. we are convinced that they can prevent and even manage swine crises if they should occur again. so, by means of flexible, complementary and therefore inseparable instruments, and at a reasonable cost to the union, let us admit it, we can make the future less problematic for our farmers. (applause) i would like to thank
- mr president, at a time when food safety is more than ever on the agenda and especially at a time when the whole meat sector in europe is affected by the mad cow crisis, it is particularly important that the reform of the pmo for pigmeat be adopted without delay. the pigmeat market is subject to cyclical fluctuations, well known to economists, but the crisis of 1998/99 was of unprecedented duration and scale, which highlighted the amplification of this phenomenon, which each time bankrupted many family farms and pushed the sector more and more towards concentration and integration. the crisis has clearly demonstrated the inadequacy of the current very lightweight mechanisms of the pmo for pigmeat and the need to provide for a regulatory mechanism to stabilise producers' incomes through a system of levies in good times and payments in times of crisis, as proposed by the european commission on the model of the french stabi-porc system. but this proposal would be quite insufficient if it left it to the member states to refuse these regulation systems and if it left it to the producers' contributions alone to build up the reserves to support incomes in times of crisis, because then we would see a two-speed pig production. on the one hand, the largest producers or those integrated with the downstream companies would stay out of this system, preferring the systems they already have: individual savings, bank loans, equalization fund. they would not have to make any commitment to limit production and would keep their growth rights. they would thus be the very source of the next crisis of overproduction which would inevitably cause the bankruptcy of the regulating funds. on the other hand, the smallest producers, the family farms, would play the solidarity game, agree to limit their production, contribute to a national regulatory fund which would bankrupt them in the next crisis of overproduction. the present ocm-pork is extremely light and far too timid. this is the first reform proposal, of any significance, that the commission has put forward since 1975. the amendments tabled by our committee on agriculture, under the impetus of georges garot, whose work i commend, transform this limited text into a major text. the amendments made by our committee are indeed essential. the participation of all member states in this new system will be compulsory. any farmer, wherever he is in the union, can subscribe to this scheme. the community budget is also essential because without it, those who join one of these regulatory funds would in fact only have constraints and the system would not be attractive at all. the efforts cannot be made by the producers alone. the rapporteur therefore proposes a greater commitment by the union through co-financing of the regulatory funds. far from creating a system which is exceptional in international practice, this flexible and reasonably costly mechanism for crisis prevention and management is on the contrary close to what is practised in certain third countries, such as the income insurance systems in force in the united states and canada. we therefore support the commission's proposal as it has been substantially amended by the work of our committee on agriculture and we shall vote in favour of the garot report.

- mr president, madam commissioner, mr president of the court of auditors, ladies and gentlemen, this new report from the court of auditors which has just been sent to us is of interest to the committee on budgetary control in making a number of observations on the problems of the management of the community budget, while warning us against the restrictive interpretations which we might draw from the crude exploitation of certain data. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. i will quickly elaborate on three points. first, a question of terminology: while the concepts of fraud and irregularity are too often not clearly separated, the court of auditors warns against the temptation to equate irregularities or errors with cases of fraud. it should be noted in this connection that the court of auditors itself notes that the number of cases of fraud is limited. another point raised in this report is the problems of vat. vat represents a significant part of the revenue of the community budget. it is clear that we are dealing with a complex system. the rates vary from one state to another and the composition of the rates differs from one state to another. for example, in some countries there is a regional vat. we must therefore continue to ask ourselves about the implementation of tax harmonization. the third point i would like to mention concerns the discussion which took place last night when the court of auditors' annual report was presented to the committee on budgetary control. it was asked - as has been repeatedly stated today - that the court should explicitly name the states in which fraud and irregularities were allegedly discovered. i would like to warn against the temptation to engage in such practices. we do not need to look for scapegoats, either in our institutions or in our states. moreover, since the court of auditors' working method is based on surveys, we have only a partial picture of the situation. the court of auditors' report emphasizes the situation of the member states in the management and control of community funds a little more than in the past. this analysis should lead us, the european parliamentarians, and the commission, to make proposals to improve the financial management and control systems in the member states. they must implement them to ensure the protection of the financial interests of the union. i would therefore like to call for better cooperation with the council.

sensitivity. the sensitivity of this test therefore guarantees that it is impossible for contaminated animals to enter the food chain. it can provide the result of the test in 5 hours and it can be made available because it can be produced without much difficulty at hundreds of millions of copies per year. its immediate use on a very large scale in veterinary laboratories would simply require is legislation in place setting out how the meat-and-bone meal, how this feed, is to be processed – another safeguard that is introduced into the system to protect public health and food safety. by saying that you must ban meat-and-bone meal from feed for pigs and poultry that cannot contract bse by this vector, what you are saying is not that you are protecting pigs and poultry, but that you are protecting cattle. you are therefore saying that the legislation that is in place is in some way inadequate or not being complied with. if there is a belief that there is a widespread disregard for the law on this issue, what does that say about what has been happening over the last few months and years in relation to feed for cattle? it raises the question that i am afraid to even ask. ask yourselves what is the answer to that question. i believe that there has been compliance with the legislation and if i believe that – and i do not think i am being naïve – i do not believe that it is essential to have a widespread ban on meat-and-bone meal to be fed to pigs and poultry. but i am willing to listen to the evidence on this issue. if people from member states come and tell me that the legislation has not been properly or fully implemented then maybe we will have to think again, but it will not be because the scientists tell us it is necessary, but because there is a failure to comply with the law in the european union. that is an issue we must seriously reflect on. let me move on to the question of testing. mr whitehead asked me for more details in relation to this and i think he is correct in that i should have stressed this a bit more in what i had to say. there are two kinds of testing involved here. firstly there is the one already in place, legislation having been brought before parliament some time ago by the commission for random post-mortem testing throughout the member states amounting to 170 000 tests. the purpose of those tests was to identify the level of infectivity in the european union. it was to get information. i welcome the fact that france moved quickly and, before any other member state, started doing this work at a higher level than was set out in the legislation. now it is getting this information. therefore it is faced with the current situation. it has been fully transparent in the provision of information relating to these tests. that is also to be welcomed and applauded. let us reflect on another issue here which causes me some concern. if there is a widespread adverse reaction against the authorities in france for doing the right thing, i hope it does not instil timidity in other member states when they do exactly the same. if they conduct the tests in a similar way to france, ensuring that they focus on animals that are most at risk, and carry out the number of tests that are required, we will get exactly the kind of information that france has and that will be available right throughout the european union so we can make the required decisions and move on. the tests that i am referring to now are somewhat different. they are not intended to give us information relating to the level of infectivity. they are more focused on the question of trying to keep out of the food chain carcasses that may be infected. it has been said that this will be very expensive, will involve a large number of carcasses and so on. let us focus on facts. the three tests available – french, swiss and irish – are unable to detect bse in animals under a certain age. the result will be negative. you will go to the expense and trouble of carrying out those tests and you will get negative findings. therefore, what is the value of carrying out those tests on young animals? none in my opinion. but we also have the weight of scientific evidence that animals under a certain age do not manifest symptoms of bse. therefore, i have asked the standing veterinary committee, sitting today as we speak, to examine this issue to determine at what age these tests should be carried out. what i am talking about is carrying out these tests on carcasses of animals over a certain age to detect whether infectivity exists and, if it does, eliminate the animal from the food chain. we have a situation of younger animals where there is no bse, we are told by the scientists, and the older animals above that certain age, all of them having been tested to determine whether there is bse or not, and they are eliminated from the food chain. this is a consumer protection measure and also a measure to enhance consumer confidence. that is why i have suggested that we take this route and i am looking forward to the advice we get from the svc this afternoon which i intend to bring before the council of ministers next week to discuss this particular issue in relation to the question of the age at which the demarcation should take place. i believe that is the right way forward. there are a number of disputes on this and, as i see in this chamber, there are different views in relation to it, but it is important that we row together on this. it is important that we try and achieve a consensus as to the right way forward and find proportionate responses and not make accusations to others who, when they identify a proportionate response, say that you are not doing enough to protect consumer public health and consumer protection. it is legitimate to draw lines in circumstances where you are fairly sure of the line you are drawing in the sand – safe on one side and not on the other. we must make sure we are fair to one another in identifying these measures which all of us believe to be necessary, because the aim of this exercise is the protection of public health and food safety and the enhancement of consumer confidence. finally, i listened with great interest to my friend, mr patriat's, comments both earlier and just now and i look forward to working closely with him in relation to these issues over the next number of weeks. i should tell you that he and i have had a discussion on this very issue as recently as last week in paris, so i am confident that parliament, the council and the commissioner can work together in a non-acrimonious manner to produce answers to this serious difficulty that we are faced with.

commission - the resources allocated by the tv channels pursuant to a legal obligation are therefore state resources. the fact that there is a legal obligation for tv channels to invest does not necessarily imply that such investments constitute state aid within the meaning of article 87 (1) of the eec treaty, but does imply that the commission must exercise control with a view to the application of article 87 of the eec treaty. the principle on the basis of which the commission determines whether such investments constitute aid and, if so, quantifies them is the principle of the private investor operating under normal market economy conditions. the purchase of audiovisual products for their subsequent broadcasting programmes is part of the normal commercial activities of tv channels. the investments made to finance such products would only contain state aid elements if the tv channels did not obtain sufficient compensation and/or remuneration from them. this remuneration may take the form of supplies, purchases of audiovisual products, co-production shares or broadcasting rights. it could also consist of other forms of commercial compensation for their investments. in other words, investments are likely to contain an aid element when they finance production projects that would not have been financed by the channels in the absence of a legal obligation. it is clear that the aid element for these projects does not consist of the entire funding provided by the channels. it would rather consist of the difference between a normal return and the actual return of the financed production. finally, it should be noted that the aid character of some of these investments does not prejudge their ultimate compatibility with the treaty rules. they could be considered compatible because of their particular supporting effect on cultural production.

- mr president, i should first like to thank our rapporteur and welcome the initiative she has taken in opening a dialogue with the council and the commission at this first reading to work towards better taking account of the amendments requested by parliament. after the mass unemployment of the 1980s and 1990s, exclusion is likely to become the new disease that will eat away at europe for the next decade. as growth returns, this is a challenge to be met if we are to ensure that growth really benefits everyone. this is not self-evident, because this new growth is highly unequal and can be accompanied, as we have seen in the united states for the last ten years, by persistent phenomena of precariousness, exclusion, poverty and urban ghettoization. this is growth in the conditions inherited from the crisis: many jobs are being created but there have never been so many precarious, temporary, part-time jobs. i think we must ensure that the phenomenon of working poor does not become widespread in our own country. in addition to economic exclusion, many are excluded from decent housing and lack access to health care, education and culture, with some groups being particularly vulnerable. this community programme is not intended to take over the entire fight against exclusion in the union, but it must enable europe to carry out this action in a more determined, effective and coordinated way. to do this, it must be closely linked to the commitment made by the heads of state and government in lisbon in march 2000 to give - i quote - 'decisive impetus to the eradication of poverty by setting appropriate objectives which must be approved by the council by the end of the year', that is to say by the nice council which is due to take place in a few weeks' time. i believe that the programme will only make sense if it is linked to the achievement of this objective. how did you do that ? first, by improving the understanding of exclusion through the development of indicators and evaluation criteria, focusing in particular on target groups. secondly, by allowing greater consideration to be given to the experience of actors on the ground, ngos, local authorities, social organisations and people who are themselves in situations of exclusion. thirdly, by helping to assess the impact of public policies in the various member states, to draw lessons, to identify good practices and to consider good strategies, including coherence with other economic and social policies. fourthly, by contributing to the definition of national guidelines and action plans in the same way as the luxembourg process for employment, based on indicators and objectives, not minimum but of a high level of demand corresponding to the idea we have of the european social model. the amendments proposed by the rapporteur - which we support - are intended to strengthen the programme in this respect. i believe that they are in line with the proposals made by the high level group on social protection - proposals made to the employment council for the nice summit - particularly on the idea of promoting access to sustainable and quality employment and access to social protection and care, as well as access for everyone to decent and safe housing and essential services - the high level group mentions in this respect electricity, water, heating, but also effective access to education, justice and public services. in conclusion, i believe that we can only combat exclusion effectively by guaranteeing access to fundamental rights for all, since these rights are the precondition for the dignity of each person and for genuine participation in citizenship.
