in writing. - the debate in this house yesterday on mad cow disease and feed safety showed above all the extreme confusion of responsibilities and minds. the current competence is shared between the community, which has already enacted some partial regulations (the ban on animal flours for feeding ruminants, the rules for heating flours, the mandatory separation of 'specific risk material'), and the states, which want to preserve their right to make regulations adapted to their own situation, as well as their right to safeguard and react quickly to protect the health of their populations. on this already unclear basis, the confusion is compounded by a double difficulty: the difficulty of further standardizing towards high controls, as some states, such as germany, do not want to impose additional costs on their farmers, while they are little affected by the disease; conversely, the difficulty of managing diversified national rules, because border controls have almost disappeared and the labelling does not mention national origin, there is a high risk of eating pigmeat fed with animal flours, even in a country where they are prohibited. we are at the height of confusion at the moment, as was shown yesterday by the speeches of the french minister for the patriot and the european commissioner byrne, who seemed completely disoriented. this situation shows how irresponsibly the unification of the internal market has been carried out in recent years. the first of the initiatives to be taken would be to put everything back on the table, to revise the labelling rules, to restore certain national controls, to create others, and to always clearly articulate, in a clear and practicable way, the minimum european regulation with the indispensable right of each state either to go further or to take safeguard measures. if we do not begin by carrying out this work of clarifying competences, rationalizing, recognizing the primary right of nations, europe will only play, as it does today, a harmful role of diluting responsibilities. on the merits of the case, my group recommended the most severe measures to combat the epidemic. but we must not stop there. it's very good to put out fires, but it's even better to prevent them from starting. we therefore want to draw four important lessons for the future. lesson one. we must reject unnatural production methods which inevitably lead to such tragedies. quality farming may cost a little more, but in reality the apparent savings of productivist farming turn out to be terrible costs for society as a whole. in this connection, we are afraid to see that the commission is looking for every means to reinstate the authorization of gmos, when their consequences are not at all under control, and that they may, in ten or twenty years, cause new "mad cow" dramas. lesson two. quality agriculture, with a certain degree of food independence, will not survive in europe in a world free trade context. however, we now feel that commissioner lamy is anxious to restart a new round of international trade negotiations after seattle, and to introduce an agricultural component, with the intention of bringing about, once again, a new alignment on the world market. this is not acceptable. lesson three. the commission must be more closely monitored by the states in international negotiations, so that there is no renewal of the false manoeuvres - i should say the treachery - such as the blair house and marrakesh agreements which, by limiting our production of vegetable protein for the benefit of the americans, have pushed us to develop in return the animal flours which are at the origin of the present problems. we believe that the future treaty of nice should not give the commission more powers in international negotiations, as is currently envisaged, but should place it more closely under the control of national governments and parliaments. lesson four. the policy of total abolition of internal border controls should be thoroughly revised, as it favours all traffic and makes health control more difficult. similarly, the dogma of free movement at any cost, which led the commission in 1996 to threaten states wishing to impose an embargo on british beef, and which led it in 1999 to take france to the court of justice for refusing to lift the same embargo, should be tempered. despite all that is happening today, the commission has the audacity to maintain its complaint, thus showing how free movement of goods is a superior dogma for it. if member states want to put an end to these aberrations, they must take advantage of the treaty of nice to clearly re-establish a national safeguard right on public health grounds.

in writing. - 18% of europeans, or 61 million people, live on less than 60% of the national average income (the low-income threshold used to measure relative poverty). the mere mention of these data should spur us to action, and that is what the heads of state and government did in lisbon by putting poverty and exclusion on the european agenda for the first time. europe can only be economically strong if it is socially just, and we can only rejoice in this progress. i therefore have no choice but to vote in favour of the report by our colleague, who not only approves the commission's proposal but also strengthens its content. the report calls for the establishment of qualitative and quantitative indicators of social exclusion. it is essential that in the 15 member states we can all speak about the same thing with the same data. the report also calls on member states to be more proactive and to set specific targets when drawing up their national action plans. finally, the open method of coordination is taken up with the encouragement of dialogue between the actors concerned (social partners, ngos, local and regional authorities, etc.) and networking. in conclusion, the financial envelope proposed by our committee on social affairs is 100 million euros instead of the 70 proposed by the executive commission. all in all, this is a step forward which we must confirm and encourage, since economic progress is certainly not enough to ensure a better quality of life for citizens.
in writing. - this report has the merit of revealing the true face of the present european construction: that of the 62 million poor and the 18 million unemployed. the restructuring and merger operations in progress are bringing with them new plans for redundancies. while economic growth is strong and unemployment is declining, working today does not protect against exclusion. the "working poor", most of whom are women, employed part-time, at a discount and in the most complete precariousness, join the procession of misery that official speeches on recovery superbly ignore. quality work, health care, housing and education are indeed basic rights which, if they were binding on employers and governments, could protect against social exclusion. that is why we shall be voting on the report on combating exclusion. however, the members who approve this text today did not have that flash of solidarity yesterday when they voted for a charter without social rights, which, by relegating the fight against exclusion to the level of assistance, represents a regression in relation to many existing legislation. it would be more effective to combat exclusion by creating, for example, a european minimum wage.
in writing. - we certainly do not dispute the usefulness of 'promoting electricity produced from renewable energy sources'. the report also states that this will create 500 000 jobs. we also see no problem in supporting research into, or even the implementation of, these sources of electricity so that consumers do not hesitate to choose them in preference to electricity produced by more polluting processes. but why should this support involve private profit? this is the case today, because the planned subsidy would go to private companies engaged in research or marketing, including trusts such as total énergie, shell solaire, abb alstom power, dalkia, a subsidiary of vivendi, arthur andersen, tiru, a joint subsidiary of suez-lyonnaise des eaux and vivendi, and other industrial groups that make profits large enough to avoid having to ask the taxpayers again. the production and distribution of electricity should be a public service. why then should the states or the european institutions not take over this public service through a board, directly hiring the 500,000 workers needed? with the savings made by not paying profits to the shareholders of a private company, it would be possible to pay correct wages and to ensure a proper public electricity service.
in writing. - last night in the plenary debate many of us spoke about the need to promote renewable energy sources at the time of the hague conference on global warming. more and more, scientists and climate scientists are speaking out about the consequences of greenhouse gases: citizens themselves are beginning to realise this. these dramatic forecasts in the very short term must impress upon us the need to adopt clear and voluntary measures at european and world level to curb this process of deterioration in the quality of the environment. the commission proposal and the rothe report, which we voted on today, go in this direction in promoting res as environmentally friendly alternative sources of electricity. it follows the commission's announcements and the european parliament's call for a major step forward towards the white paper target of doubling the share of renewable energy in energy consumption by 2020. member states must now embark on this path in order to meet the environmental objectives they have agreed to at both european and international level, but also to ensure their energy independence and security of supply. the dependence, which is around 50% for the union as a whole, is likely to rise to 70% by 2020 in the absence of renewable energy development. the european union is now at the forefront of the construction of installations in the various fields of energy production. if the union is to remain competitive in this sector, it will have to contribute to it by using and developing the relevant technologies, which implies substantial public funding. for all these reasons and because the rothe report is an excellent report, i voted for it, hoping that the commission and the council will follow us.

- mr president, côte d'ivoire has long been a pillar of stability and relative prosperity in a west african country with a troubled future. that is why we were very worried and saddened to see the slow political, economic and human collapse of that country, orchestrated by the military junta of general gueï. in order to cling to power, general gueï has hijacked the constitution adopted by the ivorian people for his own benefit and used it as a tool to exclude his political opponents. to cling to power, he did not hesitate to seize the hot debate on "ivorianity", causing an outbreak of xenophobia: hatred of the other, of the foreigner, of burkinabe or malian, and yet many of them have lived and worked on ivorian soil for many years. thus he brought côte d'ivoire to the brink of civil and ethnic war. but the ivorian people did not let the junta play out its game of massacre: they forced the tyrant to flee and, by electing a long-time opponent - laurent gbagbo - as head of state, they put côte d'ivoire back on the track of the democratic process. now this process must be confirmed rapidly by the organisation of free, transparent, pluralist parliamentary elections in which all political forces can participate. this is what politicians and citizens alike are demanding today. the ivorian political forces have already shown their responsibility by playing the card of appeasement, constitutional legality and national reconciliation in the past few weeks. we must take note of the resumption of a democratic process which is not yet complete, but which we must continue to support. i believe that this is also in the interest of stability in the whole region, because west africa is going through a particularly vulnerable period in this respect. the european union must therefore support côte d'ivoire on the path it has chosen: the path of return to constitutional legality, civil peace, economic and social progress, by providing material and financial support for the organisation of the parliamentary elections scheduled for 10 december, and by ensuring, of course, that they are fair and pluralist, and by continuing cooperation with côte d'ivoire in order to help it find solutions more suited to the social crisis in urban areas and the tensions between the functions in rural areas. that is the whole point of our resolution.

in writing. - we are resolutely opposed to this totally hypocritical and dangerous resolution for the public social protection systems of the union. in fact, despite very fair considerations on the achievements of existing systems, aimed at ensuring a high level of protection for each citizen, independent of personal resources and individual risks, including stressing the risks of transfers between public and private schemes, describing the growing share of these in overall expenditure and the resulting inequalities of situation, all the concrete proposals in the resolution are only encouragements for an accelerated and community development of private insurance schemes. and this encouragement is not to move towards efficient community public services, but, under the cover of costs and the principle of subsidiarity, to minimise the public service, reduced to a 'basic service' or 'minimum standards' called 'safety net', the care basket of which would be defined. in the rest, a very wide field is thus opened up to private insurers, provided only that they do not (at first) select patients and insurance premiums by pathology. the resolution is in fact aimed at organizing the insurance market, whereas europe should be organized towards progress in high-quality collective schemes accessible to all.

in writing. - (de) when evaluating the directive on the own funds of credit institutions, a number of conflicting interests must be carefully considered. each of the spokesmen makes justified claims for the protection of its interests, and a just solution requires dialogue. first, there are savers, who would benefit from harmonised eu-wide rules because their deposits would be protected against losses according to the same criteria. on the other hand, there are smes which fear that this directive will mean they will no longer have access to credit because they cannot compete with the guarantees offered by a large company. one possible consequence could be the loss of jobs in these branches of industry. another conflict of interest arises from the fact that, on the one hand, a longer transitional phase is required to allow as many banks, and in particular smaller institutions, to integrate the necessary new regulations into their organisation. on the other hand, late implementation favours us banks which benefit from the current regulation and can make better offers than european banks. this disadvantage for our companies must be removed, but without the large european companies abusing their power to the detriment of the smaller ones. we support the demand for a solution to the conflict between the united states and the european union arising from the discriminatory gramm-leach-bliley legislation. overall, we can say that the requirement for european harmonisation is justified and that an increase in security and fairness implies for all parties concerned that no one can be favoured at the expense of others.
- doc. a5-0316/2000 by mr posselt, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, on the initiative of the portuguese republic with a view to the adoption of a council decision on the provisional establishment of the european police college (epc).
the commission is aware of the fact that the european police college is a very important institution in the european union, both in terms of cooperation in the field of justice and home affairs and in the context of enlargement. from the very first reflections on this matter, which were made at european level at the initiative of the european parliament, the commission has undertaken to take action before the member states to develop what we might call a european police culture based on the highest standards of ethics, respect for the rights and freedoms of citizens and effectiveness in the fight against crime. the commission welcomes the rapid progress made by the portuguese presidency, which took this initiative, and by the french presidency, which intends to adopt it by the end of the year. i therefore see that the efforts of each of us will lead to the european police academy being able to be established effectively only one year after the decision taken by the tampere european council. i would also like to congratulate and thank the committee on civil liberties and human rights of the european parliament and particularly its rapporteur, mr posselt, not only for his personal commitment but also for the excellent analytical work he has done and the way he has encouraged the creation of the european police college. as regards the future of the academy, the commission is of the opinion - as you will be aware - that the tampere european council's conclusion 47 very clearly foresaw that the networking of the academy, what is also now called a virtual academy, will be only a first step. like the european parliament, the commission considers it desirable that a formula be adopted within a specific and defined time limit to ensure greater continuity of training activities, or even their development beyond the police's senior management. but i would also like to make it clear that we are not talking about the creation of a european police force. we are talking about the need to exchange experience and information, to exchange best practices in the fight against crime in order to make respect for citizens' rights and the fight against transnational crime more effective. i would like to stress above all that, from the point of view of someone who has always advocated the concept of a local police force, as in the case of the united kingdom, i would welcome the fact that this concept of british origin is being increasingly subscribed to by a number of countries in what is known as 'continental europe'. those who believe in the good solutions they advocate should not be afraid to confront them with the solutions of others. the commission considers that the transition from a police academy or virtual police college to a police academy as an institution is justified not only in terms of the operational capacity of the police forces of the present member states but also in terms of being able to include the applicant countries as soon as possible in a systematic way in a strategy for training police forces. and i believe that this priority is extremely important not only for the applicant countries but also for the assurances we have to give our citizens that enlargement is done with the safeguarding of the security of the member states. i would like to assure parliament that the commission is ready to continue to cooperate, both in setting up the academy and in ensuring its proper functioning. i noted mr posselt's proposal that the commission could draw up a report in 2003 on the future of the academy, based on an analysis by its board of directors. the commission is prepared to do so if so decided. however, that does not seem to be the council's intention at the moment. the aim of the new law is to ensure that the police academy develops from an intergovernmental perspective. we must not forget that the european union is a major player in the world economy. but the fact that the commission is not at the heart of this process does not mean that we will not follow the process and make sure that it is a success. i am convinced that this project will help to strengthen security in the area of freedom, security and justice, since there is no freedom and no justice unless it is lived in an environment of effective security.

in writing. - in line with the extraordinary summit in tampere, the portuguese presidency tabled an initiative in june this year for the council to establish a european police college. we think this proposal is very good in its objectives: to set up training sessions for police officers and personnel from the member states, but also from the candidate countries, in all areas of the fight against crime requiring crossborder cooperation. this initiative also seems to us to be quite timely in terms of the method chosen: we are not going to create a new european structure which would be at risk of being poorly connected to national realities; it is proposed instead to create this college in the form of a network of existing national institutes for the training of police officers. each of these national units would house a section of the european police college. the european college would not be based anywhere, but everywhere. its board of directors would be made up of all the directors of the national institutes, who would thus define their needs in full knowledge of the facts. this would ensure that the college is always up to date with developments in the field and that there is no divergence between it and the national technicians facing the real problems. in addition, its organisation would be flexible and scalable, with training sessions being held, in each case, at the most qualified national institute. it is a good illustration of what is now being called a networked europe, a europe that puts nations in direct contact without maintaining superstructures. unfortunately, this arrangement, which we find very satisfactory, does not seem to be very much to the european parliament's liking. the amendments tabled by the committee on civil liberties and internal affairs go in a different direction, insisting that this structure is temporary, that the time limit for revising it must be short, and that it should be given a permanent seat. at this rate, there is a high risk that in a few years' time we will have a new, expensive superstructure which will think it is superior to the national services, which will work poorly with them and which will eventually be inadequately efficient. i am told that this is the direction europol is taking if we do not quickly correct its trajectory. we believe that for the european police college, as for most other areas of cooperation, especially in the area of police, justice and security, the most effective working method is to network the national services.

- many colleagues have asked that we commemorate mr gaetano martino on the occasion of the 100th anniversary of his birth. it is an honour for me to pay tribute today to the memory of this great european, whose name is inextricably linked to the messina conference, which in 1955 laid the foundations of the european community. mr. gaetano was a distinguished doctor and politician. he was elected twice as president of the assembly in the 1960s. this presidency crowned a long political career, leading him to occupy very high positions, first in the chamber of deputies and then in the italian government, where he was successively minister of national education and minister of foreign affairs. as a minister and as a member of the european parliament, he led a very courageous campaign in favour of the european university in florence. he believed that the common foundations of europe were cultural and spiritual. from the outset, the construction of europe proved difficult and fraught with obstacles. but gaetano martino, with his deep humanist culture and his unshakable faith in europe, overcame them successfully. the proof of this is that on 1 june 1955, less than a year after the failure of the european defence community, which was an ambitious project, he began to weave the web of unification again by proposing the messina conference which, as everyone knows, commission. – madam president, thank you for your support and a special thanks to the european parliamentary delegation who were there in the hague. i actually remember meeting mrs corbey, who was there the whole time, going to a session at 5.30 one morning. you were all very supportive during the session and i thank you for that. we sometimes discuss the climate change issue as if its effects will only be felt in the long term by our children and grandchildren. however, climate change has already happened, it is already there. the ice caps are measurably melting. small island states in the pacific are slowly disappearing because of the rise in sea level. we see the effects in our everyday lives. even though the experts are very careful not to say that any particular storm or extreme weather condition is due to climate change, we will see more extreme weather as climate change continues. so it is also for us. of course it is an issue for coming generations, but it is a fact, especially for people living in poor countries, as has also been said. what can we do now? now is not the time to apportion blame or to point fingers. now is the time to decide that we cannot fail once more. failing to achieve an agreement at the next cop6 meeting is not an option. i am quite optimistic because i felt we came so close and that all the ministers there understand that a five per cent reduction as in the kyoto protocol is only a small part of the commitment we will have to make for the future. this is only the start. maybe we should not be too worried about taking a little more time, a few months more, to decide on the rules and the framework, the legal framework, that must be put in place in order to operate the huge economic market that will be created. of course we need some clear operational rules to regulate an emissions trading market worth twelve billion dollars. we had too much left on the table for these negotiations and we will have to try to sort that out. we will have to make our own assessment of what happened, and prepare the documents to make contacts with different parties, and of course with the “umbrella group”. it is very much up to the american administration to tell us with whom we should speak. we will also have to continue our contacts with developing countries. that is how we can take this issue forward constructively. now let me just answer the questions on whether we were flexible. sometimes these negotiations are extremely chaotic, and i think that you can always go home and look back saying that we made this mistake or that mistake. however, for the environment ministers present at the hague, and you know we have also set the tone here, the main objectives were to defend the credibility and integrity of the kyoto protocol. so we would not allow any creative accounting on, for example, certain issues. the americans presented us with a proposal that would have reduced their commitment by between 70 and 90 per cent. we simply could not accept that. should we lower our ambitions when we know we need to do more? at the same time, we made concessions. we opened up discussions on what we had earlier said were big loopholes, or potentially of big loopholes. we were very constructive and we negotiated until the last minute of these talks in the hague. we will continue to be willing to make concessions, but i think we were flexible while at the same time defending our main objectives, and we should continue to do that. we now know what kind of questions we will have on the table for this last part. i am hopeful, i really think that the awareness is there. all ministers know that they cannot escape this huge task of combating climate change; this was also clear from the meeting in the hague. we will do everything to be able to turn this into an agreement and actually be able to sign it. of course the follow up of the next cop6 or the continuation of cop6 will be to ratify an agreement inside the union. we can start emissions trading earlier. we can take a lot of measures, which the commission will propose. as soon as we get the chance, as soon as the legal framework is in place, we will move. i again thank you for this debate. i have taken note of everything that has been said, we will of course follow up and be willing to come back whenever parliament asks us to. the rapporteur. - mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr minister of defence, mr commissioner, as we deal this afternoon with european security and defence policy, we are, as president brok has just said, in an area which gives us optimism about european construction. since the european council in cologne, then helsinki, then feira and tomorrow, i hope, the council in nice, we have been happy to see the progress of this new policy. it is not so often that this is the case. mr. secretary of defense, we welcome that. as it did before the feira summit, voting a resolution on 15 june, the european parliament is expected to vote tomorrow on a text summarising its position on the eve of the nice council. i hope, of course, that a clear majority will vote for the proposed resolution. but i already know that this text will not be unanimous, and that is normal, because it is a difficult terrain where different political options are expressed on the role of the union in relation to that of the member states, on the place of the military in relation to the civilian, on the place of the union in relation to nato and the united states, on the role of the union in the world and the choice it must make between pacifism and non-intervention on the one hand, and the will to control crises on the other. these choices sometimes oppose us, but gradually today a majority emerges. this majority should, unless there is a quarrel, support the line followed for the last year and a half by the council of ministers, the high representative, mr solana, and the commission, particularly in the area of competence of commissioner patten, who is responsible for civilian crisis management. but this support, which i hope will be clear and lucid, is accompanied by many questions, and sometimes warnings. i'll just mention a few. first, a brief comment on a key issue, namely the relations of the new european policy with nato. we have talked a lot about this in the committee on foreign affairs. the proposed text confirms the european council's choices. it is not a question of competing with nato, or of removing from it the responsibility for defending our territory, but of making europe a credible partner of the united states by rebalancing the alliance and giving a margin of autonomy to the european union in the event of a crisis. secondly, you will find in the resolution the very clear intention of parliament to base security and defence policy on two balanced pillars: civilian crisis management and, in the event of failure, military management, the two pillars being complementary. this concern for balance leads parliament to be careful to ensure that financial resources are shared equitably, even though we are well aware that the former is the responsibility of the community budget, while the latter is still the responsibility of national budgets. thirdly, we welcome the fact that the ecsc treaty is beginning to be implemented in a concrete way, namely by the rapid reaction force. and we welcome the work already done, including at the recent capacity engagement conference. all this has the merit of making this policy credible. this is also an opportunity to take stock of the state of our armies and to strengthen the will to reform, as i recently saw in berlin with regard to the bundeswehr. regarding the institutional reforms you have undertaken, i would like to stress our wish that the union should have a coherent, clear and efficient chain of command. it is not enough to create bodies such as the cops, the military committee and the general staff, but also the vertical and horizontal articulation between them must work well and in real time. we are not entirely satisfied with this and would like to see the powers of the commission, the council and the high representative in the event of a crisis clarified. mr president, i would like to mention briefly a major problem for the credibility of this policy, namely the budgetary resources. there are certainly savings to be made, but we cannot exclude the need for new resources if we are to fill the gaps identified, particularly in high technology. i would like to stress, mr president, as did president brok, the role of the european parliament and parliamentary institutions. there are many other things to talk about. i would like to tell the council representatives that the european parliament is determined to develop a culture of security and defence which we are not used to, and we wish the nice summit a complete success.
commission. – perhaps i can begin by commenting on what my honourable friend mr hume has just said. he has done more than most as a personalised version of conflict resolution in a part of the world which i know well and has been properly commended globally for his efforts. of course, he is right in what he says about the contribution which the european union has made to conflict resolution. a japanese-american political scientist wrote a book with the unhappy title of “the end of history" in 1989. as we know, we have actually witnessed a good deal of history since 1989, but one point on which he was absolutely correct was that we saw in 1989 the end of a particularly shaming, and all too long, period in european history. we all know that the genesis of the european union, the main objective of the founding fathers was to prevent europe tearing itself apart in yet another civil war. that has been not the least of the achievements of the last few years, as we have consolidated liberal democracy throughout our continent, which is the great task that the french presidency will steer us towards accomplishing in nice. we are now faced with the problem of ensuring that when we talk about consolidation of liberal democracy in europe, we mean the whole of continental europe, because that is what enlargement and the enlargement process is all about. that is why the enlargement process is not just a strategic issue – not just an economic issue for us, but a moral issue as well – an issue very close to what the honourable gentleman was talking about when he referred to conflict resolution. i did not come to talk about that and i should respond to my honourable friend, mr brok, and the honourable lady, mrs lalumière, and thank them for their excellent reports. they militarily but morally as well. the recent history of kosovo underlines the importance of europe doing more for itself. now we are trying to do that, and frankly it is both fatuous and malicious to suggest that this is the creation of a european army or an attempt to kick the americans out of europe. i fully agree with what my honourable friend mr brok has said in his overall conclusions on the common foreign and security policy. we have come a long way since the decision in maastricht in 1991 to take the step from political cooperation towards a common foreign policy. much remains to be done to develop a strong cfsp. there is need for further reinforcement of coherence and effectiveness in the external activities of the european union cutting across the pillars. experience over the past few years has made clear that european union external action is more than just a juxtaposition of declaratory politics and technical cooperation. we need to integrate three strands into a coherent whole, community policies, cfsp, including esdp, and national action by member states. there needs to be a sensible and sensitive partnership in the external field between the institutions of the union, including the european parliament, and a very close coordination with member states. our challenge is to ensure that the world’s largest trading group and provider of development aid also makes its presence felt politically. we have a real contribution to make and we must not be afraid of doing it. for the community, this means reforming our external assistance, improving our internal procedures and creating a framework within which we can mobilise the whole range of community instruments in support of our agreed external objectives. we are not seeking new competences. we do not need new competences, but we want to exercise the powers we already have under the treaty more effectively and i have every sympathy for the european parliament’s desire to do the same. mr védrine pointed out in his remarks the priority which we have given to reforming our external actions and to delivering our programmes more effectively and more wisely. i have spoken a number of times to significant part of the displaced and refugee populations. clearly, there is no military solution in this area, as we have already said, and i have therefore taken note of the statements made by the therefore be put in place as a matter of urgency. i think that was already asked. a deposit must be arranged at duchambe. i think we should consider, we have done it in other times and in other mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, mr vice-president of the commission, another member of my group, mr modrow, will be speaking on defence matters. i would like to see the report by mr brok calling for the cornerstone of the cfsp to be the preservation of peace and freedom and the prevention of conflict. i shall confine myself to one example - so intensely topical and so are impressive. with a european flag on your car, you drive everywhere, even to the most destitute of the refugee camps. we must not disappoint those expectations. what do they expect from us ? in essence, three things, which are within our reach, if we, and each of our governments, have a little political courage. the first of these expectations was that we were asking for international observers to be sent to protect the population. let us simply say what mrs mary robinson has already said to the un commissioner for human rights: no more, no less. what we have seen, for example, in hostility but of a spirit of responsibility, in the well-understood interests of israel and all the countries of the mediterranean basin. of course, we must firmly condemn any attack on israeli civilians, such as this horrible attack on a school bus. we did it immediately, on the spot. but it is not by bombing gaza, after having plunged it into darkness to better impress the population, nor by bombing the villages in the bethlehem area, which we also visited, fifteen times, that we can hope to break the cycle of violence. thirdly, we should call for new peace negotiations based on the same principles as those we defend in all other parts of the world, namely the requirement of respect for international law and the geneva conventions, the requirement of respect for united nations resolutions. in this case, this means an end to the occupation, including east jerusalem, the dismantling of settlements and the recognition of the refugee problem. the persistence of violations of these fundamental rights, despite seven years of negotiations, and the resulting exasperation, are at the heart of this popular revolt. these are the problems that must be addressed if peace is to be restored and to be sustainable. indeed, many israelis agree, and opinion polls reveal that, beyond voting intentions, an absolute majority of them accept the idea of a comprehensive peace agreement with the palestinians, including the dismantling of settlements. as an association of soldiers' mothers says, we took our children out of lebanon, not to die for the settlements. that is why, mr president, europe must, in my view, decide to act now. if it does so in the sense i have just mentioned, it will not only meet the expectations of the palestinian people, it will strengthen the current in favour of a just peace in israel itself and it will give the world a dignified and respectable image of itself. then, and only then, will it have a chance to overcome its impotence in the middle east and the mediterranean region.
the commission's resignation in march 1999 revealed the need to reform its structures and working methods. the reform effort it is now undertaking must first and foremost seek to restore public confidence. the need for reform is undeniable and it must make the commission an administration of excellence at the service of the political project. this is an essential condition for the credibility of the construction of the european union. following the reports of the independent experts, the commission, at the instigation of mr kinnock, proposed a reform of its operation in a white paper. officially, our parliament is consulted to give a simple opinion, but commissioner kinnock has confirmed to us how important our position will be for the further work of the commission, after which we will be associated. given the scale of the task, four committees were involved and a new procedure was set up, with four parallel reports. i welcome the work done with my colleagues from the epp, mr pomés ruiz, mr harbour and mr lamassoure. so we decided on a method to deal with the whole subject without overlapping. this method was respected and required a great deal of consultation. it has enabled us to adopt a common approach, respecting the areas of competence of each committee and seeking real consistency in substance between our reports. however, i would like to stress that it is essential for the pes that this reform be carried out in a very pragmatic manner, in compliance with the treaties. the cohesion between all the sectors of the reform must ensure that european citizens have a good view of the european project and that there is real transparency in the methods of political management. it is clear that the modernisation of a complex structure such as the commission requires skill, patience and trust on the part of the various actors, and particularly the staff. we therefore want to ensure that it is not affected, but it is essential for us that all staff are effectively involved in this whole modernisation process. the reform, if it can be designed from the top, must be clear and exposed to the unions, to all the staff, and all the staff must be effectively involved in the whole process. our desire to revitalise the european civil service is very strong, and to do this we must respect certain principles: to maintain the european civil service with a single interinstitutional status which ensures equal basic treatment for each staff member and allows for real mobility, real training. the development of recruitment must always guarantee equal opportunities for all community nationals. the cobu opinion on the reform focuses on these major aspects, while respecting our competences. in substance, it is always recalled that, in parallel with any legislative procedure, all budgetary decisions will have to be taken in the framework of the annual procedures and the relevant interinstitutional agreement. parliament has a special responsibility to the citizens. and as one of the branches of the budgetary authority, it has to ensure that public funds are used properly. moreover, before any consideration is made, we will be even more vigilant in the future to ensure that the budget voted is actually spent by the commission and not redirected in accordance with the functional incapacity to implement the few political changes democratically chosen by our assembly. the measures proposed in the white paper must help to modernise and make the commission's entire operation more efficient. we will support it, ensuring that these procedures enable, as soon as possible, the establishment of a management culture oriented towards results and performance criteria which take into account the cost-benefit ratio, but also our policy choices, taking into account the fact that decentralisation and delegation of authority are essential, but provided that the power of decision-making and control is ensured. the communication from the european commission must convey a common message to the various institutions. in concrete terms, it is essential that the procedures for honouring budgetary votes be reviewed. the non-implementation of the budget, the excessive lag between budgeting and commitment and then payment of appropriations, is caricatural. it is urgently necessary to find the appropriate procedures to restore credibility to the commission's management. this requires a review of procedures by setting realistic targets to absorb the lurs in a short time, to reduce the gap between commitments and payments, which discredits a large part of the budget, and to allow contracts to be suspended if the coherence between budget appropriations and political commitments no longer exists, and by paying grants and commitments on short notice. the credibility of the commission, and therefore of the european union, is at stake in the rapid reform of its financial management systems. in the medium term, it is essential to refine the budgetary procedures in a better concertation between the budgetary authority and the commission at the beginning of each financial year, to avoid falling into the great difficulties we are experiencing in november or december and in conditions which do not allow the political expectations of parliament to be translated correctly and to take account of the real modernisation of the commission's functioning. an annual assessment of the changes in the operation and the additional cost of this reform requires consultation at the beginning of each financial year. this will take time, but it is inevitable and essential for reform. the introduction of global project management must be accompanied by a new nomenclature allowing for management transparency. we are very much in favour of this. we will ensure that all technical arrangements can be made in full respect of parliament's budgetary authority. it is with great satisfaction that our committee has seen the conclusions of the bourlanges report on outsourcing incorporated in the letter of amendment. in the case of comitology, however, member states too often express national interests which are in conflict with those of the community and their consultation slows down the decision-making process by increasing the cost. it would therefore be good if the reform provided an opportunity to limit their intervention to the only areas which do not involve expenditure. i shall not go into the human resources at length, since they are handled by mr harbour. the commission's human resources are clearly out of step with the new tasks it has been given, and with those that are to come, and the redeployment of the letter of amendment, which covers only 4%, will not solve the human resources problem. by accepting the letter of amendment on the main points last thursday during the budgetary conciliation, the council proved that the other branch of the budgetary authority was nevertheless willing to support the reform of our commission. the main focus on audit, management and financial control is in the report by mr pomés ruiz. the commission's position on the revision of the financial regulation has been known since 22 november. we have already expressed our views on the reform of the fast track by voting on the van hulten report. we would, however, like to stress the absolute need for the independence of financial control. it is also quite illogical that only the council can amend the financial regulation, and we reiterate our request for conciliation on this point. the reform of the commission is an essential act for the future of our institutions. the method of work chosen by the conference of presidents, which had seemed somewhat risky to some, required time. but when we looked at all four reports together, this consultation time allowed for a broader and more refined view, which enriched parliament's opinion. this report represents the very first steps in the reform of the commission, a major step towards a genuine modernisation of the union's management. it will be followed by many other reports and, for my part, enriched by these few weeks of working in concert, i would like this method to be retained for the future. i would like to thank in particular the three other rapporteurs, because i really appreciated our work and the clarity of their positions. the differences in appreciation which have emerged are not only political in nature but reflect even more the cultural differences between the fifteen. they reveal very different approaches to public service management, which are found every day in the different institutions of the european union, including in our political groups. the implementation of this reform reflects the difficulties we are facing, but we know that this exercise, as difficult as it is, is indispensable. together we have contributed to this first essential step for the political future of the union, we have modernised its management so that it becomes more transparent and thus more accessible to our citizens, so that they are more convinced that their future can only be built in a stronger european union.
the rapporteur. - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, despite its scope, the content of the white paper presented by commissioner kinnock does not directly raise an institutional issue. however, it is the first step in a broader reflection, initiated by president prodi himself, on what is known as the governance of the union. a further document on this subject is being prepared at the commission. it is in this spirit that our constitutional committee, after the three other committees it has consulted, has asked itself whether the executive commission is politically effective, in order to start the debate immediately. is the commission today in a position to fulfil the tasks, and beyond that, the political function, which the treaties have conferred on it? in a europe which will have 30 members tomorrow, with a council that has become a plethora, with a parliament of 700 members speaking 20 languages, the role of the european commission in defining and defending the common european interest will be more important than ever. the commission is also committed to a strong, independent, efficient, transparent and politically accountable executive. and to guarantee these qualities, we emphasize five points. firstly, the spirit of good governance must not be limited to the commission's management tasks. it must also inspire its legislative function of proposing, for example by developing an internal procedure for monitoring the principle of subsidiarity, by keeping a timetable of procedures in order to avoid excessive delays in the preparation of texts. another important point is that the commission is the only body capable of coordinating all the work involved in preparing and monitoring european decisions. where it does not, the results are felt, and this is clearly seen, particularly in the second and third pillars. we therefore call on the member states to give the commission the lead role in preparing and monitoring the meetings of the european council itself and all the formations of the council of ministers, which can be done without formally changing the institutions. the commission, however, is not meant to manage the implementation of european policies or the corresponding appropriations itself. the white paper states that at present about half of the commission's staff are assigned to management tasks. this is too little if we consider that the commission has to manage it itself. it is far too much if we consider that it has to discharge the bulk of this management, which is our case. decentralisation should be the rule, to the benefit of national administrations or external agencies. with regard to these agencies, the reflection on governance should be an opportunity for the three institutions to define a common doctrine of what is called externalisation. the creation of independent agencies is justified whenever scientific or technical expertise is needed, or decentralised management seems preferable. this was the case, for example, with the european monitoring centre for drugs. this will be the case tomorrow for food safety or aviation safety, but only if the commission's political responsibility is not dismantled and if it is ensured that it has the legal means to be accountable to parliament and the council for the way these agencies carry out their tasks. finally, it is time to look at the external representation of the union. we have already discussed this this afternoon in the debate on the common foreign policy. here again we are at the borderline between what is good governance and what can justify elements of institutional reform, as the reflections of commissioner patten have shown. the constitutional committee proposes that an overall assessment be made of the union's external representation, both vis-à-vis third countries in international negotiations and in international organisations, and that the creation of a joint diplomatic service be considered. the debate on governance is thus launched. we will continue this in the spring on the basis of the conclusions of nice and the new commission proposals.
- mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to emphasize the quality of mrs sauquillo's own-initiative report on the reform of the commission and its impact on the effectiveness of the european union's relations with developing countries. one of the great merits of this report is that it highlights the absolute need for the european union and its member states to pursue a major development policy, the only one capable of keeping pace with the culture and influence of our continent. i would like to start by making a brief recap of the figures, to avoid any complexities in relation to the present action. it must be said and repeated that the european union, together with its member states, provides more than half of official development assistance, and thus, contrary to a commonly held belief, the community is increasingly involved in european aid in the strict sense. its share of world aid was 7% 30 years ago, and is 17% today. in 1990, the european union's total external aid rose from eur 3 billion a decade ago to almost eur 9 billion today. of course, this is not enough, but it should still protect us from caricatures about the weakness of our development aid. but we must also consider a fundamental reality. this is due to the existence of development policies pursued by a number of member states alongside european policy. the overall improvement, therefore, in my view, lies in a pragmatic approach which consists in trying to coordinate the actions of the member states and those of the community as much as possible. i believe that this is the price at which complementarity will be achieved. this is the meaning of the declaration on regional policy, the important policy of the council and the commission of 10 november last. it introduces a division of labour between the commission and the member states, according to their comparative advantages. in my view, we must guard against two equally dangerous pitfalls: a gradual renationalisation of development aid, on the one hand, or a utopian approach aimed at making the european commission the sole actor in development aid. however, the reform of the european commission is a step in the right direction, proposing both more effective action for the commission itself and greater accountability for the beneficiaries of development projects. this obviously raises the problem of the human resources to be deployed, which are still insufficient, as the speakers pointed out. i shall not insist on that. i would like to conclude, mr president, by emphasizing three amendments which i tabled on behalf of the epp group, amendments nos 1, 2 and 4, the philosophy of which is to make the european union an active and not a passive partner in development aid, but also concerned with a better use of the funds allocated. the epp group will vote on mrs sauquillo's report, hoping that the amendments she proposes can be taken into consideration.

the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's environmental policy is not distorted. mr president, the proposal to amend directive 95/21 concerns the selection of vessels to be inspected and the points to be inspected. amending the directive to ensure that it is applied more rigorously, to harmonise legislation, particularly as regards the selection of vessels to be inspected and the scope of the different types of inspection, is obviously a positive step. the european union should also be able to enforce existing legislation in the member states. belgium, denmark, portugal, france, ireland and the netherlands, which are required to inspect 25% of vessels, do not do so. worse still, the existing directives, which date from 1995, are still not transposed into law in italy and portugal. in order for member states to apply existing legislation, they must allocate sufficient resources to controls to ensure the proper application of international conventions and the directive as amended by parliament. this means in concrete terms the hiring of additional inspectors, the extension of the powers and areas of control, in particular with regard to compliance with social standards, living and working conditions of crews and their publication. since 70% of accidents are caused by human error, inspection of crews, their living and working conditions, their level of training and their manpower must be an integral part of the inspection of a ship. failure to comply with these standards shall be grounds for the immobilization of the vessel and for penalties. the commission's proposals are still a little timid. in fact, they concern only about 20 vessels at most, and the positions of the french presidency, which we have heard unacceptable. i fully agree with the rapporteur that the port should be denied to vessels of any age and flagged for more than three years that pose a serious risk. it is also a matter of going report, the commission's amendments, but i would also ask members to support the amendments of the committee on the environment concerning social standards.

mr president, a year ago three french regions were hit by one of the worst oil spills in european maritime history, the sinking of the oil tanker erika. a few weeks ago, western france was hit by another ecological disaster, the sinking of the chemical tanker ievoli sun. and it is only today that the european parliament is called upon to give its opinion on strengthening maritime security. i am elected from a coastal region which is suffering every day from the very serious consequences of the sinking of the erika, the profound and lasting damage caused by this black tide to the flora and fauna of the countries of the loire, brittany and the charentes, the dramatic consequences for their economy - the 2000 tourist season was disastrous - the fisheries, marine cultures, aquaculture and marshlands have been hit very hard. the people of these regions would have appreciated more prompt action by the community institutions. i am glad, however, that the commission's proposals have taken up the main demands of the elected representatives of the french coast: a ban on single-hull tankers, increased controls in ports and the evaluation of classification societies. on the other hand, it is unacceptable for parliament to weaken the commission's original proposal for a ban on single-hull tankers. as mrs de palacio reminded us in rennes a few days ago, the united states of america managed to adopt draconian regulations on maritime safety unilaterally in just one year. why should the european union need such a long timetable as that proposed by parliament in the rapporteur's amendments to eliminate single-hull tankers? even if the double hull is not the panacea, it is an important measure which is likely to receive substantial technical improvements and it seems to me very dangerous to disconnect the american and european calendars. this shows to which waters and ports the most dangerous ships would be heading. it would be better if our parliament, in the face of a voluntarist united states, did not give the impression of a soft europe, which is always in line with the least-favoured. how can we justify, if another accident happens, that the european parliament has adopted such a slow timetable to wait for the imo to reach a compromise at world level, when the countries hosting flags of complacency occupy a large part of it and are not the most zealous advocates of security. how can we explain to our fellow citizens, in the midst of the french presidency of the union, that the european parliament has removed the necessary financial incentives and disincentives that were proposed to it to speed up the transition to double-deckers. the role of our parliament should be to support swiftly and fully the most stringent and effective provisions proposed by the commission, not to water down them. on the contrary, we should propose to go further. this first package is only a first step. it is essential to set up a system that makes the whole transport chain responsible if we are to finally get out of the current opacity. we hope that the second package of measures which will be proposed to us will meet this need. finally, whatever technical measures are taken, one of the major sources of insecurity will remain until the exponential growth in traffic linked to the expansion of north sea ports is balanced in the channel and north atlantic area. is it really reasonable that the extension of the rotterdam port's catchment area extends to the south of france? would it not be one of the most effective security measures to reduce traffic in this area by revitalizing the port infrastructure of the atlantic and the mediterranean? that is the meaning of the two amendments i tabled on behalf of my group on the reports by mr watts and mr hatzidakis. this is a line of thinking that the member states and the commission should explore, because if the overcrowding of the channel-north sea area is not addressed, it will inevitably become a veritable highway of marine pollution, a permanent threat to the safety of our seafarers, the attractiveness of our coastlines and the quality of our marine resources. the french coast is not destined to become the dumping ground for european shipping traffic and to receive on its shores detonators, heavy fuel oil and styrene.

commission. – madam president, i first would like to thank you all for this interesting and valuable debate. i am glad to say that the commission will support many of the amendments put forward in these three reports. there still remain some areas where we have somewhat different approaches. but i hope that these can be cleared today. allow me to give the commission’s view on each of the reports on the three proposals. i would like to start with the proposal on port state control. i thank parliament for its strong commitment to our proposal and especially mr watts for his series of amendments which sends a clear and strong message to sub-standard operators and negligent flag states. most of the amendments are focused on the proposed refusal of access to community waters. these are amendments nos 1, 3, 6, 7 and 8. the core of parliament’s amendments is amendment no 3, amending article 7a of the commission proposal. it includes three elements: firstly, the deletion of the age criterion is acceptable to the commission since there is no absolute correlation between age and the quality of a ship. secondly, regarding the criterion based on the absence of a black box on board, the commission supports the principle of a widened accelerated introduction of black boxes on board ships plying eu ports, but this is a matter which should not be dealt with in the port state control directive. so this is not a matter of principle but a matter of the formal place for this specific proposal. the port state control directive is designed to check compliance with international requirements and not to introduce new rules. within a few days the commission will adopt a proposal for a directive on safety of navigation including such an obligation to be equipped with a black box. the third element of amendment no 3 is a proposal to ban all ships that have flown for three years the flag of a state included in the blacklist published by the paris memorandum of understanding. in parliament’s proposal, this criterion alone would be decisive to ban whole fleets. should the directive enter into force today with the proposed amendment of parliament, 32 fleets including malta, cyprus, russia, panama, the largest fleet of the world, would be banned. this means thousands of ships including ships of high quality which is contrary to the objectives of port state control. we prefer our proposal where the flag criterion is linked to the detention record of a ship so as to give a clear and strong signal to sub-standard operators. in brief, the commission can only partially accept amendment no 3. amendments nos 1, 6, 7 and 8 also relate to the refusal of access. the commission can accept amendment nos 6, 7 and 8, but can only partially accept amendment no 1. the deletion of the age criterion is acceptable but not the extension of banning the territorial waters of member states. this is not reflected in the text of the directive where the refusal of access only concerns eu ports. as regards the other amendments, the commission can accept amendments nos 2, 4, 5, 21, 22, 23 and 24 subject to some redrafting. the commission cannot accept amendments nos 9 to 20, amendment nos 25 and 26. most are new proposed recitals that do not reflect the contents of the directive. many are either outside the scope of the port state control or are already covered by this or another directive. more specifically, amendments nos 9 to 17 and 25 introduce new recitals most of which are not linked in any way to the text of the directive. amendment no 18 introduces port state control in relation to the seafarers’ rest period, however the enforcement of the provisions in respect of seafarers’ hours of work is already fully covered by existing directive 99/95. amendment no 19 is redundant since the current procedures already provide that non-compliance with the required health and working standards as established by ilo conventions are reported as deficiencies and can also lead to the detention of a vessel. amendment no 20 is irrelevant to port state control as it concerns competition between ports of the atlantic and north sea and not maritime safety. amendment no 26 reflects the amendments of banding proposed by the rapporteur in amendment no 3 but extends the scope of the measure to the exclusive economic zone of member states and in this light it is contrary to the law of the sea. let me now turn to the proposal for the accelerated phasing in of double-hull oil tankers. i am happy to say that we almost entirely agree. following pressure by member states on the international maritime organisation, there is a proposed phase-out schedule which meets the main concerns of europe and at the same time aligns with the american oil pollution act 90 and which is to be fully supported. in this respect, the commission insists on 2015 as the final end date. in order to achieve the main objective of this proposal, namely to phase out old single-hull oil tankers quickly, we are prepared to go along with the deletion of the proposed financial incentive system setting up differential charging of port and pilotage dues. it is expected that the imo will formally adopt the phase out schedule at its april meeting next year. however, should the international maritime organisation fail to do so, the commission agrees with parliament that we will have to adopt a eu regulation based on the ep text and introduce a system for european union waters. amendment no 12 of the report says exactly the same, but it is more of a political commitment than a legal text. therefore, we do not need it in the final text and i hope you will not insist on this point. for similar reasons, the commission cannot accept the new amendment no 22 which relates to the very important area of safety of navigation but is of no relevance to the proposed regulation. the commission also rejects amendments nos 10 and 18 since this would mean setting up an additional committee just for this regulation and this is inconsistent with our policy line of reducing the number of committees by making use of existing committees. i am happy to see that the rapporteur has introduced a reference in amendment no 21 to the condition assessment scheme and we agree with the main thrust of the approach suggested but there is need for some fine tuning of the wording to make it clearer. last but not least, the proposal for amendments to the classification societies directive. here again, there is no great divergence of views and the commission can accept amendments nos 6, 12, 14, 15 and 8 with the exception of the additional paragraphs 3a and 3b to that amendment. there is a set of amendments which the commission feels could create confusion because they introduce new terminology in an area where the language of the international fora, imo, is well established. i am referring to amendments nos 2, 3, 7 and 9 and the commission feels that these are not really substantial problems, more drafting language matters which could possibly be cleared by the jurist-linguists. the issue of assessments to be carried out over the classification societies by the member states on the one hand and by the commission on the other is of primary importance. the objectives of parliament and the commission are the same. we must maintain the clear difference in substance of the tasks at hand for either party. member states must satisfy themselves that the classification society they have chosen to work on their behalf, fulfils the tasks to their full satisfaction. the commission’s task is to confirm that the classification society continues to meet the qualitative criteria in the directive and to monitor the performance of the classification societies. in that respect, the control tasks of member states and the commission are different and should not be undertaken at the same time. this is why the commission would favour amendment no 28 now on the table which reintroduces the obligation for member states to carry out their assessment and therefore rejects amendment no 13. ethics is an equally important issue that should be tackled. i share parliament’s concern that there should be no undue influence from a shipowner over a classification society. in this respect, amendments nos 26 and 29 are making clarifications of the text in their spanish versions and would be acceptable to the commission. amendment no 4 and part of amendment no 18 relating to point “k” are not acceptable. there are some other amendments which the commission has difficulties in accepting mainly on the grounds that we feel that the concerns expressed have already been sufficiently taken care of in other parts of the existing text. here i have in mind amendments nos 5, 16 and the additions 3a and 3b to amendment no 8: 3a because we feel this is adequately covered in article 9 and 10 and 3b because this is covered in the directive on port state control. further, amendment no 1 and part of amendment no 18 relating to point “k” are not acceptable on legal grounds. amendment no 1 because only the community is a legal person and not the union and 18 “k” as it may contravene horizontal commitments made in the general agreement on trade in services. amendment no 11 and a part of amendment no 18 relating to point “h” which deal with the issue of setting clear performance targets and indicators for classification societies are rather ambiguous. they seem to suggest limitations which are unacceptable and should be rejected. the aim of our proposal is to allow for a tightening of supervision of classification societies and the possibility to suspend or withdraw recognition in situations where the performance of a classification society is not up to standard. in this respect, the commission cannot accept any limitation or involvement of classification societies in the judgment over themselves. as regards amendments nos 19 to 25, i am afraid none of them is acceptable either because they are already covered in the existing directive or simply fall outside the scope of this directive and are covered by other directives. that leaves amendment no 10 dealing with the important issue of liability limits. the commission appreciates the support for its originally proposed limit. also, the commission agrees with the revision clause but would prefer the more flexible formula suggested in amendment no 12, commitology, over that in amendment no 10, full legislative procedure. i have two comments on issues raised by mr stenmarck about oil spills in the baltic sea. we have two instruments at hand. firstly there is a directive on waste reception facilities recently approved by the european parliament and council. all ships are obliged to discharge waste in european union ports. secondly, in our proposal on ‘erika ii’ concerning surveillance of navigation, member states will be required to intervene even on the high seas in such cases. i would say to mrs peijs about cambodia and honduras ships, that we are perfectly aware of the threat to safety and these are precisely the kinds of flags targeted in our proposal on the port state directive. i can assure you that if a shipowner thinks of registering a ship on these registers, he should think twice after our proposal. may i conclude by expressing once again my gratitude to parliament and to the four rapporteurs for their expeditious work and excellent reports. it is a curious coincidence that parliament is considering the final stage of the adoption of the european parliament and council decision on accidental or deliberate marine pollution, at the same time as the first set of measures proposed by the commission following the erika disaster. indeed, even with the best preventative legislation, zero risk does not exist. we are sometimes struggling against the forces of nature. in order to be better prepared against maritime disasters, this decision has established a solid framework for cooperation at community level. it creates the conditions that will allow the sharing of experience gathered by member states to better protect our marine environment against the risk of accidental or deliberate pollution. the conciliation process was demanding, but a well-balanced compromise has been found and the amendments of parliament and council have produced a better decision. the scope and content of the decision are now clearer, in particular concerning operational discharges and munitions as well as regarding the link with international conventions or in relation to the polluter-pays principle. this has largely been due to the excellent work of the european parliament and the rapporteur, mrs mckenna, whom i would particularly like to thank along with the members of parliament’s delegation. let me conclude by recalling that one month ago the ievoli sun sank near cherbourg with 6 000 tonnes of dangerous cargo. once again, this demonstrates how urgent the adoption of strengthened, preventative and restoratory community measures for the protection of our seas is. we now count on the council and, of course, mr gayssot personally to crown this remarkable work with our good, solid, ambitious agreement during the next council.
