- the next item is the report (a5-0354/2000) by mr markov, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the draft commission communication to the member states entitled 'regions in the new economy - guidelines for innovative actions of the erdf for the period 2000-06.
commission. - mr president, my first words will be to thank and congratulate helmuth markov for the constructive, extremely competent and serious presentation of the draft communication on these innovative erdf actions for the period 2000-2006. i have noted with great attention, mr rapporteur, ladies and gentlemen, the ideas and suggestions which have been expressed by many of you, and i will return to them, but i will begin with what is contained in mr markov's report, which in many respects supplements and reinforces the commission's guidelines or concerns, and in any case, mr markov, on two points. the first is the need for the poorest or least developed regions not to be left out of technological progress and to enter the knowledge economy head-on. you yourself have mentioned the differences between the poorest regions, the ten poorest regions and the ten richest regions, but when you look at the figures in detail, you must see and be struck by the fact that the differences are even greater in these regions in terms of the simple criterion of, for example, internet connections. we have therefore noted these differences, we have identified the risk of a digital divide, the digital divide, as it is called in the great american debate at the moment, and that is why, ladies and gentlemen - i may come back to this in a moment - i have chosen to propose, on behalf of the commission, that two of the three innovative actions, two of the main priorities, should be focused on this digital divide, particularly by thinking of the poorest or most peripheral regions. that is the first point on which we meet. the second point, which you mention in your report, is our common concern to integrate innovative actions into a regional policy which keeps economic and social cohesion and sustainable development as priorities. following the opinion of your assembly during this part-session and that of the member states, final adoption of these guidelines is planned for the very beginning of 2001. the preparation of the regional programmes for innovative actions can therefore begin so that we can approve them and submit them by 31 may 2001. i would like to remind members of the objective of these guidelines. in relation to the priority themes which were selected and which i wanted to present personally to the committee on regional policy on 11 september last, i would like to recall that these innovative actions are above all an instrument of regional development. as mr rack has very well said, i have never understood and will never understand this regional policy and cohesion policy as a kind of charity to the poorer regions. it is a question of solidarity, and it is a question of saying and making it clear that access to new technologies, access to the information society, is not a luxury for the richer regions, and you will continue to see me acting and hearing me say this demand that the poorer or more peripheral regions - which is sometimes the same thing - have the same right as others to enter this information society head-on. that's what these priorities are. the commission wishes to use these innovative measures, as mr berend has just said, as laboratories for experimentation and good practice, in order to improve the quality of the structural fund programmes which are co-financed by the erdf. this is why we have chosen these three strategic priorities: technological innovation, the information society, but also regional identity and sustainable development. separately or together, in combination, these themes have a decisive role to play in regional development in the years to come, especially - i repeat it for the third time - for the poorest regions. mr mastorakis and mr nogueira have stressed this point. i would now like to respond more specifically to points which have been raised in the draft report or in one or other of your questions. first, the energy efficiency. mrs schroedter or mr rack have raised this point. i'm sensitive to that, as you know. don't forget, i have an old commitment to environmental issues. i have had the honour of being the minister for the environment in my country and i keep this concern in mind and as a priority in the actions we are taking under the structural funds. energy efficiency and environmental policy aspects are not forgotten in these guidelines. they may give rise to innovative actions under the third theme, which concerns regional identity and sustainable development. i would add that, as you know, the european commission is already supporting energy efficiency through the save programme and through one of the thematic programmes of the fifth research framework programme 1998-2002. in addition, the alterner programme is devoted to supporting renewable energies. i can say this about this point, which i shall continue to attach great importance to. as regards the scale of regional partnerships - mr bradbourn has again stressed this point, and i know his tenacity - i see that we agree on the need to strengthen links with the private sector, and beyond the private sector, with universities, research centres, non-governmental organisations. in this respect, the steering committee we have foreseen for each programme will play a key role in stimulating these cooperation and defining regional strategies for innovation. but what i say here about the partnership with regard to innovative actions, i also keep in mind to check the reality of the same partnership with regard to all the programming documents of the community support frameworks or the structural funds in general. thirdly, the emphasis on education and training opportunities, which you mention in your report, mr markov. i naturally agree with the importance of improving vocational skills in europe. we have also taken up some aspects in order to enable small and mediumsized enterprises to find solutions to their needs in terms of computer skills and staff. that is why, when i am currently negotiating spds, apart from the innovative actions, i am talking here about the mainstream, i am extremely careful to find in each of the programming documents a regional plan for access to the information society and i check the quality, beyond the size of this regional programme, particularly as regards small and mediumsized enterprises, educational establishments and even farms. that is what we wanted to take up on this point. however, i understand that this concern will have to be coordinated with other instruments and in particular, as you suggested earlier, mr markov, with the european social fund. i would now like to return for a moment to the regret expressed by many of you and in your report about the programme-based approach we have proposed in this report. i understand your concern to maintain direct links between the european union and regional and local actors. that is why we have asked the competent authorities in the regions to submit regional programmes of innovative actions. we would like, however, for the projects to be chosen at regional level, as mr berend has also understood in his speech. regional and local actors are obviously better placed than the commission to meet the expectations of the field and it is probably easier for small and medium-sized enterprises to express their need for financing by also convinced that, even with necessarily limited amounts, the leverage and impact can be significant across all structural fund programmes. i also share your concern to use the appropriations - doc. a5-0371/2000 by mr langen, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the second report from the commission to the council on the state of shipbuilding in the world (com (2000) 0371 - c5-0370/2000)
mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, on behalf of the group of the party of european socialists, i would like to express my satisfaction at the fact that the commission and the council have finally recognized what we have been saying for several years and more intensively for several months: firstly, europe has imposed on itself greater and faster constraints and obligations in the field of shipbuilding than its main competitors and, secondly, south korea has outrageously violated the rules of competition, with shameless financial dumping. we therefore welcomed the commission's very recent efforts, even though i am wrong to object to the method of calculation used to show a very high rate of european aid in chapter 5 of the report to the council of 5 december. if i have not time today, i will explain this directly in writing to the commissioner. we also took note, above all, of the conclusions of the council of 5 december. the council has agreed to safeguard the future by being firm towards south korea and by not closing the door on the possibility of reintroducing aid to shipbuilding in may in very specific segments of markets which are heavily affected by korean competition. this is in line with the treaty. i don't have time to go into more detail. another positive point of the council meeting was the updating of the ships' arrangement at the cde on export credits dating from 1981. finally, we noted with interest the openness of the council with regard to aid for research and development. this is very important in companies, for companies that are, indeed, very innovative. what we are asking for, and what i am asking for today, is the full and above all immediate implementation of the council's conclusions. if, in may 2001, it should prove necessary to implement aid again, this should be done without delay. another concern about the 6th framework programme for research and development: the 'marine technology' line which existed in the fifth seems to have disappeared. this is something which, in my view, is unacceptable and should be put back, not only in terms of quantity but also in terms of the method of using these appropriations to make them easier. finally, of course, we expect that the shipping arrangement will be discussed at the oecd group 6 meeting on 18 december. i would like to end by congratulating mr langen - whose support for the workers and the need for state intervention to defend the economy i appreciate - and by wishing the commission to make good use in the future of the lessons it has learned in the field of shipbuilding and the unbridled competition of a number of other countries in the world.
- the author of this report and the authors of the proposed amendments belong to political groups which believe in the free market economy and are opposed to the excessive role of the state in supporting public services or in ensuring a certain social protection for workers. but as soon as the capitalist groups whose interests they defend find themselves in difficulty on the market, they demand that the states or the european institutions intervene to subsidize and protect the threatened sector. alstom-atlantique, which has just won a contract to build a luxury liner, will receive a subsidy equivalent to 9% of the contract price. thus, the state pays for a large part, if not all, of the profits of this enterprise. the british company harland and wolff, which was given the contract by alstom, blames its government for not having defended it effectively enough. for the big trusts and their political lawyers, demanding less state means only that the state and its finances must be at their exclusive disposal. i am for my part against any form of subsidy to private enterprises and for the states to spend the money thus saved directly on creating jobs, particularly in public services and in any case without generating private profit.
commission. – mr president, i thank you for the opportunity to update parliament on the market situation in world shipbuilding and on the conclusions of the council last week. i want to thank mr langen for his report. although the report refers to the commission's second shipbuilding report of may 2000, it has been noted here that the third report was done by mid-november and i limit my comments to that third report in this delicate issue. the market analysis contained in the third report does not indicate improvement in the market situation. south korea has continuously increased its market share, both to the detriment of the japanese and eu yards, and despite strenuous efforts by the commission, including contacts at the highest level, the bilateral negotiations with the government of south korea have not yielded concrete results that could remedy the market situation. this is despite the conclusions of accurate minutes in june which pointed to the way forward. as a result of this failure, a complaint by industry under the trade barrier regulation has been launched in october this year and commissioner lamy announced on 4 december the commission's decision to open an investigation. this process will not give quick results and if it goes to its ultimate conclusion, it will take up to two years. under regulation no 1540/98, the commission is obliged to propose measures. in reality, there are limited instruments available to the commission and member states in order to defend the eu shipbuilding industry. the potential of trade principles has not yet been seen and their effectiveness needs to be proved. discussions in the oecd have made little progress, very little progress, and the possibility of an internationally binding agreement on shipbuilding seems remote. the imf is also cautious on the issue of korean shipbuilding, as it sees itself as dealing only with macroeconomic conditions rather than with sectoral problems. improving competitiveness of the eu yards is encouraged by the commission but, in the face of massive price undercutting by korean yards, the achievable progress in productivity is not sufficient. nevertheless, all the available instruments should be used better, including aids for research and development. in the light of these factual elements, the commission concluded at its meeting of 29 november that if the commission does not achieve a satisfactory negotiated solution with korea in the framework of the tbr procedure, the commission will report to the council by 1 may next year and will propose to bring the case to the wto. in addition, and importantly, the commission will, at the same time, propose a defensive temporary support mechanism designed to counter the unfair korean practices. the commission is also ready to explore the possibilities of greater use of national support for research and development and it is noted that the general operating aids will expire after 31 december 2000. i would like to explain the rationale behind the position adopted by the commission. the commission believes that the community should seek to strengthen its negotiating position vis-à-vis korea by providing an incentive to reach a rapid agreement that would resolve the current problems. this is why the commission decided on a defensive temporary support mechanism designed to counter the unfair korean practices. this would be proposed if a satisfactory agreement with korea cannot be achieved during the course of the investigation procedure under the trade barriers regulation. the mechanisms would apply until the outcome of that wto procedure is decided. the details of the mechanisms will need to be further elaborated. they would be limited to those market segments where it has been demonstrated that eu industry has been directly injured by unfair korean practices. on the question of research and development in the shipbuilding sector, the commission concluded that in addition to the substantial community funding available under research framework programmes which provide eur 130 m in five years, the possibility of improving the aids allowed for this purpose should be explored. industry should seriously reflect about how these instruments can be used to adapt their activities in a way which will ensure the future of the sector on a lasting basis. the industry council of 5 december this year discussed at length the shipbuilding issue based on the commission's third report and its decision of 29 november 2000. it requested the commission to continue with its market monitoring, to follow up closely on the tbr case with a view to bring the problem to the wto if required and to address the issue in all relevant international fora. the council also took note of the commission's initiative to propose a temporary support mechanism for eu shipbuilding in case no progress is made with korea by 1 may 2001. the council emphasised that such a support mechanism must not distort competition inside the eu. the commission will be reporting on this situation again in april and, of course, we are also available in the european parliament.

- doc. a5-0319/2000 by mrs sbarbati, on behalf of the committee on employment and social affairs, on the communication from the commission 'towards a europe for all ages - promoting prosperity and solidarity between generations'.
- mr president, i too, like our rapporteur, whom i congratulate, will start from the observation that everyone makes without difficulty: europe is an ageing continent in terms of the age pyramid. at first glance, this may seem to many to be a handicap. i am personally, like many others, and i am becoming more and more, of those who believe that it can be an asset if we know how to do what is necessary to ensure that every citizen, regardless of age, remains a full citizen and that experience becomes a primary value in a society which, in recent years, has given too much priority to speed, ephemerality and fashion over time, duration and experience, not to mention the human being. that is why i can only welcome the existence of this communication and report, which aims to build a europe for all ages and to promote prosperity and solidarity between generations. the challenges, particularly economic ones, are well known. i'm not going back. to face them and to turn real problems into real assets, i believe, requires a strong will and a strong moral, philosophical and political mobilization. it also requires considerable financial resources. this last point of course runs counter to a fashionable individualistic ideology which leads to less public expenditure and less taxation of assets. this is a miscalculation, given the current and future demographic situation, and also given that today's active are tomorrow's inactive in economic terms. and finally, for me, and this is probably the most important, investing in life is a good economic investment anyway. and adding life to years is a process that is fundamental to human dignity. it alone gives full meaning to the mathematical lengthening of life that medical advances have made possible. (applause) i would like to thank
- the title of the report is 'promoting prosperity and solidarity between generations', an intention which we can only endorse. unfortunately, alongside the affirmation of a number of good intentions, which we shall be voting on, there are several convoluted formulations suggesting that older people should find so-called prosperity by working beyond the normal retirement age. well, it's not up to the workers to work longer hours so that their contributions compensate for the big business's whimsy of wanting to reduce the employer's share of the old-age pension. we are absolutely opposed to any move to postpone the retirement age, because we are thinking above all of the workers in production, many of whom are worn out well before the legal age, even in countries where this age is relatively low. how can we promise prosperity and solidarity to the elderly without affirming the right of every worker to a decent pension, and i call a decent pension the full salary. we shall therefore abstain on this report.
the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the report. i would like to begin by congratulating the rapporteurs and the two committees on this report on behalf of the commission. i am particularly pleased that the commission and the european parliament have shown a high degree of agreement and have developed a common understanding of the challenges of ageing. the debate showed a broad consensus on the appropriate policy responses in the areas of employment, social security, health and social inclusion. we are certainly facing enormous challenges. only a concerted and sustained effort can help us. i think it's important to maintain a high level of consensus if we're going to be able to achieve a proper adaptation to the aging process in our society. secondly, i would like to stress the importance of this communication. the communication does not contain many concrete proposals for action and initiatives. however, it provides an innovative diagnosis of the major challenges of ageing, resulting in a very important set of appropriate policy responses in employment, social protection, health and social inclusion. the agenda, which was so roughly outlined, was followed very closely in subsequent commission proposals. it will no doubt continue to inform policy trends in the future. the concern to close the age gap in europe's labour performance balance has been very strongly reflected in the employment process, from the guidelines and recommendations to the nlp and peer review processes. this was also reflected in the plans for the equal community initiative and in the use of the esf funds from 2001 to 2006. the commission has also been active in the development of the social dialogue with the member states, and has been involved in the preparation of the social dialogue with the member states. the key idea in the recent pensions communications is that 'mobilising the full potential of society', i.e. increasing the employment rate of all persons of working age, is the key instrument for sustainable pensions in an ageing society. initiatives in areas such as equal opportunities, anti-discrimination and social inclusion are analogous expressions of aspects of an active ageing scenario. i would like to emphasise here that the directive on anti-discrimination in the workplace, adopted on 12 october 2000, prohibits discrimination on grounds of age. future public health initiatives will focus more on health and care in old age and on promoting healthy ageing. finally, a section of the fifth framework programme deals with research on ageing issues, including the health effects of active practices in old age. the policy paradigm of active ageing is thus clearly reflected in many important initiatives, and we can safely assume that it will continue to inspire a number of future initiatives. in conclusion, let me respond to some of the points on which parliament expressed its concern about the impact of the measures proposed by the commission. a recurring concern in your report is whether the emphasis on policies to promote active and healthy ageing is accompanied by poorer conditions and fewer rights for those in need of care, the very elderly and the disabled. i would like to assure you that this is certainly not the commission's intention. on the contrary, in the communication the commission has placed great emphasis on the fact that policies address the differences between people. early retirement must continue to be possible for persons who are no longer able to work. not everyone can or should voluntarily leave the workforce. there must be a margin of discretion for individual preferences and decisions. we also believe that the consequences of overemphasizing active policy are the opposite. in fact, it is a prerequisite to our ability to raise sufficient funds for those in need of care so that the wealthy among us are able and motivated to make higher contributions and become more self-sufficient as they age.

- doc. a5-0385/2000 by mr dary, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council regulation on information and promotion measures for agricultural products on the internal market.
the commission has proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work. this is a very desirable approach, as is already being done for the promotion of agricultural products in third countries. the proposal covers both product information and production methods. it does not duplicate the advertising or promotional operations of the operators of the sectors or those of the public authorities. the idea is to emphasise themes addressed at european level such as information on the intrinsic characteristics of products: quality, nutritional aspect, organic production, etc. it should make it possible to launch complementary actions with certain synergy effects. the proposal has immediate advantages: a single system ensuring information and promotion of all agricultural products and production methods, measures to streamline the provision of correct information to consumers on food products, decentralization and the general application of the specifications for the sectors concerned. but, while the whole proposal seems interesting and well structured, i thought it would be useful to clarify and improve certain points in order to exploit to the full the potential of such a proposal. my colleagues in the committees on agriculture, budgets and the environment have done the same and the text is strengthened by the amendments which have been accepted; i'll mention a few. i thought it important to include production methods in this information policy because they are determinants of product quality. i also think it is necessary to provide for a greater financial contribution from the community in specific circumstances where this would be justified, for example, by a serious market crisis or a clear community interest. as regards the way in which the regulation is to be implemented, i do not think that the use of the various existing management committees is the best way of responding to this horizontal initiative. it is proposed to set up an ad hoc management committee responsible for the promotion of agricultural products. the guidelines for the lists of themes and products covered should be drawn up more regularly. in order to maintain a certain degree of flexibility in the system, it is suggested that the commission should report to the council and parliament every two years, as proposed, assessing the implementation of the proposal and examining, inter alia, the state of use of appropriations and possible needs. furthermore, since the initiative for action lies with the professionals, it is important to ensure that they are not confronted with too rigid guidelines, which would block their initiatives rather than provide a framework for them. the new system is not expected to be operational until 2002. it would be appropriate to set the date of entry into force of the regulation at the date of adoption of the implementing regulation in order not to lose the appropriations available in 2001. finally, the possibility of actions in favour of the outermost regions and their logo should be explicitly reintroduced in the text. this proposal, as amended, deserves our full support. a coherent product promotion policy is one of the tools for giving tangible life to european agricultural models. it is also a major communication tool with consumers who nowadays do not know where to put their plates. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, the president recalled that he was chairing the last session of the millennium today. i would draw your attention to the fact that the vote on this report will also be the last of this period. it could lead you to a unanimity which, knowing the commission's great spirit, would probably lead it to accept all our amendments. i thank you, ladies and gentlemen, and i wish everyone in this house a very good end to the year. arranged for the five-day session of the second millennium to end today. mr. dary, you have a great way of communicating. and you were therefore the one who was appointed to present the report we are now discussing. more seriously, i would like to stress the importance of this proposal for a council regulation on information and promotion measures for agricultural products on our internal market. the rapporteur has just said the main points on this subject. i would simply add that, at a time when the bse is highlighting certain deviations from productivist agriculture, it is particularly appropriate to promote, within the framework of our internal market, the specific qualities of agricultural products by including, as the rapporteur proposes, the mention of production methods. if european agriculture can reasonably expect to be present on international markets, its future is still more closely linked to the penetration of its internal market, which today has 370 million consumers and will probably have almost 500 million consumers in the future. in this context, information and promotion measures, co-financed by the european union and the member states, are therefore necessary, both to help restore the tarnished image of agriculture to consumers and to promote recognition of the excellence of the vast majority of our agricultural products. of course, these institutional communication measures should rather complement the advertising operations orchestrated by the large distribution sector in particular. this should include regularly presenting information to certain audiences or to consumers in general, for example on food safety, traceability, nutritional qualities, the specific nature of production methods or the efforts made for animal welfare. and while these campaigns achieve their objectives with consumers, we must not underestimate the impact they will have in return on the producers themselves, who will find in this the reward for their efforts and the encouragement to pursue them. mr dary, the committee on agriculture has followed your various recommendations. we now hope that this parliament will follow them very broadly and naturally i invite my group to support you fully.
